en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 8 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 30(b) states providing Shari'ah expertise to courts of law when requisitioned is 'subject to its approval / acceptance'; (2) Par. 54 requires members to always disclose conflicts of interest 'whether permanent or temporary in nature' to be dealt with professionally in line with the code of conduct; (3) Par. 22 & BC9 reserve voting on Shari'ah rulings solely to scholar members (3 of 4 scholars = majority), and Par. 36 requires dissenting opinions to be documented and attached with majority decisions; (4) Par. 43 stipulates that the board and the appointing authority/regulator 'with mutual coordination shall agree on all or part of the report to be made public'.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: According to AAOIFI GS 9, where does the primary responsibility for ensuring the existence and continuous operation of a robust and effective Shari'ah compliance function within an IFI lie?
en.A: With the management of the IFI, while those charged with governance (TCWG) ensure management discharges this responsibility and the SSB maintains oversight of the overall function.
en.B: Exclusively with the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB), which directly executes day-to-day compliance operations across all business units.
en.C: With the external Shari'ah auditor, who designs and operates the institution's preventive compliance controls.
en.D: With the internal Shari'ah audit function, which reports directly to the CEO to enforce operational compliance.
en.True answer: With the management of the IFI, while those charged with governance (TCWG) ensure management discharges this responsibility and the SSB maintains oversight of the overall function.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Preface PR2, Par. 5–7, 16 & BC2 (Management shall ensure a robust and effective Shari'ah compliance function exists and remains in operation [Par. 5]; TCWG shall ensure management discharges its responsibilities [Par. 6]; management and TCWG are collectively responsible and accountable in their respective areas [Par. 7]; SSB keeps an oversight of the overall function and provides input [Par. 16, BC2]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: How does AAOIFI GS 9 distinguish between the Shari'ah compliance function and internal/external Shari'ah audit or review functions in terms of control approaches?
en.A: Both the Shari'ah compliance function and external Shari'ah audit are ex-post detective controls independent of management.
en.B: The Shari'ah compliance function is a management function forming a crucial part of preventive controls (mainly concerned with ex-ante work), whereas internal Shari'ah review/audit and external Shari'ah audit are primarily detective controls concerned with ex-post work.
en.C: The Shari'ah compliance function is an ex-post detective control, whereas internal Shari'ah review is an ex-ante preventive management function.
en.D: In jurisdictions where the Shari'ah compliance function is called 'Shari'ah review,' it replaces the independent internal Shari'ah review function under GSIFI No. 3.
en.True answer: The Shari'ah compliance function is a management function forming a crucial part of preventive controls (mainly concerned with ex-ante work), whereas internal Shari'ah review/audit and external Shari'ah audit are primarily detective controls concerned with ex-post work.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 3(c) Footnote 1 & Par. 13–14 (Par. 13: Shari'ah compliance function is a crucial part of preventive controls and mainly concerned with ex-ante work; Par. 14: internal Shari'ah review/audit and external Shari'ah audit are concerned with ex-post work and are primarily detective controls; Footnote 1 clarifies that Shari'ah compliance is a management function not independent of management and must not be confused with independent internal Shari'ah review under GSIFI 3).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Under AAOIFI GS 9, how is Shari'ah non-compliance risk classified and integrated into an IFI's risk and regulatory reporting?
en.A: It is classified exclusively as a market risk sub-category and is excluded from regulatory capital calculations.
en.B: It is treated solely as a reputational issue managed informally by the marketing department without risk department involvement.
en.C: It is defined as a sub-set of operational risks (which may also result in legal, financial, or reputational risks) and must be given adequate coverage in internal and regulatory risk reporting, including for the computation of regulatory capital requirements.
en.D: It is classified as a credit risk component that applies only when an IFI's financing counterparty defaults on a Murabaha installment.
en.True answer: It is defined as a sub-set of operational risks (which may also result in legal, financial, or reputational risks) and must be given adequate coverage in internal and regulatory risk reporting, including for the computation of regulatory capital requirements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 3(k) & Par. 25–26 (Shari'ah non-compliance risk is a sub-set of operational risks that may result in legal, financial, or reputational risks [Par. 3(k)]; it is documented by the risk management department in close coordination with SCD and given adequate coverage in internal and regulatory risk reporting, including for computation of regulatory capital requirements [Par. 25]; potential financial impacts include forfeiture of Shari'ah non-compliant income and/or regulatory penalties [Par. 26]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Which sequence accurately reflects the hierarchy of 'Shari'ah principles and rules' defined in Paragraph 3(l) of AAOIFI GS 9 (from highest to lowest)?
en.A: IFI's SSB rulings → AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards → Central Shari'ah Board rulings → Regulator's Shari'ah regulations → AAOIFI FAS Shari'ah requirements.
en.B: Regulator's Shari'ah regulations → AAOIFI FAS Shari'ah requirements → AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards → IFI's SSB rulings → Central Shari'ah Board rulings.
en.C: Central Shari'ah Board rulings → AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards → IFI's SSB rulings → Regulator's Shari'ah regulations → AAOIFI FAS Shari'ah requirements.
en.D: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards → Regulator's Shari'ah regulations → Central Shari'ah Board rulings (if any) → Shari'ah-related requirements of applicable AAOIFI FAS → Approvals and rulings of the IFI's SSB.
en.True answer: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards → Regulator's Shari'ah regulations → Central Shari'ah Board rulings (if any) → Shari'ah-related requirements of applicable AAOIFI FAS → Approvals and rulings of the IFI's SSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 3(l)(i)–(v) (Defines the five-tier hierarchy: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah standards; (ii) regulations issued by the respective jurisdiction's regulator insofar as these entail regulatory Shari'ah requirements; (iii) rulings of the Central Shari'ah Board for the respective jurisdiction, if there is one; (iv) requirements of applicable AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards insofar as these entail Shari'ah-related requirements; and (v) approvals and rulings given by the SSB of the IFI).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Which of the following accurately reflects AAOIFI GS 9 requirements regarding human resources, training, and personnel performance appraisals?
en.A: Regular orientation and training programs for TCWG and senior management must be organized at least annually, periodic diagnostic assessments of employees guide training plans, and non-tolerance toward Shari'ah non-compliance must be reflected in performance appraisals, increments, bonuses, and promotions.
en.B: Mandatory Shari'ah training applies only to front-office branch tellers, while TCWG and senior management are exempt from annual orientation programs.
en.C: Shari'ah compliance breaches are excluded from employee bonus and promotion evaluations so that commercial sales targets remain unaffected.
en.D: Independent contractors and agents appointed by an IFI are excluded from Shari'ah suitability and product-understanding expectations.
en.True answer: Regular orientation and training programs for TCWG and senior management must be organized at least annually, periodic diagnostic assessments of employees guide training plans, and non-tolerance toward Shari'ah non-compliance must be reflected in performance appraisals, increments, bonuses, and promotions.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 30–34 (Par. 30 covers employees, independent contractors, and agents as 'personnel'; Par. 32 requires regular orientation and training for TCWG and senior management at least on an annual basis; Par. 33 requires periodic diagnostic assessments of employees' Shari'ah knowledge; Par. 34 mandates non-tolerance towards Shari'ah non-compliance reflected in performance appraisals, increments, bonuses, and promotions, alongside rewards for high compliance).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: According to AAOIFI GS 9 and its Specimen Fit and Proper Criteria (Appendix B), how is the Head of the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD) appointed, and what is the required work experience?
en.A: Appointed unilaterally by the SSB Chairman, requiring at least 15 years of experience in conventional commercial banking.
en.B: Appointed by management subject to the concurrence/approval of the SSB, with preferably 10 years (and in no case less than 5 years, e.g., in new markets if allowed by the SSB) of relevant work experience.
en.C: Appointed by the external auditor, requiring at least 2 years of experience in any corporate administrative function.
en.D: Elected by the bank's shareholders at the Annual General Meeting, requiring a doctoral degree in Islamic jurisprudence with no experience requirement.
en.True answer: Appointed by management subject to the concurrence/approval of the SSB, with preferably 10 years (and in no case less than 5 years, e.g., in new markets if allowed by the SSB) of relevant work experience.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 40, Appendix B(c)–(d) & BC10 (Appointment and hiring of head and staff of SCD is the responsibility of management, and appointment of the head of SCD is subject to the concurrence/approval of the SSB; Appendix B specifies preferably 10 years, but in no case less than 5 years—e.g. in new markets, if so allowed by the SSB—of work experience in Shari'ah compliance, advisory, internal/external Shari'ah audit, internal audit, or other relevant areas).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the reporting lines and performance evaluation structure of the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD) under AAOIFI GS 9?
en.A: SCD reports exclusively to the SSB; senior management has no authority over SCD's reporting line or performance appraisal.
en.B: SCD reports solely to the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and has no reporting relationship with the SSB.
en.C: SCD is principally part of management with a solid-line reporting relationship to, and performance evaluation/appraisal by, senior management in consultation with the SSB, alongside a dotted-line reporting relationship with the SSB.
en.D: SCD reports directly to the national banking regulator and is appraised annually by the external financial auditor.
en.True answer: SCD is principally part of management with a solid-line reporting relationship to, and performance evaluation/appraisal by, senior management in consultation with the SSB, alongside a dotted-line reporting relationship with the SSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 41, Par. 49 & BC4 (Par. 41: SCD is principally a part of management and shall report to, be accountable to, and be evaluated and appraised for performance by senior management in consultation with the SSB; Par. 49 & BC4: SCD shall also establish a dotted-line reporting relationship with the SSB).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Under Paragraph 51 of AAOIFI GS 9, to preserve segregation of duties and neutrality, the SCD must remain independent from five specific functions (except for providing reviews and inputs). Which of the following lists those five functions?
en.A: Internal Shari'ah audit, external Shari'ah audit, SSB secretariat, risk management, and human resources training.
en.B: Customer complaint resolution, regulatory reporting, IT system security, internal audit, and board governance.
en.C: Treasury operations, branch administration, external audit, central bank liaison, and Shari'ah research.
en.D: Managerial decision making, finance-related functions, legal, marketing and sales, and product development.
en.True answer: Managerial decision making, finance-related functions, legal, marketing and sales, and product development.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 51(a)–(e) & BC5 (SCD shall be independent of five specific functions, except for providing reviews and inputs: (a) managerial decision making; (b) finance-related functions; (c) legal; (d) marketing and sales; and (e) product development).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Under AAOIFI GS 9, when may the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD) perform the functions of the SSB Secretariat, and how is the Secretary to the SSB appointed?
en.A: In situations where resources are constrained, SCD may perform the SSB secretariat function provided such dual functionality does not result in self-review threats; the Secretary to the SSB is appointed by management on the advice of the SSB and supervised by the SSB.
en.B: SCD is strictly prohibited from ever performing SSB secretariat duties under any circumstances, and the Secretary is appointed unilaterally by the external auditor.
en.C: SCD must always serve as the SSB secretariat in every IFI regardless of size, and the Secretary is appointed solely by the CEO without SSB input.
en.D: When SCD assumes the SSB secretariat role, self-review threats are waived automatically, and the Secretary reports exclusively to the head of HR.
en.True answer: In situations where resources are constrained, SCD may perform the SSB secretariat function provided such dual functionality does not result in self-review threats; the Secretary to the SSB is appointed by management on the advice of the SSB and supervised by the SSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 3(f), Par. 52–55 & BC8 (Where resources are constrained, SCD may perform the function of SSB secretariat subject to the condition that such dual functionality shall not result in self-review threats [Par. 52, BC8]; if SCD takes up this role, the head of SCD can absorb the role of secretary to SSB [Par. 53]; the secretary to the SSB is appointed by management on the advice of the SSB, and performance is supervised by the SSB [Par. 55]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: A newly licensed small Islamic financial institution with limited internal specialists asks whether it may outsource its entire Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD) to an external advisory firm. According to AAOIFI GS 9 (Basis of Conclusion BC12), what is the Board's position?
en.A: Full outsourcing of the SCD to external consultants is actively encouraged for all IFIs during their first five years of operation.
en.B: There should be no outsourcing of the SCD because it is a unique management function; however, in case of need, the function may be allocated internally to different organs or departments in line with the requirements of GS 9.
en.C: Outsourcing is permitted provided the external firm also serves as the institution's statutory external Shari'ah auditor.
en.D: Outsourcing is mandatory whenever an IFI has fewer than 50 full-time employees.
en.True answer: There should be no outsourcing of the SCD because it is a unique management function; however, in case of need, the function may be allocated internally to different organs or departments in line with the requirements of GS 9.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Appendix C, BC12 ('It was discussed and concluded that there should be no outsourcing as the function is a management function and is unique in nature. However, in case of need the function may be allocated to different organs / departments in line with the requirements of this standard').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Which of the following accurately reflects AAOIFI GS 9 requirements for SCD's ongoing compliance review process (Paragraphs 47–48)?
en.A: All compliance checks must be conducted strictly on an annual post-audit basis, and routine review plans must be kept secret from business departments.
en.B: SCD may only review transactions exceeding USD 1 million and is prohibited from conducting unannounced snap checks.
en.C: Ongoing reviews may include pre-approvals by SCD on selected high-risk transactions as well as routine, random, and real-time snap checks, while routine review process plans and identification of high-risk transactions should be shared with relevant departments reasonably in advance to avoid unnecessary processing delays.
en.D: Business departments must pre-approve SCD's compliance review plans before SCD can examine any transaction files.
en.True answer: Ongoing reviews may include pre-approvals by SCD on selected high-risk transactions as well as routine, random, and real-time snap checks, while routine review process plans and identification of high-risk transactions should be shared with relevant departments reasonably in advance to avoid unnecessary processing delays.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 47–48 (Par. 47: ongoing reviews may include pre-approvals by SCD on selected transactions involving potential high risk of Shari'ah non-compliance, as well as routine, random, and, if necessary, snap checks of transactions on a real-time basis; Par. 48: routine compliance review process plans shall be shared with relevant departments reasonably in advance along with identification of high-risk transactions to ensure smooth functioning and avoid unnecessary delays).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Which statement accurately describes the Compliance Report of the SCD under Paragraphs 67–70 of AAOIFI GS 9?
en.A: SCD prepares a report once every two years solely for the external financial auditor, and the SSB issues its annual Shari'ah review report independently without considering SCD reports.
en.B: SCD submits monthly reports exclusively to the marketing department, and quantitative Shari'ah non-compliance risk ratings are prohibited.
en.C: SCD submits an annual report solely to the CEO, who decides whether any summary may ever be shared with the SSB.
en.D: SCD develops periodic (quarterly and annual) reports for senior management and the SSB; senior management reviews the annual report and coordinates with the SSB on outstanding significant risks/issues, and the SSB must consider SCD report(s) before finalizing its annual Shari'ah review report.
en.True answer: SCD develops periodic (quarterly and annual) reports for senior management and the SSB; senior management reviews the annual report and coordinates with the SSB on outstanding significant risks/issues, and the SSB must consider SCD report(s) before finalizing its annual Shari'ah review report.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 67–70 & BC11 (Par. 67: SCD develops periodic—quarterly and annual—reports for senior management and SSB; Par. 69 & BC11: senior management reviews the annual report and coordinates with SSB on outstanding significant risks/issues, and SSB shall consider the SCD report(s) before finalizing its annual Shari'ah review report; Par. 70: SCD may introduce a quantitative Shari'ah non-compliance risk rating in its report).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.A: (1) Control activities; (2) Monitoring; (3) Control environment; (4) Risk assessment.
en.B: (1) Control environment; (2) Risk assessment; (3) Information and communication; (4) Monitoring.
en.C: (1) Risk assessment; (2) Control activities; (3) Monitoring; (4) Information and communication.
en.D: (1) Control environment; (2) Control activities; (3) Risk assessment; (4) Monitoring.
en.True answer: (1) Control environment; (2) Risk assessment; (3) Information and communication; (4) Monitoring.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 22 & BC3: (1) Control environment covers setting the tone at the top, governance organs, values/culture, delegation of authority, and setting up SCD; (2) Risk assessment covers assessing Shari'ah non-compliance risks across departments/units and developing risk mitigation strategies; (3) Information and communication covers communicating compliance considerations, manuals, policies, standardized documentation, and Fatwas via information systems/technology; (4) Monitoring covers monitoring mechanisms, review requirements, and detective organs (Shari'ah review, internal Shari'ah audit, external Shari'ah audit).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: In a smaller Islamic bank with limited staff, the Product Development unit asks the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD) to design the commercial features and legal structure of a new Diminishing Musharakah home-finance product, and then treat SCD's sign-off as final product approval to expedite launch. Additionally, a branch requests a one-off deviation from a standard Murabaha workflow. According to AAOIFI GS 9, which assessment is correct?
en.A: SCD must not develop the product itself due to self-review threat, and while SCD's technical input during product development is valuable (especially in smaller IFIs), it shall NOT be considered final approval of the product (which requires SSB approval); for transaction deviations, SCD coordinates with the SSB to provide pre-approval or uses powers specifically vested in it by the SSB.
en.B: In smaller IFIs, SCD is fully authorized to both design new financial products from scratch and grant final Shari'ah approval without consulting the SSB.
en.C: SCD is strictly barred from providing any input during product development, and all deviations from standard transactions must be approved solely by the branch manager.
en.D: SCD may grant final product approval if endorsed by the CFO, whereas transaction deviations can never be pre-approved under any circumstances.
en.True answer: SCD must not develop the product itself due to self-review threat, and while SCD's technical input during product development is valuable (especially in smaller IFIs), it shall NOT be considered final approval of the product (which requires SSB approval); for transaction deviations, SCD coordinates with the SSB to provide pre-approval or uses powers specifically vested in it by the SSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 42(a), (k)–(l), Par. 51(e), BC6 & BC9 (BC6 explicitly explains that SCD's role is to review products and provide input rather than developing them to avoid a self-review threat, and while SCD input is especially important in smaller IFIs/windows, 'it shall not be considered as final approval of the product'; Par. 42(l) & BC9 state SCD coordinates with SSB to provide pre-approval of deviations from standard transactions or uses powers vested in it by the SSB).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: An Islamic bank maintains both a dedicated SSB Secretariat and a Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD). To avoid role overlap, how does AAOIFI GS 9 delineate responsibilities between the SSB Secretariat and the SCD regarding (1) conducting Fiqhi/technical research on new products and practices, (2) arranging SSB meetings and taking minutes, and (3) issuing an 'Actions Taken Report' on SSB pronouncements?
en.A: (1) SSB Secretariat; (2) SCD; (3) External Shari'ah auditor.
en.B: (1) SSB Secretariat; (2) SSB Secretariat; (3) Internal Shari'ah audit.
en.C: (1) SCD; (2) SCD; (3) CEO's executive office.
en.D: (1) SCD (primary research contributor); (2) SSB Secretariat (logistical and documentation support); (3) SSB Secretariat (communicating SSB pronouncements, following up compliance, and submitting an 'Actions Taken Report' to management and the SSB).
en.True answer: (1) SCD (primary research contributor); (2) SSB Secretariat (logistical and documentation support); (3) SSB Secretariat (communicating SSB pronouncements, following up compliance, and submitting an 'Actions Taken Report' to management and the SSB).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 42(i), Par. 54(a)–(c) & Appendix C, BC7 (BC7 clarifies that the secretariat provides logistical support to the SSB—such as arranging meetings, minute taking, preparing working papers—while performing research is the primary function of the SCD [Par. 42(i)], not the secretariat; Par. 54(c) assigns the SSB secretariat the duty of communicating/explaining SSB pronouncements, following up compliance, and submitting an 'Actions Taken Report' to management and the SSB).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 27–29 of AAOIFI GS 9, an IFI must establish formal protocols for both internal and external communication regarding Shari'ah compliance. Which pair of protocol requirements is mandatory under these paragraphs?
en.A: Internal protocols must restrict SCD from permanent IT system access to protect customer privacy; external protocols allow relationship managers to publish Shari'ah explanations directly to investors without business-head review.
en.B: Internal protocols apply solely to annual board meetings; external protocols require SSB pre-approval for every routine customer account statement.
en.C: Internal protocols must define document types to be shared, level of detail, frequency of exchange, permanent access level to IT systems, mode of communication, and authorities to communicate between SCD and other departments; external protocols must define the nature of information, level of detail, and a review process with relevant business heads before disseminating information to regulators, customers, and investors.
en.D: Internal and external communication protocols are optional guidelines that apply only after an IFI experiences a regulatory enforcement penalty.
en.True answer: Internal protocols must define document types to be shared, level of detail, frequency of exchange, permanent access level to IT systems, mode of communication, and authorities to communicate between SCD and other departments; external protocols must define the nature of information, level of detail, and a review process with relevant business heads before disseminating information to regulators, customers, and investors.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 28–29 (Par. 28 lists required elements of internal communication protocols: types of documents shared, level of detail, frequency of communication exchange, permanent access level to IT systems, mode of communication, and authorities to communicate between SCD and other departments; Par. 29 lists required elements of external communication protocols with regulators, customers, and investors: nature of information, level of detail, and review process with relevant business heads before dissemination).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: During its routine compliance reviews, the SCD identifies repeated operational breaches in how a branch executes Tawarruq agency steps. According to Paragraphs 63–66 of AAOIFI GS 9, how should SCD apply compliance techniques, issue tracking, and escalation?
en.A: SCD should close each breach once the individual transaction settles without logging it, and avoid transaction walk-throughs so business operations are never observed directly.
en.B: SCD should incorporate transaction walk-throughs and materiality/tolerance standards, maintain an inventory of open issues with coordinated action plans, escalate occasional, first-time, frequent, and continuous non-compliance events per defined protocols, and analyze occurrence/frequency patterns to identify and eliminate root causes through process and control improvements.
en.C: SCD should escalate only continuous breaches occurring for more than 12 months, while first-time and occasional breaches are permanently ignored.
en.D: SCD should independently rewrite the bank's core software code and impose monetary fines directly on branch customers.
en.True answer: SCD should incorporate transaction walk-throughs and materiality/tolerance standards, maintain an inventory of open issues with coordinated action plans, escalate occasional, first-time, frequent, and continuous non-compliance events per defined protocols, and analyze occurrence/frequency patterns to identify and eliminate root causes through process and control improvements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 63–66 (Par. 63(c), (e): incorporate transaction walk-throughs and standards for periodically assessing materiality and tolerance levels; Par. 64: escalation protocol must clearly define how occasional, first-time, frequent, and continuous events of non-compliance are escalated to management and TCWG; Par. 65: maintain an inventory of open issues and develop coordinated action plans; Par. 66: analyze occurrence and frequency patterns to identify and eliminate root causes via changes in processes and improvements in controls).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question: How does AAOIFI GS 9 (Paragraphs 35–37) define the role of technology and automation in strengthening the Shari'ah compliance function?
en.A: Automating routine transactions reduces reliance on human judgment and the risk of bypassing mandatory transaction steps; SCD should coordinate with the IT/information systems team and business units to embed system-based checks and flags that act as preventive controls and trigger non-compliance alerts, freeing SCD capacity for complex areas.
en.B: Technology should be used solely for post-year-end archival storage of signed Fatwas, while routine transactions must always remain manual so staff exercise individual judgment.
en.C: Once an IFI automates its core banking system, the SCD is no longer needed and should be dissolved.
en.D: System-based checks and flags are detective controls managed exclusively by the external financial auditor rather than SCD and IT.
en.True answer: Automating routine transactions reduces reliance on human judgment and the risk of bypassing mandatory transaction steps; SCD should coordinate with the IT/information systems team and business units to embed system-based checks and flags that act as preventive controls and trigger non-compliance alerts, freeing SCD capacity for complex areas.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9, Par. 35–37 (Par. 35: automating routine transactions moves dependence away from human judgment and choice of bypassing steps, increasing Shari'ah compliance; Par. 36: SCD coordinates with information systems team and business units to incorporate system-based checks and flags providing preventive controls and initiating alerts, saving time for special-attention areas; Par. 37: where resources permit, SCD adopts a technology-based mechanism for its own functioning).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question:
A newly established Islamic bank in a developing market makes four governance decisions regarding its Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD):
(1) To save costs, management outsources the entire SCD function to an external Shari'ah consultancy firm for a 3-year contract.
(2) After the regulator blocks outsourcing, management appoints a candidate as Head of SCD who holds a bachelor's degree in Islamic finance and has 6 years of internal Shari'ah audit experience in that new market, but management finalizes the appointment without seeking SSB concurrence.
(3) Once operational, the Head of SCD directly drafts the legal contracts and pricing structure of a new Istisna'a product and issues the final product sign-off without SSB approval.
(4) At year-end, the CEO conducts the Head of SCD's annual performance appraisal unilaterally without consulting the SSB.
Based on AAOIFI GS 9, how many of these four actions violate the standard, and why?
en.A: Only 1 violates GS 9 (action 3), because outsourcing is permitted for new banks, 6 years of experience meets the 5-year minimum, and the CEO solely appraises management staff.
en.B: Only 2 violate GS 9 (actions 1 and 4), because 6 years of experience automatically qualifies the Head of SCD without SSB concurrence, and SCD may grant final product sign-off in new markets.
en.C: All 4 violate GS 9: (1) SCD cannot be outsourced as it is a unique management function (BC12); (2) although 5–9 years of experience may be accepted in a new market, it is allowed only IF permitted by the SSB, and appointing the Head of SCD requires SSB concurrence/approval (Par. 40, Appendix B); (3) SCD must remain independent of product development except for providing reviews/inputs, and its input is never final product approval (Par. 51(e), BC6); (4) senior management must evaluate/appraise SCD in consultation with the SSB (Par. 41).
en.D: 3 violate GS 9 (actions 1, 2, and 3), while action 4 is compliant because dotted-line reporting to the SSB excludes the SSB from performance appraisal consultations.
en.True answer: All 4 violate GS 9: (1) SCD cannot be outsourced as it is a unique management function (BC12); (2) although 5–9 years of experience may be accepted in a new market, it is allowed only IF permitted by the SSB, and appointing the Head of SCD requires SSB concurrence/approval (Par. 40, Appendix B); (3) SCD must remain independent of product development except for providing reviews/inputs, and its input is never final product approval (Par. 51(e), BC6); (4) senior management must evaluate/appraise SCD in consultation with the SSB (Par. 41).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9: (1) BC12 concludes there should be no outsourcing of SCD as it is a unique management function; (2) Par. 40 & Appendix B(c)–(d) require Head of SCD appointment to have SSB concurrence/approval, and experience below 10 years (minimum 5 years in new markets) is valid only 'if so allowed by the SSB'; (3) Par. 51(e) & BC6 prohibit SCD from developing products (self-review threat) and state SCD input shall not be considered final product approval; (4) Par. 41 mandates that SCD be evaluated and appraised for performance by senior management 'in consultation with the SSB'.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 09: Shari'ah Compliance Function
en.Question:
A conventional bank operates a dedicated Islamic Banking Window. Due to tight staffing budgets, management merges the SSB Secretariat into the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD), having the Head of SCD also act as Secretary to the SSB. During the year, four events occur:
(1) Management argues that because the entity is an Islamic window of a conventional bank rather than a standalone Islamic bank, GS 9 is not binding.
(2) In its dual role as SSB Secretariat, the SCD is asked to conduct an independent Shari'ah review verification of new IT automated workflows that the SCD itself designed and implemented earlier in the year.
(3) SCD uncovers a recurring pattern where relationship managers repeatedly skip the asset-ownership transfer step in Murabaha financing; management grants those managers full sales bonuses anyway and closes each case without root-cause remediation.
(4) Senior management withholds SCD's annual compliance report (which lists unresolved material Murabaha breaches) from the SSB, and the SSB proceeds to issue its annual Shari'ah review report without considering SCD's report.
Which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate under AAOIFI GS 9?
en.A: (1) Correct—windows are exempt; (2) Compliant—dual roles carry no restrictions; (3) Compliant—bonuses are purely commercial; (4) Compliant—SSB reports independently of SCD reports.
en.B: (1) Incorrect—GS 9 covers windows; (2) Compliant—Head of SCD may always review SCD's own work; (3) Non-compliant—breaches must affect bonuses and undergo root-cause fix; (4) Compliant—senior management has discretion to withhold SCD reports from SSB.
en.C: (1) Incorrect—GS 9 covers windows; (2) Non-compliant—self-review threat arises; (3) Compliant—closing individual cases suffices; (4) Non-compliant—SSB must consider SCD reports.
en.D: (1) Incorrect—GS 9 explicitly defines IFIs to include stand-alone branches, divisions, and windows of conventional financial institutions (Par. 3(d)); (2) Non-compliant—merging SSB secretariat into SCD is allowed under resource constraints ONLY if it does not create a self-review threat, which is violated when reviewing work SCD itself performed earlier (Par. 3(f), 52–53); (3) Non-compliant—non-tolerance requires reflecting breaches in bonuses/appraisals and eliminating root causes of frequent non-compliance (Par. 34, 65–66); (4) Non-compliant—senior management must coordinate with SSB on outstanding significant issues in SCD's annual report, and the SSB must consider SCD report(s) before finalizing its annual Shari'ah review report (Par. 69).
en.True answer: (1) Incorrect—GS 9 explicitly defines IFIs to include stand-alone branches, divisions, and windows of conventional financial institutions (Par. 3(d)); (2) Non-compliant—merging SSB secretariat into SCD is allowed under resource constraints ONLY if it does not create a self-review threat, which is violated when reviewing work SCD itself performed earlier (Par. 3(f), 52–53); (3) Non-compliant—non-tolerance requires reflecting breaches in bonuses/appraisals and eliminating root causes of frequent non-compliance (Par. 34, 65–66); (4) Non-compliant—senior management must coordinate with SSB on outstanding significant issues in SCD's annual report, and the SSB must consider SCD report(s) before finalizing its annual Shari'ah review report (Par. 69).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 9: (1) Par. 3(d) defines IFIs to include stand-alone branches, divisions, and windows of conventional financial institutions; (2) Par. 52–53 & BC8 permit SCD to perform SSB secretariat functions under resource constraints 'subject to the condition that such dual functionality shall not result in self-review threats' (defined in Par. 3(f) as reviewing work one was responsible for earlier); (3) Par. 34 requires non-tolerance in appraisals/bonuses/increments/promotions, and Par. 65–66 require maintaining an open-issue inventory and eliminating root causes of frequent breaches; (4) Par. 69 requires senior management to coordinate with SSB on significant unresolved issues in SCD's annual report and mandates that 'SSB shall consider the SCD report(s) before finalizing its annual Shari'ah review report'.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope, frequency, and regulatory status of Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings under AAOIFI GS 10?
en.A: GS 10 applies to secondary-market Sukuk instruments and mandates all IFIs globally to obtain a rating semi-annually.
en.B: GS 10 applies to institutional-level assessments conducted by independent rating agencies; it is issued as a non-mandatory good-practice standard (unless mandated by local regulators) and encourages IFIs to obtain and publicly announce ratings once in three years, and preferably annually.
en.C: GS 10 is a mandatory standard enforced directly by AAOIFI on all Islamic banks every five years, with results kept strictly confidential from the public.
en.D: GS 10 applies exclusively to standalone full-fledged Islamic banks and excludes Islamic banking windows and Takaful operators.
en.True answer: GS 10 applies to institutional-level assessments conducted by independent rating agencies; it is issued as a non-mandatory good-practice standard (unless mandated by local regulators) and encourages IFIs to obtain and publicly announce ratings once in three years, and preferably annually.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 2–5, Par. 6(a), Footnote 1 & BC31–BC32 (Applies to institutional-level assessments [Par. 3; Footnote 1 notes publicly traded instruments belong to part two of the project]; IFIs include Islamic banking, Takaful, capital markets, and stand-alone branches/divisions/windows [Par. 6(a)]; IFIs are encouraged to have ratings conducted once in three years, and preferably annually, and publicly announce them [Par. 5]; issued as a non-mandatory good-practice initiative unless regulators adopt it as mandatory [BC31–BC32]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Under AAOIFI GS 10 and its Specimen Fit and Proper Criteria (Appendix B), which entities are eligible to conduct Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings, and what minimum criteria apply to the rating agency's Board of Directors?
en.A: Either a duly licensed credit rating agency or a Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agency with developed capacity and methodology (involving experts with suitable credit rating experience); its Board of Directors must include members with relevant financial/markets/legal/risk/ratings background, at least one director with 10 years of rating experience, and at least one independent director.
en.B: Exclusively international accounting firms registered with AAOIFI, whose Board of Directors must consist entirely of Fiqh al-Muamalat scholars.
en.C: Any financial consultancy firm without regulatory recognition, provided at least one director has 2 years of commercial banking experience.
en.D: Exclusively central banks or national Shari'ah boards, as private rating agencies are prohibited from issuing fiduciary ratings.
en.True answer: Either a duly licensed credit rating agency or a Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agency with developed capacity and methodology (involving experts with suitable credit rating experience); its Board of Directors must include members with relevant financial/markets/legal/risk/ratings background, at least one director with 10 years of rating experience, and at least one independent director.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 8(a)–(b), Par. 9(c), Appendix B(a)–(b) & Footnote 8 (Eligible agencies are (a) duly licensed credit rating agencies or (b) Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies with developed capacity/methodology involving experts with suitable credit rating experience; Appendix B Footnote 8 specifies minimum criteria for the board of directors: financial, markets, legal, risk, or ratings background sufficient to exercise governance; at least one director with 10 years rating experience; and at least one independent director).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 15–16 of AAOIFI GS 10, what restrictions govern business relationships, investments in the rated IFI's securities, and the cooling-off period required to eliminate a conflict of interest?
en.A: The rating agency may hold up to 5% of the rated IFI's shares as a passive investment and requires only a 3-month cooling-off period after providing advisory services.
en.B: The rating agency's staff may freely trade the rated IFI's Sukuk on stock exchanges, and a 6-month cooling-off period applies to former consultancy engagements.
en.C: The rating agency, its rating committee, management, and respective staff must not engage in any business, advisory, or consultancy relationship with the IFI, nor invest in or deal with any securities/instruments of such IFI (except arm's length over-the-counter transactions), and any existing threat/conflict requires elimination plus a cooling-off period of 12 months before accepting the rating service.
en.D: A rating agency is strictly barred forever from rating any IFI with which it ever had a prior conflict of interest; no cooling-off period can cure a past conflict.
en.True answer: The rating agency, its rating committee, management, and respective staff must not engage in any business, advisory, or consultancy relationship with the IFI, nor invest in or deal with any securities/instruments of such IFI (except arm's length over-the-counter transactions), and any existing threat/conflict requires elimination plus a cooling-off period of 12 months before accepting the rating service.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 15(a)–(c), Par. 16 & Appendix C Par. 20 (Par. 15(c) prohibits the rating agency, its rating committee, management, and staff from engaging in business, advisory, or consultancy relationships with the IFI, or investing in/dealing with its securities and instruments except for arm's length transactions on an over-the-counter basis; Par. 16 & Appendix C Par. 20 require eliminating all independence threats and conflict-of-interest situations and allowing a cooling-off period of 12 months).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: According to Paragraph 18 of AAOIFI GS 10, what maximum activity period does the assessment scope of a rating service cover, and how many core aspects of an IFI's state of affairs are assessed?
en.A: Activities conducted during a rolling 5-year period across 3 core aspects (Shari'ah audit, financial solvency, and Zakah payment).
en.B: Activities conducted during a 3-year period across 4 core aspects (Shari'ah compliance, credit risk, liquidity risk, and board diversity).
en.C: Activities conducted during a 2-year period across 5 core COSO internal control pillars.
en.D: An IFI's state of affairs as of a specific date and activities conducted during a period of not more than one year completing on such date, covering 6 core aspects: compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules, Shari'ah governance framework, corporate governance practices related to Shari'ah governance, transparency and disclosure, ethics and values, and fiduciary responsibilities and performance.
en.True answer: An IFI's state of affairs as of a specific date and activities conducted during a period of not more than one year completing on such date, covering 6 core aspects: compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules, Shari'ah governance framework, corporate governance practices related to Shari'ah governance, transparency and disclosure, ethics and values, and fiduciary responsibilities and performance.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 6(f) & Par. 18(a)–(f) (The assessment scope comprises the IFI's state of affairs as of a specific date and activities conducted during a period of not more than one year completing on such date, covering six aspects: (a) compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules; (b) Shari'ah governance framework; (c) corporate governance practices related to Shari'ah governance; (d) transparency and disclosure; (e) ethics and values; and (f) fiduciary responsibilities and performance).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Under Paragraph 21 of AAOIFI GS 10, how does a rating agency assess individual instruments or products when conducting an institutional-level Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating?
en.A: Although the objective is not to issue an opinion or rating on individual instruments, the agency must assess the compliance state of all material instruments or products (considering both financial materiality and qualitative factors) because overall institutional Shari'ah compliance cannot be determined otherwise.
en.B: The rating agency examines only the IFI's written Shari'ah governance policies and is prohibited from reviewing individual financing or investment contracts.
en.C: The rating agency must issue a separate published letter-grade rating for every single financial product offered by the IFI.
en.D: Individual products are assessed solely on quantitative revenue volume, ignoring qualitative Shari'ah structuring factors.
en.True answer: Although the objective is not to issue an opinion or rating on individual instruments, the agency must assess the compliance state of all material instruments or products (considering both financial materiality and qualitative factors) because overall institutional Shari'ah compliance cannot be determined otherwise.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 21 ('For the purpose of determining compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules, a rating agency shall assess the state of compliance of all material instruments or products, including financial materiality as well as qualitative factors. While the objective of a rating service under this standard is not to provide an opinion or rating on individual instruments, the level of overall Shari'ah compliance cannot be determined unless it is assessed at the level of individual instrument or product (at least those that are material)').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: In the suggested weightage distribution for benchmarked parameters under Paragraph 30 of AAOIFI GS 10, which component carries the highest suggested weightage range, and what is that range?
en.A: Fiduciary responsibility and performance, carrying a suggested weightage of 35% to 45%.
en.B: Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules, carrying a suggested weightage of 30% to 35%.
en.C: Shari'ah governance framework, carrying a suggested weightage of 25% to 30%.
en.D: Transparency and disclosure, carrying a suggested weightage of 20% to 30%.
en.True answer: Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules, carrying a suggested weightage of 30% to 35%.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 30 & Appendix D, BC23 (Par. 30 table sets suggested weightages: Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules: 30%–35%; Shari'ah governance framework: 15%–20%; Fiduciary responsibility and performance: 15%–20%; Corporate governance practices related to Shari'ah governance: 10%–15%; Transparency and disclosure: 10%–15%; Ethics and values: 10%–15%. BC23 confirms Shari'ah compliance is given the highest weight).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: In the suggested rating scale table in Paragraph 36 of AAOIFI GS 10, how are the 'BB' (60–69%), 'B' (50–59%), and 'C' (<50%) grades distinguished in terms of Shari'ah non-compliance instances?
en.A: None of BB, B, or C allows any Shari'ah non-compliance instances; all three differ solely by return on equity.
en.B: BB has unresolved material non-compliance, whereas B and C have zero non-compliance instances.
en.C: BB exhibits certain non-compliance instances within tolerable limits and resolved per Shari'ah; B exhibits certain material non-compliance instances (at times exceeding tolerable limits) that are mostly resolved per Shari'ah; C exhibits significant Shari'ah non-compliance instances with some remaining unresolved by management.
en.D: BB is reserved for institutions scoring 80–89%, B for 70–79%, and C for 60–69%.
en.True answer: BB exhibits certain non-compliance instances within tolerable limits and resolved per Shari'ah; B exhibits certain material non-compliance instances (at times exceeding tolerable limits) that are mostly resolved per Shari'ah; C exhibits significant Shari'ah non-compliance instances with some remaining unresolved by management.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 36 table (BB [60–69%]: certain non-compliance instances noted within tolerable limit and resolved as per Shari'ah; B [50–59%]: certain material non-compliance instances noted, at times more than tolerable limit, and mostly resolved as per Shari'ah; C [<50%]: significant Shari'ah non-compliance instances noted, some remaining unresolved by management).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Which of the following accurately states the composition, independence threshold, and voting rules of a Rating Committee under AAOIFI GS 10?
en.A: A rating committee must have at least 7 members, at least 50% must be independent of the rating agency, and decisions require a unanimous vote of all members.
en.B: A rating committee may consist of a single lead analyst, and non-scholar members may outvote Shari'ah experts on Shari'ah compliance rulings.
en.C: A rating committee must comprise at least 5 members, 100% must be external to the rating agency, and dissenting views are never recorded.
en.D: A rating committee generally comprises five members (in no case less than three), with not less than 33% independent of the rating agency; decisions are taken by majority vote with dissents noted for record purposes, and on Shari'ah compliance related matters the view of the majority of Shari'ah experts within the committee prevails.
en.True answer: A rating committee generally comprises five members (in no case less than three), with not less than 33% independent of the rating agency; decisions are taken by majority vote with dissents noted for record purposes, and on Shari'ah compliance related matters the view of the majority of Shari'ah experts within the committee prevails.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 41–42, Par. 52, Appendix C Par. 1, 8–9 & Appendix D, BC19 (Rating committee generally comprises 5 members, in no case less than 3; not less than 33% independent of the rating agency [BC19 explicitly notes the Board rejected raising this to 50%]; decisions by majority vote, dissents noted for record purposes, and on Shari'ah compliance related matters the view of the majority of Shari'ah experts within the rating committee prevails).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: In the 9-step principal procedure flow outlined in Paragraph 37 of AAOIFI GS 10, which step immediately follows 'Initial analysis' (Paragraphs 46–47) and precedes 'Rating committee meeting(s)' (Paragraphs 50–52)?
en.A: Due-diligence meetings (Paragraphs 48 and 49), aimed at confirming initial analysis, gathering supporting evidence, resolving identified issues, and understanding management's and Shari'ah supervisors' perspectives.
en.B: Public press release issuance (Paragraph 61), conducted prior to rating committee deliberations.
en.C: Benchmarked parameters assessment (Paragraph 43), which occurs after initial analysis is completed.
en.D: Subsequent update (Paragraph 54), performed before the rating report is drafted.
en.True answer: Due-diligence meetings (Paragraphs 48 and 49), aimed at confirming initial analysis, gathering supporting evidence, resolving identified issues, and understanding management's and Shari'ah supervisors' perspectives.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 37 & Par. 46–52 (The 9-step flow is: (1) Rating service acceptance [Par. 38] → (2) Team deployment [Par. 39–42] → (3) Benchmarked parameters assessment [Par. 43] → (4) Initial information [Par. 44–45] → (5) Initial analysis [Par. 46–47] → (6) Due-diligence meetings [Par. 48–49] → (7) Rating committee meeting(s) [Par. 50–52] → (8) Rating report [Par. 53] → (9) Subsequent update [Par. 54]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Under Paragraph 54 of AAOIFI GS 10, what is a rating agency's responsibility regarding events or facts discovered after the delivery date of a rating service?
en.A: The rating agency is legally liable for all post-rating operational breaches committed by the IFI over the subsequent 12 months and must continuously monitor daily bank transactions.
en.B: The rating agency is not responsible for events arising after the date of delivery of the rating service; however, if it becomes aware of situations, circumstances, or facts that existed when the rating was provided and would have affected the rating outcome, it shall consider issuing a revised rating and rating report.
en.C: Once a rating report is issued, it can never be revised or withdrawn under any circumstances, even if material fraud during the rated period is later uncovered.
en.D: The rating agency must automatically downgrade the IFI by two notches whenever new macroeconomic regulations are enacted after the report date.
en.True answer: The rating agency is not responsible for events arising after the date of delivery of the rating service; however, if it becomes aware of situations, circumstances, or facts that existed when the rating was provided and would have affected the rating outcome, it shall consider issuing a revised rating and rating report.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 54 ('A rating agency is not and shall not be held responsible for any events arising after the date of delivery of the rating service. However, if a rating agency becomes aware of situations and circumstances or facts, which, if known at the time the rating service was provided, would have an effect on the outcome of the rating, it shall consider issuing a revised rating and rating report').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 61–62 of AAOIFI GS 10, a rating output comprises three components (rating score, full version report to management, and public report/press release). Which items are required in the Full Version Report to management but marked 'Not applicable' for the Public Report?
en.A: The rating score and the date on which the report is issued.
en.B: The statement about involvement of subject matter experts (including Shari'ah scholars) and limitations of the rating report.
en.C: Key issues and significant matters (including risks and observations/findings) AND suggestions for improvement.
en.D: Identification of benchmarked parameters and statement of respective responsibility and scope.
en.True answer: Key issues and significant matters (including risks and observations/findings) AND suggestions for improvement.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 61 & Par. 62 table items (k) and (l) (In Par. 62's comparative table, item (k) 'Key issues and significant matters including risks and observations / findings' and item (l) 'Suggestions for improvement' are included in the Full version report to the IFI's management, whereas both are explicitly marked 'Not applicable' in the Public report / press release).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: According to the Illustrative Terms of Reference for the Rating Committee (Appendix C of AAOIFI GS 10), what rights exist regarding rating reconsideration, rating appeals, and advance notice to issuers before rating assignments or changes?
en.A: Neither committee members nor rated clients may ever request reconsideration or appeal once a preliminary score is drafted, and ratings are published without prior notice to the issuer.
en.B: Only the national central bank may file a rating appeal, and issuers must be given 30 days' advance notice before any rating action.
en.C: A rating appeal is available solely after the public press release has been circulated for 90 days, with no advance notice requirement.
en.D: A rating reconsideration process is available if a committee member strongly disagrees with the outcome; a rating appeal option is available for new analyst information provided between the committee meeting and decision communication or upon client request for consideration of material information; and the rating agency must give a minimum of 24 hours' notice to issuers before rating assignments and changes.
en.True answer: A rating reconsideration process is available if a committee member strongly disagrees with the outcome; a rating appeal option is available for new analyst information provided between the committee meeting and decision communication or upon client request for consideration of material information; and the rating agency must give a minimum of 24 hours' notice to issuers before rating assignments and changes.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Appendix C, Par. 13–15 & Par. 21 (Par. 13: rating reconsideration process available if any committee member strongly disagrees with outcome; Par. 14: rating appeal option available for new information provided by analyst between committee meeting and communicating decision to ratee, or on client request for consideration of material information; Par. 21: rating agency shall give a minimum of 24 hours notice to issuers before rating assignments and changes to allow provision of new material information).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: AAOIFI GS 10 (Paragraphs 20–24) establishes distinct benchmark hierarchies for different rating components. Comparing (1) Shari'ah Governance Framework (Par. 22), (2) Corporate Governance Practices related to Shari'ah Governance (Par. 23), and (3) Transparency and Disclosure (Par. 24), which option states the exact top-to-bottom source hierarchy for each?
en.A: (1) AAOIFI governance standards → IFSB Shari'ah governance standard(s) → Regulator's Shari'ah governance regulations; (2) IFSB corporate governance standard(s) → AAOIFI governance standards → Regulator's corporate governance regulations; (3) Applicable AAOIFI FAS transparency/disclosure requirements → IFSB transparency/disclosure standard(s) → Regulator's transparency/disclosure regulations.
en.B: (1) IFSB Shari'ah governance standard(s) → AAOIFI governance standards → Regulator's regulations; (2) AAOIFI governance standards → IFSB corporate governance standard(s) → Regulator's regulations; (3) IFSB standards → AAOIFI FAS → Regulator's regulations.
en.C: (1) Regulator's regulations → AAOIFI governance standards → IFSB standards; (2) Regulator's regulations → IFSB standards → AAOIFI governance standards; (3) Regulator's regulations → AAOIFI FAS → IFSB standards.
en.D: All three components share the identical hierarchy: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards → Central Shari'ah Board rulings → IFSB standards → Regulator's regulations.
en.True answer: (1) AAOIFI governance standards → IFSB Shari'ah governance standard(s) → Regulator's Shari'ah governance regulations; (2) IFSB corporate governance standard(s) → AAOIFI governance standards → Regulator's corporate governance regulations; (3) Applicable AAOIFI FAS transparency/disclosure requirements → IFSB transparency/disclosure standard(s) → Regulator's transparency/disclosure regulations.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 22–24: In Par. 22 (Shari'ah governance framework), AAOIFI governance standards rank first, followed by IFSB Shari'ah governance standards, then local regulatory regulations. Conversely, in Par. 23 (Corporate governance practices related to Shari'ah governance), IFSB corporate governance standards rank first, followed by AAOIFI governance standards, then local regulatory regulations. In Par. 24 (Transparency and disclosure), applicable AAOIFI FAS requirements rank first, followed by IFSB transparency/disclosure standards, then local regulatory regulations.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: A rating agency is commissioned to provide a jurisdiction-specific Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating for an Islamic bank in a country whose central bank mandates local Shari'ah regulations ahead of AAOIFI standards and omits IFSB standards. Under Paragraphs 27–28 of AAOIFI GS 10, how must the rating agency handle this modified hierarchy?
en.A: The rating agency is strictly prohibited from modifying the standard hierarchy under any circumstances and must refuse the engagement.
en.B: The rating agency may change the hierarchy or omit one or more resources depending on the jurisdiction's regulations, provided it (a) documents and publicly announces the changed hierarchy applied, and (b) does NOT claim such tiered or jurisdiction-specific rating to be in line with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general.
en.C: The rating agency may apply the local hierarchy silently without public announcement and still state in its press release that the rating fully complies with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general.
en.D: The rating agency may issue a jurisdiction-specific rating only if it simultaneously assigns an international benchmark rating and averages the two scores.
en.True answer: The rating agency may change the hierarchy or omit one or more resources depending on the jurisdiction's regulations, provided it (a) documents and publicly announces the changed hierarchy applied, and (b) does NOT claim such tiered or jurisdiction-specific rating to be in line with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 27–28 & Appendix D, BC15, BC20–BC21 (Par. 28 permits changing the hierarchy or ignoring one or more resources in a tiered or jurisdiction-specific rating depending on the jurisdiction's regulations, subject to two strict conditions: (a) document and publicly announce the changed hierarchy applied; and (b) not claim such tiered or jurisdiction-specific rating to be in line with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: During a rating engagement, a rating agency encounters two challenges: (1) for a novel fintech product, benchmarked parameters related to Shari'ah compliance are missing, and (2) management refuses access to key Mudaraba pool allocation records, creating an unavoidable significant limitation of scope. According to Paragraphs 31–34 of AAOIFI GS 10, what actions should the rating agency take?
en.A: For missing parameters, invent internal commercial benchmarks unilaterally; for the scope limitation, issue an 'A' rating with a footnote disclaimer.
en.B: For missing parameters, skip the Shari'ah compliance category entirely; for the scope limitation, rely solely on management's verbal assurances.
en.C: For missing parameters related to Shari'ah compliance, coordinate with the IFI's Shari'ah supervisor(s)—normally the IFI's SSB or its nominee, unless regulations mandate the regulator or CSB—to develop the parameters (and withdraw if unable to conclude on their suitability); for an unavoidable significant limitation of scope impacting performance or quality, consider withdrawing from the rating service.
en.D: Refer both matters to the external financial auditor and suspend the engagement for five years.
en.True answer: For missing parameters related to Shari'ah compliance, coordinate with the IFI's Shari'ah supervisor(s)—normally the IFI's SSB or its nominee, unless regulations mandate the regulator or CSB—to develop the parameters (and withdraw if unable to conclude on their suitability); for an unavoidable significant limitation of scope impacting performance or quality, consider withdrawing from the rating service.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 31–34 (Par. 31: if a significant limitation of scope impacting performance or quality cannot be avoided after due efforts, the rating agency shall consider withdrawing from the rating service; Par. 32–34: in respect of missing parameters related to compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules, coordinate with the Shari'ah supervisor(s)—normally the IFI's SSB or their nominee unless regulations mandate regulators or CSB—to develop them, and if unable to conclude as to suitability, withdraw from the rating service).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: In Appendix D (Basis of Conclusions) of AAOIFI GS 10, how does the Board justify (1) the need for Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings in addition to Shari'ah audit, and (2) allowing the rated IFI to pay the rating agency's fee?
en.A: (1) Ratings legally replace annual external Shari'ah audits; (2) Rating fees are paid out of a government subsidy fund rather than by the IFI.
en.B: (1) Shari'ah audit is forward-looking while ratings examine only past tax filings; (2) Ratee-paid fees are permitted only when the IFI receives a rating of 'A' or higher.
en.C: (1) Ratings evaluate only financial profitability; (2) Fee independence is maintained by prohibiting the rating agency from disclosing its methodology.
en.D: (1) Shari'ah audit provides a backward-looking opinion on past compliance, whereas a rating is forward-looking, differentiates relative compliance quality on a comparable scale, and focuses on processes, governance continuity, and fiduciary trust; (2) Ratee-paid remuneration does not impair independence and reflects established market practice for credit rating agencies, external auditors, and Shari'ah scholars.
en.True answer: (1) Shari'ah audit provides a backward-looking opinion on past compliance, whereas a rating is forward-looking, differentiates relative compliance quality on a comparable scale, and focuses on processes, governance continuity, and fiduciary trust; (2) Ratee-paid remuneration does not impair independence and reflects established market practice for credit rating agencies, external auditors, and Shari'ah scholars.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Appendix D, BC4, BC9, BC11–BC13 & BC27–BC28 (BC12–BC13 highlight three reasons why Shari'ah audit alone is insufficient: Shari'ah audit opines on past compliance whereas rating is forward-looking; rating provides a comparable scale across market participants; and rating focuses on processes, governance, and continuity alongside fiduciary trust [BC9]. BC27–BC28 conclude that ratee-paid remuneration does not impair independence, mirroring credit rating agencies, external auditors, and Shari'ah scholars).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question: Before accepting a Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating engagement under Paragraphs 14–17 and Appendix B of AAOIFI GS 10, a rating agency must complete a self-assessment of capacity and fulfill methodology publication requirements. Which statement accurately captures these mandatory pre-acceptance conditions?
en.A: The agency must confirm independence, perform a self-assessment of capacity covering (a) availability of methodology and knowledge base, (b) availability and strength of the rating committee, and (c) qualitative (capability) and quantitative (time allocation) availability of rating staff including subject-matter/Shari'ah experts, and have a consistent methodology made publicly available for free.
en.B: The agency may accept the engagement first and develop its rating methodology during the due-diligence phase, keeping the methodology proprietary and confidential.
en.C: The self-assessment of capacity examines only the financial liquidity of the rating agency and ignores staff time allocation or Shari'ah expert availability.
en.D: The rating methodology must be sold exclusively to rated clients for a licensing fee before they can sign an engagement letter.
en.True answer: The agency must confirm independence, perform a self-assessment of capacity covering (a) availability of methodology and knowledge base, (b) availability and strength of the rating committee, and (c) qualitative (capability) and quantitative (time allocation) availability of rating staff including subject-matter/Shari'ah experts, and have a consistent methodology made publicly available for free.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 14(a)–(c), Par. 17(a)–(c) & Appendix B(g) (Par. 14 requires: (a) independence, (b) self-assessment of capacity per Par. 17, and (c) developed and publicized consistent rating methodology; Par. 17 specifies three capacity pillars: (a) methodology and knowledge base, (b) availability and strength of rating committee, and (c) qualitative capability and quantitative time allocation of rating staff including subject-matter/Shari'ah experts; Appendix B(g) specifies methodologies should be made publicly available for free).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question:
A rating agency assigns the following component weights and scores to an Islamic bank:
• Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules (weight 30%): Score 30% (severe unresolved material Shari'ah non-compliance in core financing contracts)
• Shari'ah governance framework (weight 20%): Score 95%
• Corporate governance related to Shari'ah governance (weight 10%): Score 90%
• Transparency and disclosure (weight 10%): Score 95%
• Ethics and values (weight 10%): Score 95%
• Fiduciary responsibility and performance (weight 20%): Score 95%
The weighted average score equals (0.30×30) + (0.20×95) + (0.10×90) + (0.10×95) + (0.10×95) + (0.20×95) = 9 + 19 + 9 + 9.5 + 9.5 + 19 = 75.0%. Under Paragraph 30 (Footnote 5), Paragraph 36, and BC24 of AAOIFI GS 10, what rating conclusion applies?
en.A: The bank must be assigned an 'A' rating (70–79% band) because component weights are strictly independent and mathematical weighted averages cannot be overridden.
en.B: Despite the 75.0% mathematical average falling in the 'A' band, Footnote 5 and BC24 stipulate that a failure in a significant category such as compliance with Shari'ah rules and principles shall be considered an overall failure (and unresolved material non-compliance corresponds to 'C' / overall failure rather than 'A').
en.C: The bank must be assigned an 'AA' rating because five out of six governance and disclosure categories scored 90% or above.
en.D: The rating agency must average the 30% Shari'ah score with 100% to bring the category above 60% and assign a 'BB' rating.
en.True answer: Despite the 75.0% mathematical average falling in the 'A' band, Footnote 5 and BC24 stipulate that a failure in a significant category such as compliance with Shari'ah rules and principles shall be considered an overall failure (and unresolved material non-compliance corresponds to 'C' / overall failure rather than 'A').
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10, Par. 30 Footnote 5, Par. 36 & Appendix D, BC24 (Footnote 5 & BC24 explicitly state: 'Although the weightage of different categories is independent of each other, yet a failure in a significant category for example compliance with Shari'ah rules and principles shall be considered an overall failure.' Furthermore, under Par. 36, significant Shari'ah non-compliance instances with some remaining unresolved by management characterize grade 'C' [<50%, unsatisfactory/overall failure]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question:
A newly licensed rating agency prepares to accept its first Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating engagement for Bank Al-Noor (an Islamic bank). Review the four governance and independence facts:
(1) The rating agency's Board of Directors includes one independent director and one director with 12 years of credit rating agency experience.
(2) Eight months ago, the rating agency completed a paid consultancy project designing Bank Al-Noor's risk management framework; the agency argues that terminating the contract suffices without waiting longer.
(3) One analyst assigned to the rating team is married to an internal auditor currently employed by Bank Al-Noor.
(4) The agency forms a 5-member Rating Committee comprising 3 internal experts (2 Shari'ah scholars, 1 financial analyst) and 2 independent external members (1 Shari'ah scholar, 1 banking expert)—so 2 of 5 (40%) are independent. During voting on a Shari'ah compliance ruling, 2 Shari'ah scholars vote 'Non-Compliant' while 1 Shari'ah scholar and both non-scholar members vote 'Compliant' (3–2 overall).
Under AAOIFI GS 10, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Invalid—at least 3 independent directors are required; (2) Valid—6 months' cooling-off suffices; (3) Valid—spouses of analysts are exempt; (4) The Shari'ah ruling passes 3–2 by overall committee majority.
en.B: (1) Valid; (2) Invalid—24-month cooling-off is required; (3) Invalid; (4) Invalid committee—at least 50% of the rating committee must be independent.
en.C: (1) Valid—meets Appendix B Footnote 8 (≥1 director with 10+ years rating experience and ≥1 independent director); (2) Invalid—Par. 16 & Appendix C Par. 20 require a minimum 12-month cooling-off period after eliminating prior consultancy conflicts (8 months is insufficient); (3) Invalid—BC18 & Footnote 16 prohibit staff and their spouses/second-degree filial relations serving the ratee in any capacity from being on the rating team or committee; (4) Committee independence (2/5 = 40% ≥ 33% minimum per Par. 41 & BC19) is valid, and on the Shari'ah ruling, 'Non-Compliant' prevails because Par. 52 states the view of the majority of Shari'ah experts within the committee (2 of 3 scholars) prevails.
en.D: (1) Invalid; (2) Valid; (3) Valid; (4) Committee independence (40%) is valid, and 'Compliant' prevails because non-scholar votes count equally on Shari'ah matters.
en.True answer: (1) Valid—meets Appendix B Footnote 8 (≥1 director with 10+ years rating experience and ≥1 independent director); (2) Invalid—Par. 16 & Appendix C Par. 20 require a minimum 12-month cooling-off period after eliminating prior consultancy conflicts (8 months is insufficient); (3) Invalid—BC18 & Footnote 16 prohibit staff and their spouses/second-degree filial relations serving the ratee in any capacity from being on the rating team or committee; (4) Committee independence (2/5 = 40% ≥ 33% minimum per Par. 41 & BC19) is valid, and on the Shari'ah ruling, 'Non-Compliant' prevails because Par. 52 states the view of the majority of Shari'ah experts within the committee (2 of 3 scholars) prevails.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10 integrates four rules: (1) Appendix B Footnote 8 requires relevant background, at least one director with 10 years rating experience, and at least one independent director (12 yrs + 1 independent passes); (2) Par. 15(c), Par. 16 & Appendix C Par. 20 require eliminating consultancy conflicts and a minimum 12-month cooling-off period (8 months fails); (3) Appendix D, BC18 & Footnote 16 prohibit staff/service providers and their family members including spouses and second-degree filial relations serving the ratee in any capacity from being on the rating team or committee; (4) Par. 41 & BC19 require not less than 33% independent members on the rating committee (2/5 = 40% passes; Board rejected 50%), and Par. 52 stipulates that on Shari'ah compliance related matters, 'the view of the majority of Shari'ah experts within the rating committee shall prevail' (2 of 3 Shari'ah scholars voted Non-Compliant).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 10: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings for IFIs
en.Question:
A rating agency conducts a Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating for Al-Baraka Takaful as of 31 December 2025, issuing the report on 15 March 2026. Evaluate the following four actions during and after the engagement:
(1) The rating team assesses Al-Baraka Takaful's activities over the 12-month period from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2025.
(2) Because local Takaful regulations prioritize national Shari'ah board rulings ahead of AAOIFI standards, the agency modifies the benchmark hierarchy, publicly announces the changed hierarchy, and still states in its public press release that the rating is 'in line with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general.'
(3) In the public press release, the agency omits the 'Key issues and significant matters' and 'Suggestions for improvement' sections (including them only in the Full Version Report delivered to Al-Baraka Takaful's CEO).
(4) In May 2026, two separate developments occur: (i) a cyberattack happens in April 2026 disrupting Al-Baraka's IT system, and (ii) the agency discovers concealed side-agreements signed in October 2025 that invalidated Al-Baraka's major Wakalah contracts during 2025. The agency refuses to consider issuing a revised rating for either development.
According to AAOIFI GS 10, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
