en.A: (1) Invalid—the assessment period must cover at least 3 full years; (2) Valid—publicly announcing the changed hierarchy permits claiming general AAOIFI alignment; (3) Invalid—suggestions for improvement must be published in the press release; (4) Valid—a rating agency never revises an issued rating.
en.B: (1) Valid; (2) Valid; (3) Valid; (4) Invalid for both events—the agency must revise its rating for the April 2026 cyberattack as well.
en.C: (1) Valid; (2) Invalid—hierarchy can never be modified; (3) Invalid—both reports must be identical; (4) Partially valid—must revise only for the April 2026 cyberattack.
en.D: (1) Valid—Par. 18 specifies an assessment period of not more than one year completing on the assessment date; (2) Invalid—under Par. 28(b), when modifying the hierarchy for jurisdiction-specific ratings, the agency must NOT claim the rating to be in line with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general; (3) Valid—under Par. 62, 'Key issues/significant matters' and 'Suggestions for improvement' belong in the Full Version Report to management and are 'Not applicable' in the Public Report; (4) Partially invalid—under Par. 54, the agency is not responsible for post-delivery events like the April 2026 cyberattack, BUT because the concealed October 2025 side-agreements existed when the rating was provided and would have affected the rating outcome, it MUST consider issuing a revised rating and rating report.
en.True answer: (1) Valid—Par. 18 specifies an assessment period of not more than one year completing on the assessment date; (2) Invalid—under Par. 28(b), when modifying the hierarchy for jurisdiction-specific ratings, the agency must NOT claim the rating to be in line with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general; (3) Valid—under Par. 62, 'Key issues/significant matters' and 'Suggestions for improvement' belong in the Full Version Report to management and are 'Not applicable' in the Public Report; (4) Partially invalid—under Par. 54, the agency is not responsible for post-delivery events like the April 2026 cyberattack, BUT because the concealed October 2025 side-agreements existed when the rating was provided and would have affected the rating outcome, it MUST consider issuing a revised rating and rating report.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 10 integrates four core provisions: (1) Par. 18 defines the assessment scope as state of affairs as of a specific date and activities conducted during 'a period of not more than one year completing on such date'; (2) Par. 28(a)–(b) requires documenting and publicly announcing any changed hierarchy AND prohibits claiming such tiered or jurisdiction-specific rating to be in line with AAOIFI's Shari'ah and governance standards in general; (3) Par. 62 table explicitly marks items (k) 'Key issues and significant matters including risks and observations/findings' and (l) 'Suggestions for improvement' as required in the Full version report to management and 'Not applicable' in the Public report (press release); (4) Par. 54 relieves the agency of responsibility for post-delivery events (April 2026 cyberattack) while requiring it to consider issuing a revised rating and rating report upon discovering pre-existing facts (October 2025 concealed side-agreements) that would have affected the rating outcome.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the relationship of AAOIFI GS 11 ('Internal Shari'ah Audit') with prior AAOIFI standards, the IIA's International Professional Practices Framework (IPPF), and its effective date?
en.A: GS 11 supplements GS 3 ('Internal Shari'ah Review') without superseding it, prohibits referring to IIA's IPPF, and became effective on 1 January 2018.
en.B: GS 11 supersedes the earlier GS 3 ('Internal Shari'ah Review'), allows internal Shari'ah auditors to refer to the IIA's IPPF unless contrary to GS 11 or Shari'ah requirements, and is effective for internal Shari'ah auditors' reports covering periods beginning on or after 1 July 2021.
en.C: GS 11 supersedes GS 9 ('Shari'ah Compliance Function') and requires internal Shari'ah auditors to apply IFRS audit standards exclusively.
en.D: GS 11 is a non-binding advisory note with no effective date and leaves GS 3 in full legal force.
en.True answer: GS 11 supersedes the earlier GS 3 ('Internal Shari'ah Review'), allows internal Shari'ah auditors to refer to the IIA's IPPF unless contrary to GS 11 or Shari'ah requirements, and is effective for internal Shari'ah auditors' reports covering periods beginning on or after 1 July 2021.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Preface PR1, Intro note (p. 4), Par. 2, Par. 65 & Par. 67 (GS 11 supersedes GS 3 'Internal Shari'ah Review' adopted in June 1999 [PR1, Par. 67]; internal Shari'ah auditors may refer to IIA's IPPF unless contrary to or inconsistent with GS 11 or a requirement in Shari'ah [Par. 2]; effective for internal Shari'ah auditors' reports covering periods beginning on or after 01 July 2021 [Par. 65]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: According to Paragraph 5 and Appendix C (BC16–BC17) of AAOIFI GS 11, how does the Internal Shari'ah Audit (ISA) function differ from the Shari'ah Compliance Function?
en.A: ISA is independent of management and acts as a detective control that periodically assesses the adequacy and effectiveness of intended controls pertaining to adherence to Shari'ah guidelines, whereas the Shari'ah compliance function is a management function acting as a preventive/deterrent control through ongoing monitoring of daily activities.
en.B: ISA is a management function reporting to the CEO that pre-approves daily transactions, whereas the Shari'ah compliance function is an independent board organ conducting annual ex-post audits.
en.C: Both functions are part of executive management and share identical preventive pre-approval responsibilities over new products.
en.D: ISA evaluates only financial accounting ratios, whereas the Shari'ah compliance function conducts external statutory assurance.
en.True answer: ISA is independent of management and acts as a detective control that periodically assesses the adequacy and effectiveness of intended controls pertaining to adherence to Shari'ah guidelines, whereas the Shari'ah compliance function is a management function acting as a preventive/deterrent control through ongoing monitoring of daily activities.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 4(c) Footnote 3, Par. 5 & Appendix C, BC16–BC17 (Par. 5 states internal Shari'ah audit assesses the adequacy and effectiveness of intended controls pertaining to adherence of Shari'ah guidelines, whereas the Shari'ah compliance function is an ongoing process of monitoring overall activities and compliance environment; BC17 clarifies that ISA is a detective control commenting periodically on the control environment, while Shari'ah compliance is a preventive/deterrent control providing ongoing day-to-day feedback; Footnote 3 warns against confusing ISA with the management-level Shari'ah compliance function).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Which of the following accurately reflects the ethical, quality control, and independent/peer review requirements imposed on the Internal Shari'ah Audit function under Paragraphs 7–11 of AAOIFI GS 11?
en.A: Internal Shari'ah auditors follow only national civil service codes and are exempt from IIA's Quality Assurance and Improvement Program (QAIP).
en.B: Quality assurance reviews are conducted exclusively by the bank's executive management without documented guidelines.
en.C: Internal Shari'ah auditors must comply with AAOIFI's Code of Ethics and IIA's Code of Ethics, fulfill IIA's QAIP requirements, ensure active involvement of Shari'ah expert(s) throughout the process, and maintain a quality assurance assessment mechanism featuring independent senior/peer review governed by documented guidelines covering frequency, scope, and reviewer qualifications.
en.D: Involvement of Shari'ah experts in internal Shari'ah audit is prohibited so that auditors rely solely on conventional internal audit checklists.
en.True answer: Internal Shari'ah auditors must comply with AAOIFI's Code of Ethics and IIA's Code of Ethics, fulfill IIA's QAIP requirements, ensure active involvement of Shari'ah expert(s) throughout the process, and maintain a quality assurance assessment mechanism featuring independent senior/peer review governed by documented guidelines covering frequency, scope, and reviewer qualifications.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 7–11 & BC14–BC15 (Par. 7: comply with AAOIFI Code of Ethics and IIA Code of Ethics; Par. 8: fulfill IIA's QAIP requirements; Par. 9: ensure adequate resources and knowledge including active involvement of Shari'ah expert(s) throughout the process; Par. 10–11: maintain QA assessment mechanism including independent senior or peer review with clear documented guidelines covering (a) frequency, (b) scope, and (c) qualification and skill set of person(s) responsible).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 13–16 of AAOIFI GS 11, which rule governs the organizational independence and operational boundaries of internal Shari'ah auditors?
en.A: Internal Shari'ah auditors must be external to the IFI's legal entity and may never communicate directly with business line managers.
en.B: Internal Shari'ah auditors may assist management by designing new financing products and performing Shari'ah compliance pre-approvals when staffing is tight.
en.C: Management may restrict internal Shari'ah auditors from accessing confidential customer files and board minutes.
en.D: The internal Shari'ah audit function must be independent of management (though not necessarily independent of the IFI itself), have unrestricted access to all documents, reports, and systems, and internal Shari'ah auditors must NOT undertake any operational activities or perform any management function, including product development and Shari'ah compliance functions.
en.True answer: The internal Shari'ah audit function must be independent of management (though not necessarily independent of the IFI itself), have unrestricted access to all documents, reports, and systems, and internal Shari'ah auditors must NOT undertake any operational activities or perform any management function, including product development and Shari'ah compliance functions.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 13–16 (Par. 13: ISA function shall be independent of management but may not necessarily be independent of the entity/IFI; Par. 14: management shall ensure unrestricted access to all documents, reports, systems, etc.; Par. 16: internal Shari'ah auditors shall not undertake any operational activities of the IFI, or perform any management function, including product development and Shari'ah compliance functions).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 17–18 of AAOIFI GS 11, in addition to its primary objective of providing assurance on adherence to Shari'ah principles and rules, on which three specific areas must the Internal Shari'ah Audit function provide an assurance opinion to TCWG and the SSB?
en.A: (a) Adequacy of the governance structure/framework (including fiduciary responsibilities); (b) design and implementation of adequate internal controls by management to ensure Shari'ah adherence; and (c) establishment by management of adequate risk assessment criteria and management mechanisms for Shari'ah compliance and Islamic finance transaction risks.
en.B: (a) External market share growth; (b) dividend payout ratios to common shareholders; and (c) tax optimization strategies.
en.C: (a) Approval of sovereign Sukuk prospectuses; (b) licensing of external rating agencies; and (c) setting central bank reserve requirements.
en.D: (a) Drafting new Fatwas on behalf of the SSB; (b) executing daily treasury Murabaha trades; and (c) managing customer complaint hotlines.
en.True answer: (a) Adequacy of the governance structure/framework (including fiduciary responsibilities); (b) design and implementation of adequate internal controls by management to ensure Shari'ah adherence; and (c) establishment by management of adequate risk assessment criteria and management mechanisms for Shari'ah compliance and Islamic finance transaction risks.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 17 & Par. 18(a)–(c) (In addition to the primary objective in Par. 17, Par. 18 requires providing assurance in the form of an opinion to TCWG and the SSB as to whether: (a) an adequate governance structure/framework is in place including fiduciary responsibilities; (b) adequate internal controls have been designed and implemented by management to ensure adherence with Shari'ah principles and rules; and (c) management has established adequate risk assessment criteria and management mechanism to ensure compliance and cater to specific Islamic finance transaction risks).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 20–22 of AAOIFI GS 11, what is the default organizational form of the Internal Shari'ah Audit function, and when may it be established as a unit within the conventional Internal Audit department?
en.A: By default it must be part of the Shari'ah Compliance Department, and it may become a separate department only when assets exceed USD 10 billion.
en.B: By default all IFIs must establish a separate independent internal Shari'ah audit department; it may take the form of a unit within the internal audit department IF AND ONLY IF: (a) the IFI is very small in relative size and/or operates in a new market, (b) the internal audit department has adequate qualitative and quantitative capability, (c) the head of internal audit (or a separate appointed head of ISA) meets the fit and proper criteria in Appendix B, and (d) overall operational efficiency is achieved by combining them.
en.C: By default it is a unit within the Finance Department, and it may move into Internal Audit if approved by the external financial auditor.
en.D: Any IFI of any size in a mature market may freely merge internal Shari'ah audit into internal audit without meeting fit and proper criteria.
en.True answer: By default all IFIs must establish a separate independent internal Shari'ah audit department; it may take the form of a unit within the internal audit department IF AND ONLY IF: (a) the IFI is very small in relative size and/or operates in a new market, (b) the internal audit department has adequate qualitative and quantitative capability, (c) the head of internal audit (or a separate appointed head of ISA) meets the fit and proper criteria in Appendix B, and (d) overall operational efficiency is achieved by combining them.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 20–22 & Appendix C, BC10–BC13 (Par. 21: all IFIs shall, by default, establish separate independent internal Shari'ah audit departments; Par. 22 & BC11 list four cumulative conditions required to operate as a unit within the internal audit department: (a) very small relative size and/or operating in a new market; (b) internal audit department has adequate quantitative and qualitative capability; (c) head of internal audit or a separate appointed head of ISA meets Appendix B fit and proper criteria; and (d) overall operational efficiency is achieved).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Paragraph 23 of AAOIFI GS 11, what specific conditions apply when an IFI outsources its Internal Shari'ah Audit function to a professional firm?
en.A: Outsourcing of internal Shari'ah audit is strictly prohibited under all circumstances, just like the Shari'ah compliance function.
en.B: Any consulting firm may accept internal Shari'ah audit engagements for up to 10 Islamic banks simultaneously per assigned lead auditor.
en.C: The professional firm must have adequate qualitative and quantitative capability and meet Appendix B fit and proper criteria, AND the individual assigned as Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit must meet Appendix B criteria and must NOT be involved in internal Shari'ah audit assignments of more than three IFIs (with multiple collective investment schemes/funds managed by IFIs counted as a single IFI).
en.D: Outsourcing is permitted only if the professional firm simultaneously serves as the IFI's external financial auditor and external Shari'ah auditor.
en.True answer: The professional firm must have adequate qualitative and quantitative capability and meet Appendix B fit and proper criteria, AND the individual assigned as Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit must meet Appendix B criteria and must NOT be involved in internal Shari'ah audit assignments of more than three IFIs (with multiple collective investment schemes/funds managed by IFIs counted as a single IFI).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 23(a)–(b) & Appendix B Section 2 (Unlike GS 9 which prohibits outsourcing SCD, GS 11 Par. 23 permits outsourcing ISA if and only if: (a) the professional firm has adequate capability and meets Appendix B criteria; and (b) the person assigned as head of internal Shari'ah audit meets Appendix B criteria and is not involved in ISA assignments of more than three IFIs—except that multiple collective investment schemes/funds managed by IFIs are considered a single IFI for this limit).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: According to Paragraphs 24–26 (including the reporting flow chart) of AAOIFI GS 11, what is the reporting line and draft-to-final report workflow for the Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit (HISA)?
en.A: Primary reporting is to the CEO, with dotted-line reporting to the Chief Risk Officer, and final reports are approved by management before going to the Audit Committee.
en.B: Primary reporting is to the SSB, with dotted-line reporting to the CFO, and draft reports are reviewed by executive management before going to the SSB.
en.C: Primary reporting is to the external Shari'ah auditor, with no reporting relationship to the Audit Committee.
en.D: Primary reporting is to those charged with governance (the Audit Committee) and dotted-line reporting is to the SSB; HISA first shares initial draft reports and observations with the SSB for its Shari'ah views, comments, and interpretations, and then issues the final report to both the SSB and the Audit Committee.
en.True answer: Primary reporting is to those charged with governance (the Audit Committee) and dotted-line reporting is to the SSB; HISA first shares initial draft reports and observations with the SSB for its Shari'ah views, comments, and interpretations, and then issues the final report to both the SSB and the Audit Committee.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 24–26 & Reporting Flow Chart (p. 14), Appendix C, BC8 (Par. 24: primary reporting to TCWG, namely the audit committee, and dotted-line reporting to the SSB; Par. 25–26 chart: Step 1 HISA sends Draft report → Step 2 SSB review and comments back to HISA → Step 3 Final report → SSB & Audit Committee).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: According to Paragraph 30 and Appendix B of AAOIFI GS 11, who holds the authority to appoint the Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit, who hires the ISA staff, and what minimum experience is specified for the Head of ISA?
en.A: The Audit Committee holds the responsibility and authority to appoint the Head of ISA (subject to SSB approval regarding Shari'ah/Fiqh al-Muamalat knowledge and skills, preferably with ≥10 years of relevant experience, subject to regulatory relaxation in newer markets), while the Head of ISA in coordination with HR hires the ISA staff.
en.B: The CEO appoints the Head of ISA without Audit Committee or SSB involvement, requiring at least 2 years of experience in retail banking sales.
en.C: The external financial auditor appoints both the Head of ISA and all ISA staff, requiring a Ph.D. in conventional economics.
en.D: The Head of SCD appoints the Head of ISA so that internal Shari'ah audit remains aligned with management priorities.
en.True answer: The Audit Committee holds the responsibility and authority to appoint the Head of ISA (subject to SSB approval regarding Shari'ah/Fiqh al-Muamalat knowledge and skills, preferably with ≥10 years of relevant experience, subject to regulatory relaxation in newer markets), while the Head of ISA in coordination with HR hires the ISA staff.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 30–31, Appendix B Section 1, Footnote 6 & Appendix C, BC21 (Par. 30: appointment of head of ISA is the responsibility and authority of the audit committee; head of ISA in coordination with HR is responsible for hiring relevant staff; Appendix B Section 1(c)–(d) & Footnote 6: preferably not less than 10-year work experience in relevant areas, with regulatory relaxation allowed in newer markets [BC21], plus SSB approval on Shari'ah/Fiqh al-Muamalat knowledge and skills).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 37–39 of AAOIFI GS 11, who develops the Internal Shari'ah Audit Charter and Manual (SOPs), and who approves them?
en.A: Both documents are drafted by the Shari'ah Compliance Department and approved solely by the Chief Executive Officer.
en.B: The Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit develops the charter and manual (subject to periodic review and update), and they are approved by the Audit Committee after due consultation with the SSB.
en.C: The external Shari'ah auditor drafts both documents, and they are approved by the bank's shareholders at the Annual General Meeting.
en.D: The SSB drafts both documents unilaterally without input from the Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit or the Audit Committee.
en.True answer: The Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit develops the charter and manual (subject to periodic review and update), and they are approved by the Audit Committee after due consultation with the SSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 37–39 ('The head of the internal Shari'ah audit shall be responsible for developing an internal Shari'ah audit charter and manual, which shall be subject to periodic review and update, as appropriate. The same shall be approved by the audit committee, after due consultation with the SSB').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 55–57 of AAOIFI GS 11, what are the mandatory maximum deadlines for (1) submitting final periodic ISA reports, (2) SSB providing final comments on draft periodic reports, and (3) submitting engagement (audit entity) reports?
en.A: (1) Within 6 months of period-end; (2) Within 3 months of receiving the draft; (3) Within 3 months of engagement completion.
en.B: (1) Within 1 month of period-end; (2) Within 14 days of receiving the draft; (3) Within 6 months of engagement completion.
en.C: (1) Periodic reports (quarterly, half-yearly, or at least annual) not later than 3 months from the end of the respective period; (2) SSB final comments/conclusions on the draft periodic report within 1 month of receipt; (3) Engagement (audit entity) reports not later than 1 month from completion of the respective audit engagement (if desired by SSB and Audit Committee).
en.D: GS 11 specifies no numerical deadlines for either periodic reports or engagement reports.
en.True answer: (1) Periodic reports (quarterly, half-yearly, or at least annual) not later than 3 months from the end of the respective period; (2) SSB final comments/conclusions on the draft periodic report within 1 month of receipt; (3) Engagement (audit entity) reports not later than 1 month from completion of the respective audit engagement (if desired by SSB and Audit Committee).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 55–57 (Par. 55(a): periodic reports within a reasonable time, but not later than 3 months from the end of the respective period; Par. 55(b): engagement/audit entity reports within a reasonable time, but not later than 1 month from completion of the respective engagement, if so desired by SSB and audit committee; Par. 56: upon receipt of draft periodic report, SSB shall provide its final comments and conclusions thereon to HISA within 1 month; Par. 57: quarterly, half-yearly, or at least annual basis).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: According to Paragraphs 63–64 of AAOIFI GS 11, how are responsibilities allocated for rectifying Shari'ah non-compliance findings, agreeing on follow-up action plans, and implementing those follow-up plans?
en.A: Internal Shari'ah auditors directly execute operational rectifications inside business branches and rewrite customer contracts.
en.B: The external Shari'ah auditor is responsible for implementing internal audit follow-up plans on a monthly basis.
en.C: The SSB is solely responsible for implementing operational corrective actions across bank branches.
en.D: Management is responsible for rectifying and preventing recurrence of non-compliance; after discussing observations and developing mutual action plans with management, the follow-up plan is agreed with the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD), which is responsible for its implementation, while internal Shari'ah auditors prioritize following up earlier observations in subsequent audits.
en.True answer: Management is responsible for rectifying and preventing recurrence of non-compliance; after discussing observations and developing mutual action plans with management, the follow-up plan is agreed with the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD), which is responsible for its implementation, while internal Shari'ah auditors prioritize following up earlier observations in subsequent audits.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 63–64 ('The management is responsible for rectifying and preventing recurrence of instances of non-compliance... At the conclusion of the internal Shari'ah audit, observations and proposed recommendations should be discussed with the management and subsequently action plans should be mutually developed... Such follow up plan shall be agreed with the Shari'ah compliance department, who shall be responsible for implementation of the same. While performing the engagement (audit entity) audit for a future period, the internal Shari'ah auditors shall assign due priority to the follow up of the earlier observations...').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 40–43 of AAOIFI GS 11, what two overarching areas form the primary scope of the annual/periodic internal Shari'ah audit process, and who must approve the periodic audit plans?
en.A: The process covers (a) auditing the overall organizational governance structure and management control environment (including Shari'ah governance, related corporate governance, and fiduciary responsibilities), and (b) conducting an organizational-level risk assessment of Shari'ah adherence to drive the selection and audit cycle of individual audit entities (branches, departments, functions); periodic plans must be developed at least annually and approved by BOTH the SSB and the Audit Committee.
en.B: The process covers only branch cash counts and ATM reconciliations, and periodic plans are approved solely by the Chief Financial Officer.
en.C: The process covers only IT software licensing and tax compliance, and periodic plans are approved exclusively by the SSB without Audit Committee input.
en.D: Periodic plans are prepared once every three years and require approval solely from the Head of the Shari'ah Compliance Department.
en.True answer: The process covers (a) auditing the overall organizational governance structure and management control environment (including Shari'ah governance, related corporate governance, and fiduciary responsibilities), and (b) conducting an organizational-level risk assessment of Shari'ah adherence to drive the selection and audit cycle of individual audit entities (branches, departments, functions); periodic plans must be developed at least annually and approved by BOTH the SSB and the Audit Committee.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 40–43 (Par. 40 defines two primary areas of the annual/periodic ISA process: (a) audit of governance structure and management control environment at the overall organizational level including fiduciary responsibilities; and (b) overall risk assessment at the organizational level with regard to adherence with Shari'ah principles and rules forming the basis for selection and performance of audits of individual organizational units/engagements. Par. 41 mandates developing periodic plans at least annually, approved by BOTH the SSB and the Audit Committee).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: In the 12-step Engagement (Audit Entity) Audit Process Flow depicted in Paragraph 44 of AAOIFI GS 11, what happens during Steps 10, 11, and 12 regarding the closing meeting, unresolved observations, and post-issuance rating revisions?
en.A: Step 10 issues the final report directly to regulators without discussing observations with the auditee; Step 12 prohibits any revision to the final audit rating once issued.
en.B: In Step 10 (Closing meeting), all major observations are discussed with the auditee (noting any spot rectification) and documented; in Step 11, a draft report is issued to the auditee for reply; in Step 12, the final report and audit rating are issued after considering auditee responses, unresolved observations are sent to the SSB for corrective actions, and the final rating can be revised based on the SSB's decision on unresolved observations or material information coming to the auditor's knowledge after issuance.
en.C: Unresolved observations in Step 12 are permanently dropped if the auditee disagrees with them, and the SSB reviews observations only once every five years.
en.D: Step 11 sends the draft report exclusively to the external financial auditor, while Step 12 leaves audit rating decisions solely to branch managers.
en.True answer: In Step 10 (Closing meeting), all major observations are discussed with the auditee (noting any spot rectification) and documented; in Step 11, a draft report is issued to the auditee for reply; in Step 12, the final report and audit rating are issued after considering auditee responses, unresolved observations are sent to the SSB for corrective actions, and the final rating can be revised based on the SSB's decision on unresolved observations or material information coming to the auditor's knowledge after issuance.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 44 Process Flow Chart (Steps 10–12, p. 18): Step 10 (Closing meeting): all major observations discussed with auditee, spot rectification noted, results documented; Step 11 (Reporting of audit observation - draft report): draft report issued to auditee for reply; Step 12 (Issuance of final reports and audit ratings): final report issued after considering auditee responses; audit opinion formed on approved rating mechanism; unresolved observations sent to Shari'ah Board for corrective actions; final rating can be revised based on Shari'ah board's decision on unresolved observations or any material information coming to auditor's knowledge after issuance of final report.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: According to Paragraphs 45–47 and 49 of AAOIFI GS 11, how should an internal Shari'ah auditor calibrate (1) materiality, (2) sample sizes when Shari'ah non-compliance is detected, and (3) the extent of detailed audit procedures across Low, Medium, and High residual risk areas?
en.A: (1) Materiality is defined solely as ≥5% of net profit; (2) sample sizes remain fixed even when breaches are found; (3) exhaustive detailed procedures are mandatory even in Low residual risk areas.
en.B: (1) Materiality is set unilaterally by branch managers; (2) sample selection relies solely on non-statistical convenience sampling; (3) High residual risk areas require no detailed procedures.
en.C: (1) Materiality reflects quantitative or qualitative significance beyond the 'risk appetite' and 'tolerable limit' defined by TCWG and the SSB; (2) statistical approaches and judgment are used, and when instances of Shari'ah non-compliance are identified, sample sizes must be increased adequately; (3) detailed procedures depend on residual risk: Low risk requires no or minimum detailed procedures (as performing them may be counterproductive and inefficient), Medium risk requires minimum to reasonable detailed procedures, and High risk requires reasonable detailed procedures.
en.D: (1) Qualitative materiality is ignored in Shari'ah audits; (2) sample sizes are reduced when breaches are discovered; (3) Low, Medium, and High residual risk areas require identical detailed testing.
en.True answer: (1) Materiality reflects quantitative or qualitative significance beyond the 'risk appetite' and 'tolerable limit' defined by TCWG and the SSB; (2) statistical approaches and judgment are used, and when instances of Shari'ah non-compliance are identified, sample sizes must be increased adequately; (3) detailed procedures depend on residual risk: Low risk requires no or minimum detailed procedures (as performing them may be counterproductive and inefficient), Medium risk requires minimum to reasonable detailed procedures, and High risk requires reasonable detailed procedures.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 45–47 & Par. 49(a)–(c) (Par. 45: materiality is quantitative or qualitative significance beyond the 'risk appetite' and 'tolerable limit' defined by TCWG and SSB; Par. 47: statistical techniques and judgment are used, and in case of identified instances of Shari'ah non-compliance, sample sizes shall be increased adequately; Par. 49: (a) low residual risk—normally no or minimum detailed procedures as counterproductive and inefficient; (b) medium risk—minimum to reasonable detailed procedures; (c) high risk—reasonable detailed procedures).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Which of the following accurately captures AAOIFI GS 11 requirements on IT auditing techniques, audit documentation, working paper review, and archiving (Paragraphs 48 and 50–54)?
en.A: IT general controls and CAATs are outside the scope of internal Shari'ah audit; working papers are reviewed by the CEO and may be freely altered after archiving.
en.B: Documentation is sufficient only if it records every single bank transaction in full; working papers require no supervisory review.
en.C: Internal Shari'ah auditors are prohibited from using audit software and must maintain handwritten ledgers exclusively.
en.D: Internal Shari'ah auditors may assess IT general controls relating to Shari'ah compliance (e.g., flags, authorizations, transaction computation controls) and use CAATs; documentation must be quantitatively sufficient and qualitatively appropriate for an experienced Shari'ah auditor (or experienced internal audit/assurance professional) to understand procedures, results, and conclusions; working papers must be reviewed by the Head of ISA (or designee); and a consistent policy must govern completion, archiving, and any post-archiving changes.
en.True answer: Internal Shari'ah auditors may assess IT general controls relating to Shari'ah compliance (e.g., flags, authorizations, transaction computation controls) and use CAATs; documentation must be quantitatively sufficient and qualitatively appropriate for an experienced Shari'ah auditor (or experienced internal audit/assurance professional) to understand procedures, results, and conclusions; working papers must be reviewed by the Head of ISA (or designee); and a consistent policy must govern completion, archiving, and any post-archiving changes.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 48(a)–(b), Par. 50–54 & Appendix C, BC18–BC19 (Par. 48 covers assessing IT general controls relating to Shari'ah compliance controls—flags, authorizations, transaction computations—and using CAATs; Par. 50 sets the documentation benchmark: sufficient quantitatively and appropriate qualitatively for an experienced Shari'ah auditor or experienced internal audit/assurance professional to understand procedures, results, and conclusions; Par. 51 requires working papers to be reviewed by HISA or his designee; Par. 53–54 require consistent completion/archiving/post-archiving change policy and openness to emerging audit software).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Comparing the required contents of a Periodic Internal Shari'ah Audit Report (Paragraph 59) versus an Engagement (Audit Entity) Report (Paragraph 61) under AAOIFI GS 11, which statement is accurate?
en.A: Both reports are addressed to TCWG (Audit Committee, or Board of Directors in its absence) and the SSB; the Periodic Report provides an opinion on the IFI's overall Shari'ah adherence, references completed engagements with their key observations/ratings, covers overall governance/control environment and Shari'ah non-compliance risks, and reports status against the periodic plan, whereas the Engagement Report describes the specific audit entity/period/procedures, expresses an opinion/rating on that entity, and summarizes key observations separately identifying follow-up issues from previous periods along with management's and SSB's comments.
en.B: Periodic reports are addressed solely to the CEO, while engagement reports are published publicly in national newspapers.
en.C: Engagement reports omit follow-up issues from previous periods and never include management's or SSB's comments.
en.D: Periodic reports omit any opinion on the IFI's overall adherence to Shari'ah principles and rules, leaving that exclusively to external auditors.
en.True answer: Both reports are addressed to TCWG (Audit Committee, or Board of Directors in its absence) and the SSB; the Periodic Report provides an opinion on the IFI's overall Shari'ah adherence, references completed engagements with their key observations/ratings, covers overall governance/control environment and Shari'ah non-compliance risks, and reports status against the periodic plan, whereas the Engagement Report describes the specific audit entity/period/procedures, expresses an opinion/rating on that entity, and summarizes key observations separately identifying follow-up issues from previous periods along with management's and SSB's comments.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Par. 59(a)–(g) & Par. 61(a)–(e) (Both list addressees as TCWG [audit committee, and in its absence the board of directors] and the SSB. Par. 59 Periodic Report includes: (c) overall scope; (d) opinion on overall state of adherence by the IFI; (e) reference to engagements completed since last periodic report + summary of key observations + ratings; (f) key matters/risks/findings on governance/control environment and Shari'ah non-compliance risks; (g) status of work performed against periodic plan and changes thereto. Par. 61 Engagement Report includes: (c) scope/description of audit entity/period/principal procedures; (d) opinion on audit entity adherence + rating; (e) summary of key observations separately identifying issues under follow up from previous periods along with management's and SSB's comments/opinions).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question: Under Appendix B (Specimen Fit and Proper Criteria) of AAOIFI GS 11, which comparison between the criteria for (1) Head of Internal Shari'ah Audit and (2) an outsourced Professional Shari'ah Audit Firm is accurate?
en.A: (1) Head of ISA must hold a Ph.D. in Islamic theology with zero audit experience; (2) any general IT software vendor qualifies as an outsourced Shari'ah audit firm.
en.B: (1) Head of ISA must hold a university degree or professional qualification (preferably in accountancy, audit, internal audit, and/or Shari'ah audit), be well-versed in Islamic finance operations and Paragraph 4(k) Shari'ah hierarchy, have preferably ≥10 years relevant experience (subject to regulatory relaxation in newer markets), and hold SSB and regulatory approvals; (2) an outsourced firm must be either a professional firm of accountants or a dedicated Shari'ah audit/advisory firm with regulatory approval, SSB approval on Shari'ah/Fiqh al-Muamalat capability and suitability to the IFI's operations, adequate qualitative and quantitative resources, and compliance with professional standards, QA, ethics, independence, and confidentiality.
en.C: (1) Head of ISA requires only Audit Committee approval without SSB approval; (2) outsourced firms are exempt from independence and confidentiality rules.
en.D: (1) Head of ISA must be an external consultant; (2) outsourced firms may only be law firms rather than professional firms of accountants.
en.True answer: (1) Head of ISA must hold a university degree or professional qualification (preferably in accountancy, audit, internal audit, and/or Shari'ah audit), be well-versed in Islamic finance operations and Paragraph 4(k) Shari'ah hierarchy, have preferably ≥10 years relevant experience (subject to regulatory relaxation in newer markets), and hold SSB and regulatory approvals; (2) an outsourced firm must be either a professional firm of accountants or a dedicated Shari'ah audit/advisory firm with regulatory approval, SSB approval on Shari'ah/Fiqh al-Muamalat capability and suitability to the IFI's operations, adequate qualitative and quantitative resources, and compliance with professional standards, QA, ethics, independence, and confidentiality.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11, Appendix B, Sections 1(a)–(e) & 2(a)–(d), Footnote 6 (Section 1 covers Head of ISA—whether full-time, assigned by an outsourced firm, or Head of IA acting as Head of ISA—requiring degree/qualification preferably in accountancy/audit/internal audit/Shari'ah audit, knowledge of Islamic finance & Par. 4(k) hierarchy/Fiqh al-Muamalat, preferably ≥10 yrs experience with regulatory relaxation in newer markets, SSB approval, and regulatory approvals. Section 2 requires an outsourced firm to be a professional firm of accountants or dedicated Shari'ah audit/advisory firm meeting regulatory approval, SSB approval, qualitative/quantitative capacity, and professional/QA/ethics/independence/confidentiality compliance).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question:
Evaluate the following four organizational arrangements regarding the Internal Shari'ah Audit (ISA) function under AAOIFI GS 11:
(1) A large, long-established Islamic bank in a mature market embeds its ISA function as a unit inside its conventional Internal Audit department, and the Head of Internal Audit (who also leads ISA) has not obtained SSB approval or Shari'ah qualifications.
(2) A small Islamic investment company outsources its ISA function to a qualified professional accounting firm; the partner assigned as Head of ISA currently serves as Head of ISA for two other Islamic banks plus four separate Islamic collective investment funds managed by one of those banks.
(3) Because the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD) is understaffed, the Audit Committee instructs internal Shari'ah auditors to temporarily draft SOPs and perform pre-approval compliance checks for new Murabaha transactions.
(4) The Head of ISA reports primarily to the Audit Committee with a dotted-line to the SSB, shares initial draft audit reports with the SSB for Shari'ah comments, and then submits the final report to both the SSB and the Audit Committee.
According to AAOIFI GS 11, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—any bank may merge ISA into Internal Audit; (2) Non-compliant—the partner is auditing 6 entities (>3 limit); (3) Compliant—temporary support to SCD is allowed; (4) Non-compliant—final reports go only to the Audit Committee.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant—outsourcing ISA is completely prohibited; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant—draft reports go to the CEO first.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant—ISA may be a unit within Internal Audit ONLY if all four cumulative conditions in Par. 22 are met (small size/new market, adequate IA capability, Head of IA or separate ISA head meeting Appendix B fit & proper criteria including SSB approval, and overall operational efficiency); (2) Compliant—under Par. 23(b), multiple collective investment schemes/funds managed by IFIs count as a SINGLE IFI, so the partner serves 2 banks + 1 fund group = 3 IFIs (within the ≤3 limit); (3) Non-compliant—Par. 16 strictly prohibits internal Shari'ah auditors from undertaking operational activities or management functions, including product development and Shari'ah compliance functions; (4) Compliant—follows Par. 24–26 reporting lines and draft-to-final workflow.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant—SSB must never see draft ISA reports.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—ISA may be a unit within Internal Audit ONLY if all four cumulative conditions in Par. 22 are met (small size/new market, adequate IA capability, Head of IA or separate ISA head meeting Appendix B fit & proper criteria including SSB approval, and overall operational efficiency); (2) Compliant—under Par. 23(b), multiple collective investment schemes/funds managed by IFIs count as a SINGLE IFI, so the partner serves 2 banks + 1 fund group = 3 IFIs (within the ≤3 limit); (3) Non-compliant—Par. 16 strictly prohibits internal Shari'ah auditors from undertaking operational activities or management functions, including product development and Shari'ah compliance functions; (4) Compliant—follows Par. 24–26 reporting lines and draft-to-final workflow.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 21–22 require a separate department by default, allowing a unit within Internal Audit ONLY when all four conditions in Par. 22(a)–(d) are met (violated here because the bank is large/mature and lacks Appendix B/SSB approval); (2) Par. 23(b) limits an outsourced Head of ISA to ≤3 IFIs, explicitly stipulating that 'multiple collective investment schemes / funds managed by IFIs... shall be considered a single IFI for the purpose of this requirement' (2 banks + 1 fund group = 3 IFIs, compliant); (3) Par. 16 prohibits internal Shari'ah auditors from performing any management function, including product development and Shari'ah compliance functions; (4) Par. 24–26 require primary reporting to the Audit Committee, dotted-line to SSB, draft report review by SSB, and final report issuance to both SSB and Audit Committee.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 11: Internal Shari'ah Audit
en.Question:
During the annual Internal Shari'ah Audit cycle of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank for the year ended 31 December 2025, examine four audit execution and reporting actions:
(1) In auditing the Treasury department, the ISA team assesses residual risk as High and discovers multiple Shari'ah non-compliance instances in commodity Tawarruq confirmations, yet performs minimal detailed procedures and keeps the original sample size unchanged.
(2) For the annual periodic ISA report covering FY2025, the Head of ISA submits the draft periodic report to the SSB on 15 February 2026; the SSB takes 6 weeks to return its final comments, and the Head of ISA submits the final periodic report to the Audit Committee and SSB on 20 April 2026.
(3) During the engagement audit of the Retail Financing branch, the ISA team holds a closing meeting with branch management to discuss major observations and document spot rectifications, issues a draft report for auditee reply, and upon issuing the final report sends unresolved observations to the SSB for corrective actions.
(4) To ensure rectification of the Retail Financing branch's findings, the ISA team and branch management mutually develop an action plan and agree on the follow-up plan with the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD), assigning implementation responsibility to the SCD.
According to AAOIFI GS 11, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—initial sample sizes never need expansion; (2) Compliant—6 months are allowed for periodic reports; (3) Non-compliant—unresolved observations must not go to the SSB; (4) Non-compliant—ISA itself must implement the follow-up plan.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant—SSB has 60 days to comment and ISA has 4 months to issue final report; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant—SCD has no role in follow-up plans.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 47 & 49(c), identified Shari'ah non-compliance instances require adequately increasing sample sizes, and High residual risk requires reasonable detailed procedures; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 55(a) & 56, the SSB must provide final comments on the draft periodic report within 1 month (not 6 weeks), and the final periodic report must be submitted within 3 months of period-end (by 31 March 2026, not 20 April 2026); (3) Compliant—follows Steps 10–12 of the engagement process flow (Par. 44); (4) Compliant—follows Par. 63, under which mutually developed action plans are agreed with the SCD, which is responsible for implementation.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 47 & 49(c), identified Shari'ah non-compliance instances require adequately increasing sample sizes, and High residual risk requires reasonable detailed procedures; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 55(a) & 56, the SSB must provide final comments on the draft periodic report within 1 month (not 6 weeks), and the final periodic report must be submitted within 3 months of period-end (by 31 March 2026, not 20 April 2026); (3) Compliant—follows Steps 10–12 of the engagement process flow (Par. 44); (4) Compliant—follows Par. 63, under which mutually developed action plans are agreed with the SCD, which is responsible for implementation.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 11 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 47 requires increasing sample sizes adequately when instances of Shari'ah non-compliance are identified, and Par. 49(c) requires reasonable detailed procedures when residual risk is High; (2) Par. 56 requires the SSB to provide final comments on the draft periodic report within 1 month of receipt, and Par. 55(a) mandates submitting periodic reports not later than 3 months from the end of the respective period (31 March 2026 for FY ended 31 December 2025); (3) Par. 44 Steps 10–12 require a closing meeting with auditee, draft report for auditee reply, and sending unresolved observations in the final report to the SSB for corrective actions; (4) Par. 63 requires mutually developing action plans with management and agreeing the follow-up plan with the SCD, who is responsible for implementation.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope, applicability to Sukuk programs, and primary responsibility for implementing AAOIFI GS 12 ('Sukuk Governance')?
en.A: GS 12 covers the entire Sukuk lifecycle (issuance, investment, maturity/termination, and restructuring/rescheduling), applies equally to instruments similar to Sukuk irrespective of nomenclature, requires each issuance or tranche in a Sukuk program to fulfill GS 12, and places responsibility for implementation on those charged with governance and management of the originator.
en.B: GS 12 applies solely to the initial issuance phase of sovereign Sukuk, allows a single program-level compliance check to exempt all subsequent tranches, and assigns primary implementation responsibility to the rating agency.
en.C: GS 12 applies only to instruments explicitly titled 'Sukuk' on public stock exchanges and places implementation responsibility exclusively on the Sukuk's Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSSB).
en.D: GS 12 governs secondary-market equity shares and delegates primary compliance responsibility to the external financial auditor.
en.True answer: GS 12 covers the entire Sukuk lifecycle (issuance, investment, maturity/termination, and restructuring/rescheduling), applies equally to instruments similar to Sukuk irrespective of nomenclature, requires each issuance or tranche in a Sukuk program to fulfill GS 12, and places responsibility for implementation on those charged with governance and management of the originator.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 3–6 & Appendix C, BC10–BC12 (Par. 3: governs overall lifecycle including issuance, investment, maturity/termination, and restructuring/rescheduling, and applies equally to instruments similar to Sukuk irrespective of nomenclature; Par. 4: responsibility for implementation rests with those charged with governance and management of the originator; Par. 6: in a Sukuk program comprising a series of issuances or multiple tranches, each issuance or tranche shall fulfill GS 12).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 7 of AAOIFI GS 12, how are a 'Provisional Fatwa' and a 'Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV)' defined in the context of a Sukuk issuance?
en.A: A Provisional Fatwa is a legally binding post-maturity audit opinion, while an SPV is merely a transparent pass-through accounting ledger with no separate legal personality.
en.B: A Provisional Fatwa is an initial Fatwa issued by the SSSB to approve the basic Sukuk structure to assist the documentation team in drafting documents (remaining valid until the Final Fatwa is issued, provided the structure is unchanged), while an SPV is a legal entity created to fulfill specific financial objectives that is NOT a pass-through entity, rather an entity in itself.
en.C: A Provisional Fatwa is issued by the originator's legal counsel before consulting the SSSB, while an SPV is a wholly owned operating subsidiary controlled directly by the originator's CEO.
en.D: A Provisional Fatwa permanently replaces the Final Fatwa for sovereign Sukuk, while an SPV is prohibited from holding legal title to tangible Sukuk assets.
en.True answer: A Provisional Fatwa is an initial Fatwa issued by the SSSB to approve the basic Sukuk structure to assist the documentation team in drafting documents (remaining valid until the Final Fatwa is issued, provided the structure is unchanged), while an SPV is a legal entity created to fulfill specific financial objectives that is NOT a pass-through entity, rather an entity in itself.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 7(c), Par. 7(i), Par. 7(n) & Appendix C, BC8–BC9 (Par. 7(i): Provisional Fatwa is an initial Fatwa issued by the SSSB to approve the basic structure of Sukuk to help the documentation team in drafting relevant documents, remaining valid until the final Fatwa is issued as long as the structure is unchanged; Par. 7(n): SPV/SPE is a legal entity created to fulfill specific financial objectives, and in the context of Sukuk, is NOT a pass-through entity and rather is an entity in itself).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 8 of AAOIFI GS 12, Sukuk governance rests on five key pillars—one specific to Islamic finance and four coinciding with principles recommended by the OECD. Which option correctly lists all five pillars?
en.A: Capital adequacy, liquidity coverage, credit enhancement, market listing, and tax neutrality.
en.B: Shari'ah compliance, profit maximization, regulatory immunity, confidentiality, and collateralization.
en.C: Shari'ah compliance (specific to Islamic finance) plus the four OECD-aligned pillars: accountability, fairness, transparency, and responsibility.
en.D: Independent rating, sovereign guarantee, pass-through accounting, external audit, and secondary-market liquidity.
en.True answer: Shari'ah compliance (specific to Islamic finance) plus the four OECD-aligned pillars: accountability, fairness, transparency, and responsibility.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 8(a)–(e) (Lists the five key pillars of Sukuk governance, noting that pillars (b) to (e) coincide with OECD principles: (a) Shari'ah compliance; (b) accountability; (c) fairness; (d) transparency; and (e) responsibility).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 10 and 16–17 of AAOIFI GS 12, which seven organs constitute the normal governance structure of a Sukuk issuance, and what due diligence must the originator perform before appointing a Trustee?
en.A: Only three organs exist (Originator, Central Bank, and Rating Agency), and trustee due diligence examines solely the trustee's marketing network.
en.B: Five organs exist (excluding external Shari'ah audit and internal audit), and trustee due diligence is waived whenever the trustee is a subsidiary of the originator.
en.C: Six organs exist (excluding the trustee), and trustee selection is decided exclusively by the external financial auditor.
en.D: The seven organs are (a) TCWG of the originator, (b) management, (c) the Sukuk Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSSB), (d) the trustee, (e) internal audit function, (f) external auditor, and (g) external Shari'ah auditor; before appointing a trustee, the originator must perform due diligence covering (a) demonstrable compliance with and understanding of Shari'ah principles and rules, (b) independence and objectivity, (c) creditworthiness, financial stability, and regulatory approvals, and (d) compliance with best practices.
en.True answer: The seven organs are (a) TCWG of the originator, (b) management, (c) the Sukuk Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSSB), (d) the trustee, (e) internal audit function, (f) external auditor, and (g) external Shari'ah auditor; before appointing a trustee, the originator must perform due diligence covering (a) demonstrable compliance with and understanding of Shari'ah principles and rules, (b) independence and objectivity, (c) creditworthiness, financial stability, and regulatory approvals, and (d) compliance with best practices.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 10(a)–(g) & Par. 16–17(a)–(d) (Par. 10 lists the 7 organs of governance for a normal Sukuk issuance; Par. 17 mandates pre-appointment due diligence of the trustee covering (a) demonstrable compliance/understanding of Shari'ah principles and rules, (b) independence and objectivity, (c) creditworthiness, financial stability, and regulatory approvals, and (d) compliance with best practices).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Which of the following accurately reflects AAOIFI GS 12 rules on appointing a Sukuk Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSSB), utilizing an originator's existing SSB or a Shari'ah advisory firm, and proclaiming Shari'ah compliance?
en.A: If the originator already has an SSB meeting GS 12 requirements, it may also be appointed as the SSSB (with regulatory approval); Shari'ah advisory firms are not barred from acting as SSSB provided they have at least three Shari'ah board members and fulfill GS 12 requirements; and the authority to proclaim Shari'ah compliance of a Sukuk issuance rests solely with the SSSB and/or the Central Shari'ah Board of the jurisdiction.
en.B: An originator's internal SSB is strictly prohibited from ever serving as the SSSB for that originator's Sukuk issuances.
en.C: Shari'ah advisory firms are completely barred from acting as SSSB, and the lead investment bank arranger holds joint authority to proclaim Shari'ah compliance.
en.D: An SSSB requires at least 9 Shari'ah scholars in all jurisdictions without any regulatory flexibility.
en.True answer: If the originator already has an SSB meeting GS 12 requirements, it may also be appointed as the SSSB (with regulatory approval); Shari'ah advisory firms are not barred from acting as SSSB provided they have at least three Shari'ah board members and fulfill GS 12 requirements; and the authority to proclaim Shari'ah compliance of a Sukuk issuance rests solely with the SSSB and/or the Central Shari'ah Board of the jurisdiction.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 19, Par. 22–23, Par. 33 & Appendix C, BC13 (Par. 19: originator's existing SSB meeting GS 12 requirements may additionally be appointed as SSSB with necessary regulatory approvals; Par. 22–23: normally constituted per GS 1 with regulatory flexibility on member count/eligibility; BC13: GS 12 does not bar Shari'ah advisory firms from acting as SSSB as long as they have at least three Shari'ah board members and fulfill GS 12 requirements; Par. 33: authority of proclaiming Shari'ah compliance rests solely with the SSSB and/or the central Shari'ah board).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 36 of AAOIFI GS 12, which condition must be satisfied regarding the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) used in a Sukuk structure?
en.A: The originator must hold at least 51% of the voting shares of the SPV to guarantee operational oversight and provide unconditional loss compensation to the SPV.
en.B: Sukuk assets must be transferred to the SPV absolutely (creating a legal impediment against the originator and its creditors even in originator bankruptcy), all rights and obligations must be legally and beneficially transferred, the originator must have neither effective control over SPV management nor any direct or indirect equity stake in the SPV, and the SPV must have no recourse to the originator for asset losses unless via a Shari'ah-compliant credit enhancement duly approved by the SSSB.
en.C: The SPV formation documents are approved solely by the originator's external tax counsel without SSSB review.
en.D: If the originator acts as asset management agent for the SPV, operational control of the Sukuk assets permanently transfers from the SPV and trustee back to the originator.
en.True answer: Sukuk assets must be transferred to the SPV absolutely (creating a legal impediment against the originator and its creditors even in originator bankruptcy), all rights and obligations must be legally and beneficially transferred, the originator must have neither effective control over SPV management nor any direct or indirect equity stake in the SPV, and the SPV must have no recourse to the originator for asset losses unless via a Shari'ah-compliant credit enhancement duly approved by the SSSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 36(a)–(f) & Appendix C, BC15 (Par. 36 requires: (a) absolute transfer creating legal impediment for originator or its creditors even in bankruptcy; (b) legal and beneficial transfer of all rights and obligations; (c) originator has neither effective control on SPV management nor direct or indirect equity stake in SPV; (d) no recourse to originator for losses generated from Sukuk assets unless there is a Shari'ah-compliant credit enhancement arrangement duly approved by SSSB; (e) SPV formation process and documentation approved by SSSB; (f) if originator acts as asset management agent, arm's length relationship and control of Sukuk assets always rests with SPV exercised by trustee).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Which of the following accurately reflects AAOIFI GS 12 requirements regarding Sukuk trading (including OTC trading), underwriter mandate letters, and agency relationships (Paragraphs 37–43)?
en.A: Unlisted Sukuk traded over-the-counter (OTC) are exempt from Shari'ah tradability rules, and underwriters' mandate letters are reviewed solely by commercial investment bankers.
en.B: Once an originator is appointed as an asset management or maintenance agent, the principal (Sukuk-holders/trustee) permanently waives the right to remove or replace the agent.
en.C: Shari'ah compliance applies to both listed and unlisted/OTC Sukuk trading (including communicating tradability, valuation restrictions, and any temporary bar on trade before back-end execution); all mandate letters for underwriters and arrangers must be reviewed by the SSSB; and in agency relationships, the principal retains at all times the right of removal or replacement of an agent in line with Shari'ah principles and rules.
en.D: Originators may freely issue unconditional principal guarantees to underwriters without SSSB review.
en.True answer: Shari'ah compliance applies to both listed and unlisted/OTC Sukuk trading (including communicating tradability, valuation restrictions, and any temporary bar on trade before back-end execution); all mandate letters for underwriters and arrangers must be reviewed by the SSSB; and in agency relationships, the principal retains at all times the right of removal or replacement of an agent in line with Shari'ah principles and rules.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 37–43 (Par. 37–39: Shari'ah compliance applies to listed and unlisted/OTC trading, requiring communication of tradability, valuation restrictions, and temporary bars on trade e.g. till back-end transaction is executed; Par. 40–41: underwriter appointments and any guarantees/undertakings must be Shari'ah compliant, and ALL mandate letters for all parties including underwriters, arrangers, etc. shall be reviewed by the SSSB; Par. 42: in agency relationships, the principal retains, at all times, the right of removal or replacement of an agent in line with Shari'ah principles and rules).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 46 of AAOIFI GS 12, which rule governs the valuation, registration, relocation, and damage reporting of Sukuk assets during the continuity of a Sukuk issuance?
en.A: Sukuk assets may be transferred to the SPV at any arbitrary book discount agreed by management and registered solely in the originator's corporate name.
en.B: The originator may relocate Sukuk assets across jurisdictions at will without notifying Sukuk-holders as long as insurance is maintained.
en.C: Material damage to Sukuk assets need only be disclosed in the final liquidation report at maturity.
en.D: Sukuk assets must be transferred at fair market value (or reasonably close thereto, never at an inappropriate or exploitative value), registered in the name of the SPV identifying Sukuk-holders as their owners, relocated ONLY with proper justification and pre-approval of Sukuk-holders or their representatives (without jeopardizing their interests), and any damage or material changes (especially affecting tradability) must be immediately reported to Sukuk-holders and relevant stakeholders.
en.True answer: Sukuk assets must be transferred at fair market value (or reasonably close thereto, never at an inappropriate or exploitative value), registered in the name of the SPV identifying Sukuk-holders as their owners, relocated ONLY with proper justification and pre-approval of Sukuk-holders or their representatives (without jeopardizing their interests), and any damage or material changes (especially affecting tradability) must be immediately reported to Sukuk-holders and relevant stakeholders.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 46(a)–(i) (Par. 46(d): transferred at fair market value or reasonably close thereto, never inappropriate/exploitative; Par. 46(f): not relocated without proper justification, must not jeopardize Sukuk-holders' interests, and requires pre-approval of Sukuk-holders or their representatives; Par. 46(g): registered in name of SPV identifying Sukuk-holders as owners; Par. 46(i): any damage or material changes, particularly affecting tradability conditions, immediately reported to Sukuk-holders and relevant stakeholders).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 55–63 of AAOIFI GS 12, what are the SSSB's powers regarding impermissible income, escalation of unresolved non-compliance, periodic reporting, and approval of changes in SSSB membership?
en.A: The SSSB approves impermissible amounts payable to charity and their disposal; may escalate unresolved non-compliance to regulators and/or Sukuk-holders; issues an annual (or more frequent) report addressed to TCWG of the originator and made available to Sukuk-holders and regulators; and any change in SSSB membership requires approval of (a) the trustee, (b) the Sukuk-holders or their representatives, and (c) the regulator.
en.B: The originator's CEO independently decides charity disbursements, SSSB reports are confidential to management, and the originator may replace SSSB members unilaterally.
en.C: SSSB reports are issued once every three years solely to the external auditor, and changes in SSSB require only the rating agency's consent.
en.D: Impermissible income is retained by the originator as a management performance fee, and SSSB escalation to regulators is strictly prohibited.
en.True answer: The SSSB approves impermissible amounts payable to charity and their disposal; may escalate unresolved non-compliance to regulators and/or Sukuk-holders; issues an annual (or more frequent) report addressed to TCWG of the originator and made available to Sukuk-holders and regulators; and any change in SSSB membership requires approval of (a) the trustee, (b) the Sukuk-holders or their representatives, and (c) the regulator.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 55–63 (Par. 55: SSSB approves impermissible amounts payable to charity and disposal of charity funds; Par. 56: escalation protocol allowing SSSB to inform regulators and/or Sukuk-holders upon non-compliance and refusal to remediate; Par. 57, 59–60: SSSB report issued at least annually, addressed to TCWG of originator, and made available to Sukuk-holders, owners, regulator, and CSB; Par. 63: changes in SSSB subject to approval of (a) trustee, (b) Sukuk-holders or their representatives, and (c) regulator).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 67–74 of AAOIFI GS 12, which two scenarios give rise to restructuring or rescheduling of Sukuk before intended maturity, and who must thoroughly review and approve any restructuring proposition?
en.A: Restructuring occurs whenever market interest rates drop by 1%, and requires approval solely from the originator's Board of Directors.
en.B: Restructuring or rescheduling may occur due to (a) the originator's default or potential default, or (b) acquisition, merger, or corporate restructuring of the originator; any restructuring proposition must be thoroughly reviewed and approved by the SSSB, representatives of Sukuk-holders, and the regulator.
en.C: Restructuring is initiated primarily whenever the originator claims the original Sukuk structure had Shari'ah compliance issues, and requires approval solely from the trustee.
en.D: Restructuring is strictly prohibited under AAOIFI GS 12; any distressed Sukuk must be liquidated immediately without rescheduling.
en.True answer: Restructuring or rescheduling may occur due to (a) the originator's default or potential default, or (b) acquisition, merger, or corporate restructuring of the originator; any restructuring proposition must be thoroughly reviewed and approved by the SSSB, representatives of Sukuk-holders, and the regulator.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 69–74 (Par. 69: restructuring or rescheduling may occur in two scenarios: (a) originator's default or potential default, or (b) acquisition, merger, or corporate restructuring of the originator; Par. 72: any restructuring or rescheduling proposition shall be thoroughly reviewed and approved by the SSSB, representatives of Sukuk-holders, and the regulator; Par. 74: no restructuring may be initiated merely on the premise that the original structure has Shari'ah compliance issues unless Change in Fatwa requirements in Par. 64–66 are first fulfilled).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 83–89 of AAOIFI GS 12, what rules govern the External Shari'ah Audit of a Sukuk issuance and the Annual Review Meeting of Sukuk-holders?
en.A: External Shari'ah audit is conducted once every five years, and the draft audit report is finalized by the originator's CFO without consulting the SSSB.
en.B: Annual review meetings of Sukuk-holders are prohibited for corporate Sukuk, and external Shari'ah audit reports are confidential to the originator's management.
en.C: An external Shari'ah audit must be performed at least annually by an auditor appointed by the originator in consultation with the trustee, SSSB, and (if applicable) Sukuk-holders' representatives; the draft report must first be submitted to and finalized in consultation with the SSSB; and the originator must assemble an annual review meeting of Sukuk-holders or their representatives (in person or via webcast) to review periodic financial reporting/auditors' report, the SSSB report, and the external Shari'ah auditor report.
en.D: The originator's financial statement auditor is strictly barred from ever conducting the external Shari'ah audit of the Sukuk issuance.
en.True answer: An external Shari'ah audit must be performed at least annually by an auditor appointed by the originator in consultation with the trustee, SSSB, and (if applicable) Sukuk-holders' representatives; the draft report must first be submitted to and finalized in consultation with the SSSB; and the originator must assemble an annual review meeting of Sukuk-holders or their representatives (in person or via webcast) to review periodic financial reporting/auditors' report, the SSSB report, and the external Shari'ah auditor report.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 83–89 & Par. 101 (Par. 83: external Shari'ah audit at least annually; Par. 84 & 101: appointed by originator in consultation with trustee, SSSB, and Sukuk-holders' representatives, and originator's financial statement auditors are eligible if qualified unless disallowed by regulator; Par. 87: draft report first submitted to SSSB and finalized after due consultation with SSSB; Par. 88–89: annual review meeting of Sukuk-holders or representatives in person or via webcast to review financial reporting/auditors' report, SSSB report, external Shari'ah auditor report, and updates).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 90–93 and 102–103 of AAOIFI GS 12, which AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards govern reporting by the originator and reporting to Sukuk-holders, and what transitional exemption applies at initial implementation?
en.A: IFRS 9 and IFRS 17 govern Sukuk reporting, and GS 12 became mandatory retroactively for all historical Sukuk issued since 2010.
en.B: AAOIFI FAS 1 and FAS 2 govern Sukuk reporting, and transitional exemptions apply only to sovereign Sukuk with maturities exceeding 10 years.
en.C: Accounting policies for Sukuk reporting are approved solely by the external financial auditor without SSSB review, and no transitional provisions exist.
en.D: Financial reporting by the originator follows AAOIFI FAS 29 and financial reporting to Sukuk-holders follows AAOIFI FAS 34 (with accounting policies in both cases subject to SSSB approval); GS 12 is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 July 2021, and originators may elect not to apply GS 12 to already-completed lifecycle phases (if no other non-compliance results) or to Sukuk issuances whose remaining time to maturity is less than 24 months from the effective date.
en.True answer: Financial reporting by the originator follows AAOIFI FAS 29 and financial reporting to Sukuk-holders follows AAOIFI FAS 34 (with accounting policies in both cases subject to SSSB approval); GS 12 is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 July 2021, and originators may elect not to apply GS 12 to already-completed lifecycle phases (if no other non-compliance results) or to Sukuk issuances whose remaining time to maturity is less than 24 months from the effective date.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 90–93 & Par. 102–103 (Par. 90–91: originator financial reporting in line with FAS 29, accounting policies approved by SSSB; Par. 92–93: financial reporting to Sukuk-holders in line with FAS 34, accounting policies approved by SSSB; Par. 102: effective for financial periods beginning on or after 01 July 2021; Par. 103: transitional exemption for (a) lifecycle phases already completed, provided no non-compliance with another provision results, and (b) Sukuk issuances with remaining time to maturity less than 24 months from the effective date).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 27–32 and Appendix C (BC14) of AAOIFI GS 12, which set of rules governs the preparation, content, language review disclosure, and public availability of the Sukuk Fatwa document?
en.A: The Final Fatwa is issued after reviewing the final rating certificates and final legal documents; contracts must state that terms are interpreted in light of the Fatwa; the Fatwa is a mandatory part of the prospectus (though SSSB remuneration is NOT disclosed in the prospectus); any dissenting opinions/reservations with reasons, names, and signatures must be included; and if contracts were reviewed in translation or if not every SSSB member reviewed the entire documentation in detail, those facts (and the names of members who performed detailed review) must be stated in the Fatwa.
en.B: The Final Fatwa is issued prior to drafting any legal contracts, dissenting opinions of SSSB scholars are omitted to present unanimity, and SSSB members' exact fee schedules must be published inside the Fatwa.
en.C: SSSB members may review English summaries of Arabic contracts without disclosing that a translation was used, and the Fatwa is kept confidential from Sukuk-holders.
en.D: Only the SSSB Chairman signs the Fatwa, and partial document review by a single scholar requires no disclosure in the Fatwa.
en.True answer: The Final Fatwa is issued after reviewing the final rating certificates and final legal documents; contracts must state that terms are interpreted in light of the Fatwa; the Fatwa is a mandatory part of the prospectus (though SSSB remuneration is NOT disclosed in the prospectus); any dissenting opinions/reservations with reasons, names, and signatures must be included; and if contracts were reviewed in translation or if not every SSSB member reviewed the entire documentation in detail, those facts (and the names of members who performed detailed review) must be stated in the Fatwa.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 28–32 & Appendix C, BC14 (Par. 28: Fatwa is part of legal documentation and contracts state terms are interpreted/construed in light of the Fatwa; Par. 29: mandatory part of prospectus, though BC14 states SSSB remuneration is NOT disclosed in the prospectus; Par. 30: Final Fatwa issued after reviewing final rating certificates and legal documents; Par. 31(g)–(h): includes reservations/dissenting opinions with reasons, name, and signature, plus signatures of all consenting members; Par. 32(a)–(b): states if translated version was reviewed and states if entire documentation was not reviewed in detail by each member along with names of members who performed detailed review).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 64–66 and 74 of AAOIFI GS 12, under what grounds may an SSSB change a previously issued Fatwa, what standard governs that process, and how does a Fatwa change interact with Sukuk restructuring?
en.A: An SSSB may never change an issued Fatwa under any circumstances, even if an error is discovered or AAOIFI Shari'ah standards are amended.
en.B: The SSSB may change its Fatwa upon becoming aware of previously unknown facts/circumstances, significant changes in business/operations, changes in Sukuk terms/documentation, changes in relevance of applied Shari'ah principles/rules (e.g., amendments in AAOIFI standards, regulations, or CSB rulings), or an earlier error in the Fatwa; it must follow AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 29 and consider stakeholder justice/equity; and no restructuring may be initiated merely on the premise of original Shari'ah compliance issues until Change in Fatwa requirements are complied with.
en.C: An SSSB may change its Fatwa whenever the originator requests lower profit distributions, without following Shari'ah Standard No. 29 or considering stakeholder equity.
