en.D: An originator may unilaterally declare its own Sukuk structure non-compliant to force a restructuring without obtaining a changed Fatwa from the SSSB.
en.True answer: The SSSB may change its Fatwa upon becoming aware of previously unknown facts/circumstances, significant changes in business/operations, changes in Sukuk terms/documentation, changes in relevance of applied Shari'ah principles/rules (e.g., amendments in AAOIFI standards, regulations, or CSB rulings), or an earlier error in the Fatwa; it must follow AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 29 and consider stakeholder justice/equity; and no restructuring may be initiated merely on the premise of original Shari'ah compliance issues until Change in Fatwa requirements are complied with.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 64(a)–(e), Par. 65–66 & Par. 74 (Par. 64 lists five grounds for changing a Fatwa: (a) newly discovered pre-existing facts/circumstances, (b) significant changes in business/operations of originator or Sukuk assets, (c) changes in terms/conditions of structure/documentation, (d) changes in relevance of earlier applied Shari'ah principles/rules e.g. amendments in AAOIFI standards/regulations/CSB rulings, (e) earlier error in the Fatwa; Par. 65 requires following AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 29; Par. 66 requires considering stakeholder impact based on justice and equity, especially for (c) and (d); Par. 74 prohibits initiating restructuring merely on the premise of original Shari'ah compliance issues unless Change in Fatwa requirements in Par. 64–66 are complied with).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: An originator prepares a cross-border Sukuk issuance in a secular legal jurisdiction where local commercial courts might not recognize Shari'ah principles and rules when interpreting contractual agreements. Additionally, the originator obtains only a conventional credit rating for the Sukuk instrument. According to Paragraphs 80–82 of AAOIFI GS 12, what is required?
en.A: The legal risk regarding secular courts should be omitted from the prospectus so investors are not alarmed, and a conventional credit rating is fully sufficient without any fiduciary rating.
en.B: Cross-border Sukuk cannot be issued in secular jurisdictions under any circumstances, and credit ratings are prohibited for Sukuk.
en.C: The prospectus must disclose the risk that courts of law in the jurisdiction may not accept Shari'ah principles and rules for interpreting contractual agreements, together with a summary of remedial options (such as Shari'ah-based arbitration before referring to courts of law), and GS 12 further recommends publishing Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings (for both the originator and the instrument) because a normal credit rating alone is generally insufficient to capture non-credit Shari'ah and fiduciary considerations.
en.D: The prospectus must state that secular court judgments automatically override the SSSB's Fatwa, and fiduciary ratings apply only to the SPV.
en.True answer: The prospectus must disclose the risk that courts of law in the jurisdiction may not accept Shari'ah principles and rules for interpreting contractual agreements, together with a summary of remedial options (such as Shari'ah-based arbitration before referring to courts of law), and GS 12 further recommends publishing Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings (for both the originator and the instrument) because a normal credit rating alone is generally insufficient to capture non-credit Shari'ah and fiduciary considerations.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 80(f) & Par. 81–82 (Par. 80(f): in case there is a risk that the courts of law of the relevant jurisdiction may not accept Shari'ah principles and rules for interpreting contractual agreements, such risk shall be disclosed in the prospectus along with a summary of remedial options e.g. Shari'ah-based arbitration before referring to courts of law; Par. 81–82: recommends published ratings for Sukuk and originators, and further recommends publishing Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings for both originator and instrument because normal credit ratings might not be sufficient to account for non-credit considerations).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: A large non-financial corporate entity issues Sukuk frequently to fund infrastructure projects. Under Paragraphs 50–52 and Appendix C (BC18–BC20) of AAOIFI GS 12, how must idle Sukuk proceeds be parked prior to deployment, and what internal audit governance practice is recommended for frequent non-IFI Sukuk originators?
en.A: Idle proceeds may be parked in conventional interest-bearing treasury bills as long as the interest is donated to charity, and non-IFI corporates are exempt from internal audit oversight of Sukuk.
en.B: Idle proceeds must be held exclusively in non-interest cash vaults at the central bank, and internal audit of Sukuk may only be performed by the rating agency.
en.C: The originator may invest idle proceeds in any high-yield corporate bonds without SSSB approval, and internal Shari'ah audit is strictly restricted to licensed Islamic banks.
en.D: Idle Sukuk proceeds must be parked in safe and sound Shari'ah-compliant deposits/institutions approved by the SSSB with acceptable credit ratings (if applicable) during and before deployment, and GS 12 recommends that frequent Sukuk originators (even non-IFIs such as corporations and governments) establish an internal Shari'ah audit function to verify compliance with GS 12, contractual terms, financial reporting accuracy, regulations, and Shari'ah principles.
en.True answer: Idle Sukuk proceeds must be parked in safe and sound Shari'ah-compliant deposits/institutions approved by the SSSB with acceptable credit ratings (if applicable) during and before deployment, and GS 12 recommends that frequent Sukuk originators (even non-IFIs such as corporations and governments) establish an internal Shari'ah audit function to verify compliance with GS 12, contractual terms, financial reporting accuracy, regulations, and Shari'ah principles.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 50(e), Par. 51–52 & Appendix C, BC18–BC20 (Par. 50(e) requires ensuring Sukuk proceeds are parked in safe and sound Shari'ah-compliant deposits/institutions, as may be approved by the SSSB, having acceptable credit rating(s), if applicable, during and before deployment in Sukuk assets; Par. 51–52 & BC19 state internal audit must review compliance with GS 12, contracts, financial reporting, regulations, and Shari'ah, and explicitly recommend that frequent Sukuk originators—even non-IFIs like governments and corporates—establish an internal Shari'ah audit function).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: When a Sukuk issuance undergoes early termination or liquidation (Paragraphs 67–68, 75–77, and 94 of AAOIFI GS 12), which core governance principles apply and what must be included in the Termination Report submitted to stakeholders?
en.A: The SSSB must specifically approve the modus operandi and causes of termination/early redemption as Shari'ah compliant, termination must not cause unjustifiable material loss to Sukuk-holders, and the originator must submit a Termination Report including: final financial reporting to Sukuk-holders with balance/return computations and auditors' report, final SSSB report, final external Shari'ah audit report, reasons/timeframe/method of returning funds, details of any claims/pending lawsuits/penalties impacting settlement value, and IFSB Standard No. 19 disclosures.
en.B: Early termination requires no SSSB approval if exercised via a contractual call option, and the Termination Report omits pending lawsuits or penalties until after settlement distributions are completed.
en.C: Only the trustee receives a brief cash-settlement receipt, while final SSSB and external Shari'ah audit reports are waived upon early termination.
en.D: The originator may terminate Sukuk unilaterally at a 20% discount to asset value without consulting stakeholders or disclosing the method of returning investment funds.
en.True answer: The SSSB must specifically approve the modus operandi and causes of termination/early redemption as Shari'ah compliant, termination must not cause unjustifiable material loss to Sukuk-holders, and the originator must submit a Termination Report including: final financial reporting to Sukuk-holders with balance/return computations and auditors' report, final SSSB report, final external Shari'ah audit report, reasons/timeframe/method of returning funds, details of any claims/pending lawsuits/penalties impacting settlement value, and IFSB Standard No. 19 disclosures.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 68(a)–(c), Par. 76–77 & Par. 94(a)–(f) (Par. 68: SSSB specifically approves modus operandi and causes of termination/early redemption; termination occurs after due deliberations/communication and approval as necessary; shall not result in unjustifiable material loss to Sukuk-holders; Par. 77: SSSB issues final SSSB report considering final financial reporting and auditors'/external Shari'ah auditors' reports; Par. 94(a)–(f): Termination report includes final financial reporting + auditors' report, final SSSB report, final external Shari'ah audit report, details/reasons/timeframe/method of returning investment and profit, claims/pending lawsuits/penalties adversely impacting settlement value, and IFSB Standard No. 19 disclosures).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question: Regarding external audits of Sukuk-related financial statements (Paragraphs 95–101 of AAOIFI GS 12), which statement accurately describes (1) the external audit of financial reporting to Sukuk-holders and (2) special audit considerations for the originator's own financial statements?
en.A: (1) Financial reporting to Sukuk-holders requires an external audit only at maturity; (2) during the audit of the originator's financial statements, Sukuk disclosures are evaluated solely on quantitative revenue thresholds, and the Sukuk's external financial auditor can never conduct the external Shari'ah audit.
en.B: (1) Financial reporting to Sukuk-holders must undergo external audit at least annually by an auditor appointed by the originator in consultation with the trustee and (if applicable) Sukuk-holders' representatives (with the originator's financial statement auditor eligible unless disallowed by regulators); (2) when auditing the originator's own financial statements, the auditor must consider the qualitative significance of Sukuk instruments and disclosures when determining planning materiality, and—subject to meeting external Shari'ah auditor criteria—the external auditors of the Sukuk issuance may also conduct the external Shari'ah audit.
en.C: (1) The SSSB conducts the financial statement audit of the SPV; (2) planning materiality for the originator's audit excludes all off-balance-sheet Sukuk structures.
en.D: (1) External audit of Sukuk financial reporting is optional for corporate originators; (2) dual appointment as both Sukuk financial auditor and external Shari'ah auditor is strictly prohibited in all jurisdictions.
en.True answer: (1) Financial reporting to Sukuk-holders must undergo external audit at least annually by an auditor appointed by the originator in consultation with the trustee and (if applicable) Sukuk-holders' representatives (with the originator's financial statement auditor eligible unless disallowed by regulators); (2) when auditing the originator's own financial statements, the auditor must consider the qualitative significance of Sukuk instruments and disclosures when determining planning materiality, and—subject to meeting external Shari'ah auditor criteria—the external auditors of the Sukuk issuance may also conduct the external Shari'ah audit.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12, Par. 95–101 (Par. 95–96: external audit of financial reporting to Sukuk-holders at least annually, appointed by originator in consultation with trustee and Sukuk-holders' representatives; originator's financial statement auditors eligible unless disallowed by regulator; Par. 99–100: auditors of originator's financial statements must consider qualitative significance of Sukuk instruments and relevant reporting when determining planning materiality; Par. 101: subject to fulfilling criteria for appointment as external Shari'ah auditors, external auditors of the Sukuk issuance may also conduct external Shari'ah audit).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question:
In August 2022, a corporate originator launches a 5-year multi-tranche Sukuk program and makes four pre-issuance governance decisions:
(1) Management applies GS 12 governance requirements only to Tranche 1 and exempts Tranches 2 and 3, arguing that a single program-level approval covers all tranches.
(2) The originator establishes an SPV in which the originator holds a 10% direct equity stake and grants the SPV unconditional recourse against the originator for any commercial losses on the Sukuk assets without any SSSB-approved Shari'ah credit enhancement.
(3) The SSSB issues its Final Fatwa before final rating certificates and final legal documents are completed; furthermore, only two of the three SSSB members reviewed the legal contracts in detail, and the Fatwa omits stating which members performed the detailed review.
(4) The prospectus discloses the qualifications, experience, responsibilities, and powers of the SSSB members, but omits the individual remuneration figures paid to the SSSB members.
According to AAOIFI GS 12, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—program-level compliance covers all tranches; (2) Compliant—up to 20% SPV equity is permitted; (3) Compliant—Final Fatwa may precede final rating certificates; (4) Non-compliant—SSSB fees must be published in the prospectus.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant—partial document review by 2 scholars requires no disclosure; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant—Par. 6 mandates that each issuance or tranche in a Sukuk program must fulfill GS 12 requirements (and the transitional exemption in Par. 103(b) applies only if remaining maturity is <24 months from 1 July 2021); (2) Non-compliant—Par. 36(c) prohibits the originator from maintaining any direct or indirect equity stake in the SPV, and Par. 36(d) bars SPV recourse to the originator for asset losses absent a Shari'ah-compliant credit enhancement duly approved by the SSSB; (3) Non-compliant—Par. 30 requires issuing the Final Fatwa AFTER reviewing final rating certificates and legal documents, and Par. 32(b) mandates stating in the Fatwa if each member did not review the entire documentation in detail along with the names of members who performed such detailed review; (4) Compliant—Par. 80(a) requires SSSB qualifications/experience/responsibilities/powers in the prospectus, while Appendix C (BC14) explicitly concludes that SSSB remuneration should NOT be disclosed in the Sukuk prospectus.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—Par. 6 mandates that each issuance or tranche in a Sukuk program must fulfill GS 12 requirements (and the transitional exemption in Par. 103(b) applies only if remaining maturity is <24 months from 1 July 2021); (2) Non-compliant—Par. 36(c) prohibits the originator from maintaining any direct or indirect equity stake in the SPV, and Par. 36(d) bars SPV recourse to the originator for asset losses absent a Shari'ah-compliant credit enhancement duly approved by the SSSB; (3) Non-compliant—Par. 30 requires issuing the Final Fatwa AFTER reviewing final rating certificates and legal documents, and Par. 32(b) mandates stating in the Fatwa if each member did not review the entire documentation in detail along with the names of members who performed such detailed review; (4) Compliant—Par. 80(a) requires SSSB qualifications/experience/responsibilities/powers in the prospectus, while Appendix C (BC14) explicitly concludes that SSSB remuneration should NOT be disclosed in the Sukuk prospectus.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 6 requires each issuance or tranche in a Sukuk program to fulfill GS 12 (and Par. 103(b) transitional exemption applies only if remaining maturity is <24 months from the 1 July 2021 effective date); (2) Par. 36(c) prohibits any direct or indirect equity stake in the SPV by the originator, and Par. 36(d) prohibits recourse to the originator for losses generated from Sukuk assets unless via a Shari'ah-compliant credit enhancement duly approved by SSSB; (3) Par. 30 mandates issuing the Final Fatwa AFTER reviewing final rating certificates and legal documents, and Par. 32(b) mandates stating in the Fatwa if the entire documentation was not reviewed in detail by each SSSB member along with the names of members who performed detailed review; (4) Par. 80(a) covers SSSB qualifications/powers in the prospectus, and Appendix C, BC14 confirms SSSB remuneration should NOT be disclosed in the Sukuk prospectus.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 12: Sukuk Governance
en.Question:
During Year 2 of a 7-year Ijarah Sukuk issuance, four events occur:
(1) The originator relocates key underlying Sukuk industrial equipment to a neighboring country after obtaining the SSSB's consent, without seeking pre-approval from the Sukuk-holders or their representatives.
(2) Following the resignation of one SSSB member, the originator appoints a replacement scholar with formal approvals from the Trustee and the Regulator, without obtaining approval from the Sukuk-holders or their representatives.
(3) Experiencing cash-flow strain, the originator initiates a Sukuk restructuring solely on the claim that the original Sukuk structure has Shari'ah compliance issues—without any Change in Fatwa procedure—and submits the restructuring proposal exclusively to the SSSB.
(4) For the annual external Shari'ah audit, the originator appoints its own financial statement auditor (who meets all regulatory and external Shari'ah auditor criteria) in consultation with the trustee, SSSB, and Sukuk-holders' representatives, and the auditor submits the draft report first to the SSSB before finalizing it.
According to AAOIFI GS 12, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—SSSB consent suffices for relocating assets; (2) Compliant—trustee and regulator approvals suffice; (3) Compliant—alleged Shari'ah flaws allow immediate restructuring; (4) Non-compliant—financial statement auditors cannot conduct external Shari'ah audits.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant—draft reports go to the CEO first.
en.C: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 46(f), Sukuk assets shall not be relocated without proper justification, must not jeopardize Sukuk-holders' interests, and may be relocated ONLY with the pre-approval of the Sukuk-holders or their representatives; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 63, changes in the SSSB require approval of ALL three: (a) the trustee, (b) the Sukuk-holders or their representatives, AND (c) the regulator; (3) Non-compliant—Par. 74 prohibits initiating restructuring merely on the premise of original Shari'ah compliance issues unless Change in Fatwa requirements (Par. 64–66) are first complied with, and Par. 72 requires restructuring propositions to be reviewed and approved by the SSSB, representatives of Sukuk-holders, AND the regulator; (4) Compliant—Par. 84 & 101 permit the originator's financial statement auditor to serve as external Shari'ah auditor if qualified and appointed in consultation with trustee, SSSB, and Sukuk-holders' representatives, and Par. 87 mandates submitting the draft report first to the SSSB and finalizing after due consultation with the SSSB.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 46(f), Sukuk assets shall not be relocated without proper justification, must not jeopardize Sukuk-holders' interests, and may be relocated ONLY with the pre-approval of the Sukuk-holders or their representatives; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 63, changes in the SSSB require approval of ALL three: (a) the trustee, (b) the Sukuk-holders or their representatives, AND (c) the regulator; (3) Non-compliant—Par. 74 prohibits initiating restructuring merely on the premise of original Shari'ah compliance issues unless Change in Fatwa requirements (Par. 64–66) are first complied with, and Par. 72 requires restructuring propositions to be reviewed and approved by the SSSB, representatives of Sukuk-holders, AND the regulator; (4) Compliant—Par. 84 & 101 permit the originator's financial statement auditor to serve as external Shari'ah auditor if qualified and appointed in consultation with trustee, SSSB, and Sukuk-holders' representatives, and Par. 87 mandates submitting the draft report first to the SSSB and finalizing after due consultation with the SSSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 12 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 46(f) requires proper justification, non-jeopardy of Sukuk-holders' interests, and pre-approval of Sukuk-holders or their representatives before relocating Sukuk assets; (2) Par. 63 requires approval of (a) trustee, (b) Sukuk-holders or their representatives, AND (c) regulator for any change in SSSB; (3) Par. 74 bars initiating restructuring merely on the premise of original Shari'ah compliance issues unless Change in Fatwa requirements (Par. 64–66) are complied with first, and Par. 72 requires approval of restructuring by SSSB, Sukuk-holders' representatives, AND regulator; (4) Par. 84 & 101 permit appointing the originator's financial statement auditor as external Shari'ah auditor if qualified and consulted with trustee, SSSB, and Sukuk-holders' representatives, and Par. 87 requires submitting the draft report first to the SSSB before finalizing.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Which of the following accurately states the authoritative hierarchy between AAOIFI GS 13 ('Waqf Governance') and its accompanying Guidance Note, its relationship with AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard (SS) 60, and its effective date?
en.A: GS 13 is read in conjunction with AAOIFI SS 60 on Waqf and the Guidance Note for GS 13; in case of any inconsistency between GS 13 and the Guidance Note, the requirements of GS 13 prevail, and GS 13 is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 July 2021.
en.B: In case of any inconsistency between GS 13 and its Guidance Note, the Guidance Note overrides GS 13, and GS 13 became effective on 1 January 2018.
en.C: GS 13 supersedes AAOIFI SS 60 on Waqf and applies solely to sovereign state-owned endowments beginning on 1 January 2025.
en.D: GS 13 is a non-binding appendix to FAS 37 with no effective date and no authoritative hierarchy.
en.True answer: GS 13 is read in conjunction with AAOIFI SS 60 on Waqf and the Guidance Note for GS 13; in case of any inconsistency between GS 13 and the Guidance Note, the requirements of GS 13 prevail, and GS 13 is effective for financial periods beginning on or after 1 July 2021.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Introductory Note (p. 5) & Par. 91 (GS 13 shall be read in conjunction with AAOIFI's Shari'ah Standard (SS) 60 on Waqf and the Guidance Note for GS 13; in case of any inconsistencies between this standard and the guidance note, the requirements of the standard shall prevail; Par. 91 sets effective date for financial periods beginning on or after 01 July 2021).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 2–3 (including Footnote 1) and Appendix B (BC3–BC7) of AAOIFI GS 13, how does the standard apply to Family Waqf and Temporary Waqf?
en.A: Both Family Waqf and Temporary Waqf of any duration are strictly excluded from GS 13.
en.B: Family Waqf are encouraged to adopt GS 13 principles insofar as applicable (provided this is NOT used to legitimize violating the Shari'ah rules of inheritance), while GS 13 is applicable to a temporary Waqf created for a reasonably long period (generally no less than 5 years) and encourages shorter-period temporary Waqf to adopt it as well.
en.C: GS 13 applies mandatorily to temporary Waqf of less than 6 months, while Family Waqf may use GS 13 to override Islamic inheritance shares.
en.D: GS 13 applies solely to perpetual Waqf structured as public limited companies and excludes trusts, foundations, and temporary Waqf.
en.True answer: Family Waqf are encouraged to adopt GS 13 principles insofar as applicable (provided this is NOT used to legitimize violating the Shari'ah rules of inheritance), while GS 13 is applicable to a temporary Waqf created for a reasonably long period (generally no less than 5 years) and encourages shorter-period temporary Waqf to adopt it as well.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 2–3, Footnote 1 & Appendix B, BC3–BC7 (Par. 2 & Footnote 1: Family Waqf are not included in SS 60; GS 13 encourages Family Waqf to adopt GS 13 principles insofar as applicable, provided it is not used to legitimize violating Shari'ah rules of inheritance. Par. 3 & BC7: GS 13 is applicable to all types of Waqf irrespective of legal structure, including temporary Waqf created for a reasonably long period—generally no less than 5 years—while shorter-term temporary Waqf are encouraged to adopt it).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Appendix D (Paragraph PP3), Appendix B (BC8–BC10), and Paragraph 4(a) Footnote 2 of AAOIFI GS 13, where does conceptual ownership of a Waqf rest once created, and how is 'Ghallah' (yield) defined?
en.A: Ownership transfers jointly to the Nazir and the beneficiaries, while Ghallah represents gross cash donations received prior to expenses.
en.B: Ownership remains with the Waqif's legal heirs, while Ghallah represents the unrealized fair-value appreciation of endowed land.
en.C: Upon creating a Waqf, the Waqif loses ownership and the ability to transfer it; conceptually, ownership belongs to Allah Almighty alone (and is NOT transferred to the Waqif's heirs, beneficiaries, the Nazir, or the state), while Ghallah (per FAS 37) represents the net surplus from financial activities and other gains/losses attributable (adjusted for non-cash items and items not available for distribution) to the beneficiaries.
en.D: Ownership vests in the state treasury upon registration, while Ghallah represents the initial endowed corpus.
en.True answer: Upon creating a Waqf, the Waqif loses ownership and the ability to transfer it; conceptually, ownership belongs to Allah Almighty alone (and is NOT transferred to the Waqif's heirs, beneficiaries, the Nazir, or the state), while Ghallah (per FAS 37) represents the net surplus from financial activities and other gains/losses attributable (adjusted for non-cash items and items not available for distribution) to the beneficiaries.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 4(a) Footnote 2, Appendix B BC8–BC10 & Appendix D PP3 (PP3 & BC10 state that at the time the Waqif creates a Waqf, he loses ownership and the ability to transfer it, and ownership belongs to Allah Almighty alone—hence it is NOT transferred to the Waqif's heirs, beneficiaries, the Nazir, or the state; Par. 4(a) Footnote 2 defines Ghallah per FAS 37 as the net surplus from financial activities and other gains/losses attributable, adjusted for non-cash items and items not available for distribution, to the beneficiaries).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 4(d), Paragraph 62, and Appendix B (BC13–BC15) of AAOIFI GS 13, how are unpaid volunteers and external service providers treated with respect to the 'management' of a Waqf?
en.A: Unpaid volunteers are excluded from governance and ethical standards because they receive no salary, and outsourcing management functions is strictly prohibited.
en.B: Only full-time salaried executives are considered part of management, and volunteers cannot be assigned operational responsibilities.
en.C: Volunteers are classified as beneficiaries rather than management, and management outsourcing is permitted only for sovereign state Waqfs.
en.D: Management includes employees and may also include volunteers (as well as a Nazir involved in management functions) because from a governance perspective there is no difference whether a person is paid or unpaid as long as responsibility remains the same; additionally, the management function may be outsourced to professional service providers subject to GS 13 and local regulations.
en.True answer: Management includes employees and may also include volunteers (as well as a Nazir involved in management functions) because from a governance perspective there is no difference whether a person is paid or unpaid as long as responsibility remains the same; additionally, the management function may be outsourced to professional service providers subject to GS 13 and local regulations.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 4(d), Par. 62 & Appendix B, BC13–BC15 (Par. 4(d) & BC13–BC14 explicitly include volunteers in the definition of management because from a governance perspective there is no difference whether a person is paid or unpaid as long as responsibility remains the same; Par. 62 & BC15 confirm that management may comprise paid employees, volunteers, or a combination of both, and may also be outsourced to professional service providers subject to GS 13 and jurisdiction regulations).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 11–12 of AAOIFI GS 13, which of the following accurately describes the rights of a Waqif after establishing a Waqf?
en.A: Subject to Shari'ah principles, applicable law, and the original Waqf deed, a Waqif generally has the right to access timely financial and operational information, define the use of surplus funds (if permitted by law), appoint/suspend/remove the Nazir, become a Nazir of the Waqf (though a board of Nazirs is preferred), be a beneficiary of the Waqf, and make changes to the Waqf deed to the extent allowed by the original deed.
en.B: Once a Waqf deed is signed, a Waqif is strictly prohibited from ever being a beneficiary of the Waqf, serving as Nazir, or receiving financial reports.
en.C: A Waqif retains unconditional power to revoke the Waqf at any time and reclaim all endowed corpus assets for personal heirs.
en.D: A Waqif may stipulate conditions in a Family Waqf deed that deliberately exclude female heirs from statutory Shari'ah inheritance rights.
en.True answer: Subject to Shari'ah principles, applicable law, and the original Waqf deed, a Waqif generally has the right to access timely financial and operational information, define the use of surplus funds (if permitted by law), appoint/suspend/remove the Nazir, become a Nazir of the Waqf (though a board of Nazirs is preferred), be a beneficiary of the Waqf, and make changes to the Waqf deed to the extent allowed by the original deed.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 11(a)–(b) & Par. 12(a)–(f) (Par. 12 enumerates the general rights of a Waqif: (a) access to timely and pertinent financial and operational information; (b) define use of surplus funds if permitted by law; (c) appoint, suspend, and remove the Nazir subject to good governance; (d) become a Nazir of the Waqf [though board of Nazirs is preferred]; (e) be a beneficiary of the Waqf; (f) make changes to the Waqf deed in line with Shari'ah and to the extent allowed by the original Waqf deed. Par. 11(a) prohibits stipulating conditions conflicting with Shari'ah, particularly inheritance/gift/will rules in Family Waqf).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 16–20 of AAOIFI GS 13, which rules govern the determination, eligibility verification, document access, and treatment of Waqf beneficiaries?
en.A: Beneficiaries are strictly prohibited from seeing the Waqf deed, and the Nazir may favor relatives among beneficiaries at his personal discretion.
en.B: If no determinable beneficiaries exist, benefits must be allocated to recognized/registered charitable activities consistent with Waqf objectives; eligibility verification must rely on observable, verifiable indicators without compromising beneficiaries' privacy and dignity; beneficiaries are entitled to a copy of the Waqf deed; and there shall be no preferential treatment among beneficiaries unless specifically required in the Waqf deed.
en.C: If the Waqif's named beneficiaries are no longer alive, the Waqf assets automatically revert to the Nazir's personal estate.
en.D: Eligibility verification may involve publishing beneficiaries' private financial and medical records publicly to ensure transparency.
en.True answer: If no determinable beneficiaries exist, benefits must be allocated to recognized/registered charitable activities consistent with Waqf objectives; eligibility verification must rely on observable, verifiable indicators without compromising beneficiaries' privacy and dignity; beneficiaries are entitled to a copy of the Waqf deed; and there shall be no preferential treatment among beneficiaries unless specifically required in the Waqf deed.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 16–20 (Par. 17: in case of no determinable beneficiaries, benefits shall be allocated to recognized/registered charitable activities by the Nazir in accordance with Waqf objectives; Par. 18: determining eligibility involves reliable background checks and analytical diagnosis based on observable/verifiable indicators without compromising privacy and dignity; Par. 19: beneficiaries are entitled to a copy of the Waqf deed; Par. 20: no preferential treatment among beneficiaries unless specifically required in the Waqf deed).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 21–23 and Appendix B (BC16–BC19) of AAOIFI GS 13, which governance form of Nazir is strongly recommended, and what is expected when a natural person is appointed as an individual Nazir by the Waqif?
en.A: An individual Nazir is strongly preferred over a board, and he must serve alone for life without delegating authority.
en.B: A state government agency is mandatory for all private Waqfs, and natural persons are prohibited from serving as Nazir.
en.C: A Board of Nazirs is strongly recommended; if a natural person is appointed as Nazir by the Waqif, as a preferred governance practice, he is expected to nominate within three years of his appointment a Board of Nazirs (including a reasonable representation of independent members) in whom all responsibilities and authority of the Nazir will be vested.
en.D: An individual Nazir must resign automatically after 12 months and transfer ownership of the Waqf assets to a commercial bank.
en.True answer: A Board of Nazirs is strongly recommended; if a natural person is appointed as Nazir by the Waqif, as a preferred governance practice, he is expected to nominate within three years of his appointment a Board of Nazirs (including a reasonable representation of independent members) in whom all responsibilities and authority of the Nazir will be vested.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 21(a)–(d), Par. 23 & Appendix B, BC16–BC19 (Par. 21 lists four forms: (a) board of Nazirs [strongly recommended], (b) individual Nazir, (c) juristic person Nazir, (d) state Nazir; Par. 23 stipulates that in the event a natural person is appointed as Nazir by the Waqif, such Nazir, as a preferred governance practice, is expected to nominate, within three years of his appointment, a board of Nazirs—including a reasonable representation of independent members—in whom will be vested all the responsibilities and authority of the Nazir).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 39(l) and 51 (and BC33–BC34) of AAOIFI GS 13, what rules govern (1) risk coverage/insurance for Waqf assets and (2) determining the remuneration of a Nazir?
en.A: (1) Conventional insurance is preferred over Takaful even where Takaful is readily available; (2) a Nazir is strictly prohibited from ever receiving any remuneration.
en.B: (1) Waqf assets may never be covered by Takaful or insurance; (2) the Nazir may unilaterally fix his own remuneration at up to 50% of gross Waqf donations.
en.C: (1) Takaful is mandatory regardless of cost even if it consumes 100% of Waqf yield; (2) Nazir remuneration is set exclusively by the external auditor.
en.D: (1) The Nazir must maintain Takaful coverage (or, if unavailable, insurance coverage if allowed by Shari'ah principles and rules) considered appropriate and reasonable based on a cost-versus-benefit analysis; (2) if permissible by law, the Nazir receives remuneration specified by the Waqif, or if silent, determined by a competent authority (if any), or otherwise no more than a fair remuneration per Waqf deed limits or comparable fair market practice.
en.True answer: (1) The Nazir must maintain Takaful coverage (or, if unavailable, insurance coverage if allowed by Shari'ah principles and rules) considered appropriate and reasonable based on a cost-versus-benefit analysis; (2) if permissible by law, the Nazir receives remuneration specified by the Waqif, or if silent, determined by a competent authority (if any), or otherwise no more than a fair remuneration per Waqf deed limits or comparable fair market practice.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 39(l), Par. 51 & Appendix B, BC33–BC34 (Par. 39(l): maintain Takaful coverage, or in case of its unavailability, insurance coverage if allowed by Shari'ah principles and rules, considered appropriate and reasonable considering cost vs. benefit analysis; Par. 51: if permissible by law, Nazir receives remuneration specified by Waqif; if Waqif is silent, determined by competent authority if any; otherwise no more than a fair remuneration in line with Waqf deed principles/limits or comparable fair market practice).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 52–54 of AAOIFI GS 13, which independence requirements apply to the Audit Committee of a Waqf, and when may a Waqif serve as a member of the Audit Committee?
en.A: All members of the audit committee must be independent of the Waqf and its management; the majority of members (including the chairman) must also be independent of the Nazir if the Nazir is not a board of Nazirs; and a Waqif may be a member of the audit committee provided he is NOT involved in active management of, and does NOT have a business relationship with, the Waqf.
en.B: A Waqif is strictly barred from ever serving on the audit committee under any circumstances, and the CEO of the Waqf chairs the audit committee.
en.C: Only the chairman of the audit committee needs to be independent of management, while active senior managers may form the majority of the committee.
en.D: A Waqif may serve on the audit committee even while acting as the full-time managing director and primary commercial supplier of the Waqf.
en.True answer: All members of the audit committee must be independent of the Waqf and its management; the majority of members (including the chairman) must also be independent of the Nazir if the Nazir is not a board of Nazirs; and a Waqif may be a member of the audit committee provided he is NOT involved in active management of, and does NOT have a business relationship with, the Waqf.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 52–54 ('All members of the audit committee shall be independent of the Waqf and its management. The majority of them, including the chairman, shall also be independent of the Nazir, if the Nazir is not in the form of the board of Nazirs. A Waqif may be a member of the audit committee, if he is not involved in active management of or does not have a business relationship with, the Waqf').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 55–60 and Appendix B (BC20–BC24) of AAOIFI GS 13, what is the minimum member requirement for a Waqf's Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB), and how did the Board treat internal versus external Shari'ah audit for Waqf institutions?
en.A: A Waqf SSB must have at least 5 scholars in all cases, and external Shari'ah audit is strictly mandatory for every Waqf regardless of size.
en.B: Considering the nature and relative size of the Waqf, its SSB may comprise one or more members (preferably three or more members); furthermore, the Board considered internal Shari'ah audit mandatory (possible within the existing internal audit function), whereas external Shari'ah audit may not be mandatory/necessary as cost vs. benefits might not justify it for most types of Waqf.
en.C: A Waqf is prohibited from establishing its own SSB and must rely exclusively on the external financial auditor for Fatwas.
en.D: Both internal Shari'ah audit and external Shari'ah audit are strictly optional for all Waqf institutions.
en.True answer: Considering the nature and relative size of the Waqf, its SSB may comprise one or more members (preferably three or more members); furthermore, the Board considered internal Shari'ah audit mandatory (possible within the existing internal audit function), whereas external Shari'ah audit may not be mandatory/necessary as cost vs. benefits might not justify it for most types of Waqf.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 55–60, Par. 71 & Appendix B, BC20–BC24 (Par. 56: considering nature and relative size of the Waqf in terms of resources and operations, an SSB may comprise of one or more members [preferably three or more members]; Par. 71 & BC24: internal audit function shall include an internal Shari'ah audit function—considered mandatory by the Board—whereas external Shari'ah audit may not be mandatory/necessary as it might not justify cost vs. benefits for most types of Waqf).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 65, 68, and 72 of AAOIFI GS 13, what are the reporting lines of a Waqf's internal audit function, who approves its charter and annual plan, and how may it be outsourced?
en.A: It reports functionally to the CEO, its charter is approved by the external auditor, and outsourcing is permitted only to international accounting firms.
en.B: It reports functionally and administratively to the Waqif, and outsourcing is strictly prohibited.
en.C: It reports functionally to the audit committee (or the Nazir if there is no audit committee) and administratively to senior management; its charter and annual plan are approved by the Nazir on the recommendation of the audit committee; and TCWG may outsource the internal audit / internal Shari'ah audit function wholly or partially to a professional service provider, whether a firm or an individual.
en.D: It reports functionally to the SSB, its annual plan is approved by beneficiaries, and partial outsourcing to an individual practitioner is prohibited.
en.True answer: It reports functionally to the audit committee (or the Nazir if there is no audit committee) and administratively to senior management; its charter and annual plan are approved by the Nazir on the recommendation of the audit committee; and TCWG may outsource the internal audit / internal Shari'ah audit function wholly or partially to a professional service provider, whether a firm or an individual.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 65, Par. 68 & Par. 72 (Par. 65: functionally reports to audit committee or Nazir if there is no audit committee, and administratively to senior management; Par. 68: charter and annual plan submitted to and approved by the Nazir on the recommendation of the audit committee; Par. 72: TCWG may decide to outsource, wholly or partially, the internal audit / internal Shari'ah audit function to a professional service provider, be it a firm or an individual).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 77 and 80 (including Footnote 10) of AAOIFI GS 13, what hierarchy of accounting standards governs a Waqf's financial reporting, and what ethical rule governs public relations and disclosures?
en.A: IFRS → National Tax Code → AAOIFI FAS 37; public disclosures should actively promote the personal generosity of the Waqif and Nazir.
en.B: Local GAAP → IFRS → AAOIFI FAS 1; public disclosures are optional for non-governmental Waqfs.
en.C: AAOIFI FAS 1 → IFRS → Local GAAP; public relations may exaggerate social impact to attract larger donations.
en.D: The financial reporting hierarchy is: (a) AAOIFI's Financial Accounting Standard on Waqf (FAS 37), (b) other applicable AAOIFI FASs, and (c) generally accepted accounting principles in the jurisdiction insofar as they do not contravene Shari'ah principles and rules; ethical disclosure principles require truthful, fair, and unbiased dissemination and avoiding unnecessary and excessive self-projection and self-praise for the Waqf, Waqif, TCWG, and senior management.
en.True answer: The financial reporting hierarchy is: (a) AAOIFI's Financial Accounting Standard on Waqf (FAS 37), (b) other applicable AAOIFI FASs, and (c) generally accepted accounting principles in the jurisdiction insofar as they do not contravene Shari'ah principles and rules; ethical disclosure principles require truthful, fair, and unbiased dissemination and avoiding unnecessary and excessive self-projection and self-praise for the Waqf, Waqif, TCWG, and senior management.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 77(a)–(c) & Par. 80(a)–(c), Footnote 10 (Par. 80 establishes preference hierarchy: (a) financial accounting standard issued by AAOIFI on Waqf [FAS 37, Footnote 10], (b) other applicable AAOIFI FASs, and (c) local GAAP insofar as not contravening Shari'ah principles and rules; Par. 77(b)–(c) requires truthful, fair, and unbiased information dissemination and avoidance of unnecessary and excessive self-projection and self-praise for the Waqf, Waqif, TCWG, and senior management).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 49–50 and Appendix B (BC31–BC32) of AAOIFI GS 13, how does the standard regulate pledging or creating a charge over Waqf assets?
en.A: Waqf assets shall in NO case be subjected to a pledge or charge created for the benefit of any party (including the Nazir or Waqif); however, in rare circumstances when the Nazir determines it necessary to obtain Shari'ah-compliant financing for Waqf operations, pledging or creating a charge against Waqf assets is permitted ONLY if governed by a well-documented risk policy duly approved by the Nazir, compliant with Shari'ah principles and rules, AND approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB) of the Waqf.
en.B: Pledging Waqf assets is completely prohibited under all circumstances without exception, even for Shari'ah-compliant Waqf development financing approved by the SSB.
en.C: The Nazir may freely pledge Waqf real estate as collateral for a conventional bank overdraft or for the Waqif's personal business loan without SSB approval.
en.D: Pledging Waqf assets requires only the oral consent of the senior accountant and is exempt from risk policy documentation.
en.True answer: Waqf assets shall in NO case be subjected to a pledge or charge created for the benefit of any party (including the Nazir or Waqif); however, in rare circumstances when the Nazir determines it necessary to obtain Shari'ah-compliant financing for Waqf operations, pledging or creating a charge against Waqf assets is permitted ONLY if governed by a well-documented risk policy duly approved by the Nazir, compliant with Shari'ah principles and rules, AND approved by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB) of the Waqf.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 49–50 & Appendix B, BC31–BC32 (Par. 49: 'The Waqf assets shall in no case be subjected to a pledge or a charge created for the benefit of any party (including the Nazir or Waqif).' Par. 50 & BC32: in rare circumstances when financing a Waqf, if the Nazir determines it necessary to obtain Shari'ah-compliant financing for the Waqf operations and pledging or creating a charge against the Waqf assets, it shall be subjected to a well-documented risk policy duly approved by the Nazir, in compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules, and subject to the approval of the SSB of the Waqf).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 15(i)–(j) of AAOIFI GS 13, what rules govern modifying the conditions stipulated in a Waqf deed and reinvesting part of the Waqf yield (Ghallah)?
en.A: Conditions in a Waqf deed can never be modified even during the Waqif's lifetime, and 100% of Ghallah must be distributed immediately each month with zero retention for maintenance reserves.
en.B: The Waqf deed must specify the authority of the Waqif (during his lifetime) or the Nazir (after the death of the Waqif) to modify conditions provided it is in the interest of the Waqf (measured by the actions/behavior of a trustworthy, prudent, conscientious, and insightful person or competent authority), permitted by regulators, and in line with Shari'ah and the original Waqf deed; it must also address the right to invest part of Ghallah for development, yield optimization, sustainability, and maintenance/restoration reserves in a balanced and fair manner without unduly compromising beneficiaries' rights.
en.C: After the Waqif's death, the Nazir may modify Waqf objectives solely to increase administrative salaries, and may retain 95% of Ghallah indefinitely without justification.
en.D: Only the external auditor has legal authority to amend the Waqf deed after the Waqif's death.
en.True answer: The Waqf deed must specify the authority of the Waqif (during his lifetime) or the Nazir (after the death of the Waqif) to modify conditions provided it is in the interest of the Waqf (measured by the actions/behavior of a trustworthy, prudent, conscientious, and insightful person or competent authority), permitted by regulators, and in line with Shari'ah and the original Waqf deed; it must also address the right to invest part of Ghallah for development, yield optimization, sustainability, and maintenance/restoration reserves in a balanced and fair manner without unduly compromising beneficiaries' rights.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 15(i)–(j) (Par. 15(i): authority of Waqif during his lifetime or Nazir after death of Waqif to modify conditions stipulated in the Waqf deed, provided it is in the interest of the Waqf, permitted by regulatory authorities, and in line with Shari'ah principles/rules and the original Waqf deed—where 'in the interest of the Waqf' means in line with the actions/behavior of a trustworthy, prudent, conscientious, and insightful person or competent authority; Par. 15(j): right to invest part of Ghallah for development, optimization of yield, sustainability, and maintenance/restoration reserves in a balanced and fair manner without unduly compromising beneficiaries' rights).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 40–41 of AAOIFI GS 13, how must a Waqf's Risk Management Policy categorize identified risks, and what core principles must its Investment Policy incorporate?
en.A: Risks are categorized solely into credit risk and currency risk; the investment policy must maximize short-term speculative trading returns regardless of corpus preservation.
en.B: Risk management is optional for charitable endowments; the investment policy permits retaining non-Shari'ah-compliant equity holdings indefinitely if they pay high dividends.
en.C: The Risk Management Policy must categorize risks into four categories: (i) risks to be avoided and prevented, (ii) risks to be transferred and hedged, (iii) risks to be mitigated partially or fully, and (iv) risks to be taken on a calculated basis within tolerable limits; the Investment Policy must balance revenue/cash flows against sustainability, liquidity, and perpetuity, produce stable cash flows, preserve intrinsic asset value, avoid speculative/excessively risky investments, achieve Ghallah consistent with acceptable risk, and establish a process for disposing of investments (and/or income) no longer considered Shari'ah-compliant.
en.D: All identified risks must be transferred externally via conventional derivatives, and external investment managers may be selected without written criteria.
en.True answer: The Risk Management Policy must categorize risks into four categories: (i) risks to be avoided and prevented, (ii) risks to be transferred and hedged, (iii) risks to be mitigated partially or fully, and (iv) risks to be taken on a calculated basis within tolerable limits; the Investment Policy must balance revenue/cash flows against sustainability, liquidity, and perpetuity, produce stable cash flows, preserve intrinsic asset value, avoid speculative/excessively risky investments, achieve Ghallah consistent with acceptable risk, and establish a process for disposing of investments (and/or income) no longer considered Shari'ah-compliant.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 40(a)–(d) & Par. 41(a)–(e) (Par. 40(c) defines four risk categories: (i) risks to be avoided and prevented; (ii) risks to be transferred and hedged; (iii) risks to be mitigated partially or fully, if possible; and (iv) risks to be taken on a calculated basis within tolerable limits. Par. 41 requires an investment policy balancing revenue/cash flows against sustainability, liquidity, and perpetuity; producing relatively stable cash flows; preserving intrinsic value; avoiding speculative or excessively risky investments; achieving Ghallah consistent with acceptable risk; defining asset allocation; establishing a process for disposal of non-Shari'ah-compliant investments/income; and setting criteria for selecting external investment managers/consultants).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 85–86 and 90 of AAOIFI GS 13, who holds the authority to appoint, agree the scope of, and determine the remuneration of a Waqf's external auditor, and which standard governs quarterly or half-yearly interim reviews?
en.A: The external auditor is always appointed by the Waqf's senior management, and interim reviews are prohibited under GS 13.
en.B: The external auditor is appointed by the SSB, and interim reviews follow IFRS 13.
en.C: The external auditor is appointed by the individual Waqif even if he serves as the full-time managing CEO of the Waqf.
en.D: Based on audit committee recommendations (where applicable), the external auditor is appointed (with scope and remuneration agreed) by: (a) the individual Waqif, if he is alive AND NOT involved in day-to-day operations and management of the Waqf; or (b) collectively by the Waqifs, if the Waqif is not an individual; or (c) the Nazir, if neither (a) nor (b) is met; furthermore, a Nazir may request the external auditor to perform quarterly or half-yearly reviews of interim condensed financial statements in line with ISRE 2410.
en.True answer: Based on audit committee recommendations (where applicable), the external auditor is appointed (with scope and remuneration agreed) by: (a) the individual Waqif, if he is alive AND NOT involved in day-to-day operations and management of the Waqf; or (b) collectively by the Waqifs, if the Waqif is not an individual; or (c) the Nazir, if neither (a) nor (b) is met; furthermore, a Nazir may request the external auditor to perform quarterly or half-yearly reviews of interim condensed financial statements in line with ISRE 2410.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 85(a)–(c), Par. 86 & Par. 90 (Par. 85 establishes a strict three-tier hierarchy for appointing, agreeing scope, and setting remuneration of the external auditor [based on audit committee recommendations where applicable]: (a) individual Waqif, if alive AND not involved in day-to-day operations and management; (b) collectively by the Waqifs, if the Waqif is not an individual; (c) the Nazir, if both of the above conditions are not met. Par. 90 specifies ISRE 2410 'Review of Interim Financial Information Performed by the Independent Auditor of the Entity' for quarterly or half-yearly interim reviews).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 87–89 of AAOIFI GS 13, which auditing standards apply to the external audit of a Waqf, what two additional matters must the external auditor specifically opine on in its report, and what meeting attendance right does the external auditor hold?
en.A: The external auditor performs the audit under AAOIFI Auditing Standards (and ISAs in matters not specifically addressed by AAOIFI ASs); documents in its report (as part of other matters) whether in its opinion (a) the revenue, expenditure, and operations of the Waqf during the period were in line with the objective(s) of the Waqf as well as Shari'ah principles and rules, and (b) the assets of the Waqf have been adequately safeguarded; and is entitled to attend meetings of the board of Nazirs and meeting of Waqifs where the annual report and financial statements are presented.
en.B: The external auditor applies exclusively local tax rules, opines only on mathematical trial-balance accuracy, and is barred from attending meetings of the board of Nazirs.
en.C: The external auditor opines solely on whether the Waqf outperformed stock market benchmarks and attends only confidential SSB meetings.
en.D: AAOIFI Auditing Standards are optional for Waqf audits, and the auditor's report omits any statement on safeguarding Waqf assets.
en.True answer: The external auditor performs the audit under AAOIFI Auditing Standards (and ISAs in matters not specifically addressed by AAOIFI ASs); documents in its report (as part of other matters) whether in its opinion (a) the revenue, expenditure, and operations of the Waqf during the period were in line with the objective(s) of the Waqf as well as Shari'ah principles and rules, and (b) the assets of the Waqf have been adequately safeguarded; and is entitled to attend meetings of the board of Nazirs and meeting of Waqifs where the annual report and financial statements are presented.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 87–89 (Par. 87: audit performed in accordance with AAOIFI Auditing Standards and International Standards on Auditing in matters not specifically addressed by AAOIFI ASs; Par. 88: in addition to normal scope, documents in its report as part of other matters whether, in its opinion: (a) revenue, expenditure, and operations of the Waqf during the period under audit have been in line with the objective(s) of the Waqf as well as Shari'ah principles and rules, and (b) the assets of the Waqf have been adequately safeguarded; Par. 89: entitled to attend meetings of the board of Nazirs and meeting of Waqifs where annual report and financial statements are presented).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 79 and 82–83 of AAOIFI GS 13, what three core reports must be included in a Waqf's Annual Report, and what specialized accounting and cost-disclosure rules apply?
en.A: The Annual Report contains only a brief 1-page cash receipt summary, and all Zakat, charity, and Waqf yield funds may be commingled in a single undivided account without separate cost disclosure.
en.B: The Annual Report must include: (a) annual financial statements (with statement of service performance per FAS 37) and external auditor's report, (b) a report by the Nazir (covering multi-year financial performance and long-term social impact with tables/charts, summary of activities, investment activities and risk mitigation, and donations received/grants disbursed segregated by nature), and (c) the SSB's annual Shari'ah compliance report; furthermore, funds accounting must segregate different fund categories (including Zakat and other charity funds), and costs attributable to management, the Nazir, and TCWG must be reported separately alongside related-party transactions and conflicts of interest.
en.C: The SSB report is excluded from the Annual Report, and remuneration paid to the Nazir and TCWG is combined with charitable grants disbursed to beneficiaries.
en.D: Only governmental Waqfs must prepare an Annual Report, and multi-year social impact commentary is prohibited.
en.True answer: The Annual Report must include: (a) annual financial statements (with statement of service performance per FAS 37) and external auditor's report, (b) a report by the Nazir (covering multi-year financial performance and long-term social impact with tables/charts, summary of activities, investment activities and risk mitigation, and donations received/grants disbursed segregated by nature), and (c) the SSB's annual Shari'ah compliance report; furthermore, funds accounting must segregate different fund categories (including Zakat and other charity funds), and costs attributable to management, the Nazir, and TCWG must be reported separately alongside related-party transactions and conflicts of interest.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13, Par. 79(a)–(c), Footnote 9 & Par. 82–83 (Par. 79 mandates three components in the Annual Report: (a) financial statements [with statement of service performance per FAS 37, Footnote 9] + external auditor's report; (b) Nazir's report containing 5 sub-elements including multi-year financial performance & long-term social impact with tables/charts/graphs, activities, investments/risks, and segregated donations received & grants disbursed; (c) SSB's report. Par. 82 requires funds accounting separating different fund categories including Zakat and charity funds; Par. 83 requires reporting related-party transactions/conflicts of interest and separately reporting costs attributable to management, Nazir, and TCWG).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question:
Examine the following four governance practices of a newly established charitable and family Waqf:
(1) The Waqif includes a clause in the Family Waqf deed stating that AAOIFI GS 13 governance principles override Islamic inheritance shares so that only eldest sons receive corpus distributions upon termination.
(2) The Waqif appoints a single natural person as individual Nazir; four years after appointment, the individual Nazir continues operating alone without nominating a Board of Nazirs.
(3) To fund a commercial real-estate expansion of the Waqf, the Nazir obtains a Shari'ah-compliant Murabaha facility and pledges a Waqf building as security without documenting a risk policy and without seeking approval from the Waqf's SSB.
(4) The Nazir establishes a 3-member Audit Committee comprising two independent external professionals (one serving as Chairman) plus the Waqif, who is not involved in active management and has no business relationship with the Waqf.
According to AAOIFI GS 13, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—GS 13 allows Family Waqfs to modify inheritance shares; (2) Compliant—individual Nazirs never need to form a board; (3) Compliant—Shari'ah-compliant financing needs no SSB approval for pledging; (4) Non-compliant—a Waqif can never sit on the Audit Committee.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant—Par. 2 Footnote 1 & BC5 explicitly warn that encouraging Family Waqfs to adopt GS 13 must NOT be used to legitimize violating Shari'ah rules of inheritance; (2) Non-compliant with preferred governance practice—Par. 23 expects a natural-person individual Nazir to nominate within three years of appointment a Board of Nazirs (including reasonable independent representation); (3) Non-compliant—Par. 50 permits pledging Waqf assets for Shari'ah-compliant operational financing ONLY if subject to a well-documented risk policy duly approved by the Nazir AND approved by the Waqf's SSB; (4) Compliant—Par. 53 requires all members to be independent of the Waqf/management, the majority (including the Chairman) to be independent of a non-board Nazir (2 of 3 + Chairman are independent), and explicitly permits a Waqif to be a member if not involved in active management and having no business relationship with the Waqf.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—Par. 2 Footnote 1 & BC5 explicitly warn that encouraging Family Waqfs to adopt GS 13 must NOT be used to legitimize violating Shari'ah rules of inheritance; (2) Non-compliant with preferred governance practice—Par. 23 expects a natural-person individual Nazir to nominate within three years of appointment a Board of Nazirs (including reasonable independent representation); (3) Non-compliant—Par. 50 permits pledging Waqf assets for Shari'ah-compliant operational financing ONLY if subject to a well-documented risk policy duly approved by the Nazir AND approved by the Waqf's SSB; (4) Compliant—Par. 53 requires all members to be independent of the Waqf/management, the majority (including the Chairman) to be independent of a non-board Nazir (2 of 3 + Chairman are independent), and explicitly permits a Waqif to be a member if not involved in active management and having no business relationship with the Waqf.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 2 Footnote 1, Par. 11(a) & Appendix B BC5 stipulate that Family Waqfs may consider GS 13 principles provided this is NOT used to legitimize violating Shari'ah rules of inheritance; (2) Par. 23 expects a natural person appointed as individual Nazir to nominate, within three years of appointment, a board of Nazirs (including reasonable representation of independent members); (3) Par. 49–50 & BC32 allow pledging Waqf assets for Shari'ah-compliant Waqf financing ONLY under a well-documented risk policy approved by the Nazir AND with the approval of the Waqf's SSB; (4) Par. 53 requires all audit committee members to be independent of the Waqf and management, the majority including the chairman to be independent of the Nazir when the Nazir is not a board of Nazirs (2/3 + chairman satisfied), and permits a Waqif to serve if not involved in active management or business relationships with the Waqf.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 13: Waqf Governance
en.Question:
A medium-sized educational Waqf established by a single individual Waqif (who is still alive and serves as the full-time managing Chief Executive Officer of the Waqf) undergoes its annual governance and audit cycle. Evaluate the following four actions:
(1) Because the Waqf deed was silent on Shari'ah supervision, the Board of Nazirs constitutes a Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB) consisting of a single qualified Shari'ah scholar commensurate with the Waqf's moderate size.
(2) On the recommendation of the Audit Committee, the Board of Nazirs approves the internal audit charter (which incorporates internal Shari'ah audit) and partially outsources internal Shari'ah audit fieldwork to a qualified individual Shari'ah audit practitioner.
(3) Because the individual Waqif is alive, he personally selects the external financial auditor, agrees on the audit scope, and fixes the auditor's remuneration without involving the Board of Nazirs.
(4) The external auditor conducts the audit under AAOIFI Auditing Standards and issues a clean financial statement opinion under AAOIFI FAS 37, but omits any opinion on whether the Waqf's revenue, expenditure, and operations complied with Waqf objectives and Shari'ah principles or whether Waqf assets were adequately safeguarded.
According to AAOIFI GS 13, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Non-compliant—every Waqf SSB must have at least 3 members; (2) Non-compliant—internal audit cannot be outsourced to an individual; (3) Compliant—an alive individual Waqif always appoints the external auditor; (4) Compliant—standard financial opinions require no additional Waqf-specific statements.
en.B: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant—partial outsourcing to an individual is prohibited; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.D: (1) Compliant—under Par. 56, where not stipulated in the Waqf deed, the Nazir constitutes the SSB, which may comprise one or more members (preferably three or more) considering the Waqf's nature and relative size; (2) Compliant—Par. 68 & 71–72 allow the Nazir (on audit committee recommendation) to approve the internal audit charter incorporating internal Shari'ah audit and outsource it wholly or partially to a professional service provider, 'be it a firm or an individual'; (3) Non-compliant—under Par. 85(a) & (c), an individual Waqif appoints the external auditor ONLY if he is alive AND NOT involved in day-to-day operations and management of the Waqf; since he is the active managing CEO, the Board of Nazirs must make the appointment (based on audit committee recommendation); (4) Non-compliant—under Par. 88(a)–(b), in addition to the normal audit scope, the external auditor MUST document in its report (as part of other matters) whether in its opinion (a) revenue, expenditure, and operations were in line with Waqf objectives and Shari'ah principles/rules, and (b) Waqf assets were adequately safeguarded.
en.True answer: (1) Compliant—under Par. 56, where not stipulated in the Waqf deed, the Nazir constitutes the SSB, which may comprise one or more members (preferably three or more) considering the Waqf's nature and relative size; (2) Compliant—Par. 68 & 71–72 allow the Nazir (on audit committee recommendation) to approve the internal audit charter incorporating internal Shari'ah audit and outsource it wholly or partially to a professional service provider, 'be it a firm or an individual'; (3) Non-compliant—under Par. 85(a) & (c), an individual Waqif appoints the external auditor ONLY if he is alive AND NOT involved in day-to-day operations and management of the Waqf; since he is the active managing CEO, the Board of Nazirs must make the appointment (based on audit committee recommendation); (4) Non-compliant—under Par. 88(a)–(b), in addition to the normal audit scope, the external auditor MUST document in its report (as part of other matters) whether in its opinion (a) revenue, expenditure, and operations were in line with Waqf objectives and Shari'ah principles/rules, and (b) Waqf assets were adequately safeguarded.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 13 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 56 empowers the Nazir (if not stipulated in the Waqf deed) to constitute an SSB comprising 'one or more members (preferably three or more members)' considering nature and relative size; (2) Par. 68, 71 & 72 provide for approval of the internal audit charter (including internal Shari'ah audit) by the Nazir on audit committee recommendation and allow outsourcing wholly or partially to a professional service provider, 'be it a firm or an individual'; (3) Par. 85(a)–(c) restricts an alive individual Waqif from appointing the external auditor if he IS involved in day-to-day operations and management of the Waqf, shifting appointment authority to the Nazir (on audit committee recommendation); (4) Par. 88(a)–(b) mandates the external auditor to document in its report (as part of other matters) its opinion on (a) compliance of revenue, expenditure, and operations with Waqf objectives and Shari'ah principles/rules, and (b) adequate safeguarding of Waqf assets.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope, proportionality exemptions, and effective date of AAOIFI GS 14 ('Islamic Crowdfunding Governance')?
en.A: GS 14 applies exclusively to commercial equity crowdfunding, replaces national regulatory frameworks, and became effective retroactively on 1 July 2021.
en.B: GS 14 applies at the level of each ICF issuance across all types of Islamic crowdfunding (commercial and social) in addition to—not in replacement of—jurisdictional regulations; an operator (subject to regulatory requirements) may define criteria for non-material social ICF issuances exempt from all or certain requirements; and GS 14 is effective prospectively for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023.
en.C: GS 14 exempts all social Islamic crowdfunding campaigns automatically regardless of size, and applies only to platforms operated by licensed commercial banks.
en.D: GS 14 is a non-binding technical appendix to GS 12 ('Sukuk Governance') with no standalone effective date.
en.True answer: GS 14 applies at the level of each ICF issuance across all types of Islamic crowdfunding (commercial and social) in addition to—not in replacement of—jurisdictional regulations; an operator (subject to regulatory requirements) may define criteria for non-material social ICF issuances exempt from all or certain requirements; and GS 14 is effective prospectively for financial periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Introduction IN3, Par. 3–6, Par. 140 & Appendix D, BC4–BC9 (Par. 3–5: applies to all types of Islamic crowdfunding initiatives—commercial and social [BC6–BC9]—at the level of each ICF issuance, in addition to and not in replacement of local regulatory requirements; Par. 6 & IN3: operator, subject to regulatory requirements, may define criteria of non-material social ICF issuances exempt from all or certain requirements under the proportionality principle; Par. 140: effective prospectively on ICF issuances for financial periods beginning on or after 01 January 2023).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 7 and Paragraph 16 of AAOIFI GS 14, which participant in Islamic crowdfunding is deemed an Islamic Financial Institution (IFI) subject to all relevant AAOIFI Governance Standards, and how is an 'Ongoing ICF issuance' distinguished from an 'Open-ended ICF issuance'?
en.A: The operator (and no other element, unless established specifically as an IFI) is considered an IFI subject to relevant AAOIFI GSs; an 'ongoing ICF issuance' has an ongoing transaction/venture structure (such as Ijarah, Musharaka, or Mudaraba—excluding equity ICF issuances that conclude upon issuing shares), whereas an 'open-ended ICF issuance' has no ceiling limit on investment amount and no specific investing period.
en.B: Every commercial issuer raising funds on a platform is automatically classified as an IFI; an 'ongoing ICF issuance' refers exclusively to equity share offerings, whereas an 'open-ended ICF issuance' has a fixed 12-month maturity.
en.C: Only the trustee and platform provider are deemed IFIs; 'ongoing' and 'open-ended' ICF issuances are identical synonyms for one-time charitable donations.
en.D: Neither the operator nor any other party is considered an IFI under GS 14, and equity ICF issuances remain 'ongoing ICF issuances' indefinitely.
en.True answer: The operator (and no other element, unless established specifically as an IFI) is considered an IFI subject to relevant AAOIFI GSs; an 'ongoing ICF issuance' has an ongoing transaction/venture structure (such as Ijarah, Musharaka, or Mudaraba—excluding equity ICF issuances that conclude upon issuing shares), whereas an 'open-ended ICF issuance' has no ceiling limit on investment amount and no specific investing period.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 7(k), Par. 7(n)–(o), Par. 16 & Appendix D, BC10–BC13 (Par. 7(k) Explanation & Par. 16: an operator, but no other element unless established specifically as an IFI, is considered to be an IFI and subject to relevant AAOIFI GSs; Par. 7(n): ongoing ICF issuance has an ongoing transaction/venture structure such as Ijarah, Musharaka, or Mudaraba, explicitly excluding equity ICF issuances which conclude when equity shares are issued; Par. 7(o): open-ended ICF issuance has no ceiling limit on investment amount and no specific period for investing).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 12 and 17–22 of AAOIFI GS 14, which seven elements comprise Islamic crowdfunding, and when may responsibility for the Shari'ah compliance function of an ICF issuance be passed on to the issuer?
en.A: Five elements exist (excluding the trustee and underlying operations), and the operator may never pass Shari'ah compliance responsibilities to an issuer under any circumstances.
en.B: Six elements exist (excluding the platform provider), and Shari'ah compliance responsibility passes automatically to every issuer upon signing the platform terms of service.
en.C: The seven elements are (a) operator, (b) platform, (c) platform provider (if different from operator), (d) trustee, (e) fund providers, (f) issuer, and (g) underlying operations; responsibility for the Shari'ah compliance function may be passed on to the issuer where the issuer has established a Shari'ah compliance function duly complying with the relevant AAOIFI GS (GS 9) AND with due approval of the SSB of the ICF issuance.
en.D: Eight elements exist including the central bank, and AI or smart contracts are prohibited in Islamic crowdfunding platforms.
en.True answer: The seven elements are (a) operator, (b) platform, (c) platform provider (if different from operator), (d) trustee, (e) fund providers, (f) issuer, and (g) underlying operations; responsibility for the Shari'ah compliance function may be passed on to the issuer where the issuer has established a Shari'ah compliance function duly complying with the relevant AAOIFI GS (GS 9) AND with due approval of the SSB of the ICF issuance.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 12(a)–(g) & Par. 17–22 (Par. 12 enumerates the 7 key elements of Islamic crowdfunding; Par. 17–19 require the operator to establish a Shari'ah compliance function/SCD with overarching unrestricted access to ICF records, and stipulate that where the issuer has established a Shari'ah compliance function duly complying with the relevant AAOIFI GS [GS 9], such responsibility may be passed on to the issuer with due approval of the SSB of the ICF issuance; Par. 22 encourages using AI, smart contracts, machine learning, and algorithms).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 27–29 of AAOIFI GS 14, what three conditions must be satisfied before funds held in a trust account are released to the issuer, and what is the 'cooling-off period'?
en.A: Funds are released immediately upon each individual pledge; the cooling-off period is a 90-day post-maturity lock-up during which issuers withhold profit distributions.
en.B: Funds are released once 50% of the target is raised, and fund providers canceling during the cooling-off period forfeit 10% of their principal as a penalty.
en.C: Funds are released solely at the issuer's written request, and material adverse changes exclude misleading statements discovered in the prospectus.
en.D: Funds in trust accounts administered by an independent registered trustee may only be released to the issuer after: (i) the targeted amount sought to be raised has been achieved, (ii) there is no material adverse change relating to the offer during the offer period, and (iii) the cooling-off period (if required by the regulator) has expired; the cooling-off period is the period after pledging funds during which a fund provider may cancel the investment and be refunded without incurring any loss except transaction costs or currency exchange loss.
en.True answer: Funds in trust accounts administered by an independent registered trustee may only be released to the issuer after: (i) the targeted amount sought to be raised has been achieved, (ii) there is no material adverse change relating to the offer during the offer period, and (iii) the cooling-off period (if required by the regulator) has expired; the cooling-off period is the period after pledging funds during which a fund provider may cancel the investment and be refunded without incurring any loss except transaction costs or currency exchange loss.
