en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 27(a)–(c), Par. 28(a)–(c) & Par. 29 (Par. 27(c) requires all three conditions before releasing trust funds: (i) targeted amount achieved; (ii) no material adverse change during the offer period [false/misleading statement, material omission, or material change in circumstances per Par. 28]; and (iii) cooling-off period, if required by regulator, has expired. Par. 29 defines cooling-off period as the period after pledging investment during which the fund provider may cancel and be refunded without incurring any loss except expenses related to transaction costs or currency exchange loss).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 32 and Appendix D (BC35–BC37) of AAOIFI GS 14, which entities are considered INELIGIBLE to act as an issuer on an Islamic crowdfunding platform unless specifically allowed by the respective regulator?
en.A: (a) Entities with commercially or financially complex structures (such as investment funds, companies, or financial institutions) OTHER than a licensed Islamic microfinance provider or a non-banking IFI; (b) a public-listed company or a subsidiary thereof; and (c) a start-up with no appropriate business plan, or an entity with a bad financial performance track record or whose owners/directors have a bad financial conduct track record (including blind pools).
en.B: All licensed Islamic microfinance providers and non-banking IFIs are permanently barred from raising funds via Islamic crowdfunding.
en.C: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) with audited financial statements and approved business plans are ineligible to be issuers.
en.D: Only public-listed corporations are eligible to raise funds on Islamic crowdfunding platforms, while private start-ups are completely excluded.
en.True answer: (a) Entities with commercially or financially complex structures (such as investment funds, companies, or financial institutions) OTHER than a licensed Islamic microfinance provider or a non-banking IFI; (b) a public-listed company or a subsidiary thereof; and (c) a start-up with no appropriate business plan, or an entity with a bad financial performance track record or whose owners/directors have a bad financial conduct track record (including blind pools).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 32(a)–(c) & Appendix D, BC35–BC37 (Par. 32 specifies three ineligible issuer categories unless allowed by respective regulators: (a) entities having commercially or financially complex structures e.g. investment funds, companies, or financial institutions, OTHER than a licensed Islamic microfinance provider or a non-banking IFI; (b) a public-listed company or a subsidiary thereof; and (c) a start-up entity with no appropriate business plan, or an entity with a bad track record of financial performance or whose owners/directors have a bad track record of financial conduct, including blind pools).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 45–47 and Appendix D (BC29(b)) of AAOIFI GS 14, what three practical options may an operator and issuer exercise with mutual consent to address the difficulty of appointing a separate Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB) for each individual ICF issuance?
en.A: (1) Eliminate SSB oversight for issuances under USD 5 million; (2) let the operator's CEO approve Fatwas; or (3) rely on the external financial auditor for Shari'ah rulings.
en.B: (1) The operator appoints a single SSB serving as the SSB for all ICF issuances it manages; (2) the operator appoints a large-member SSB that appoints at least three members from amongst itself as the SSB for a respective ICF issuance; or (3) the function is outsourced to a Shari'ah advisory firm subject to nominating at least three identified, individually eligible persons as SSB members.
en.C: (1) Appoint a single scholar per campaign; (2) outsource to any general law firm without identified scholars; or (3) dispense with Fatwas for Mudaraba campaigns.
en.D: (1) Require each issuer to hire 7 full-time scholars; (2) let fund providers vote on Fatwas online; or (3) apply conventional banking compliance checklists.
en.True answer: (1) The operator appoints a single SSB serving as the SSB for all ICF issuances it manages; (2) the operator appoints a large-member SSB that appoints at least three members from amongst itself as the SSB for a respective ICF issuance; or (3) the function is outsourced to a Shari'ah advisory firm subject to nominating at least three identified, individually eligible persons as SSB members.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 45–47 & Appendix D, BC29(b) (Par. 46 sets out three mutual-consent options to overcome practical difficulties in appointing an SSB per ICF issuance: (a) operator appoints an SSB serving all ICF issuances it manages; (b) operator appoints a large-member SSB which appoints at least three members from amongst themselves as the SSB of a respective ICF issuance; or (c) function is outsourced to a Shari'ah advisory firm subject to nomination of at least three identified persons to be members of the SSB who are otherwise individually eligible).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 62–63 and Appendix D (BC30–BC31) of AAOIFI GS 14, when must an Audit and Governance Committee (AGC) be appointed for an ICF issuance, and how is it composed?
en.A: An AGC is required for every one-time charity campaign and consists exclusively of the issuer's executive directors.
en.B: An AGC is required only when an issuer defaults, and is appointed unilaterally by the external financial auditor.
en.C: The operator and issuer (with mutual consent) must appoint an AGC if: (a) the issuer lacks an audit committee capable of performing GS 14 functions, (b) the ICF issuance has high investment risk factors or a relatively material investment (for issuer or operator), AND (c) the ICF issuance is ongoing and/or open-ended; it must comprise at least three members: an independent chairman appointed by mutual consent of operator and issuer, an equal number of members nominated by the issuer and operator (e.g., including operator's compliance officer), and preferably a nominee of the trustee.
en.D: An AGC must have at least 7 external Shari'ah scholars and is chaired by the issuer's Chief Financial Officer.
en.True answer: The operator and issuer (with mutual consent) must appoint an AGC if: (a) the issuer lacks an audit committee capable of performing GS 14 functions, (b) the ICF issuance has high investment risk factors or a relatively material investment (for issuer or operator), AND (c) the ICF issuance is ongoing and/or open-ended; it must comprise at least three members: an independent chairman appointed by mutual consent of operator and issuer, an equal number of members nominated by the issuer and operator (e.g., including operator's compliance officer), and preferably a nominee of the trustee.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 62(a)–(c), Par. 63(a)–(c) & Appendix D, BC30–BC31 (Par. 62 triggers AGC appointment when: (a) issuer does not have an audit committee capable of performing GS 14 functions, (b) ICF issuance has high investment risk factors or relatively material investment, AND (c) ICF issuance is ongoing and/or open-ended. Par. 63 sets composition of ≥3 members: (a) independent chairman appointed with mutual consent of operator and issuer; (b) equal number of members nominated by issuer and operator [e.g. compliance officer/employee of operator]; (c) preferably a nominee of the trustee).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraph 67 of AAOIFI GS 14, what four capabilities must an operator verify regarding the crowdfunding platform before commencing an ICF issuance?
en.A: Social media follower count, celebrity endorsement availability, automated interest compounding, and secondary-market short selling.
en.B: Cryptocurrency mining capacity, offshore tax-haven routing, manual paper ledger entry, and conventional credit scoring.
en.C: Guaranteed minimum fixed returns, automated loan rollovers, unrestricted third-party data monetization, and anonymous unverified investor onboarding.
en.D: Capability to handle: (a) transaction record keeping, (b) implementation of information security controls to safeguard parties' (especially fund providers') interests, (c) technology-based and/or authorization-based preventive controls to ensure Shari'ah and contractual compliance, and (d) financial reporting (for ongoing/open-ended transactions) complying with Shari'ah principles (preferably based on relevant AAOIFI FASs).
en.True answer: Capability to handle: (a) transaction record keeping, (b) implementation of information security controls to safeguard parties' (especially fund providers') interests, (c) technology-based and/or authorization-based preventive controls to ensure Shari'ah and contractual compliance, and (d) financial reporting (for ongoing/open-ended transactions) complying with Shari'ah principles (preferably based on relevant AAOIFI FASs).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 67(a)–(d) (Before commencement of an ICF issuance, the operator shall ensure—preferably through an independent certification body when not a dedicated ICF platform, or by the operator's SSB for (c) and (d)—that the platform can adequately handle: (a) record keeping of transactions; (b) implementation of information security controls; (c) technology-based and/or authorization-based preventive controls for Shari'ah and contractual compliance; and (d) financial reporting in respect of ongoing and/or open-ended transactions complying with Shari'ah principles, preferably based on relevant AAOIFI FASs).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 77–79 and Appendix D (BC29(c)) of AAOIFI GS 14, may an Islamic crowdfunding operator outsource its Shari'ah compliance function, and to whom must the SCD submit periodic Shari'ah non-compliance risk reports?
en.A: Yes—without any compromise on quality and effectiveness, the operator may outsource the Shari'ah compliance function where outsourcing is more effective or appropriate considering cost, HR, or efficiency constraints; the SCD must submit periodic reports highlighting significant Shari'ah non-compliance risks and mitigating measures to management, those charged with governance of the operator, and the Audit and Governance Committee (AGC) of the respective ICF issuance.
en.B: No—outsourcing the Shari'ah compliance function is strictly prohibited for Islamic crowdfunding operators under all circumstances.
en.C: Yes—outsourcing is allowed, and periodic Shari'ah non-compliance risk reports are submitted exclusively to the issuer's marketing team.
en.D: No—only the external financial auditor may perform Shari'ah compliance monitoring, and no risk reports are shared with the AGC.
en.True answer: Yes—without any compromise on quality and effectiveness, the operator may outsource the Shari'ah compliance function where outsourcing is more effective or appropriate considering cost, HR, or efficiency constraints; the SCD must submit periodic reports highlighting significant Shari'ah non-compliance risks and mitigating measures to management, those charged with governance of the operator, and the Audit and Governance Committee (AGC) of the respective ICF issuance.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 77–79 & Appendix D, BC29(c) (Par. 78 & BC29(c): operator may consider outsourcing the Shari'ah compliance function, without any compromise on quality and effectiveness, where outsourcing (a) may be considered more effective and/or (b) seems more appropriate considering cost, HR, or other constraints or for improving efficiency. Par. 79(d): SCD submits periodic reports highlighting significant Shari'ah non-compliance risks and implementation of mitigating measures to management, TCWG of the operator, and the AGC of the respective ICF issuance).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 97–103 and Appendix D (BC29(a)) of AAOIFI GS 14, when is an annual External Shari'ah Audit required for an ICF issuance, and what is the reporting workflow for the external Shari'ah auditor's report?
en.A: An external Shari'ah audit is mandatory for every one-time charity campaign of any size, and the draft report is submitted directly to the issuer's CEO without SSB review.
en.B: The operator and issuer (with mutual consent) must appoint an external Shari'ah auditor (at least annually) where: (a) the SSB considers it necessary given Shari'ah non-compliance risks, (b) the ICF issuance has high investment risk factors or a relatively large investment size, AND (c) the ICF issuance is ongoing and/or open-ended; the draft report must first be submitted to the SSB and finalized after due consultation with the SSB, and the final report is addressed to the fund providers and made available to all relevant stakeholders.
en.C: External Shari'ah audit is conducted once every three years solely by the operator's internal compliance officer, and the report is kept confidential from fund providers.
en.D: The issuer's financial statement auditor is strictly prohibited from serving as the external Shari'ah auditor of the ICF issuance.
en.True answer: The operator and issuer (with mutual consent) must appoint an external Shari'ah auditor (at least annually) where: (a) the SSB considers it necessary given Shari'ah non-compliance risks, (b) the ICF issuance has high investment risk factors or a relatively large investment size, AND (c) the ICF issuance is ongoing and/or open-ended; the draft report must first be submitted to the SSB and finalized after due consultation with the SSB, and the final report is addressed to the fund providers and made available to all relevant stakeholders.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 97–103 & Appendix D, BC29(a) (Par. 97–98: appointed by mutual consent of operator and issuer at minimum annually when (a) SSB considers it necessary given Shari'ah non-compliance risks, (b) ICF issuance has high investment risk factors or relatively large investment size, AND (c) ICF issuance is ongoing and/or open-ended [BC29(a) notes one-time and relatively small issuances may be exempted under proportionality]; Par. 100: issuer's financial statement auditor is eligible if qualified unless disallowed by regulator; Par. 102–103: draft report first submitted to SSB and finalized after due consultation with SSB, addressed to fund providers and made available to all relevant stakeholders).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 125–134 of AAOIFI GS 14, what is the minimum record retention period for an Islamic crowdfunding operator in the absence of a specific regulatory requirement, and what rules govern periodic financial reports and their external audit for ongoing/open-ended ICF issuances?
en.A: Minimum retention is 2 years; periodic financial reports are prepared every 3 years under IFRS without SSB involvement, and external financial audit is optional.
en.B: Minimum retention is 5 years; accounting policies are approved solely by the platform provider, and external auditors' reports are confidential to the issuer.
en.C: The operator must maintain all transaction records for the regulatory period, and at minimum 7 years in the absence of a regulatory requirement; for ongoing and/or open-ended ICF issuances, the issuer must prepare periodic financial reports at least annually (considering relevant AAOIFI FASs such as FAS 14 and FAS 34, with accounting policies approved by the SSB) and subject them to external audit at least annually, making the auditors' report available to all fund providers.
en.D: Minimum retention is 10 years; financial reporting applies solely to social donation campaigns, and external financial audit is prohibited for commercial Mudaraba campaigns.
en.True answer: The operator must maintain all transaction records for the regulatory period, and at minimum 7 years in the absence of a regulatory requirement; for ongoing and/or open-ended ICF issuances, the issuer must prepare periodic financial reports at least annually (considering relevant AAOIFI FASs such as FAS 14 and FAS 34, with accounting policies approved by the SSB) and subject them to external audit at least annually, making the auditors' report available to all fund providers.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 125–134 & Footnote 21 (Par. 125: operator maintains all necessary records of all transactions executed through the platform for the period defined by regulator, and at minimum 7 years in the absence of such regulatory requirement; Par. 127–129 & Footnote 21: issuer prepares periodic financial reports of ongoing/open-ended ICF issuances at minimum annually per relevant AAOIFI FASs [FAS 14, FAS 34, Conceptual Framework], with accounting policies approved by SSB; Par. 131–134: financial reports subject to external audit at minimum annually, with auditors' report made available to all fund providers).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Appendix B (Paragraphs B2–B3) and Appendix C (Paragraph C13) of AAOIFI GS 14, how frequently must the operator conduct a money-laundering risk assessment, and what three immediate actions must the operator take upon confirming a user match against a prohibited users database?
en.A: ML risk assessment every 5 years; upon confirmed match, send a 30-day courtesy warning while allowing pending withdrawals to settle.
en.B: ML risk assessment every 36 months; upon confirmed match, transfer the user's funds to the issuer and close the account silently without notifying authorities.
en.C: ML risk assessment is required only upon initial platform licensing; upon confirmed match, freeze funds only if the amount exceeds USD 100,000.
en.D: The operator must conduct periodic assessments of its money-laundering risks no later than every 24 months; upon confirming a user match against a prohibited users database, the operator must immediately: (a) freeze the user's funds or block the transaction if it is an existing user, (b) reject the user if the transaction has not commenced, and (c) report to the relevant authorities.
en.True answer: The operator must conduct periodic assessments of its money-laundering risks no later than every 24 months; upon confirming a user match against a prohibited users database, the operator must immediately: (a) freeze the user's funds or block the transaction if it is an existing user, (b) reject the user if the transaction has not commenced, and (c) report to the relevant authorities.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Appendix B Par. B2(a), B3(d) & Appendix C Par. C13(a)–(c) (Appendix B Par. B2(a): conduct periodic assessment of money laundering risks no later than every 24 months; Appendix C Par. C13: upon confirming identity match against database(s) of listed prohibited users, operator shall immediately: (a) freeze the user's funds or block the transaction, if it is an existing user; (b) reject the user, if the transaction has not commenced; and (c) report to the relevant authorities).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 57–61 and 91–96 of AAOIFI GS 14, which rules govern (1) Fatwa document disclosure when contracts are reviewed in translation or when an SSB member did not review the entire documentation in detail, and (2) unavoidable changes in SSB composition during the lifecycle of an ICF issuance?
en.A: (1) The Fatwa (with reasoning) is a mandatory part of the prospectus and available on the platform/website throughout the lifecycle; if contracts were reviewed in translation, that fact must be stated in the Fatwa, and if an SSB member(s) did NOT perform a detailed review of the entire documentation, that fact must be clearly stated along with the name(s) of the SSB member(s) who have NOT performed such detailed review; (2) any unavoidable change in the SSB requires the mutual consent of the operator and the issuer and must be communicated without delay to fund providers, regulators, and other relevant stakeholders.
en.B: (1) Translation review requires no disclosure, and partial review by scholars is prohibited unless all scholars sign a waiver; (2) the issuer may unilaterally remove and replace SSB members without consulting the operator.
en.C: (1) The Fatwa is kept confidential until maturity; (2) changes in the SSB require approval solely from the external financial auditor.
en.D: (1) Only the SSB Chairman's signature is required on the Fatwa, and dissenting opinions are excluded; (2) SSB changes need only be announced in the following year's annual report.
en.True answer: (1) The Fatwa (with reasoning) is a mandatory part of the prospectus and available on the platform/website throughout the lifecycle; if contracts were reviewed in translation, that fact must be stated in the Fatwa, and if an SSB member(s) did NOT perform a detailed review of the entire documentation, that fact must be clearly stated along with the name(s) of the SSB member(s) who have NOT performed such detailed review; (2) any unavoidable change in the SSB requires the mutual consent of the operator and the issuer and must be communicated without delay to fund providers, regulators, and other relevant stakeholders.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 57–61 & Par. 91–93 (Par. 58: Fatwa along with reasoning made public as mandatory part of prospectus and available on platform/website throughout lifecycle; Par. 60(a): state in Fatwa if translated version was reviewed; Par. 60(b): where review of entire documentation in detail is not performed by a member(s) of the SSB, state such fact clearly in the Fatwa along with the name(s) of the SSB member(s) who have NOT performed such detailed review; Par. 92–93: unavoidable change in SSB takes place only with mutual consent of operator and issuer and must be communicated to fund providers, regulators, and relevant stakeholders without delay).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 72 and 74 of AAOIFI GS 14, which rules govern an issuer's management of underlying operations—specifically regarding asset transfer valuation, disposal/cessation, geographic relocation, and deployment of ICF proceeds into new sub-projects?
en.A: Underlying operations may be transferred at any negotiated discount, relocated freely without notifying fund providers, and used to cross-subsidize unrelated conventional product lines.
en.B: Underlying operations must be transferred at fair market value (or reasonably close thereto, never at an unfair/exploitative value, with independent valuers recommended for material amounts); any disposal, partial cessation, or change requires business justification in fund providers' best interest, SSB approval, and communication to fund providers/regulators; relocation requires proper justification, must not jeopardize fund providers' interests, and requires pre-approval of fund providers if having a significant impact; and ICF proceeds must NOT be invested in non-Shari'ah-compliant product-line extensions or new sub-projects.
en.C: Disposal of underlying assets requires only the operator's internal marketing approval, and geographic relocation requires pre-approval solely from the external financial auditor.
en.D: Independent valuers are prohibited for material asset transfers, and proceeds may be invested in new non-Shari'ah-compliant sub-projects if purified at year-end.
en.True answer: Underlying operations must be transferred at fair market value (or reasonably close thereto, never at an unfair/exploitative value, with independent valuers recommended for material amounts); any disposal, partial cessation, or change requires business justification in fund providers' best interest, SSB approval, and communication to fund providers/regulators; relocation requires proper justification, must not jeopardize fund providers' interests, and requires pre-approval of fund providers if having a significant impact; and ICF proceeds must NOT be invested in non-Shari'ah-compliant product-line extensions or new sub-projects.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 72(a)–(f) & Par. 74(a)–(e) (Par. 72(d): transferred at fair market value or reasonably close thereto, never unfair/exploitative, independent valuers/experts highly recommended for material amounts; Par. 72(e): disposal/partial cessation/change justified from business perspective in best interest of fund providers, approved by SSB, and communicated to fund providers and regulators; Par. 72(f): no relocation without proper justification, must not jeopardize fund providers' interests, and any act having significant impact requires pre-approval of fund providers; Par. 74(e): proceeds shall not be invested in extensions of product lines or new sub-projects outside originally envisaged operations which are not Shari'ah compliant).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Comparing early termination of an ICF issuance (Paragraphs 104–105) versus restructuring or rescheduling of an ICF issuance (Paragraphs 106–110) under AAOIFI GS 14, which statement is completely accurate?
en.A: Early termination may be executed unilaterally by the issuer at any time without SSB approval, whereas restructuring is permitted for any commercial reason upon simple majority vote of the operator's board.
en.B: Early termination requires no stakeholder communication if triggered by a regulatory order, whereas restructuring allows shifting all commercial losses onto fund providers while preserving issuer equity returns.
en.C: Early termination occurs via five triggers (material breach self-initiating termination per prospectus, mutual agreement, issuer call option, trustee/fund providers unilateral termination upon default/potential default, or regulator order) and requires SSB approval of both the acceptability of the termination reason and the modus operandi, regulator/court approval where applicable, stakeholder communication/approval, and no unjustifiable material loss to fund providers (unless inevitable to prevent greater losses); restructuring or rescheduling occurs as an exception in two scenarios (issuer default/potential default or acquisition/merger/corporate restructuring), must preserve the initial equilibrium of financial benefits/rights (or achieve an equitable arrangement), and requires thorough review and approval by the SSB, fund providers (through the trustee if applicable), and (where required) the regulator.
en.D: Restructuring and early termination are completely prohibited for all Islamic crowdfunding issuances.
en.True answer: Early termination occurs via five triggers (material breach self-initiating termination per prospectus, mutual agreement, issuer call option, trustee/fund providers unilateral termination upon default/potential default, or regulator order) and requires SSB approval of both the acceptability of the termination reason and the modus operandi, regulator/court approval where applicable, stakeholder communication/approval, and no unjustifiable material loss to fund providers (unless inevitable to prevent greater losses); restructuring or rescheduling occurs as an exception in two scenarios (issuer default/potential default or acquisition/merger/corporate restructuring), must preserve the initial equilibrium of financial benefits/rights (or achieve an equitable arrangement), and requires thorough review and approval by the SSB, fund providers (through the trustee if applicable), and (where required) the regulator.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 104–110 (Par. 104–105: 5 triggers for termination and 4 core principles: (a) regulator/court approval where applicable, (b) SSB decides if reason is acceptable under Shari'ah and specifically approves modus operandi, (c) deliberation/communication and approval of stakeholders, (d) unless inevitable [e.g. not terminating would increase losses], shall not result in unjustifiable material loss to fund providers. Par. 106–110: restructuring/rescheduling occurs as an exception in 2 scenarios [issuer default/potential default or acquisition/merger/corporate restructuring], preserves initial equilibrium of financial benefits/rights or achieves equitable arrangement, and requires thorough review and approval by SSB, fund providers [through trustee if applicable], and regulator where required).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 44 and 118–121 of AAOIFI GS 14, which combination of prospectus disclosures and platform disclaimers is mandatory?
en.A: The prospectus is static and may never be updated after launch; the operator is barred from ever investing in any ICF issuance; and the operator guarantees the issuer's commercial profit projections.
en.B: Secular court risks regarding Shari'ah contract interpretation are omitted from the prospectus, and the operator assumes primary legal responsibility for the issuer's day-to-day Shari'ah compliance.
en.C: Fee structures and cooling-off rights are disclosed only after a fund provider transfers money into the trust account.
en.D: For an open-ended ICF issuance, the prospectus is a live document that must be updated periodically; the prospectus must disclose whether and to what extent the operator invests in the ICF issuance (along with independence, early redemption, tradability, and liquidation safeguards) as well as the risk that local courts of law may not accept Shari'ah principles for interpreting contracts (alongside remedial options like Shari'ah-based arbitration); and the operator must display disclaimers stating non-guarantee of the issuer's performance and clarifying that responsibility for Shari'ah compliance rests primarily on the issuer.
en.True answer: For an open-ended ICF issuance, the prospectus is a live document that must be updated periodically; the prospectus must disclose whether and to what extent the operator invests in the ICF issuance (along with independence, early redemption, tradability, and liquidation safeguards) as well as the risk that local courts of law may not accept Shari'ah principles for interpreting contracts (alongside remedial options like Shari'ah-based arbitration); and the operator must display disclaimers stating non-guarantee of the issuer's performance and clarifying that responsibility for Shari'ah compliance rests primarily on the issuer.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 44, Par. 118, Par. 119(i), Par. 120(d) & Par. 121(e), (i) (Par. 118 & BC34: prospectus is a live document if the ICF issuance is open-ended and shall be updated periodically; Par. 44 & Par. 119(i): discloses whether/to what extent operator invests in the ICF issuance and safeguards for independence/redemption/liquidation; Par. 120(d): discloses risk that courts of law may not accept Shari'ah principles for contract interpretation along with remedial options e.g. Shari'ah-based arbitration; Par. 121(e) & (i): operator disclaimer includes non-guarantee on issuer's performance and user disclaimer on Shari'ah compliance stating that responsibility for Shari'ah compliance is primarily on the issuer).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 138–139 of AAOIFI GS 14, which rules govern the presentation of disclosures, prospective financial projections, risk prominence, and user education on an Islamic crowdfunding platform?
en.A: Disclosures must be concise and focused (avoiding excessive confusing information and avoiding very fine print/small font sizes); investment risks must be given equal prominence with information on product benefits (without exaggerating benefits); prospective financial information may be included only when a reasonable basis exists and, where amounts are material, must be subject to independent assessment and assurance; and the operator must educate users via text/video/audio explanations, articles/webinars, and continuously updated FAQs.
en.B: Offering documents should maximize technical legal length using fine-print footnotes for risk warnings, highlight projected returns in large bold fonts while minimizing risk disclosures, and omit FAQs to prevent user inquiries.
en.C: Prospective financial projections may be published without any underlying basis whenever an early-stage start-up wants to attract retail investors faster.
en.D: User education is solely the responsibility of the external Shari'ah auditor, while the operator is prohibited from hosting webinars or educational videos.
en.True answer: Disclosures must be concise and focused (avoiding excessive confusing information and avoiding very fine print/small font sizes); investment risks must be given equal prominence with information on product benefits (without exaggerating benefits); prospective financial information may be included only when a reasonable basis exists and, where amounts are material, must be subject to independent assessment and assurance; and the operator must educate users via text/video/audio explanations, articles/webinars, and continuously updated FAQs.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Par. 138(a)–(h) & Par. 139(a)–(d) (Par. 138(b), (d): excessive information may be counter-productive and confusing, thus disclosures shall be concise and focused, and very fine print and small font sizes shall be avoided; Par. 138(g): benefits shall not be exaggerated, and investment risks should have equal prominence with information on product benefits; Par. 138(h): prospective financial information included only if reasonable basis exists, and where amounts are material, subject to independent assessments and assurance; Par. 139(b)–(d): operator provides text/video/audio explanations, videos/articles/webinars/webcasts, and continually displays and updates FAQs).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question: Under Appendix C (Paragraphs C1–C10) of AAOIFI GS 14, which requirements govern personal information sharing with third parties (including related parties) and cyber risk preparedness?
en.A: The operator may freely sell user contact lists to related corporate affiliates without user consent, and business continuity plans are optional for online platforms.
en.B: Concerned employees must sign a declaration of adherence to the personal data policy referencing AAOIFI's Code of Ethics; the operator may share user information with a third party (including a related party) ONLY after obtaining prior user permission (updating the user on the third party's identity and purpose of sharing) and must always give the user an 'opt-out' option from previously given permission; and for cyber risk management, the operator must maintain an approved and tested Business Continuity Plan / Disaster Recovery Plan (BCP/DRP) and assess cyber risk impact before undertaking new activities, M&A, new technology adoption, or outsourcing.
en.C: Once a user grants data-sharing permission during registration, that consent is irrevocable and cannot be opted out of later.
en.D: Cyber risk impact assessments apply only after a major data breach occurs, and employees are exempt from signing data-protection adherence declarations.
en.True answer: Concerned employees must sign a declaration of adherence to the personal data policy referencing AAOIFI's Code of Ethics; the operator may share user information with a third party (including a related party) ONLY after obtaining prior user permission (updating the user on the third party's identity and purpose of sharing) and must always give the user an 'opt-out' option from previously given permission; and for cyber risk management, the operator must maintain an approved and tested Business Continuity Plan / Disaster Recovery Plan (BCP/DRP) and assess cyber risk impact before undertaking new activities, M&A, new technology adoption, or outsourcing.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14, Appendix C, Par. C1(a), C5–C8 & C10(c)–(d) (Par. C1(a): concerned employees sign declaration on adherence to personal information policy referencing AAOIFI Code of Ethics; Par. C8: operator may share user information with a third party, including a related party, ONLY after obtaining prior permission including updating user about identity of third party and purpose, and the option shall always be available to the user to 'opt-out' from previously given permission; Par. C10(c)–(d): assess cyber risk impact when undertaking new activities, investment decisions, M&A, new technology adoption, and outsourcing, and maintain an approved and tested BCP/DRP).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question:
In March 2024, an Islamic crowdfunding platform operator prepares to host a high-risk, material, ongoing Mudaraba campaign. Evaluate the following four pre-issuance governance actions:
(1) The issuer applying to raise funds is a wholly owned subsidiary of a public-listed holding company; the operator accepts the issuer on its own initiative without obtaining regulatory allowance.
(2) Once fund providers pledge 100% of the targeted USD 2 million offering amount, the operator instructs the independent trustee to release the funds immediately to the issuer, even though 5 days remain in the jurisdiction's mandatory statutory cooling-off period.
(3) By mutual consent of the operator and issuer, the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB) function for the campaign is outsourced to a Shari'ah advisory firm that nominates three identified Shari'ah scholars who each individually meet all eligibility criteria.
(4) Because the issuer has no audit committee of its own, the operator and issuer establish a 3-member Audit and Governance Committee (AGC) chaired by the operator's Chief Executive Officer, with one nominee from the issuer and one nominee from the trustee.
According to AAOIFI GS 14, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—subsidiaries of listed companies are eligible; (2) Compliant—reaching 100% target overrides cooling-off periods; (3) Non-compliant—outsourcing SSB is prohibited; (4) Compliant—operator's CEO may chair the AGC.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 32(b), a public-listed company or a subsidiary thereof is ineligible to be an issuer unless specifically allowed by the respective regulator; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 27(c)(i)–(iii), trust funds may be released ONLY after ALL three conditions are met: target achieved, no material adverse change, AND expiration of the cooling-off period (if required by the regulator); (3) Compliant—Par. 46(c) explicitly permits outsourcing the SSB function to a Shari'ah advisory firm with mutual consent of operator and issuer, subject to nominating at least three identified, individually eligible persons as SSB members; (4) Non-compliant—under Par. 62–63, an AGC is required for this high-risk ongoing issuance and MUST be chaired by an INDEPENDENT member appointed by mutual consent of the operator and issuer (not the operator's CEO), with equal nominees from issuer and operator.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 32(b), a public-listed company or a subsidiary thereof is ineligible to be an issuer unless specifically allowed by the respective regulator; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 27(c)(i)–(iii), trust funds may be released ONLY after ALL three conditions are met: target achieved, no material adverse change, AND expiration of the cooling-off period (if required by the regulator); (3) Compliant—Par. 46(c) explicitly permits outsourcing the SSB function to a Shari'ah advisory firm with mutual consent of operator and issuer, subject to nominating at least three identified, individually eligible persons as SSB members; (4) Non-compliant—under Par. 62–63, an AGC is required for this high-risk ongoing issuance and MUST be chaired by an INDEPENDENT member appointed by mutual consent of the operator and issuer (not the operator's CEO), with equal nominees from issuer and operator.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 32(b) declares a public-listed company or a subsidiary thereof ineligible to be an issuer unless allowed by the respective regulator; (2) Par. 27(c)(i)–(iii) prohibits releasing trust funds until (i) targeted amount is achieved, (ii) no material adverse change occurs during the offer period, AND (iii) the cooling-off period (if required by regulator) has expired; (3) Par. 46(c) permits outsourcing SSB to a Shari'ah advisory firm by mutual consent of operator and issuer subject to nominating at least three identified, individually eligible persons; (4) Par. 62–63 mandate an AGC for a high-risk/material ongoing ICF issuance lacking an issuer audit committee, requiring an INDEPENDENT chairman appointed by mutual consent of operator and issuer and an equal number of nominees from issuer and operator (making the operator's CEO invalid as chairman).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 14: Islamic Crowdfunding Governance
en.Question:
During the operational lifecycle of an open-ended, high-risk Ijarah Islamic crowdfunding issuance, examine the following four actions by the operator and issuer:
(1) Due to internal HR constraints, the operator outsources its Shari'ah compliance function to a specialized Islamic finance compliance firm without compromising quality or effectiveness.
(2) To lower operating expenses, the issuer relocates the core underlying leased machinery to a distant region—a move having a significant impact on fund providers—after obtaining SSB approval, without seeking pre-approval from the fund providers.
(3) Over two years of operation, the issuer never updates the initial prospectus and conducts no external Shari'ah audit, arguing that a one-time pre-launch Fatwa suffices for an open-ended issuance.
(4) The operator shares fund providers' personal contact and investment records with a related marketing affiliate without obtaining prior user permission, and sets its transaction record retention policy at 3 years (in a jurisdiction with no statutory retention period).
According to AAOIFI GS 14, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Non-compliant—operators may never outsource their Shari'ah compliance function; (2) Compliant—SSB approval suffices for relocating underlying operations; (3) Compliant—open-ended prospectuses remain static and external Shari'ah audits are optional; (4) Compliant—sharing data with related affiliates requires no user permission and 3-year retention suffices.
en.B: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.D: (1) Compliant—under Par. 78 & BC29(c), the operator may outsource the Shari'ah compliance function without compromising quality/effectiveness where appropriate due to cost/HR constraints or efficiency; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 72(f), relocating underlying operations with a significant impact on fund providers may be performed ONLY with the pre-approval of the fund providers; (3) Non-compliant—under Par. 118, the prospectus of an open-ended ICF issuance is a live document that must be updated periodically, and under Par. 97–98, a high-risk ongoing/open-ended ICF issuance MUST undergo an external Shari'ah audit at minimum annually; (4) Non-compliant—Appendix C Par. C8 prohibits sharing user information with any third party (including a related party) without prior user permission (specifying third-party identity and purpose), and Par. 125 requires retaining transaction records for at minimum 7 years in the absence of a regulatory requirement.
en.True answer: (1) Compliant—under Par. 78 & BC29(c), the operator may outsource the Shari'ah compliance function without compromising quality/effectiveness where appropriate due to cost/HR constraints or efficiency; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 72(f), relocating underlying operations with a significant impact on fund providers may be performed ONLY with the pre-approval of the fund providers; (3) Non-compliant—under Par. 118, the prospectus of an open-ended ICF issuance is a live document that must be updated periodically, and under Par. 97–98, a high-risk ongoing/open-ended ICF issuance MUST undergo an external Shari'ah audit at minimum annually; (4) Non-compliant—Appendix C Par. C8 prohibits sharing user information with any third party (including a related party) without prior user permission (specifying third-party identity and purpose), and Par. 125 requires retaining transaction records for at minimum 7 years in the absence of a regulatory requirement.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 14 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 78 & Appendix D BC29(c) allow the operator to outsource the Shari'ah compliance function without compromising quality/effectiveness when more effective or appropriate for cost/HR/efficiency reasons; (2) Par. 72(f) requires proper justification, non-jeopardy of fund providers' interests, and pre-approval of fund providers before relocating underlying operations in a manner having a significant impact; (3) Par. 118 mandates periodic updates to the prospectus of an open-ended ICF issuance as a live document, and Par. 97–98 require at least an annual external Shari'ah audit for high-risk/large ongoing or open-ended ICF issuances; (4) Appendix C Par. C8 prohibits sharing user data with third parties (including related parties) without prior user permission updating identity and purpose, and Par. 125 mandates retaining transaction records for at minimum 7 years when local regulations specify no period.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope of AAOIFI GS 15 ('Syndicated Financing'), its relationship with AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard (SS) 24 and Sukuk issuances, and its effective date?
en.A: GS 15 supersedes AAOIFI SS 24 ('Syndicated Financing'), excludes all guidance relevant to Sukuk issuances, and became effective retroactively on 1 July 2021.
en.B: GS 15 complements and is read in conjunction with AAOIFI SS 24 ('Syndicated Financing'); its guidance—particularly regarding the awarding of mandate and transaction close phases—also applies mutatis mutandis to listed and unlisted Sukuk issuances insofar as not in conflict with GS 12 ('Sukuk Governance'); and it is effective for syndicated financing transactions executed on or after 1 July 2024.
en.C: GS 15 applies solely to bilateral single-bank Murabaha facilities and becomes effective on 1 January 2027.
en.D: GS 15 overrides AAOIFI GS 12 ('Sukuk Governance') in all sovereign Sukuk offerings and applies only to the post-maturity liquidation phase.
en.True answer: GS 15 complements and is read in conjunction with AAOIFI SS 24 ('Syndicated Financing'); its guidance—particularly regarding the awarding of mandate and transaction close phases—also applies mutatis mutandis to listed and unlisted Sukuk issuances insofar as not in conflict with GS 12 ('Sukuk Governance'); and it is effective for syndicated financing transactions executed on or after 1 July 2024.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Introductory Note (p. 3), Par. 3–6, Par. 52 & Appendix C, BC1–BC4 (Par. 3: complements and shall be read in conjunction with AAOIFI SS 24 'Syndicated Financing'; Par. 6 & Footnote 1: guidance, particularly in respect of awarding of mandate phase and transaction close phase, applies mutatis mutandis on listed and unlisted Sukuk issuances insofar as not in conflict with GS 12 'Sukuk Governance'; Par. 52: effective on syndicated financing transactions executed on or after 1 July 2024).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 7 and Appendix C (BC23–BC24) of AAOIFI GS 15, how are the roles of 'Facility agent' and 'Security agent' defined in a syndicated financing transaction?
en.A: A facility agent (if appointed) is a participant IFI responsible for ongoing coordination with the customer on behalf of the syndication participants and delegated with all or certain responsibilities of the lead arranger through the inter-financier agreement, whereas a security agent (fiduciary/trustee) is an entity appointed by the syndication participants (or lead arranger on their behalf) to hold and/or enforce rights on the syndicated financing underlying assets and/or securities on their behalf.
en.B: A facility agent must always be a conventional commercial bank, whereas a security agent is an internal department of the borrowing customer.
en.C: Both the facility agent and security agent are appointed exclusively by the national central bank and cannot be assumed by the lead arranger even with stakeholder consent.
en.D: A security agent handles marketing and investor roadshows prior to transaction close, whereas a facility agent issues the Provisional Fatwa.
en.True answer: A facility agent (if appointed) is a participant IFI responsible for ongoing coordination with the customer on behalf of the syndication participants and delegated with all or certain responsibilities of the lead arranger through the inter-financier agreement, whereas a security agent (fiduciary/trustee) is an entity appointed by the syndication participants (or lead arranger on their behalf) to hold and/or enforce rights on the syndicated financing underlying assets and/or securities on their behalf.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 7(c), Par. 7(p), Par. 35 & Appendix C, BC23–BC24 (Par. 7(c): facility agent, if so appointed, is a participant IFI responsible for ongoing coordination with the customer on behalf of the syndication participants and delegated with all or certain responsibilities of the lead arranger through the inter-financier agreement; Par. 7(p): security agent, also referred to as fiduciary or trustee, is an entity appointed by the syndication participants or lead arranger on their behalf to serve as an agent to hold and/or enforce rights on the syndicated financing underlying assets and/or securities).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 8–9 of AAOIFI GS 15, which governance principle addresses fee sharing among arrangers and profit/capital distribution among syndication participants, and which key governance pillar does it support?
en.A: Principle 1 ('Effective Shari'ah compliance structures'), which allows the lead arranger to retain 100% of arrangement fees regardless of work performed by co-arrangers.
en.B: Principle 6 ('Transparency and mutual disclosures'), which requires equal fee splits among all participants regardless of their contractual roles.
en.C: Principle 3 ('Equitable and fair treatment of, and amongst, syndication participants'), aligned with the pillar of Fairness, which requires equitable and unbiased treatment particularly regarding profit distribution and return of capital, and stipulates that as far as possible, fee sharing amongst arrangers should be commensurate with the responsibilities and work performed by the respective arrangers.
en.D: Principle 7 ('Code of conduct and ethics'), which prohibits arrangers from charging any arrangement or agency fees.
en.True answer: Principle 3 ('Equitable and fair treatment of, and amongst, syndication participants'), aligned with the pillar of Fairness, which requires equitable and unbiased treatment particularly regarding profit distribution and return of capital, and stipulates that as far as possible, fee sharing amongst arrangers should be commensurate with the responsibilities and work performed by the respective arrangers.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 8(c) & Par. 9 Principle 3 (Principle 3 'Equitable and fair treatment of, and amongst, syndication participants' corresponds to the pillar of Fairness and states that the lead arranger and customer shall ensure equitable and unbiased treatment amongst syndication participants regarding distribution of profit and return of capital, and that as far as possible, fee sharing amongst the arrangers should be commensurate with the responsibilities and work performed by the respective arrangers).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 14–17 of AAOIFI GS 15, what is a 'Provisional Fatwa' at the awarding of mandate phase, who procures it, and what three purposes does it serve?
en.A: A final, unchangeable Shari'ah ruling issued by the customer's legal counsel to bypass individual bank SSBs.
en.B: A credit risk rating certificate issued by an external rating agency prior to signing the mandate.
en.C: A post-close audit report issued by the external Shari'ah auditor after funds are disbursed to the customer.
en.D: An initial Fatwa procured by the lead arranger (or facility agent, as applicable) from its SSB approving the basic transaction structure for documentation purposes, which facilitates: (a) proposed syndication participants gaining confidence in the Shari'ah compliance of the proposed structure prior to review by their own SSBs, (b) the documentation team drafting the relevant transaction documents, and (c) the respective SSBs of proposed syndication participants understanding the transaction structure once final documents are presented for approval.
en.True answer: An initial Fatwa procured by the lead arranger (or facility agent, as applicable) from its SSB approving the basic transaction structure for documentation purposes, which facilitates: (a) proposed syndication participants gaining confidence in the Shari'ah compliance of the proposed structure prior to review by their own SSBs, (b) the documentation team drafting the relevant transaction documents, and (c) the respective SSBs of proposed syndication participants understanding the transaction structure once final documents are presented for approval.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 7(k) & Par. 17(a)–(c) (Par. 17 states the lead arranger or facility agent, as applicable, shall procure a provisional Fatwa from its SSB to approve the basic structure of the syndicated financing transaction for documentation purposes, facilitating: (a) proposed syndication participants gaining confidence in Shari'ah compliance prior to review of their respective SSBs; (b) documentation team drafting relevant transaction documents; and (c) respective SSBs of proposed syndication participants understanding the transaction structure once final documents are presented for approval).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 18–19 of AAOIFI GS 15, what three circumstances may give rise to a conflict of interest at the time of awarding a mandate, and when must a potential arranger decline a mandate?
en.A: Conflicts may arise from (a) an existing or prior relationship with the potential customer (or its associated entities/persons), (b) an existing financial or non-financial exposure with the potential customer (or associated entities/persons), and/or (c) a fee arrangement on terms different from market norms; a potential arranger must disclose any possible conflict (subject to regulatory customer-confidentiality rules) and shall NOT accept a mandate if it is established that accepting it will jeopardize the interest of a party or parties to the syndicated financing transaction.
en.B: Conflicts arise only when two arrangers share the same external auditor, and an arranger may accept any mandate as long as it charges below-market arrangement fees.
en.C: Existing credit exposure to the customer never constitutes a conflict of interest, and customer confidentiality rules prohibit disclosing conflicts to co-arrangers.
en.D: A potential arranger may accept a mandate that jeopardizes syndicate participants' interests provided the customer signs a private indemnity letter.
en.True answer: Conflicts may arise from (a) an existing or prior relationship with the potential customer (or its associated entities/persons), (b) an existing financial or non-financial exposure with the potential customer (or associated entities/persons), and/or (c) a fee arrangement on terms different from market norms; a potential arranger must disclose any possible conflict (subject to regulatory customer-confidentiality rules) and shall NOT accept a mandate if it is established that accepting it will jeopardize the interest of a party or parties to the syndicated financing transaction.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 18(a)–(c) & Par. 19(a)–(c) (Par. 18 identifies three sources of conflict at mandate award: (a) existing or prior relationship with potential customer or associated entities/persons; (b) existing financial or non-financial exposure with potential customer or associated entities/persons; and/or (c) fee arrangement on terms and conditions different from market norms. Par. 19(b)–(c) require disclosing possible conflicts to potential customer and other potential arrangers [subject to regulatory confidentiality rules] and prohibit accepting a mandate if established that it will jeopardize the interest of a party or parties to the transaction).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 20–21 and Appendix C (BC10–BC12) of AAOIFI GS 15, when is a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement (involving both IFIs and conventional financial institutions) permitted, and what restriction applies to an IFI participating in it?
en.A: Hybrid arrangements are encouraged as the preferred structure, and an IFI lead arranger may actively solicit conventional banks and serve as facility agent for the conventional tranche.
en.B: Hybrid arrangements are generally discouraged but permitted if the overall purpose/use of assets or proceeds is Shari'ah compliant AND either: (a) the customer's financing needs cannot be met by IFIs alone and the customer (not the IFIs, without any IFI involvement) approaches CFIs at its absolute discretion, or (b) the customer has no Shari'ah preference, has already awarded the mandate to a CFI arranger, and includes a separate Shari'ah-compliant tranche; furthermore, the Shari'ah tranche's arranger must be limited to IFIs, and an IFI must NOT in any way lead, arrange, or facilitate (including acting as an agent) for the conventional financing.
en.C: Hybrid arrangements are strictly prohibited under all circumstances, even when the customer independently arranges a separate conventional tranche.
en.D: An IFI may arrange the conventional interest-bearing tranche provided the arrangement fees earned from the conventional tranche are donated to charity.
en.True answer: Hybrid arrangements are generally discouraged but permitted if the overall purpose/use of assets or proceeds is Shari'ah compliant AND either: (a) the customer's financing needs cannot be met by IFIs alone and the customer (not the IFIs, without any IFI involvement) approaches CFIs at its absolute discretion, or (b) the customer has no Shari'ah preference, has already awarded the mandate to a CFI arranger, and includes a separate Shari'ah-compliant tranche; furthermore, the Shari'ah tranche's arranger must be limited to IFIs, and an IFI must NOT in any way lead, arrange, or facilitate (including acting as an agent) for the conventional financing.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 20(a)–(b), Par. 21(a)–(d) & Appendix C, BC10–BC12 (Par. 20 allows hybrid arrangement if overall purpose/use of assets or proceeds is Shari'ah compliant and either (a) customer's needs cannot be met by IFIs alone and customer—not IFIs, without any involvement of IFIs—approaches CFIs at customer's absolute discretion, or (b) customer has no Shari'ah preference, already mandated a CFI arranger, and includes a separate Shari'ah-compliant tranche. Par. 21(b) & (d) limit arranger(s) of the Shari'ah tranche to IFIs and prohibit an IFI from leading, arranging, or facilitating—including acting as an agent—for conventional financing in any manner whatsoever).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 7(g), Paragraphs 24–25, and Appendix C (BC5–BC7, BC13–BC15) of AAOIFI GS 15, why did the Board adopt the term 'inter-financier agreement' instead of 'inter-creditor agreement,' and why does GS 15 omit an illustrative template for this agreement?
en.A: Because Islamic banks are legally prohibited from signing written agreements with each other, and templates are banned by AAOIFI's charter.
en.B: Because 'inter-creditor' applies only to sovereign Sukuk, and AAOIFI plans to publish a mandatory rigid template in 2028.
en.C: The Board rejected 'inter-creditor agreement' to avoid similarity with conventional transactions and reflect the true nature of Islamic financing (which is not necessarily credit or borrowing), and decided to prescribe minimum contents rather than an illustrative format to avoid overlapping with the International Islamic Financial Market (IIFM), which had already initiated a documentation standard project on inter-financier agreements.
en.D: Because an inter-financier agreement is purely an informal verbal understanding among syndication participants with no minimum content requirements.
en.True answer: The Board rejected 'inter-creditor agreement' to avoid similarity with conventional transactions and reflect the true nature of Islamic financing (which is not necessarily credit or borrowing), and decided to prescribe minimum contents rather than an illustrative format to avoid overlapping with the International Islamic Financial Market (IIFM), which had already initiated a documentation standard project on inter-financier agreements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 7(g), Par. 24–25, Footnote 6 & Appendix C, BC5–BC7, BC13–BC15 (BC15: rejected 'inter-creditor agreement' to avoid similarity with conventional transactions and reflect the true nature of Islamic financing [not necessarily credit or borrowing], adopting 'inter-financier agreement'; BC6–BC7: included minimum contents in Par. 25(a)–(m) rather than an illustrative format to avoid overlap with IIFM's initiated documentation standard project on inter-creditor/inter-financier agreements).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 26–27 and Appendix C (BC16–BC19) of AAOIFI GS 15, how must inter-financier agreements be structured in a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement?
en.A: All IFIs and conventional banks sign a single unified inter-creditor agreement governed by conventional LIBOR/SOFR default waterfall rules.
en.B: Only the conventional banks sign an inter-financier agreement, while IFIs rely solely on verbal understandings.
en.C: A single joint agreement is mandatory unless the customer requests separate agreements.
en.D: Two distinct inter-financier agreements must be separately prepared and signed by the syndication participants for the Shari'ah-compliant tranche and the conventional financing tranche respectively; IFIs are not allowed to sign the same inter-financier agreement with conventional banks, and the Shari'ah tranche's agreement must identify its IFI lead arranger(s) and specify a Shari'ah-compliant mechanism for realizing and liquidating security/underlying assets upon default.
en.True answer: Two distinct inter-financier agreements must be separately prepared and signed by the syndication participants for the Shari'ah-compliant tranche and the conventional financing tranche respectively; IFIs are not allowed to sign the same inter-financier agreement with conventional banks, and the Shari'ah tranche's agreement must identify its IFI lead arranger(s) and specify a Shari'ah-compliant mechanism for realizing and liquidating security/underlying assets upon default.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 7(g) Footnote 2, Par. 26–27 & Appendix C, BC16–BC19 (Par. 26: in case of a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement, two distinct inter-financier agreements shall be separately prepared and signed by the syndication participants for the Shari'ah-compliant financing tranche and the conventional financing tranche respectively; BC18: IFIs are not allowed to sign the same inter-financier agreement; Par. 27: specifies lead arranger(s) for the Shari'ah tranche, ensures enforceability of Shari'ah principles/rules, and specifies the Shari'ah-compliant mechanism applicable in case of default for realization and liquidation of security/underlying assets).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 31–33 of AAOIFI GS 15, which disclosures must the lead arranger make to the customer during the transaction close phase?
en.A: (a) Allocation of financing among syndication participants (identifying any preferential allocations or allocations with a potential conflict of interest, e.g., to associated entities), (b) the basis of allocation particularly where total possible participation surpasses the mandated amount (oversubscription), and (c) details and basis of underwriting by itself or any other IFI—while allowing the customer reasonable time and opportunity to evaluate the legal contracts to be executed.
en.B: Only the final total profit rate, keeping syndicate allocation percentages and underwriting arrangements strictly secret from the customer.
en.C: Only the names of conventional banks in the syndicate, omitting any preferential allocations made to the lead arranger's affiliates.
en.D: Disclosures at transaction close are optional once the customer has signed the initial mandate letter.
en.True answer: (a) Allocation of financing among syndication participants (identifying any preferential allocations or allocations with a potential conflict of interest, e.g., to associated entities), (b) the basis of allocation particularly where total possible participation surpasses the mandated amount (oversubscription), and (c) details and basis of underwriting by itself or any other IFI—while allowing the customer reasonable time and opportunity to evaluate the legal contracts to be executed.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 31(a)–(c) & Par. 32 (Par. 31 requires the lead arranger to disclose to the customer until transaction close: (a) allocation of financing among syndication participants, identifying any preferential allocations or allocations with a potential conflict of interest e.g. to associated entities; (b) basis of allocation particularly where total possible participation surpasses the mandated amount; and (c) details and basis of underwriting by itself or any other IFI. Par. 32 requires apprising the customer of agreed terms and allowing reasonable time and opportunity to evaluate legal contracts).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 40–42 of AAOIFI GS 15, how are Shari'ah compliance responsibilities, issue sharing, and a Change of Fatwa handled during the continuity of a syndicated financing transaction?
en.A: Only the lead arranger's SSB is responsible for Shari'ah compliance across the entire syndicate, and other participants are barred from reviewing the transaction under their own SSBs.
en.B: Each syndication participant is responsible for ensuring Shari'ah compliance and conforming to relevant AAOIFI GSs (SSB, Shari'ah compliance function, internal and external Shari'ah audit) in respect of its own proportionate share; any participant identifying a Shari'ah compliance issue must immediately inform the lead arranger (who informs all participants after consulting the customer); and if a participant's SSB decides to change its Fatwa, it must follow AAOIFI SS 29, promptly inform other participants and the customer, and collaborate to find a Shari'ah-compliant solution.
en.C: If one participant's SSB changes its Fatwa, the entire syndicated transaction is automatically voided without notifying the customer.
en.D: Shari'ah compliance issues discovered during continuity must be kept secret from other syndication participants until final maturity.
en.True answer: Each syndication participant is responsible for ensuring Shari'ah compliance and conforming to relevant AAOIFI GSs (SSB, Shari'ah compliance function, internal and external Shari'ah audit) in respect of its own proportionate share; any participant identifying a Shari'ah compliance issue must immediately inform the lead arranger (who informs all participants after consulting the customer); and if a participant's SSB decides to change its Fatwa, it must follow AAOIFI SS 29, promptly inform other participants and the customer, and collaborate to find a Shari'ah-compliant solution.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 40–42 & Appendix C, BC8–BC9 (Par. 40: each syndication participant ensures Shari'ah compliance and conforms to relevant AAOIFI GSs [SSB, Shari'ah compliance, internal & external Shari'ah audit] insofar as its respective proportionate share is concerned; Par. 41: participant identifying an issue immediately informs lead arranger, who after due consultation with customer informs all participants so they collaborate on a solution; Par. 42: if a participant's SSB changes its Fatwa, it follows SS 29, promptly informs other participants and customer, and collaborates to find a Shari'ah-compliant solution).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 43–44 of AAOIFI GS 15, what four events may trigger an early settlement of a syndicated financing transaction before intended maturity, and what core principle applies to the modus operandi of early settlement?
en.A: Early settlement occurs only upon bankruptcy court order, and requires no SSB approval if the customer pays a 5% prepayment penalty.
en.B: Any single minority syndicate participant may unilaterally force early settlement of the entire syndicate at will without consulting co-participants.
en.C: Early settlement may occur (after regulatory clearance where applicable and SSB approvals) when: (a) parties mutually agree, (b) the customer exercises its unilateral contractual option for early settlement, (c) syndication participants collectively exercise their option of unilateral termination of underlying contract(s) due to default/potential default, or (d) the regulator orders early settlement; the SSBs of respective syndication participants must specifically approve the modus operandi of early settlement (if not already approved at the time of transaction documents), alongside stakeholder deliberation/approval and fair treatment.
en.D: Early settlement is prohibited in Islamic syndicated financing; all facilities must run strictly to their original contractual maturity date.
en.True answer: Early settlement may occur (after regulatory clearance where applicable and SSB approvals) when: (a) parties mutually agree, (b) the customer exercises its unilateral contractual option for early settlement, (c) syndication participants collectively exercise their option of unilateral termination of underlying contract(s) due to default/potential default, or (d) the regulator orders early settlement; the SSBs of respective syndication participants must specifically approve the modus operandi of early settlement (if not already approved at the time of transaction documents), alongside stakeholder deliberation/approval and fair treatment.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 43(a)–(d) & Par. 44(a)–(c) (Par. 43 lists four triggers for early settlement after regulatory clearance and SSB approvals: (a) mutual agreement of parties; (b) customer exercises unilateral contractual option of early settlement; (c) syndication participants collectively exercise unilateral termination option due to default or potential default; (d) regulator orders early settlement. Par. 44(a)–(c) requires: (a) SSBs of respective syndication participants specifically approve modus operandi of early settlement if not already approved with transaction documents; (b) deliberation, communication, and approval with participants and customer; (c) fair treatment to parties).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 45–46 of AAOIFI GS 15, what rules govern an early exit (pre-exit) by an individual syndication participant before maturity?
en.A: A syndication participant may sell its participation share freely on the open market at any price without notifying the lead arranger or complying with debt-sale Shari'ah rules.
en.B: Early exit by an individual participant is strictly prohibited until all co-participants exit simultaneously.
en.C: An exiting participant deals directly with incoming buyers behind closed doors and notifies the customer only 6 months after transferring its stake.
en.D: A participant may exit early per the inter-financier agreement while complying with contractual terms and Shari'ah principles (particularly those governing sale and settlement of debt, if a debt), and must at a minimum: (a) inform the customer (and obtain prior approval if required) through the lead arranger of early exit and replacement, (b) inform other participants through the lead arranger/facility agent/security agent with its rationale if required, (c) seek a no-objection certificate (NOC) from other participants if required, and (d) sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) if required by the inter-financier agreement.
en.True answer: A participant may exit early per the inter-financier agreement while complying with contractual terms and Shari'ah principles (particularly those governing sale and settlement of debt, if a debt), and must at a minimum: (a) inform the customer (and obtain prior approval if required) through the lead arranger of early exit and replacement, (b) inform other participants through the lead arranger/facility agent/security agent with its rationale if required, (c) seek a no-objection certificate (NOC) from other participants if required, and (d) sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) if required by the inter-financier agreement.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 45 & Par. 46(a)–(d) (Par. 45 allows early exit before maturity per terms of inter-financier agreement, complying with contractual terms and Shari'ah principles/rules—particularly those related to sale and settlement of debt in case of a debt. Par. 46 requires compliance with inter-financier agreement including at minimum: (a) informing customer [and obtaining prior approval if required] through lead arranger of early exit and replacement; (b) informing other participants through lead arranger/facility agent/security agent along with rationale if required; (c) seeking NOC from other participants if required; and (d) signing NDA with customer and/or existing/incoming participants if required).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: During the Marketing and Negotiations phase (Paragraphs 22–23 and 28–30 of AAOIFI GS 15), how must an arranger handle (1) Information Memorandum disclosures in a hybrid arrangement, and (2) customer preferences regarding pricing and potential syndication participants?
en.A: (1) The Information Memorandum must clearly describe the proposed transaction structure and, in a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement, provide a clear description of the segregation of the Shari'ah-compliant tranche from the conventional financing tranche (alongside pricing, profit/loss sharing ratios, fees, risk assessments, credit enhancements, and Shari'ah-based arbitration); (2) the customer's pricing preferences must be documented and communicated to the arranger(s) (who provide market guidance), and the customer's preferences regarding potential syndication participants must be pre-agreed and documented before marketing begins—if the arranger deems it necessary to deviate from those preferences, it must communicate the deviation to the customer along with its rationale.
en.B: (1) The Information Memorandum combines the Shari'ah and conventional tranches into a single blended yield table; (2) the arranger may freely invite any bank rejected by the customer without informing the customer or providing a rationale.
en.C: (1) Pricing and arrangement fees are omitted from the Information Memorandum until after binding commitments are signed; (2) customer pricing preferences are ignored whenever they differ from the lead arranger's target fee margin.
en.D: (1) The Information Memorandum is prepared exclusively by the customer without arranger review; (2) customer preferences on syndicate participants are legally non-binding and need never be documented.
en.True answer: (1) The Information Memorandum must clearly describe the proposed transaction structure and, in a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement, provide a clear description of the segregation of the Shari'ah-compliant tranche from the conventional financing tranche (alongside pricing, profit/loss sharing ratios, fees, risk assessments, credit enhancements, and Shari'ah-based arbitration); (2) the customer's pricing preferences must be documented and communicated to the arranger(s) (who provide market guidance), and the customer's preferences regarding potential syndication participants must be pre-agreed and documented before marketing begins—if the arranger deems it necessary to deviate from those preferences, it must communicate the deviation to the customer along with its rationale.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 22–23(a)–(r) & Par. 28–30 (Par. 23(e) requires a description of proposed transaction structure and, in a hybrid arrangement, a clear description of segregation of the Shari'ah-compliant tranche from the conventional tranche; Par. 29 requires documenting and communicating customer's pricing preferences to arranger(s); Par. 30 requires pre-agreeing and documenting customer's preferences regarding potential syndication participants before commencing marketing/negotiation, and communicating any necessary deviation to the customer along with its rationale).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 34–37 of AAOIFI GS 15, which four conflict-of-interest rules govern arrangers, associated agent appointments, and potential syndication participants that decline to join the syndicate?
en.A: Arrangers may condition syndicate allocation on the customer purchasing unrelated advisory services from the arranger's subsidiary; lead arrangers may never serve as security or facility agents even with stakeholder consent; and declining banks may freely pitch bilateral counter-deals to the customer.
en.B: (1) Arrangers must ensure that obtaining any additional financing or service business (directly or via an associated entity) is NOT leveraged on the mandated syndicated transaction in a manner jeopardizing other participants' interests; (2) associated appointments (security agent, facility agent, Takaful provider) must be made on an arm's length basis, and the lead arranger may also be appointed as security agent and/or facility agent with due stakeholder consent if no conflict of interest results; and (3) a potential syndication participant that declines participation after being approached by the arranger must NOT approach the customer directly to offer a counter-proposal or stand-alone deal, and must NOT divulge any material non-public information received during its interaction with the arranger.
en.C: Associated appointments such as the Takaful provider may be awarded at above-market captive rates without stakeholder disclosure, and declining participants are prohibited from pitching counter-deals for only 48 hours.
en.D: A lead arranger has automatic unilateral authority to appoint itself as security agent without stakeholder consent and may use syndicate negotiations to extract exclusive cross-selling mandates.
