en.True answer: (1) Arrangers must ensure that obtaining any additional financing or service business (directly or via an associated entity) is NOT leveraged on the mandated syndicated transaction in a manner jeopardizing other participants' interests; (2) associated appointments (security agent, facility agent, Takaful provider) must be made on an arm's length basis, and the lead arranger may also be appointed as security agent and/or facility agent with due stakeholder consent if no conflict of interest results; and (3) a potential syndication participant that declines participation after being approached by the arranger must NOT approach the customer directly to offer a counter-proposal or stand-alone deal, and must NOT divulge any material non-public information received during its interaction with the arranger.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 34–37 (Par. 34: obtaining additional financing or service business, directly or via associated entity, shall not be leveraged on the mandated syndicated transaction so as to jeopardize other participants' interests; Par. 35: associated appointments [security agent, facility agent, Takaful provider] must be on an arm's length basis, and lead arranger may also be appointed as security agent and/or facility agent with due consent of relevant stakeholders if no conflict of interest results; Par. 37(a)–(b): an approached potential participant deciding not to participate shall NOT (a) approach customer directly to offer a counter-proposal or stand-alone deal, and (b) divulge any material non-public information received).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: In Appendix C (Basis of Conclusions, BC8–BC9) of AAOIFI GS 15, why did the Board decline the proposal to mandate a common SSB and shared Shari'ah compliance/external Shari'ah audit functions for each syndicated financing transaction, and what option did it recognize regarding SSB delegation?
en.A: Because AAOIFI SS 24 strictly prohibits two Islamic banks from ever cooperating on Shari'ah matters, and SSBs can never delegate any authority.
en.B: Because external Shari'ah audits are prohibited for syndicated financing transactions, and individual bank SSBs have no authority once a Provisional Fatwa is issued.
en.C: The Board declined mandating a common SSB and shared Shari'ah compliance/audit functions because of implementation and administrative challenges, and because under AAOIFI GSs and national regulatory frameworks the responsibilities of individual IFIs' SSBs and Shari'ah compliance departments cannot be shared with others (while external/internal Shari'ah audit selection depends on each auditor's materiality and sampling); however, the Board noted that delegation of authorities by SSBs may take place subject to AAOIFI GSs and regulatory requirements without relieving the respective SSBs of their responsibilities and accountability.
en.D: The Board mandated that the lead arranger's SSB automatically binds all participating IFIs with zero right for participant SSBs to review or issue separate Fatwas.
en.True answer: The Board declined mandating a common SSB and shared Shari'ah compliance/audit functions because of implementation and administrative challenges, and because under AAOIFI GSs and national regulatory frameworks the responsibilities of individual IFIs' SSBs and Shari'ah compliance departments cannot be shared with others (while external/internal Shari'ah audit selection depends on each auditor's materiality and sampling); however, the Board noted that delegation of authorities by SSBs may take place subject to AAOIFI GSs and regulatory requirements without relieving the respective SSBs of their responsibilities and accountability.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Appendix C, BC8–BC9 (BC8–BC9 explain that while SS 24 Par. 5/4 provides an option—not a mandate—for a joint committee of SSBs, the Board declined mandating a common SSB or shared Shari'ah compliance/audit functions because of administrative challenges, because under AAOIFI GSs and national regulations individual IFIs' SSBs and SCDs cannot share their responsibilities with others, and because audit selection depends on each auditor's materiality/sampling; however, delegation of authorities by SSBs may occur per AAOIFI GSs and regulations without relieving the respective SSBs of responsibility and accountability).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 47–51 of AAOIFI GS 15, what two scenarios justify restructuring or rescheduling a syndicated financing transaction, what core conditions must be met, and who must thoroughly review and approve the restructuring proposition?
en.A: Restructuring occurs whenever market benchmark rates rise, permits increasing profit margins on existing debt receivables, and requires approval solely from the facility agent.
en.B: Restructuring is permitted only upon formal liquidation of the customer, and requires approval solely from the lead arranger's credit committee.
en.C: Restructuring may be initiated unilaterally by the customer to extend payment dates for 10 years without consulting the syndication participants' SSBs.
en.D: Restructuring or rescheduling may generally occur as a result of (a) the customer's default or risk of potential default, or (b) acquisition, merger, or corporate restructuring of the customer; it must maintain the primary objective of the original transaction, preserve the initial equilibrium of financial benefits or rights, and safeguard stakeholders' interests; and any restructuring or rescheduling proposition must be thoroughly reviewed and approved by the respective SSBs of the syndication participants, the customer, and (where applicable) the regulator.
en.True answer: Restructuring or rescheduling may generally occur as a result of (a) the customer's default or risk of potential default, or (b) acquisition, merger, or corporate restructuring of the customer; it must maintain the primary objective of the original transaction, preserve the initial equilibrium of financial benefits or rights, and safeguard stakeholders' interests; and any restructuring or rescheduling proposition must be thoroughly reviewed and approved by the respective SSBs of the syndication participants, the customer, and (where applicable) the regulator.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 47(a)–(b), Par. 48 & Par. 49 (Par. 47: restructuring or rescheduling may generally occur in two scenarios: (a) customer's default or risk of potential default, or (b) acquisition, merger, or corporate restructuring of the customer; Par. 48: must maintain primary objective of original transaction, initial equilibrium of financial benefits or rights, and safeguard interests of relevant parties/stakeholders; Par. 49: proposition shall be thoroughly reviewed and approved by respective SSBs of syndication participants, the customer, and where applicable, the regulator).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: In Appendix C (BC16–BC19) and Paragraphs 26–27 of AAOIFI GS 15, what specific Shari'ah concern led the Shari'ah Committee and the Board to prohibit IFIs from signing a single combined inter-financier agreement with conventional banks in a hybrid syndicated financing arrangement, and how did the Board address potential legal enforceability exceptions?
en.A: The Shari'ah Committee observed that signing the same inter-financier agreement in a hybrid arrangement creates an element of cooperation between IFIs and CFIs for interest-bearing transactions; therefore, GS 15 prohibits IFIs from signing the same agreement and requires two separate inter-financier agreements—while the Board noted in BC19 that a jurisdiction's CSB or an IFI's SSB may grant a case-by-case exception on grounds of necessity (e.g., legal enforceability), though the Board declined to embed such an exception option directly in the standard text.
en.B: The Board prohibited separate agreements because conventional banks refused to sign separate agreements, and inserted a blanket exemption in Paragraph 26 allowing unified agreements whenever legal fees exceed USD 50,000.
en.C: The Shari'ah Committee concluded that signing a single agreement with conventional banks is fully permissible in all cases without any CSB or SSB review.
en.D: The Board required the conventional tranche's inter-financier agreement to be governed by AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards while the Islamic tranche is governed by conventional banking law.
en.True answer: The Shari'ah Committee observed that signing the same inter-financier agreement in a hybrid arrangement creates an element of cooperation between IFIs and CFIs for interest-bearing transactions; therefore, GS 15 prohibits IFIs from signing the same agreement and requires two separate inter-financier agreements—while the Board noted in BC19 that a jurisdiction's CSB or an IFI's SSB may grant a case-by-case exception on grounds of necessity (e.g., legal enforceability), though the Board declined to embed such an exception option directly in the standard text.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 26–27 & Appendix C, BC16–BC19 (BC16–BC18: Shari'ah Committee observed an element of cooperation between IFIs and CFIs for interest-bearing transactions if IFIs sign the same inter-financier agreement in a hybrid arrangement, so the Board amended GS 15 to prohibit IFIs from signing the same agreement and mandate two separate inter-financier agreements; BC19: Board and Shari'ah Committee concluded that a jurisdiction's CSB or an IFI's SSB may make an exception on a case-by-case basis on grounds of necessity e.g. legal enforceability, but decided it was not appropriate to provide an option for such exception in the standard itself).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question: How does AAOIFI GS 15 bind non-IFI corporate customers to its governance and Shari'ah compliance provisions (Appendix C, BC20–BC22 & Paragraph 16), and how does GS 15 apply to Sukuk issuances (Paragraph 6 & Appendix C, BC1–BC4)?
en.A: Non-IFI customers are bound automatically by AAOIFI's statutory police power without signing any contracts, whereas Sukuk issuances are completely exempt from all provisions of GS 15.
en.B: While keeping the primary compliance onus on IFIs, GS 15 binds the non-IFI customer to comply with Shari'ah principles/rules and applicable GS 15 requirements by virtue of signing the respective contracts and documents (specifically including the Mandate under Par. 16(d)); furthermore, although Sukuk issuances are excluded from the primary scope of GS 15 to avoid regulatory overlap with GS 12, Paragraph 6 makes GS 15 guidance—particularly regarding the awarding of mandate and transaction close phases—applicable mutatis mutandis to listed and unlisted Sukuk issuances insofar as not in conflict with GS 12.
en.C: Corporate customers have zero obligations under GS 15 even after signing the Mandate, whereas GS 15 replaces GS 12 for all listed Sukuk issuances.
en.D: Only sovereign government customers are bound by GS 15, and Sukuk issuances apply GS 15 solely during post-maturity restructuring.
en.True answer: While keeping the primary compliance onus on IFIs, GS 15 binds the non-IFI customer to comply with Shari'ah principles/rules and applicable GS 15 requirements by virtue of signing the respective contracts and documents (specifically including the Mandate under Par. 16(d)); furthermore, although Sukuk issuances are excluded from the primary scope of GS 15 to avoid regulatory overlap with GS 12, Paragraph 6 makes GS 15 guidance—particularly regarding the awarding of mandate and transaction close phases—applicable mutatis mutandis to listed and unlisted Sukuk issuances insofar as not in conflict with GS 12.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15, Par. 6, Par. 16(d) & Appendix C, BC1–BC4, BC20–BC22 (BC20–BC22 explain that while keeping the primary onus on IFIs, the customer is bound to comply with Shari'ah principles and rules and applicable GS 15 requirements by virtue of signing the respective contracts and documents, including the Mandate per Par. 16(d); Par. 6 & BC1–BC4 explain that while Sukuk is excluded from primary scope to avoid overlap with GS 12, GS 15 guidance—particularly regarding awarding of mandate and transaction close phases—applies mutatis mutandis to listed and unlisted Sukuk issuances insofar as not in conflict with GS 12).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question:
In October 2024, an industrial corporation seeks USD 300 million in financing for a Shari'ah-compliant manufacturing expansion. Because local IFIs can only provide USD 180 million, a hybrid syndicated arrangement is structured with USD 180 million in a Shari'ah-compliant tranche and USD 120 million in a conventional tranche. Evaluate the following four actions taken during origination, marketing, and close:
(1) At the customer's request, the IFI Lead Arranger directly approaches two conventional banks on behalf of the customer to arrange the USD 120 million conventional tranche and agrees to serve as facility agent for both the Shari'ah tranche and the conventional tranche.
(2) To save legal drafting costs, all participating IFIs and the two conventional banks sign a single combined inter-financier agreement covering both tranches.
(3) Before marketing, the customer documented a preference excluding Bank X; during marketing, the IFI Lead Arranger determines based on market expertise that inviting Bank X is necessary and communicates this deviation along with its rationale to the customer.
(4) Bank Z, after being approached by the IFI Lead Arranger and reviewing the Information Memorandum, declines to join the syndicate and immediately contacts the customer directly to offer a stand-alone bilateral financing deal at a lower profit rate.
According to AAOIFI GS 15, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—IFI lead arrangers may arrange conventional tranches if requested by the customer; (2) Compliant—a single unified agreement reduces costs; (3) Non-compliant—customer participant preferences can never be deviated from; (4) Compliant—declining banks may freely approach the customer.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 20(a), the customer (NOT the IFIs, and without any involvement of the IFIs) must approach CFIs at its absolute discretion, and under Par. 21(d), an IFI shall NOT in any way lead, arrange, or facilitate (including acting as an agent) for conventional financing; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 26 & Appendix C BC18, two distinct inter-financier agreements must be separately prepared and signed for the Shari'ah tranche and conventional tranche, and IFIs are not allowed to sign the same agreement; (3) Compliant—follows Par. 30, which allows deviating from pre-agreed customer participant preferences based on market expertise provided the deviation and its rationale are communicated to the customer; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 37(a), which prohibits an approached potential participant that decides not to participate from approaching the customer directly to offer a counter-proposal or stand-alone deal.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 20(a), the customer (NOT the IFIs, and without any involvement of the IFIs) must approach CFIs at its absolute discretion, and under Par. 21(d), an IFI shall NOT in any way lead, arrange, or facilitate (including acting as an agent) for conventional financing; (2) Non-compliant—under Par. 26 & Appendix C BC18, two distinct inter-financier agreements must be separately prepared and signed for the Shari'ah tranche and conventional tranche, and IFIs are not allowed to sign the same agreement; (3) Compliant—follows Par. 30, which allows deviating from pre-agreed customer participant preferences based on market expertise provided the deviation and its rationale are communicated to the customer; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 37(a), which prohibits an approached potential participant that decides not to participate from approaching the customer directly to offer a counter-proposal or stand-alone deal.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 20(a) requires that the customer (and not the IFIs, without any involvement of the IFIs) approaches CFIs at its absolute discretion, and Par. 21(d) strictly prohibits an IFI from leading, arranging, or facilitating (including acting as an agent) for conventional financing in any manner whatsoever; (2) Par. 26 & Appendix C BC18 require two distinct inter-financier agreements to be separately prepared and signed for the Shari'ah tranche and conventional tranche, prohibiting IFIs from signing the same agreement; (3) Par. 30 allows an arranger to deviate from pre-agreed customer preferences regarding potential participants if deemed necessary based on expertise/market understanding, provided such deviation is communicated to the customer along with its rationale; (4) Par. 37(a) bars an approached potential syndication participant that declines participation from approaching the customer directly to offer a counter-proposal or stand-alone deal.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 15: Syndicated Financing
en.Question:
During the continuity of a 6-year syndicated Murabaha/Musharakah financing facility among four Islamic banks (Lead Arranger Bank A and Participants B, C, and D), examine the following four events occurring between Year 2 and Year 5:
(1) In Year 2, Bank B's internal Shari'ah audit detects a Shari'ah compliance issue in how the customer deploys underlying project assets; Bank B bypasses Bank A (the Lead Arranger) and directly issues an ultimatum to the customer without informing Banks A, C, or D.
(2) In Year 3, Bank C's SSB decides to change its earlier Fatwa following a revision in AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards; Bank C follows AAOIFI SS 29, promptly informs Banks A, B, and D as well as the customer, and collaborates with them to find a Shari'ah-compliant solution.
(3) In Year 4, Bank D seeks an early exit (pre-exit) before maturity by transferring its remaining Murabaha debt receivable share to an incoming bank at a 12% cash discount, without informing the customer or seeking the no-objection certificate (NOC) required under the inter-financier agreement.
(4) In Year 5, following a corporate merger of the customer, the parties propose rescheduling installment dates while maintaining the primary objective and initial equilibrium of financial benefits/rights, and submit the rescheduling proposition for thorough review and approval to the respective SSBs of Banks A, B, C, and D, the customer, and the regulator.
According to AAOIFI GS 15, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—participants deal directly with the customer on audit findings; (2) Non-compliant—SSBs cannot change a Fatwa during continuity; (3) Compliant—debt receivables may be discounted upon pre-exit; (4) Non-compliant—corporate mergers cannot trigger rescheduling.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 41, a syndication participant identifying a Shari'ah compliance issue must immediately inform the Lead Arranger, who after due consultation with the customer informs all syndication participants so they can collaborate on a solution; (2) Compliant—follows Par. 42, which requires following AAOIFI SS 29, promptly informing other participants and the customer, and collaborating on a Shari'ah-compliant solution; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. 45–46, which require complying with Shari'ah rules on sale of debt (prohibiting discounting debt receivables) as well as informing the customer through the lead arranger and seeking the NOC required by the inter-financier agreement; (4) Compliant—follows Par. 47(b), 48, and 49, which permit rescheduling upon corporate merger/restructuring while preserving the primary objective and initial equilibrium of financial benefits/rights, subject to thorough review and approval by the respective SSBs of all syndication participants, the customer, and the regulator.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 41, a syndication participant identifying a Shari'ah compliance issue must immediately inform the Lead Arranger, who after due consultation with the customer informs all syndication participants so they can collaborate on a solution; (2) Compliant—follows Par. 42, which requires following AAOIFI SS 29, promptly informing other participants and the customer, and collaborating on a Shari'ah-compliant solution; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. 45–46, which require complying with Shari'ah rules on sale of debt (prohibiting discounting debt receivables) as well as informing the customer through the lead arranger and seeking the NOC required by the inter-financier agreement; (4) Compliant—follows Par. 47(b), 48, and 49, which permit rescheduling upon corporate merger/restructuring while preserving the primary objective and initial equilibrium of financial benefits/rights, subject to thorough review and approval by the respective SSBs of all syndication participants, the customer, and the regulator.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 15 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 41 requires a participant identifying a Shari'ah compliance issue to immediately inform the lead arranger, who after consulting the customer informs all participants to collaborate on a solution; (2) Par. 42 governs Change of Fatwa by requiring adherence to AAOIFI SS 29, prompt notice to other syndication participants and the customer, and collaboration to find a Shari'ah-compliant solution; (3) Par. 45–46 require an early-exiting participant to comply with Shari'ah rules on sale/settlement of debt (barring discounted debt trading) and comply with inter-financier agreement procedures including informing the customer via lead arranger and obtaining required NOCs; (4) Par. 47(b), 48 & 49 allow rescheduling resulting from acquisition, merger, or corporate restructuring provided the primary objective and initial equilibrium of financial benefits/rights are maintained and the proposition is thoroughly reviewed and approved by the respective SSBs of the syndication participants, the customer, and the regulator.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope, mandatory code requirement, and effective date of AAOIFI GS 16 ('Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics')?
en.A: GS 16 applies to IFIs along with Islamic social finance institutions (such as Waqf, Zakah, and Qard-based microfinance institutions), mandates the adoption of the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics ('AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals'), and is effective on or after 1 July 2024.
en.B: GS 16 applies exclusively to commercial Islamic banks, leaves adoption of the AAOIFI Code of Ethics optional, and becomes effective on 1 January 2028.
en.C: GS 16 excludes Islamic social finance institutions such as Waqf and Zakah funds and became effective retroactively on 26 December 2019.
en.D: GS 16 applies solely to individual Islamic finance professionals rather than institutions and has no effective date.
en.True answer: GS 16 applies to IFIs along with Islamic social finance institutions (such as Waqf, Zakah, and Qard-based microfinance institutions), mandates the adoption of the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics ('AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals'), and is effective on or after 1 July 2024.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Preface PR2–PR3, Par. 2–3 & Par. 9 (Par. 2: applies to IFIs along with Islamic social finance institutions such as Waqf, Zakah, and Qard-based microfinance institutions; Par. 3: mandates adoption of the respective AAOIFI code of ethics ['AAOIFI Code of Ethics for Islamic Finance Professionals', Footnote 5] and recommends compliance with relevant AAOIFI GSs; Par. 9: effective on or after 1 July 2024).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraph 4(b) (including Footnote 6) and Appendix B (Footnote 18) of AAOIFI GS 16, how are 'internal stakeholders' and the concept of 'Ihsaan' defined?
en.A: Internal stakeholders include solely full-time salaried head-office employees (excluding outsourced call center or Takaful agents), while Ihsaan means minimal compliance with statutory regulations.
en.B: Internal stakeholders include the board of directors, Shari'ah supervisory board (SSB), senior management (particularly the CEO), management, and staff—AND in the case of outsourcing business functions to third parties (such as Takaful agents, BancaTakaful agents, and call center agents), such third parties are ALSO viewed as internal stakeholders; Ihsaan is defined as striving for excellence in ethics, achieved when something is done in a manner that, given resources, constraints, and circumstances, cannot be done better.
en.C: Internal stakeholders include external retail depositors and borrowers, while Ihsaan refers exclusively to voluntary charitable donations above Zakah.
en.D: Outsourced third parties are strictly classified as external regulators, and SSB members are excluded from the definition of internal stakeholders.
en.True answer: Internal stakeholders include the board of directors, Shari'ah supervisory board (SSB), senior management (particularly the CEO), management, and staff—AND in the case of outsourcing business functions to third parties (such as Takaful agents, BancaTakaful agents, and call center agents), such third parties are ALSO viewed as internal stakeholders; Ihsaan is defined as striving for excellence in ethics, achieved when something is done in a manner that, given resources, constraints, and circumstances, cannot be done better.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 4(b), Footnote 6 & Appendix B Footnote 18 (Par. 4(b) & Footnote 6 define internal stakeholders to include the board of directors, SSB, senior management—particularly the CEO—management, staff, and third parties to whom business functions are outsourced, including Takaful agents, BancaTakaful agents, and call center agents; Footnote 18 cites Par. 10(e) of AAOIFI Code of Ethics defining Ihsaan as striving for excellence in ethics, achieved when something is done in a manner which, in given resources, constraints, and circumstances, cannot be done better).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Part A (Paragraph 5(a)–(f)) of AAOIFI GS 16, an institution must develop its institutional framework for the implementation of ethics based on six minimum principles. Which option accurately lists all six principles?
en.A: Profit maximization, regulatory arbitrage, market dominance, cost minimization, executive secrecy, and external outsourcing.
en.B: Shari'ah audit, credit scoring, liquidity coverage, board rotation, external rating, and capital adequacy.
en.C: (1) Commitment to ethics at all levels, (2) formalisation of ethics requirements and expectations, (3) sustained allocation of resources (human and financial) for ethics, (4) supporting internal stakeholders to understand, own, and practice ethics while encouraging others to do the same, (5) nurturing an organisational culture which encourages and incentivises ethical conduct and discourages and penalises unethical behaviour, and (6) periodic improvement of the institutional framework.
en.D: (1) Annual external audit, (2) shareholder dividend priority, (3) strict hierarchy, (4) non-disclosure, (5) automated compliance, and (6) regulatory immunity.
en.True answer: (1) Commitment to ethics at all levels, (2) formalisation of ethics requirements and expectations, (3) sustained allocation of resources (human and financial) for ethics, (4) supporting internal stakeholders to understand, own, and practice ethics while encouraging others to do the same, (5) nurturing an organisational culture which encourages and incentivises ethical conduct and discourages and penalises unethical behaviour, and (6) periodic improvement of the institutional framework.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 5(a)–(f) (Enumerates the six minimum principles in Part A: (a) commitment to ethics at all levels; (b) formalisation of ethics requirements and expectations; (c) sustained allocation of resources [human and financial] for ethics; (d) supporting internal stakeholders to understand, own and practice ethics while encouraging others to do the same; (e) nurturing an organisational culture which encourages and incentivises ethical conduct and discourages and penalises unethical behaviour; and (f) periodic improvement of the institutional framework).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Part B (Paragraph 6(a)–(g)) of AAOIFI GS 16, which seven minimum components must an institution include in its institutional framework for the implementation of ethics?
en.A: External Shari'ah audit, credit rating, Sukuk prospectus, Zakah calculation, liquidity reserve, IT firewall, and sovereign guarantee.
en.B: Shareholder charter, CEO bonus plan, marketing manual, dividend policy, tax audit, branch layout, and vendor list.
en.C: Internal Shari'ah review, external financial audit, treasury policy, FX hedging, customer survey, annual budget, and legal counsel.
en.D: (1) Code of ethics (adopting the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics), (2) board ethics committee (dedicated or assigned to an existing board committee), (3) ethics risk assessment, (4) ethics capacity building programme, (5) self-declaration, (6) ethics incentive and disciplinary mechanism, and (7) ethics violation reporting mechanism (anonymous ethics hotline without fear of retaliation).
en.True answer: (1) Code of ethics (adopting the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics), (2) board ethics committee (dedicated or assigned to an existing board committee), (3) ethics risk assessment, (4) ethics capacity building programme, (5) self-declaration, (6) ethics incentive and disciplinary mechanism, and (7) ethics violation reporting mechanism (anonymous ethics hotline without fear of retaliation).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 6(a)–(g) (Specifies the seven minimum components of the institutional framework: (a) code of ethics; (b) board ethics committee; (c) ethics risk assessment; (d) ethics capacity building programme; (e) self-declaration; (f) ethics incentive and disciplinary mechanism; and (g) ethics violation reporting mechanism).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraph 7 (including Footnote 10), Appendix B (Paragraph B8), and Appendix C (BC4–BC6, BC14–BC16) of AAOIFI GS 16, what is the authoritative status of Appendix B, and how may an institution supplement the AAOIFI Code of Ethics?
en.A: Appendix B ('A model institutional framework for the implementation of ethics') is explicitly an operative part of GS 16; an institution must adopt the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics as its primary code and may add additional ethical requirements that are not inconsistent with the AAOIFI Code of Ethics as well as supplementary implementation guidelines.
en.B: Appendix B is a purely non-binding illustrative example that institutions may ignore, and institutions may replace the AAOIFI Code of Ethics with their own commercial sales code.
en.C: Appendix B overrides the main body of GS 16 in case of conflict, and institutions are prohibited from adding any supplementary ethical guidelines.
en.D: Institutions need only confirm that their existing corporate handbook is broadly similar to the AAOIFI Code of Ethics without formally adopting the AAOIFI Code.
en.True answer: Appendix B ('A model institutional framework for the implementation of ethics') is explicitly an operative part of GS 16; an institution must adopt the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics as its primary code and may add additional ethical requirements that are not inconsistent with the AAOIFI Code of Ethics as well as supplementary implementation guidelines.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 6(a), Par. 7 Footnote 10, Appendix B Par. B8 & Appendix C, BC4–BC6, BC14–BC16 (Par. 7 Footnote 10 & BC15 explicitly designate Appendix B as an operative part of the standard; Par. 6(a), B8 & BC5–BC6 require adopting the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics as the primary code, to which the institution may add additional ethical requirements not inconsistent with the AAOIFI Code of Ethics and supplementary implementation guidelines).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraphs B9–B10 of Appendix B to AAOIFI GS 16, what accessibility requirements apply to the AAOIFI Code of Ethics for internal stakeholders?
en.A: The Code need only be kept in a locked physical binder in the CEO's office in its original Arabic or English text.
en.B: The institution must ensure that all internal stakeholders have access to the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics in their preferred language / mother tongue AND make it accessible through both electronic and non-electronic platforms.
en.C: The Code must be distributed exclusively via mobile app notifications in English only, with non-electronic copies prohibited.
en.D: Access to the Code is restricted solely to senior executives and members of the board ethics committee.
en.True answer: The institution must ensure that all internal stakeholders have access to the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics in their preferred language / mother tongue AND make it accessible through both electronic and non-electronic platforms.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix B, Par. B9–B10 (Par. B9: 'An institution shall ensure that all internal stakeholders have access to respective AAOIFI code of ethics in their preferred language / mother tongue.' Par. B10: 'An institution shall make respective AAOIFI code of ethics accessible to all internal stakeholders through electronic and non-electronic platforms').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraph 8 of AAOIFI GS 16, what conditions must be met before an institution outsources specific components of its institutional framework for the implementation of ethics?
en.A: Outsourcing of any ethics framework component is strictly prohibited under all circumstances.
en.B: The CEO may outsource any ethics component unilaterally without board committee approval or third-party risk checks.
en.C: The decision to outsource must be made with the approval of the board ethics committee AND only after conducting due diligence on the risks posed by third parties, taking into account ethical considerations such as integrity, privacy, confidentiality, and security.
en.D: Outsourcing requires approval solely from the external financial auditor and applies only to annual financial statement preparation.
en.True answer: The decision to outsource must be made with the approval of the board ethics committee AND only after conducting due diligence on the risks posed by third parties, taking into account ethical considerations such as integrity, privacy, confidentiality, and security.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 8 ('An institution may decide to outsource specific components of the institutional framework. The decision to outsource shall be made with the approval of the board ethics committee, and only after conducting due diligence on the risks posed by third parties, taking into account ethical considerations such as integrity, privacy, confidentiality and security').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraph 6(b) and Appendix B (Paragraphs B16 and B20) of AAOIFI GS 16, how may an institution establish its Board Ethics Committee, and what gender diversity recommendation applies to its ethics committees?
en.A: It must always be a brand-new standalone committee with at least 9 male Shari'ah scholars; assigning the function to an existing board committee is prohibited.
en.B: The Board Ethics Committee is optional and may be replaced entirely by the CEO's executive office.
en.C: It may only be assigned to the external financial auditor, and no diversity recommendations exist in GS 16.
en.D: The Board Ethics Committee may be either a dedicated committee or an existing board committee assigned with the function (such as the governance committee, risk committee, audit committee, or audit and governance committee), and the institution should preferably include at least one female professional in its board ethics committee and management ethics committee (if one exists), respectively.
en.True answer: The Board Ethics Committee may be either a dedicated committee or an existing board committee assigned with the function (such as the governance committee, risk committee, audit committee, or audit and governance committee), and the institution should preferably include at least one female professional in its board ethics committee and management ethics committee (if one exists), respectively.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 6(b) & Appendix B, Par. B16, B20 (Par. 6(b) & B16: board ethics committee could either be a dedicated committee or an existing board committee to which the function may be assigned—such as governance committee, risk committee, audit committee, or audit and governance committee; Par. B20: 'An institution should preferably include at least one female professional in its board ethics committee and management ethics committee (if one exists), respectively').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Appendix B (Paragraphs B17(f), B18(c), and B21–B26) of AAOIFI GS 16, how are the roles of 'Ethics Officer' and 'Ethics Champions' structured and distinguished?
en.A: The Ethics Officer (who may be appointed full-time or assigned to an existing employee on a part-time basis by decision of the board ethics committee) oversees day-to-day implementation, assists the ethics committees (serving as secretary to the management ethics committee), and investigates violation claims when delegated; Ethics Champions are designated preferably from each business function to engage informally with employees to provide guidance and raise ethics awareness alongside their primary day-to-day responsibilities.
en.B: Ethics Champions hold formal disciplinary firing power over senior executives, whereas the Ethics Officer must always be an external consultant.
en.C: Both the Ethics Officer and all Ethics Champions must be full-time dedicated staff prohibited from performing any other operational duties.
en.D: Ethics Champions investigate claims against SSB members, while the Ethics Officer manages commercial product pricing.
en.True answer: The Ethics Officer (who may be appointed full-time or assigned to an existing employee on a part-time basis by decision of the board ethics committee) oversees day-to-day implementation, assists the ethics committees (serving as secretary to the management ethics committee), and investigates violation claims when delegated; Ethics Champions are designated preferably from each business function to engage informally with employees to provide guidance and raise ethics awareness alongside their primary day-to-day responsibilities.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix B, Par. B17(f), B18(c) & B21–B26 (Par. B17(f), B23–B24: Ethics Officer oversees day-to-day implementation, assists board/management ethics committees [serving as secretary to management ethics committee per B18(c)], investigates claims when delegated, and may be full-time or assigned part-time to an existing employee; Par. B25–B26: Ethics Champions designated preferably from each business function engage informally to extend support/guidance and raise awareness within their business functions in addition to their primary day-to-day responsibilities).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraphs B29–B30 of Appendix B to AAOIFI GS 16, what minimum frequency is required for internal ethics training, which employees require specific focus, and how should external stakeholders (suppliers and customers) be engaged?
en.A: Internal ethics training is required once every three years for back-office IT staff only, while suppliers and customers are excluded from any ethics orientation.
en.B: The institution must conduct periodic (at least annually) ethics training for all internal stakeholders with a specific focus on employees dealing with customers and other external stakeholders, and should conduct ethics orientation or sensitising sessions for suppliers, customers, and other stakeholders where possible as part of its corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities.
en.C: Ethics training applies only to newly hired entry-level tellers during onboarding, with no ongoing annual refresher.
en.D: Suppliers and customers must pass a mandatory formal exam administered by the board ethics committee before opening an account.
en.True answer: The institution must conduct periodic (at least annually) ethics training for all internal stakeholders with a specific focus on employees dealing with customers and other external stakeholders, and should conduct ethics orientation or sensitising sessions for suppliers, customers, and other stakeholders where possible as part of its corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix B, Par. B29–B30 (Par. B29: 'An institution shall conduct periodic (at least annually) ethics training for all internal stakeholders, with a specific focus on employees dealing with customers and other external stakeholders.' Par. B30: 'An institution should conduct ethics orientation or sensitising sessions for the benefit of its suppliers, customers and other stakeholders, where possible, as a part of its corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraph 6(g) and Appendix B (Paragraphs B36–B37) of AAOIFI GS 16, what requirements govern an institution's ethics violation reporting mechanism and whistleblowing policy?
en.A: Whistleblowers must disclose their full identity and obtain their line manager's written permission before reporting any ethics violation.
en.B: All ethics violations are reported exclusively to the local police department rather than to internal ethics committees.
en.C: The institution must establish an ethics hotline allowing internal stakeholders to report ethics violations anonymously without fear of retaliation, maintain a timely response/action mechanism with confidentiality, route reports to the management ethics committee (or directly to the board ethics committee if no management ethics committee exists), and adopt a whistleblowing policy protecting those who disclose violations in good faith and in accordance with proper reporting protocols.
en.D: Anonymous reporting is prohibited in order to deter employees from submitting minor operational complaints.
en.True answer: The institution must establish an ethics hotline allowing internal stakeholders to report ethics violations anonymously without fear of retaliation, maintain a timely response/action mechanism with confidentiality, route reports to the management ethics committee (or directly to the board ethics committee if no management ethics committee exists), and adopt a whistleblowing policy protecting those who disclose violations in good faith and in accordance with proper reporting protocols.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 6(g) & Appendix B, Par. B36–B37 (Par. 6(g): establish an ethics hotline allowing internal stakeholders to report ethics violations anonymously without fear of retaliation, with timely response/action mechanism maintaining confidentiality; Par. B36: report instances to management ethics committee, or directly to board ethics committee if there is no management ethics committee; Par. B37: develop a policy on whistleblowing protecting those who disclose ethics violations in good faith and in accordance with proper reporting protocols).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Principle 6 (Paragraphs B39–B42 of Appendix B to AAOIFI GS 16), what requirements apply to (1) the periodic comprehensive review of the institutional framework and (2) the annual report on implementation of the AAOIFI Code of Ethics?
en.A: (1) The periodic review report is submitted solely to the marketing department; (2) publishing an annual report on implementation of the AAOIFI Code of Ethics is strictly prohibited.
en.B: (1) Comprehensive reviews are conducted once every ten years; (2) an independent assurance report is legally mandatory for every annual ethics report.
en.C: (1) Confidentiality is waived during the comprehensive review; (2) the annual ethics report replaces the institution's audited financial statements.
en.D: (1) The institution must periodically conduct a comprehensive review of its institutional framework's effectiveness (ensuring strict confidentiality during the review) and share the review report—including a comprehensive improvement plan—with the board ethics committee; (2) the institution is encouraged to publish an annual report on implementing the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics (as a section of its annual report or part of a broader ethics report), which may optionally be accompanied by an independent assurance report.
en.True answer: (1) The institution must periodically conduct a comprehensive review of its institutional framework's effectiveness (ensuring strict confidentiality during the review) and share the review report—including a comprehensive improvement plan—with the board ethics committee; (2) the institution is encouraged to publish an annual report on implementing the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics (as a section of its annual report or part of a broader ethics report), which may optionally be accompanied by an independent assurance report.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix B, Par. B39–B42 (Par. B40–B41: conduct periodic comprehensive review of effectiveness ensuring strict confidentiality during review, prepare review report including comprehensive improvement plan, and share with board ethics committee; Par. B39(b) & B42: encouraged to publish an annual report on implementing the respective AAOIFI code of ethics—as a section of annual report or part of comprehensive ethics report—which may optionally be accompanied by an independent assurance report).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraphs B17(c), B19(c), and B38(a)–(b) of Appendix B to AAOIFI GS 16, how is jurisdiction divided between the Board Ethics Committee and the Management Ethics Committee for handling ethics violation claims, and what recusal and resignation rules apply if a committee member is implicated?
en.A: Claims against members of those charged with governance (TCWG), the SSB, or senior management MUST be addressed by the Board Ethics Committee; claims against other internal stakeholders are handled by the Management Ethics Committee (if one exists, otherwise by the Board Ethics Committee); and if a reported violation involves a member of TCWG or the Management Ethics Committee, that member must recuse himself (neither participating in the investigation nor being privy to case information until decided) and MUST resign from the committee if found guilty of a material ethics violation.
en.B: The Management Ethics Committee investigates claims against senior management and SSB members, while the Board Ethics Committee handles routine branch teller infractions; an implicated member may observe the investigation privately without voting.
en.C: Claims against SSB members are investigated solely by the CEO, and a member found guilty of a material ethics violation receives only a private warning while remaining on the committee.
en.D: If no Management Ethics Committee exists, claims against operational staff are dismissed automatically without investigation.
en.True answer: Claims against members of those charged with governance (TCWG), the SSB, or senior management MUST be addressed by the Board Ethics Committee; claims against other internal stakeholders are handled by the Management Ethics Committee (if one exists, otherwise by the Board Ethics Committee); and if a reported violation involves a member of TCWG or the Management Ethics Committee, that member must recuse himself (neither participating in the investigation nor being privy to case information until decided) and MUST resign from the committee if found guilty of a material ethics violation.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix B, Par. B17(c), B19(c) & B38(a)–(b) (Par. B17(c) & B38(a): where reported ethics violation is against a member of TCWG, SSB, or senior management, it shall be addressed by the board ethics committee; otherwise handled by management ethics committee if one exists, or board ethics committee if none exists. Par. B38(b): where reported violation involves a member of TCWG or management ethics committee, that member must recuse himself—neither participating in investigation nor being privy to case-related info until decided—and shall resign from the committee if found guilty of material ethics violation).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraph B18 of Appendix B and Appendix C (BC7–BC13) of AAOIFI GS 16, what is the minimum composition of the Management Ethics Committee, and what positions did the Board adopt regarding (1) CEO participation/chairmanship and (2) middle management versus lower management employee representation?
en.A: The CEO is strictly barred from serving on the Management Ethics Committee in any capacity, and lower-level clerical employees are preferred over middle managers.
en.B: Established by the CEO after official authorization from TCWG and reporting to the Board Ethics Committee, the Management Ethics Committee must comprise at minimum: (a) a chairman appointed by the Board Ethics Committee (which has discretion to appoint the CEO or another member), (b) senior management members (e.g., heads of finance, HR, Shari'ah compliance, and operations), (c) the Ethics Officer serving as committee secretary, and (d) employee(s) from middle management (specifically middle management rather than lower management, so operational violations are surfaced while preserving confidentiality).
en.C: The Management Ethics Committee is mandatory for all institutions, is chaired by the external auditor, and excludes senior department heads.
en.D: The CEO appoints the committee chairman unilaterally without TCWG authorization, and both lower-level tellers and external vendors serve as voting members.
en.True answer: Established by the CEO after official authorization from TCWG and reporting to the Board Ethics Committee, the Management Ethics Committee must comprise at minimum: (a) a chairman appointed by the Board Ethics Committee (which has discretion to appoint the CEO or another member), (b) senior management members (e.g., heads of finance, HR, Shari'ah compliance, and operations), (c) the Ethics Officer serving as committee secretary, and (d) employee(s) from middle management (specifically middle management rather than lower management, so operational violations are surfaced while preserving confidentiality).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix B Par. B18(a)–(d) & Appendix C, BC7–BC13 (Par. B18: established by CEO after official TCWG authorization, reporting to board ethics committee, comprising at minimum: (a) chairman appointed by board ethics committee, (b) senior management members such as heads of finance, HR, Shari'ah compliance, operations, (c) ethics officer as committee secretary, and (d) employee(s) from middle management. BC10–BC11: Board unanimously agreed CEO should actively participate on the committee and left chairmanship [CEO or another member] to TCWG discretion; BC13: middle management—and NOT lower management—employee should be included to apprise committee of operational-level violations while protecting confidentiality).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: In Appendix C (Basis for Conclusions, BC1–BC6) of AAOIFI GS 16, why did the Board decide to issue GS 16 as a Governance Standard rather than a non-binding Ethics Guideline, and why did it mandate adopting the AAOIFI Code of Ethics as the primary code rather than allowing institutions merely to confirm equivalence of their own codes?
en.A: Because AAOIFI has no authority to issue guidelines, and because local regulators prohibit Islamic banks from writing any internal policies.
en.B: Because third-party Western ethics models already cover all Islamic Shari'ah principles completely, making a brief binding rulebook sufficient.
en.C: The Board classified GS 16 as a Governance Standard (rather than a non-binding guideline) because it prescribes governance controls to ensure ethical conduct rather than ethical values per se and creates moral/legal obligation, while finding third-party solutions context-heavy and incomplete; it mandated adopting the AAOIFI Code of Ethics as the primary code because verifying equivalence of diverse institutional codes would be more costly and time-consuming than direct adoption, and allowing replacement codes could result in institutions investing heavily in a framework built on a deficient or Shari'ah-non-compliant code.
en.D: Because mandatory adoption eliminates the need for any board ethics committee or periodic ethics risk assessments.
en.True answer: The Board classified GS 16 as a Governance Standard (rather than a non-binding guideline) because it prescribes governance controls to ensure ethical conduct rather than ethical values per se and creates moral/legal obligation, while finding third-party solutions context-heavy and incomplete; it mandated adopting the AAOIFI Code of Ethics as the primary code because verifying equivalence of diverse institutional codes would be more costly and time-consuming than direct adoption, and allowing replacement codes could result in institutions investing heavily in a framework built on a deficient or Shari'ah-non-compliant code.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix C, BC1–BC6 (BC2–BC3: third-party solutions were context-heavy and incomplete; since GS 16 prescribes governance controls to ensure ethical conduct rather than ethical values per se and creates moral/legal obligation, it was issued as a Governance Standard rather than a non-binding guideline. BC5–BC6: requiring institutions merely to confirm compliance/equivalence of their existing codes would be more costly and time-consuming than simply adopting the AAOIFI Code of Ethics, and allowing replacement codes risked institutions investing heavily in implementing a deficient or Shari'ah-non-compliant code).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Appendix B (Paragraphs B3, B6, B17(a), and B34–B35) of AAOIFI GS 16, how must an institution embed ethics into strategic decision-making and personnel performance management?
en.A: Revenue and market-share targets always take precedence over ethical considerations, and ethical conduct is excluded from executive bonus appraisals.
en.B: Overly ambitious sales targets are encouraged without ethics committee input, and material ethics breaches are resolved informally without disciplinary penalties.
en.C: Ethics criteria apply solely to junior administrative staff and are excluded from CEO and senior management performance evaluations.
en.D: The institution must give ethics precedence in strategic planning, decision-making, and culture-building; allow ethics to be a deciding factor when competing objectives (such as revenue, profitability, reputation, and market share) arise (with the Board Ethics Committee providing input to balance ethical conduct against overly ambitious performance targets); make ethics an essential criterion for professional success, growth, and recognition for all employees (particularly the CEO and senior management) influencing compensation, promotion, and benefits; and enforce a zero-tolerance policy for material ethics violations.
en.True answer: The institution must give ethics precedence in strategic planning, decision-making, and culture-building; allow ethics to be a deciding factor when competing objectives (such as revenue, profitability, reputation, and market share) arise (with the Board Ethics Committee providing input to balance ethical conduct against overly ambitious performance targets); make ethics an essential criterion for professional success, growth, and recognition for all employees (particularly the CEO and senior management) influencing compensation, promotion, and benefits; and enforce a zero-tolerance policy for material ethics violations.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Appendix B, Par. B3, B6(c)–(d), B17(a) & B34–B35 (Par. B3: prioritise ethics as core value giving it precedence in strategic planning, decision-making, etc.; Par. B6(c)–(d): make ethics an essential criterion for professional success/growth/recognition for all employees, particularly CEO and senior management, and allow ethics to be one of the deciding factors when competing objectives such as revenue, profitability, reputation, and market share are present; Par. B17(a): board ethics committee provides input to balance ethical conduct and overly ambitious performance targets; Par. B34–B35: integrate ethical conduct into performance appraisals influencing compensation/promotion/benefits and enforce a zero-tolerance policy for material ethics violations).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: In Appendix C (BC14, 'Cost of implementing and managing the institutional framework') and Paragraph 7 of AAOIFI GS 16, which four flexibilities did the Board recognize to help smaller or resource-constrained institutions minimize implementation costs without compromising the framework's objectives and quality?
en.A: (1) Tailor-designing and customizing the framework based on the nature of operations, size, structure, and unique circumstances (while upholding all principles and basic components); (2) assigning the Ethics Officer role to an existing employee on a part-time basis rather than hiring a full-time officer; (3) not mandating the establishment of a Management Ethics Committee; and (4) outsourcing the development and implementation of specific components to competent third parties (with Board Ethics Committee approval and due diligence).
en.B: (1) Exempting small IFIs from adopting the AAOIFI Code of Ethics; (2) waiving the Board Ethics Committee requirement; (3) eliminating annual ethics training; and (4) omitting the anonymous ethics violation reporting hotline.
en.C: (1) Merging ethics oversight into the commercial sales department; (2) conducting ethics risk assessments once every 10 years; (3) waiving self-declarations for senior management; and (4) outsourcing without due diligence.
en.D: (1) Relying solely on verbal reminders from the CEO; (2) dispensing with written ethics policies; (3) using unpaid interns as the Board Ethics Committee; and (4) ignoring third-party outsourced agents.
en.True answer: (1) Tailor-designing and customizing the framework based on the nature of operations, size, structure, and unique circumstances (while upholding all principles and basic components); (2) assigning the Ethics Officer role to an existing employee on a part-time basis rather than hiring a full-time officer; (3) not mandating the establishment of a Management Ethics Committee; and (4) outsourcing the development and implementation of specific components to competent third parties (with Board Ethics Committee approval and due diligence).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 7–8 & Appendix C, BC14(a)–(d) (BC14 lists four cost-minimizing flexibilities without compromising objectives/quality: (a) tailor-designing/customizing the institutional framework based on nature of operations, size, structure, and unique circumstances as long as principles are upheld and basic components are in place; (b) assigning the ethics officer role to an existing employee on a part-time basis rather than appointing a full-time ethics officer; (c) not mandating the establishment of a management ethics committee; and (d) outsourcing development and implementation to competent third parties per Par. 8).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 6(c), 6(e), and Appendix B (Paragraphs B13–B14, B17(d), B19(d), and B32) of AAOIFI GS 16, how are (1) ethics risk assessments and (2) periodic self-declarations of compliance executed and governed across an institution?
en.A: (1) Ethics risk assessments examine solely IT server uptime and require no follow-up improvement plan; (2) self-declarations apply only to external customers.
en.B: (1) The institution must periodically, systematically, and comprehensively conduct an ethics risk assessment to identify gaps/deficiencies across strategy and operations (including designing, sales, and implementation of products and services) and develop/implement a comprehensive improvement plan to eliminate or minimize material ethical conduct risks; (2) relevant internal stakeholders must periodically complete and submit self-declaration forms confirming compliance with the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics and organizational policies/procedures—with TCWG self-declarations managed by the Board Ethics Committee and other internal stakeholders' self-declarations managed by the Management Ethics Committee (if one exists).
en.C: (1) Ethics risk assessments are conducted once at incorporation; (2) senior executives and TCWG members are exempt from submitting periodic self-declarations.
en.D: (1) Ethics risk assessments exclude product sales practices; (2) all self-declarations are managed solely by the Human Resources clerk without committee oversight.
en.True answer: (1) The institution must periodically, systematically, and comprehensively conduct an ethics risk assessment to identify gaps/deficiencies across strategy and operations (including designing, sales, and implementation of products and services) and develop/implement a comprehensive improvement plan to eliminate or minimize material ethical conduct risks; (2) relevant internal stakeholders must periodically complete and submit self-declaration forms confirming compliance with the respective AAOIFI Code of Ethics and organizational policies/procedures—with TCWG self-declarations managed by the Board Ethics Committee and other internal stakeholders' self-declarations managed by the Management Ethics Committee (if one exists).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16, Par. 6(c), 6(e) & Appendix B, Par. B13–B14, B17(d), B19(d), B32 (Par. B13–B14: conduct periodic, systematic, and comprehensive ethics risk assessment to identify gaps/deficiencies in strategy and operations—including designing, sales, and implementation of products and services—and develop/implement an improvement plan to eliminate/minimize material risks; Par. B32: require relevant internal stakeholders to complete/submit periodic self-declaration forms confirming compliance with AAOIFI Code of Ethics and organizational policies/procedures; Par. B17(d) assigns managing self-declarations of TCWG to the board ethics committee, while Par. B19(d) assigns managing self-declarations of other internal stakeholders to the management ethics committee).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question:
In October 2024, a Qard-based Islamic microfinance and Zakah institution designs its Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics. Evaluate the following four governance and operational decisions:
(1) Management argues that because the institution is a non-profit Islamic social finance entity rather than a commercial bank, AAOIFI GS 16 is merely optional.
(2) The institution outsources its customer call center operations to an external BPO vendor, but excludes those call center agents from annual ethics training and self-declaration requirements on the grounds that they are third-party contractors rather than employees.
(3) To save costs, the CEO signs a contract outsourcing the administration of the anonymous ethics hotline to a third-party vendor without seeking approval from the Board Ethics Committee and without conducting due diligence on the vendor's privacy, confidentiality, and security controls.
(4) After receiving official TCWG authorization, the CEO establishes a Management Ethics Committee, appoints its chairman unilaterally without Board Ethics Committee involvement, and includes two junior entry-level tellers (lower management) while excluding middle management employees.
According to AAOIFI GS 16, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—social finance entities are exempt from GS 16; (2) Compliant—outsourced call center agents are external parties; (3) Compliant—CEO may outsource hotlines for cost savings; (4) Compliant—lower-level tellers are preferred over middle managers.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant—Par. 2 explicitly applies GS 16 to IFIs along with Islamic social finance institutions (such as Waqf, Zakah, and Qard-based microfinance institutions), and Par. 9 makes it effective on or after 1 July 2024; (2) Non-compliant—Par. 4(b) & Footnote 6 explicitly classify third parties to whom business functions are outsourced (specifically naming call center agents, Takaful agents, and BancaTakaful agents) as 'internal stakeholders' subject to training (B29) and self-declarations (B32); (3) Non-compliant—Par. 8 mandates that outsourcing any component of the institutional framework requires the approval of the Board Ethics Committee AND prior due diligence on third-party risks (integrity, privacy, confidentiality, security); (4) Non-compliant—Appendix B Par. B18(a), (d) & BC12–BC13 stipulate that the chairman of the Management Ethics Committee MUST be appointed by the Board Ethics Committee (not unilaterally by the CEO), and that employee(s) from middle management—and NOT lower management—should be included.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—Par. 2 explicitly applies GS 16 to IFIs along with Islamic social finance institutions (such as Waqf, Zakah, and Qard-based microfinance institutions), and Par. 9 makes it effective on or after 1 July 2024; (2) Non-compliant—Par. 4(b) & Footnote 6 explicitly classify third parties to whom business functions are outsourced (specifically naming call center agents, Takaful agents, and BancaTakaful agents) as 'internal stakeholders' subject to training (B29) and self-declarations (B32); (3) Non-compliant—Par. 8 mandates that outsourcing any component of the institutional framework requires the approval of the Board Ethics Committee AND prior due diligence on third-party risks (integrity, privacy, confidentiality, security); (4) Non-compliant—Appendix B Par. B18(a), (d) & BC12–BC13 stipulate that the chairman of the Management Ethics Committee MUST be appointed by the Board Ethics Committee (not unilaterally by the CEO), and that employee(s) from middle management—and NOT lower management—should be included.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 2 & Par. 9 apply GS 16 mandatorily to IFIs along with Islamic social finance institutions (Waqf, Zakah, Qard-based microfinance) on or after 1 July 2024; (2) Par. 4(b) & Footnote 6 define third parties performing outsourced business functions (specifically including call center agents) as internal stakeholders subject to annual training (Par. B29) and self-declarations (Par. B32); (3) Par. 8 prohibits outsourcing components of the institutional framework without Board Ethics Committee approval AND prior third-party risk due diligence covering integrity, privacy, confidentiality, and security; (4) Appendix B Par. B18(a), (d) & Appendix C BC12–BC13 require the chairman of the Management Ethics Committee to be appointed by the Board Ethics Committee and require middle management—specifically NOT lower management—representation.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 16: Institutional Framework for the Implementation of Ethics
en.Question:
During its annual ethics governance cycle, an Islamic bank encounters the following four situations:
(1) An anonymous whistleblower uses the ethics hotline to report that the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) pressured branch managers into mis-selling complex Mudaraba investment accounts to elderly retail clients; the Ethics Officer routes the claim to the Management Ethics Committee for investigation.
(2) During a subsequent investigation handled by the Board Ethics Committee involving alleged insider conflict of interest by one of the Board Ethics Committee's own members, that implicated member attends all investigative meetings and reviews confidential evidence; after the committee finds him guilty of a material ethics violation, he refuses to resign from the committee.
(3) The bank uploads the AAOIFI Code of Ethics solely as an English-language PDF on its internal intranet without translating it into the local mother tongue spoken by branch staff and without providing non-electronic copies.
(4) At year-end, the bank publishes a dedicated section in its Annual Report detailing its implementation of the AAOIFI Code of Ethics, without engaging an external firm to provide an independent assurance report on that section.
According to AAOIFI GS 16, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—Management Ethics Committee investigates all internal claims including against the CEO; (2) Compliant—committee members have the right to review evidence against themselves; (3) Compliant—English PDF on the intranet suffices; (4) Non-compliant—an independent assurance report is mandatory.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—under Appendix B Par. B17(c), B19(c) & B38(a), any reported ethics violation against a member of TCWG, the SSB, or senior management (including the CEO) MUST be addressed by the Board Ethics Committee, NOT the Management Ethics Committee; (2) Non-compliant—violates Par. B38(b), which mandates that a member of TCWG or an ethics committee involved in a reported violation must recuse himself (neither participating in the investigation nor being privy to case information until decided) AND must resign from the committee if found guilty of a material ethics violation; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. B9–B10, which require access to the AAOIFI Code of Ethics in internal stakeholders' preferred language / mother tongue AND via both electronic and non-electronic platforms; (4) Compliant—under Par. B39(b) & B42, publishing an annual report on implementation of the AAOIFI Code of Ethics is encouraged, and accompanying it with an independent assurance report is explicitly optional.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Appendix B Par. B17(c), B19(c) & B38(a), any reported ethics violation against a member of TCWG, the SSB, or senior management (including the CEO) MUST be addressed by the Board Ethics Committee, NOT the Management Ethics Committee; (2) Non-compliant—violates Par. B38(b), which mandates that a member of TCWG or an ethics committee involved in a reported violation must recuse himself (neither participating in the investigation nor being privy to case information until decided) AND must resign from the committee if found guilty of a material ethics violation; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. B9–B10, which require access to the AAOIFI Code of Ethics in internal stakeholders' preferred language / mother tongue AND via both electronic and non-electronic platforms; (4) Compliant—under Par. B39(b) & B42, publishing an annual report on implementation of the AAOIFI Code of Ethics is encouraged, and accompanying it with an independent assurance report is explicitly optional.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 16 integrates four provisions in Appendix B: (1) Par. B17(c), B19(c) & B38(a) assign exclusive jurisdiction over ethics violation claims against TCWG, SSB members, and senior management (including the CEO) to the Board Ethics Committee; (2) Par. B38(b) requires an implicated member of TCWG or the ethics committee to recuse himself (neither participating in investigation nor being privy to case info until decided) AND mandates resignation from the committee if found guilty of a material ethics violation; (3) Par. B9–B10 mandate providing the AAOIFI Code of Ethics in internal stakeholders' preferred language / mother tongue AND via both electronic and non-electronic platforms; (4) Par. B39(b) & B42 encourage publishing an annual report on implementing the AAOIFI Code of Ethics and state that it 'may optionally be accompanied by an independent assurance report'.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope, applicability to public instruments, and effective date of AAOIFI GS 17 ('Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments')?
en.A: GS 17 applies exclusively to secondary-market equity shares and mandates ratings every six months.
en.B: GS 17 applies to independent rating agency engagements providing assessment-based ratings on the state of Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary responsibilities for Sukuk and other Islamic finance instruments (including RIAs, URIA, and asset/liability/quasi-equity products); it highly recommends that all publicly offered instruments—excluding those offered by IFIs rated under GS 10—obtain ratings (preferably updated annually and announced publicly); and it is effective for ratings issued on or after 1 July 2023.
en.C: GS 17 is a mandatory SEC-enforced standard replacing GS 10 entirely for all Islamic financial institutions.
en.D: GS 17 applies only to conventional bonds and exempts all Islamic finance instruments from rating requirements.
en.True answer: GS 17 applies to independent rating agency engagements providing assessment-based ratings on the state of Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary responsibilities for Sukuk and other Islamic finance instruments (including RIAs, URIA, and asset/liability/quasi-equity products); it highly recommends that all publicly offered instruments—excluding those offered by IFIs rated under GS 10—obtain ratings (preferably updated annually and announced publicly); and it is effective for ratings issued on or after 1 July 2023.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Preface PR2, Par. 2–6 & Par. 60 (Par. 2–4: applies to Sukuk, RIAs, URIA, and asset/liability/quasi-equity products; Par. 6: highly recommends that all publicly offered instruments—excluding those offered by IFIs rated under GS 10—be subject to rating, updated annually and announced publicly; Par. 60: effective for ratings issued on or after 1 July 2023).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 8–9 and 57–58 of AAOIFI GS 17, which agencies are eligible to conduct Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary ratings for instruments, and what standards govern their principal procedures and documentation?
en.A: Either duly licensed credit rating agencies (with capacity and methodology developed per GS 10 and GS 17) or specialized Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies (with due involvement of credit rating experts), meeting ethical, quality control, and fit-and-proper criteria, while principal procedures and documentation follow Paragraphs 37–54 of GS 10 (suitably amended).
en.B: Exclusively central banks, while credit rating agencies are strictly barred from rating any Islamic finance instruments.
en.C: Any general accounting firm without credit rating expertise, following standard IFRS auditing guidelines.
en.D: Exclusively the issuer's internal audit department, with documentation exempt from archiving.
en.True answer: Either duly licensed credit rating agencies (with capacity and methodology developed per GS 10 and GS 17) or specialized Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies (with due involvement of credit rating experts), meeting ethical, quality control, and fit-and-proper criteria, while principal procedures and documentation follow Paragraphs 37–54 of GS 10 (suitably amended).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 8(a)–(b), Par. 9(a)–(d) & Par. 57–58 (Par. 8: eligible agencies are (a) credit rating agencies licensed/recognized by RSAs with capacity/methodology per GS 10 and GS 17, or (b) Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies with capacity/methodology per GS 10 and GS 17 involving credit rating experts; Par. 9: must meet ethics, quality control, engagement acceptance, and fit-and-proper criteria per GS 10; Par. 57–58: principal procedures, documentation, archiving, and confidentiality follow Par. 37–54 of GS 10, suitably amended).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraph 4 of AAOIFI GS 17, which four broad instrument types are brought into the scope of the standard?
en.A: Common equities, treasury bills, municipal bonds, and commercial paper.
en.B: Life insurance policies, commodity futures, foreign exchange forwards, and real estate deeds.
en.C: (a) Sukuk (including those issued by IFIs, corporates, or governments); (b) investment management instruments including restricted investment accounts (RIA) not registered as separate legal entities; (c) unrestricted investment accounts (URIA) or a class of URIA or similar instruments offered as Shari'ah-compliant by non-IFIs, or by IFIs unrated under GS 10 or rated below target; and (d) any other Islamic finance instruments offered publicly as liability, quasi-equity, or asset products.
en.D: Personal unsecured bank loans, consumer credit cards, pawnshop tickets, and student loans.
en.True answer: (a) Sukuk (including those issued by IFIs, corporates, or governments); (b) investment management instruments including restricted investment accounts (RIA) not registered as separate legal entities; (c) unrestricted investment accounts (URIA) or a class of URIA or similar instruments offered as Shari'ah-compliant by non-IFIs, or by IFIs unrated under GS 10 or rated below target; and (d) any other Islamic finance instruments offered publicly as liability, quasi-equity, or asset products.
