en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 4(a)–(d) (Enumerates the four instrument types within scope: (a) Sukuk issued by IFIs, corporate entities, or governments; (b) investment management instruments including restricted investment accounts [RIA] not registered as separate legal entities; (c) unrestricted investment accounts [URIA] or a class of URIA or similar instruments offered as Shari'ah-compliant by non-IFIs, or by IFIs unrated under GS 10 or rated below target; and (d) any other Islamic finance instruments offered publicly as liability, quasi-equity, or asset products).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraph 13 of AAOIFI GS 17, how are Shari'ah-compliant financial instruments classified into four distinct types for determining the suitable assessment scope and rating scale?
en.A: Short-term, medium-term, long-term, and perpetual instruments.
en.B: Sovereign, corporate, retail, and wholesale instruments.
en.C: Primary-market, secondary-market, over-the-counter, and unlisted instruments.
en.D: (a) Equity or quasi-equity type (without guarantee or purchase undertaking) instruments; (b) quasi-equity type (with guarantee or purchase undertaking) instruments; (c) liability type instruments; and (d) asset type instruments.
en.True answer: (a) Equity or quasi-equity type (without guarantee or purchase undertaking) instruments; (b) quasi-equity type (with guarantee or purchase undertaking) instruments; (c) liability type instruments; and (d) asset type instruments.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 13(a)–(d) (Classifies instruments into four types for determining suitable scope and rating scale: (a) equity or quasi-equity type [without guarantee or purchase undertaking] instruments; (b) quasi-equity type [with guarantee or purchase undertaking] instruments; (c) liability type instruments; and (d) asset type instruments).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 14–16 of AAOIFI GS 17, which characteristics define an 'Equity or quasi-equity type (without guarantee or purchase undertaking) instrument'?
en.A: Participatory structure representing a residual interest in underlying assets, perpetual and/or convertible nature, unconditional right of originator to avoid delivering cash or assets, subordination to all liability and quasi-equity instruments (preceding only share capital), and absence of any capital or return guarantee/purchase undertaking.
en.B: Fixed maturity date exactly in 3 years backed by an unconditional sovereign bank guarantee.
en.C: Senior secured debt status with mandatory senior claims over all other bank creditors.
en.D: Purely short-term commercial murabaha trade financing with daily liquidity settlements.
en.True answer: Participatory structure representing a residual interest in underlying assets, perpetual and/or convertible nature, unconditional right of originator to avoid delivering cash or assets, subordination to all liability and quasi-equity instruments (preceding only share capital), and absence of any capital or return guarantee/purchase undertaking.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 14(a)–(d) & Par. 15–16 (Par. 14 defines equity-type instruments: participatory structure representing residual interest in underlying assets, perpetual and/or convertible, unconditional right of originator to avoid delivering cash/assets, subordinate to liabilities/quasi-equity preceding only share capital; Par. 15–16 add that quasi-equity without guarantee shares these participatory profit/loss and subordination traits, lacks capital guarantees, and carries variable returns).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraph 21 of AAOIFI GS 17, how is a hybrid or Sukuk instrument classified as a 'Liability type instrument'?
en.A: If its equity component exceeds 80% of total asset value throughout its entire lifecycle.
en.B: If the ratio of its liability component (at par value, i.e., sale price including cost and profit) mostly, or at times, during the continuity of the instrument, exceeds 50% of the total underlying assets (considering tangibility ratio), and/or the return from its liability component provides more than 66.67% of the overall instrument's return.
en.C: If the instrument is structured purely on Mudaraba participation without any sale-based contracts.
en.D: Liability classification applies only when the originator defaults on dividend payments.
en.True answer: If the ratio of its liability component (at par value, i.e., sale price including cost and profit) mostly, or at times, during the continuity of the instrument, exceeds 50% of the total underlying assets (considering tangibility ratio), and/or the return from its liability component provides more than 66.67% of the overall instrument's return.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 21(a)–(b) (Defines when a hybrid or other instrument is classified as a liability type instrument: (a) if the ratio of its liability component [at par value, i.e., sale price including cost and profit] mostly, or at times, during continuity of the instrument, is more than 50% of the total underlying assets [duly considering tangibility ratio]; and/or (b) the return from its liability component provides more than 66.67% of the return of the overall instrument).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: According to Paragraphs 27–28 and Appendix D (BC21–BC23) of AAOIFI GS 17, what rating approach is recommended regarding Shari'ah compliance/governance versus fiduciary performance and capacity, and how are jurisdiction-specific ratings distinguished?
en.A: A single blended score must be used combining all pillars into one indivisible number, and country-specific suffixes are prohibited.
en.B: Ratings are restricted exclusively to international benchmarks; jurisdiction-specific ratings are banned.
en.C: It is recommended as a preferred practice that two different scores or ratings are developed by the rating agency in respect of (i) Shari'ah compliance and governance, and (ii) fiduciary responsibilities and capacity; furthermore, jurisdiction-specific ratings must be distinguished from global ratings by adding a three-letter jurisdiction-specific suffix and must not claim to be in general alignment with AAOIFI standards.
en.D: Fiduciary performance is evaluated solely by securities market regulators rather than rating agencies.
en.True answer: It is recommended as a preferred practice that two different scores or ratings are developed by the rating agency in respect of (i) Shari'ah compliance and governance, and (ii) fiduciary responsibilities and capacity; furthermore, jurisdiction-specific ratings must be distinguished from global ratings by adding a three-letter jurisdiction-specific suffix and must not claim to be in general alignment with AAOIFI standards.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 27 & Par. 46(a)–(c) (Par. 27: recommended as preferred practice that two different scores or ratings are developed for [i] Shari'ah compliance and governance, and [ii] fiduciary responsibilities and capacity; Par. 46: jurisdiction-specific ratings must document amended hierarchy, distinguish themselves by adding a three-letter jurisdiction-specific suffix, and not claim to be in line with AAOIFI standards in general).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 49–52 of AAOIFI GS 17, what action must a rating agency take if it encounters an unavoidable significant limitation of scope or is unable to conclude on the suitability of benchmarked parameters during an instrument rating engagement?
en.A: Issue an 'AAA' rating with a footnote waiver and proceed with publishing the report.
en.B: Arbitrarily adjust financial scoring weights to mask the missing parameters.
en.C: Transfer the rating engagement to an external conventional audit firm without informing stakeholders.
en.D: Assess the limitation of scope and suitability of benchmarked parameters (coordinating with Shari'ah supervisors for missing Shari'ah compliance parameters), and if an unavoidable significant limitation of scope remains or if unable to conclude on suitability, withdraw itself from the rating engagement.
en.True answer: Assess the limitation of scope and suitability of benchmarked parameters (coordinating with Shari'ah supervisors for missing Shari'ah compliance parameters), and if an unavoidable significant limitation of scope remains or if unable to conclude on suitability, withdraw itself from the rating engagement.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 49–51 (Par. 49: if an unavoidable significant limitation of scope impacting performance or quality remains after due efforts, the rating agency shall consider withdrawing from the rating engagement; Par. 50–51: assess suitability of benchmarked parameters, coordinate with Shari'ah supervisors for missing parameters, and if unable to conclude as to suitability, withdraw itself from the rating engagement).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraph 53 and Paragraph 60 of AAOIFI GS 17, how are rating scales structured for instruments, and what is the effective date of GS 17?
en.A: A rating scale is suggested to have a span of 5 to 10 stepped grades reflecting Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary responsibilities (with failure in a significant category like Shari'ah compliance considered an overall failure), and GS 17 is effective for ratings issued on or after 1 July 2023.
en.B: A rating scale must have exactly 3 grades, and GS 17 became effective on 1 January 2015.
en.C: Rating scales are prohibited from publishing conclusion statements, and GS 17 has no effective date.
en.D: GS 17 mandates a uniform global numeric scale from 0 to 100 for all agencies without grading symbols.
en.True answer: A rating scale is suggested to have a span of 5 to 10 stepped grades reflecting Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary responsibilities (with failure in a significant category like Shari'ah compliance considered an overall failure), and GS 17 is effective for ratings issued on or after 1 July 2023.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 53 & Par. 60 (Par. 53: rating scale suggested to have span of 5 to 10 stepped grades entailing explanation of Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary responsibilities, provided failure in a significant category—particularly compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules—is considered an overall failure; Par. 60: effective for ratings issued on or after 1 July 2023).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 18–20 of AAOIFI GS 17, which characteristics define a 'Quasi-equity type (with guarantee or purchase undertaking) instrument'?
en.A: Participatory instruments that permanently lack any form of guarantee, resulting in complete equity loss absorption without originator recourse.
en.B: Quasi-equity type Sukuk or other instruments where a guarantee or purchase undertaking provides a guaranteed or promised amount of redemption or maturity, meaning recourse in potential default goes first to the originator instead of directly to underlying assets.
en.C: Purely short-term commercial bank demand deposits with zero profit-sharing features.
en.D: Conventional zero-coupon bonds issued by non-financial corporate entities.
en.True answer: Quasi-equity type Sukuk or other instruments where a guarantee or purchase undertaking provides a guaranteed or promised amount of redemption or maturity, meaning recourse in potential default goes first to the originator instead of directly to underlying assets.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 18–19 (Defines quasi-equity type with guarantee or purchase undertaking: quasi-equity type Sukuk or other instruments where a guarantee or purchase undertaking provides a guaranteed or promised amount of redemption or maturity; in potential default, recourse is first to the originator instead of direct recourse to underlying assets, and risks/rewards of underlying assets are partially absorbed by the originator).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraph 23 of AAOIFI GS 17, what scope applies to an 'Asset-type instrument' rating?
en.A: Ratings apply exclusively to government central bank reserve bonds.
en.B: Asset-type ratings are restricted to conventional stock market shares.
en.C: Asset-type ratings apply to asset-side products (financing and investment products offered through acceptable Islamic modes) by: (a) IFIs unrated under GS 10 or rated below desired rating seeking separate product ratings, and (b) other entities/institutions offering Islamic finance products publicly (such as deferred payment sales or Ijarah) either linked to their business model or offered in markets where IFIs do not exist.
en.D: Asset-type ratings apply solely to non-performing corporate loans.
en.True answer: Asset-type ratings apply to asset-side products (financing and investment products offered through acceptable Islamic modes) by: (a) IFIs unrated under GS 10 or rated below desired rating seeking separate product ratings, and (b) other entities/institutions offering Islamic finance products publicly (such as deferred payment sales or Ijarah) either linked to their business model or offered in markets where IFIs do not exist.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 23(a)–(b) (Defines asset-type instrument scope: asset-side financing/investment products offered via acceptable Islamic modes by (a) IFIs unrated under GS 10 or rated below desired rating wishing separate product ratings, and (b) other entities/institutions offering Islamic finance products publicly—such as deferred payment sales or Ijarah—linked to business model or in markets where IFIs do not exist).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 28–32 of AAOIFI GS 17, which hierarchy defines the benchmarked parameters for 'Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules' and 'Shari'ah governance framework' when rating an Islamic finance instrument?
en.A: Conventional central bank monetary policy guidelines → Basel III capital accords → IMF lending rules.
en.B: External auditors' internal checklists → Rating agency's commercial marketing manual → Local commercial court precedents.
en.C: IFSB corporate governance standards → AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards → Issuer's board resolutions.
en.D: For Shari'ah principles and rules: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, (ii) regulator's Shari'ah regulations, (iii) Central Shari'ah Board rulings, (iv) AAOIFI FAS Shari'ah-related requirements, and (v) originator's SSB approvals/rulings; for Shari'ah governance framework: (i) AAOIFI governance standards [specifically GS 12 'Sukuk Governance'], (ii) IFSB Shari'ah governance standards, and (iii) regulator's Shari'ah governance regulations.
en.True answer: For Shari'ah principles and rules: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, (ii) regulator's Shari'ah regulations, (iii) Central Shari'ah Board rulings, (iv) AAOIFI FAS Shari'ah-related requirements, and (v) originator's SSB approvals/rulings; for Shari'ah governance framework: (i) AAOIFI governance standards [specifically GS 12 'Sukuk Governance'], (ii) IFSB Shari'ah governance standards, and (iii) regulator's Shari'ah governance regulations.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 28(a)–(e) & Par. 30(a)–(c) (Par. 28 defines Shari'ah principles and rules hierarchy: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah standards; (ii) regulator Shari'ah regulations; (iii) Central Shari'ah Board rulings; (iv) AAOIFI FAS Shari'ah-related requirements; (v) originator's SSB approvals/rulings. Par. 30 defines Shari'ah governance framework hierarchy: (i) AAOIFI governance standards [specifically GS 12]; (ii) IFSB Shari'ah governance standards; (iii) regulator Shari'ah governance regulations).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraph 31 of AAOIFI GS 17, how do instrument types affect the weighting and relative significance of the 'Shari'ah governance framework' benchmarked parameter?
en.A: Shari'ah governance framework is weighted higher for equity or quasi-equity without guarantee instruments (because risk/reward depends primarily on originator governance); is relevant for trustees/service providers when assets are carved out; has lower weight for liability-type instruments (where returns attribute directly to specific transactions rather than ongoing operations); and is weighted higher for asset-type instruments issued by financial institutions due to performance dependence on originator conduct.
en.B: Shari'ah governance framework carries a uniform 50% weight across all instrument types without exception.
en.C: Shari'ah governance framework is applied exclusively to conventional bonds and carries zero weight for equity Sukuk.
en.D: Shari'ah governance framework is assessed only after maturity during final asset liquidation.
en.True answer: Shari'ah governance framework is weighted higher for equity or quasi-equity without guarantee instruments (because risk/reward depends primarily on originator governance); is relevant for trustees/service providers when assets are carved out; has lower weight for liability-type instruments (where returns attribute directly to specific transactions rather than ongoing operations); and is weighted higher for asset-type instruments issued by financial institutions due to performance dependence on originator conduct.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 31(a)–(f) (Par. 31 details considerations for Shari'ah governance significance by instrument type: (b) weighted higher for equity/quasi-equity without guarantee because risk/reward depends on originator governance; (c) relevant for trustee/service provider when assets are carved out; (d) lower weight for liability-type instruments where returns attribute directly to a transaction; (e) weighted higher for asset-type instruments issued by financial institutions due to performance dependence on originator conduct).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraph 27 (Table of Suggested Weightages, Paragraph 48) of AAOIFI GS 17, how are benchmarked parameter weight distributions structured across different instrument types?
en.A: All instrument types must allocate exactly 50% to Shari'ah compliance and 50% to credit ratings.
en.B: Suggested weight distributions vary by instrument type: for equity/quasi-equity without guarantee, Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules is 30–35%, Shari'ah governance framework is 15–20% (Originator 10%, Instrument 5%), Corporate governance is 10% (Originator 5%, Service Provider/Trustee 5%), Transparency & disclosure is 10–15%, Ethics & values is 5–10% (Originator 5%, Service Provider 2% or similar), Asset quality/returns is 20–25%, and Originator creditworthiness is 20–15%; whereas for liability-type instruments, Asset quality is N/A and Originator creditworthiness carries 35–45%.
en.C: Ethics and values carry a mandatory 80% weight across all four instrument classifications.
en.D: Fiduciary performance weights are identical for participatory equity Sukuk and senior corporate murabaha notes.
en.True answer: Suggested weight distributions vary by instrument type: for equity/quasi-equity without guarantee, Compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules is 30–35%, Shari'ah governance framework is 15–20% (Originator 10%, Instrument 5%), Corporate governance is 10% (Originator 5%, Service Provider/Trustee 5%), Transparency & disclosure is 10–15%, Ethics & values is 5–10% (Originator 5%, Service Provider 2% or similar), Asset quality/returns is 20–25%, and Originator creditworthiness is 20–15%; whereas for liability-type instruments, Asset quality is N/A and Originator creditworthiness carries 35–45%.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 48 Table (Details the suggested weight distribution across instrument types: e.g., equity/quasi-equity without guarantee allocates Shari'ah compliance 30–35%, Shari'ah governance 15–20%, Corporate governance 10%, Transparency 10–15%, Ethics & values 5–10%, Asset quality/returns 20–25%, Creditworthiness 20–15%; liability instruments set Asset quality to N/A and Creditworthiness to 35–45%).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 18–20 of AAOIFI GS 17, how are 'Quasi-equity type (with guarantee or purchase undertaking) instruments' structured, and what examples represent this category?
en.A: They are pure equity instruments with zero redemption guarantees and loss absorption identical to common shares.
en.B: They are short-term trade receivables backed by conventional bank letters of credit without underlying assets.
en.C: They are quasi-equity type Sukuk or other instruments where a guarantee or purchase undertaking provides a guaranteed or promised amount of redemption or maturity, meaning recourse in potential default goes first to the originator instead of directly to underlying assets; examples include commingled Mudaraba Sukuk with redemption guarantees, Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek with pre-promised transfer prices or promised gifts, hybrid Sukuk failing equity/liability criteria, and URIA accounts.
en.D: They are government treasury bills issued at a discount without Shari'ah review.
en.True answer: They are quasi-equity type Sukuk or other instruments where a guarantee or purchase undertaking provides a guaranteed or promised amount of redemption or maturity, meaning recourse in potential default goes first to the originator instead of directly to underlying assets; examples include commingled Mudaraba Sukuk with redemption guarantees, Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek with pre-promised transfer prices or promised gifts, hybrid Sukuk failing equity/liability criteria, and URIA accounts.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 18–20(a)–(d) (Par. 18–19 define quasi-equity with guarantee or purchase undertaking: guarantee/purchase undertaking provides guaranteed/promised redemption amount; recourse in default goes first to originator instead of underlying assets; risks/rewards partially absorbed by originator. Par. 20 lists examples: (a) commingled Mudaraba Sukuk with redemption/maturity guarantee; (b) Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek with pre-promised transfer price or promised gift; (c) hybrid Sukuk failing equity or liability criteria; (d) URIAs and similar ongoing accounts).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 55–56 of AAOIFI GS 17, how are fiduciary performance and the quality of management services evaluated across different instrument types, and what distinction applies to liability-type versus equity-type instruments?
en.A: Fiduciary performance is evaluated exclusively through stock market trading volume for all instrument types without exception.
en.B: Liability-type instruments require extensive qualitative equity assessments, whereas equity instruments omit fiduciary scoring entirely.
en.C: Management services quality is assessed solely by external credit rating agencies using conventional balance sheet leverage ratios.
en.D: For liability-type or quasi-equity (with guarantee) instruments, the element of fiduciary performance is reduced or eliminated across the scale, with performance aspects captured in credit ratings; for asset-type instruments, the fiduciary element may be eliminated; and the interconnected yet distinct nature of instrument performance versus management service quality is best addressed by separately assessing (a) asset quality/returns and (b) originator creditworthiness on distinct scales.
en.True answer: For liability-type or quasi-equity (with guarantee) instruments, the element of fiduciary performance is reduced or eliminated across the scale, with performance aspects captured in credit ratings; for asset-type instruments, the fiduciary element may be eliminated; and the interconnected yet distinct nature of instrument performance versus management service quality is best addressed by separately assessing (a) asset quality/returns and (b) originator creditworthiness on distinct scales.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 55–56 (Par. 55: for liability-type or quasi-equity [with guarantee] instruments, fiduciary performance element is reduced or eliminated across scale, with performance captured in credit ratings; for asset-side instruments, fiduciary element may be eliminated. Par. 56: distinct yet interconnected nature of performance vs management service quality is addressed by separately assessing [a] asset quality/returns and [b] originator creditworthiness on distinct scales).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 46 and 54 of AAOIFI GS 17, how are jurisdiction-specific ratings structured, and what summarized indicators characterize the suggested 'AAs' (80–89%) rating scale grade?
en.A: Jurisdiction-specific ratings document amended hierarchies, add a three-letter jurisdiction-specific suffix, and do not claim general AAOIFI standard alignment; the suggested 'AAs' grade (80–89% weighted average score) represents a very good level of compliance where the underlying instrument structure is preferred in terms of Shari'ah principles and free of controversial elements, a strong governance environment is maintained (to the extent relevant), and fiduciary performance is expected to be strong.
en.B: Jurisdiction-specific ratings omit suffixes, and the 'AAs' grade represents unsatisfactory compliance with frequent non-compliance instances.
en.C: The 'AAs' grade is reserved for instruments scoring below 50% with significant governance weaknesses.
en.D: Jurisdiction-specific ratings are governed exclusively by Basel III rules and ignore local central bank regulations.
en.True answer: Jurisdiction-specific ratings document amended hierarchies, add a three-letter jurisdiction-specific suffix, and do not claim general AAOIFI standard alignment; the suggested 'AAs' grade (80–89% weighted average score) represents a very good level of compliance where the underlying instrument structure is preferred in terms of Shari'ah principles and free of controversial elements, a strong governance environment is maintained (to the extent relevant), and fiduciary performance is expected to be strong.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 46(a)–(c) & Par. 54 Table ('AAs' grade 80–89%) (Par. 46: jurisdiction-specific ratings document amended hierarchy, add a three-letter jurisdiction-specific suffix, and do not claim to be in line with AAOIFI standards in general. Par. 54 Table 'AAs' [80–89%]: very good level of compliance; underlying instrument structure preferred in terms of Shari'ah principles and free of controversial elements; strong governance environment maintained to the extent relevant; fiduciary performance expected to be strong).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question: In Appendix D (Basis of Conclusions, BC11–BC13) of AAOIFI GS 17, how did the Board evaluate the eligibility of traditional credit rating agencies versus specialized Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies?
en.A: Traditional credit rating agencies were permanently barred from rating Islamic finance instruments due to complete lack of commercial interest.
en.B: The Board acknowledged that credit ratings and Shari'ah compliance/fiduciary ratings differ in their required approaches and skill sets; however, to support wider adoption of the standard, the Board decided NOT to restrict credit rating agencies from adopting the standard (regardless of whether they engage in institutional GS 10 ratings), including both licensed credit rating agencies and specialized Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies as eligible agencies, provided they develop the necessary capacity and methodology.
en.C: Only specialized Shari'ah boutique firms are eligible, while all conventional credit rating agencies are legally prohibited from adopting GS 17.
en.D: Credit rating agencies were granted automatic eligibility without needing to develop capacity or methodology for Shari'ah compliance.
en.True answer: The Board acknowledged that credit ratings and Shari'ah compliance/fiduciary ratings differ in their required approaches and skill sets; however, to support wider adoption of the standard, the Board decided NOT to restrict credit rating agencies from adopting the standard (regardless of whether they engage in institutional GS 10 ratings), including both licensed credit rating agencies and specialized Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies as eligible agencies, provided they develop the necessary capacity and methodology.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17, Par. 8(a)–(b) & Appendix D, BC11–BC13 (BC12 notes that credit ratings and Shari'ah compliance/fiduciary ratings differ in required approaches and skill sets; however, to support wider adoption, the Board decided not to restrict credit rating agencies from adopting the standard—whether or not they engage in GS 10 institutional ratings—and included both credit rating agencies and specialized Shari'ah compliance and fiduciary rating agencies as eligible agencies under Par. 8, subject to developing necessary capacity and methodology).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question:
In February 2024, a corporate originator issues a USD 500 million hybrid Sukuk structured as a combination of an Ijara tangible lease asset component and a Murabaha deferred payment sale component. Review the four structural and rating governance facts:
(1) The liability component (par value sale price) accounts for 65% of the total underlying assets, and returns from the liability component generate 70% of the overall instrument's return.
(2) Because the Sukuk is hybrid, the rating agency classifies it as an 'Equity-type instrument without guarantee', applying equity-only asset return volatility metrics while ignoring the Murabaha liability cash flows.
(3) The rating agency develops two distinct scores/ratings: one for Shari'ah compliance and governance, and a separate one for fiduciary responsibilities and capacity (comprising asset quality/returns and originator creditworthiness).
(4) During the rating assessment, the rating agency encounters a severe unavoidable limitation of scope impacting audit evidence on underlying asset cash flows; after exhausting due efforts, the rating agency proceeds to issue an 'AAs' rating without withdrawing.
According to AAOIFI GS 17, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—hybrid Sukuk are always equity-type; (2) Compliant—rating agencies have absolute discretion over instrument classification; (3) Non-compliant—dual ratings are prohibited; (4) Compliant—limitations of scope never require withdrawal.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant with Paragraph 21 classification rules—since the liability component exceeds 50% of underlying assets (65%) and provides more than 66.67% of the return (70%), it is correctly classified as a 'Liability-type instrument'; (2) Non-compliant—classifying a hybrid Sukuk with 65% liability as equity is wrong; (3) Compliant—Paragraph 27 recommends as a preferred practice developing two different scores/ratings for Shari'ah compliance/governance and fiduciary responsibilities/capacity; (4) Non-compliant—Paragraph 49 mandates that if an unavoidable significant limitation of scope remains after due efforts, the rating agency shall consider withdrawing from the rating engagement rather than issuing a rating.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Compliant with Paragraph 21 classification rules—since the liability component exceeds 50% of underlying assets (65%) and provides more than 66.67% of the return (70%), it is correctly classified as a 'Liability-type instrument'; (2) Non-compliant—classifying a hybrid Sukuk with 65% liability as equity is wrong; (3) Compliant—Paragraph 27 recommends as a preferred practice developing two different scores/ratings for Shari'ah compliance/governance and fiduciary responsibilities/capacity; (4) Non-compliant—Paragraph 49 mandates that if an unavoidable significant limitation of scope remains after due efforts, the rating agency shall consider withdrawing from the rating engagement rather than issuing a rating.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 21(a)–(b) classifies a hybrid instrument as a liability-type instrument if its liability component exceeds 50% of underlying assets and/or generates >66.67% of return; (2) classifying 65% liability as equity violates Par. 21; (3) Par. 27 recommends as a preferred practice developing two distinct scores/ratings for Shari'ah compliance/governance and fiduciary responsibilities/capacity; (4) Par. 49 requires considering withdrawal from the rating engagement if an unavoidable significant limitation of scope remains after due efforts.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 17: Shari'ah Compliance and Fiduciary Ratings of Sukuk and Other Islamic Finance Instruments
en.Question:
During the annual review and rating cycle of a publicly offered Tier 1 perpetual Mudaraba Sukuk issuance (classified as an equity/quasi-equity type without purchase undertaking), examine the following four governance and rating execution actions:
(1) The rating agency issues a single indivisible blended score combining Shari'ah governance and fiduciary capacity into one number, claiming that separate ratings are prohibited under AAOIFI standards.
(2) In assessing the Shari'ah compliance benchmarked parameters, the rating agency applies SEC corporate governance regulations before considering AAOIFI Shari'ah standards and regulatory Shari'ah requirements.
(3) Because the Tier 1 Sukuk lacks any capital guarantee or purchase undertaking, the rating agency evaluates its fiduciary performance by applying traditional senior corporate bond credit default probability models directly without assessing underlying asset quality or returns.
(4) The rating agency determines its rating scale span as 7 stepped grades (well within the suggested 5 to 10 grade range), provides clear explanatory conclusions for each grade, and ensures that a failure in compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules is treated as an overall failure.
According to AAOIFI GS 17, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—single blended scores are mandatory; (2) Compliant—SEC corporate governance rules always rank first; (3) Compliant—Tier 1 Sukuk use senior bond default models; (4) Non-compliant—rating scales cannot have 7 grades.
en.B: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—Paragraph 27 recommends as a preferred practice developing two different scores/ratings for Shari'ah compliance/governance and fiduciary responsibilities/capacity; (2) Non-compliant—Paragraph 28 establishes that AAOIFI Shari'ah standards and RSA Shari'ah regulations take precedence over general corporate governance codes when evaluating Shari'ah compliance parameters; (3) Non-compliant—Paragraphs 41 and 43 mandate that for equity and quasi-equity instruments without guarantee, assessing asset quality and returns (along with underlying performance) is paramount, whereas applying senior corporate bond credit models alone is improper; (4) Compliant—Paragraph 53 suggests a rating scale span of 5 to 10 stepped grades with explanatory conclusions, and explicitly mandates that a failure in a significant category (particularly compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules) shall be considered an overall failure.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—Paragraph 27 recommends as a preferred practice developing two different scores/ratings for Shari'ah compliance/governance and fiduciary responsibilities/capacity; (2) Non-compliant—Paragraph 28 establishes that AAOIFI Shari'ah standards and RSA Shari'ah regulations take precedence over general corporate governance codes when evaluating Shari'ah compliance parameters; (3) Non-compliant—Paragraphs 41 and 43 mandate that for equity and quasi-equity instruments without guarantee, assessing asset quality and returns (along with underlying performance) is paramount, whereas applying senior corporate bond credit models alone is improper; (4) Compliant—Paragraph 53 suggests a rating scale span of 5 to 10 stepped grades with explanatory conclusions, and explicitly mandates that a failure in a significant category (particularly compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules) shall be considered an overall failure.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 17 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 27 recommends as a preferred practice developing two separate scores/ratings for Shari'ah compliance/governance and fiduciary responsibilities/capacity (making single blended scores non-mandatory/sub-optimal); (2) Par. 28 establishes Shari'ah compliance hierarchy placing AAOIFI Shari'ah standards and RSA Shari'ah regulations ahead of general corporate codes; (3) Par. 41 & 43 require evaluating asset quality, returns, and underlying performance for equity/quasi-equity without guarantee instruments, rendering senior bond credit models improper; (4) Par. 53 suggests a rating scale span of 5 to 10 stepped grades with explanatory conclusions and explicitly mandates that a failure in compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules is treated as an overall failure.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope of AAOIFI GS 18 ('Shari'ah Decision-Making Process'), its relationship with AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard (SS) 29, and its effective date?
en.A: GS 18 applies to all IFIs, other Shari'ah-compliant institutions, and Islamic finance transactions (involving internal and external stakeholders as well as Central Shari'ah Boards), complements—without superseding—AAOIFI SS 29 ('Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework'), and is effective from 1 January 2026.
en.B: GS 18 supersedes AAOIFI SS 29 completely, applies exclusively to internal bank employees (excluding CSBs and external stakeholders), and became effective retroactively on 1 July 2021.
en.C: GS 18 governs solely the classical Usul al-Fiqh methodology for deriving Fatwas and exempts management from any role in Shari'ah decision-making.
en.D: GS 18 is a non-binding advisory note applicable only to sovereign Sukuk issuances beginning on 1 January 2030.
en.True answer: GS 18 applies to all IFIs, other Shari'ah-compliant institutions, and Islamic finance transactions (involving internal and external stakeholders as well as Central Shari'ah Boards), complements—without superseding—AAOIFI SS 29 ('Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework'), and is effective from 1 January 2026.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Preface PR3, Par. 1–3, Par. 91 & Appendix G, BC1–BC6 (Par. 1–3 & BC2: complements—without superseding or undermining—AAOIFI SS 29 'Stipulations and Ethics of Fatwa in the Institutional Framework', and is read in conjunction with GS 8 and AAOIFI Code of Ethics; Par. 2 & BC5–BC9: applies to all IFIs, other institutions, and Islamic finance transactions involving internal and external stakeholders as well as CSBs; Par. 91: effective from 1 January 2026).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraph 4(d)–(e) and Appendix G (BC10–BC12) of AAOIFI GS 18, how are 'Jurisprudential arbitrage' and 'Non-disciplinary Fatwa' defined?
en.A: Jurisprudential arbitrage is the lawful harmonization of accounting standards across countries, while a non-disciplinary Fatwa is any Fatwa issued by a Central Shari'ah Board.
en.B: Jurisprudential arbitrage is an effort to develop a seemingly Shari'ah-compliant transaction or product while circumventing generally applied Shari'ah principles and rules through unjustified use of options across different schools of Islamic jurisprudence, juristic stratagems (Heelas), principle of need (Hajah)/necessity (Dharurah), and/or public interest (Maslahah); a non-disciplinary Fatwa is an opinion based on self-interest rather than proper evidence, not following Fatwa principles, and/or accumulating weak opinions into an opinion unacceptable by any school of Islamic jurisprudence per AAOIFI SS 29.
en.C: Both terms refer exclusively to commercial dispute arbitration between two Islamic banks under secular commercial law.
en.D: Jurisprudential arbitrage is mandatory when structuring cross-border Sukuk, whereas a non-disciplinary Fatwa is any minority dissenting opinion recorded in SSB minutes.
en.True answer: Jurisprudential arbitrage is an effort to develop a seemingly Shari'ah-compliant transaction or product while circumventing generally applied Shari'ah principles and rules through unjustified use of options across different schools of Islamic jurisprudence, juristic stratagems (Heelas), principle of need (Hajah)/necessity (Dharurah), and/or public interest (Maslahah); a non-disciplinary Fatwa is an opinion based on self-interest rather than proper evidence, not following Fatwa principles, and/or accumulating weak opinions into an opinion unacceptable by any school of Islamic jurisprudence per AAOIFI SS 29.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 4(d)–(e) & Appendix G, BC10–BC12 (Par. 4(d): Jurisprudential arbitrage is an effort to develop a seemingly Shari'ah-compliant transaction/product while circumventing generally applied Shari'ah principles and rules through unjustified use of (i) options available under different schools of Islamic jurisprudence, (ii) juristic stratagems [Heelas], (iii) principle of need [Hajah] and necessity [Dharurah], and/or (iv) public interest [Maslahah]; Par. 4(e): Non-disciplinary Fatwa is an opinion based on self-interest and not on proper evidence, does not follow principles of Fatwa, and/or accumulates weak opinions leading to an opinion not acceptable by any school of Islamic jurisprudence per SS 29).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraph 4(h) (including its Explanation) of AAOIFI GS 18, what is the five-tier hierarchy of 'Shari'ah principles and rules,' and whose clarification prevails if an ambiguity is identified during a compliance, audit, or rating exercise?
en.A: Institutional SSB rulings override AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, and the external financial auditor's interpretation prevails in case of ambiguity.
en.B: Central Bank regulations → Institutional SSB rulings → AAOIFI FASs → AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards → CSB rulings, with the CEO's clarification prevailing in case of ambiguity.
en.C: From top to bottom: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, (ii) regulator's regulations insofar as they entail regulatory Shari'ah requirements, (iii) rulings of the Central Shari'ah Board (if one exists), (iv) Shari'ah-related requirements of applicable AAOIFI FASs, and (v) approvals and rulings given by the institution's SSB; in case of an ambiguity identified during a compliance, audit, or rating exercise regarding interpretations of (i) to (iv), the Shari'ah Supervisory Board's (SSB's) clarification shall prevail.
en.D: AAOIFI FASs rank first ahead of AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, and any ambiguity automatically invalidates the underlying contract.
en.True answer: From top to bottom: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards, (ii) regulator's regulations insofar as they entail regulatory Shari'ah requirements, (iii) rulings of the Central Shari'ah Board (if one exists), (iv) Shari'ah-related requirements of applicable AAOIFI FASs, and (v) approvals and rulings given by the institution's SSB; in case of an ambiguity identified during a compliance, audit, or rating exercise regarding interpretations of (i) to (iv), the Shari'ah Supervisory Board's (SSB's) clarification shall prevail.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 4(h)(i)–(v) & Explanation (Establishes the 5-tier hierarchy from top to bottom: (i) AAOIFI Shari'ah standards, (ii) regulator's regulations insofar as entailing regulatory Shari'ah requirements, (iii) CSB rulings [if one exists], (iv) Shari'ah-related requirements of applicable AAOIFI FASs, and (v) approvals/rulings of the institution's SSB; Explanation explicitly states: 'In case of an ambiguity, identified during a compliance, audit or rating exercise, as the case may be, with regard to interpretations related to (i) to (iv) above, the Shari'ah supervisory board's clarification shall prevail').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraph 4(j)–(k) of AAOIFI GS 18, how are 'Maqasid Al-Shari'ah' and 'Maqasid Al-Uqood' defined?
en.A: Maqasid Al-Shari'ah refers solely to maximizing shareholder return on equity, while Maqasid Al-Uqood refers to minimizing corporate tax liabilities.
en.B: Maqasid Al-Shari'ah allows overriding explicit Quranic prohibitions for commercial convenience, while Maqasid Al-Uqood permits sellers to retain legal ownership of sold goods until final installment payment.
en.C: Both terms refer to conventional civil-law contract interpretation doctrines that subordinate substance to legal form.
en.D: Maqasid Al-Shari'ah are the higher objectives of Shari'ah meant to protect and safeguard human beings through obedience to Allah Almighty in line with Shari'ah principles and rules, achieved through preserving Deen, life, intellect, progeny, and wealth and prioritizing necessities (Daruriyyat), followed by needs (Hajiyyat), followed by embellishments/complementary matters (Tahsiniyyat); Maqasid Al-Uqood are the objectives for which the relevant contract is legislated per Shari'ah (e.g., transferring ownership of the sold subject matter in a sale contract, or transferring ownership of usufruct in an Ijarah contract).
en.True answer: Maqasid Al-Shari'ah are the higher objectives of Shari'ah meant to protect and safeguard human beings through obedience to Allah Almighty in line with Shari'ah principles and rules, achieved through preserving Deen, life, intellect, progeny, and wealth and prioritizing necessities (Daruriyyat), followed by needs (Hajiyyat), followed by embellishments/complementary matters (Tahsiniyyat); Maqasid Al-Uqood are the objectives for which the relevant contract is legislated per Shari'ah (e.g., transferring ownership of the sold subject matter in a sale contract, or transferring ownership of usufruct in an Ijarah contract).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 4(j)–(k) & Appendix G, BC13–BC20 (Par. 4(j): Maqasid Al-Shari'ah are higher objectives of Shari'ah meant to protect/safeguard human beings through obedience to Allah Almighty in line with Shari'ah principles and rules, achieved through preservation of Deen, life, intellect, progeny, and wealth and prioritization of necessities, followed by needs, followed by embellishments and complementary matters; Par. 4(k): Maqasid Al-Uqood are objectives for which the relevant contract is legislated per Shari'ah—e.g., transferring ownership of subject matter in a sale contract [negated if seller retains ownership until installments are settled], or transferring ownership of usufruct in an Ijarah contract [negated if lessee bears loss of leased asset on an absolute basis]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraph 8(a)–(b) of AAOIFI GS 18, how does the SSB product approval process distinguish between 'standard products' and 'non-standard products'?
en.A: Standard products (offered on an ongoing basis in a standardized format) require reviewing at minimum six elements—product concept paper, final legal documentation, accounting recording and reporting, IT mapping in the core banking system, marketing material, and relevant SOPs/manuals/product programmes—whereas non-standard products (bespoke transactions such as Sukuk, syndication, club-deals, or investment proposals) require reviewing the structure/legal documentation, accounting recording/reporting, and/or approving after review Shari'ah pronouncements issued by other SSBs.
en.B: Standard products require only a verbal summary of the concept paper without legal or IT review, whereas non-standard products require 100% IT core-banking mapping before approval.
en.C: Both standard and non-standard products are approved solely by the Product Development Department without SSB review.
en.D: Accounting recording and financial reporting are excluded from SSB product approval for both standard and non-standard products.
en.True answer: Standard products (offered on an ongoing basis in a standardized format) require reviewing at minimum six elements—product concept paper, final legal documentation, accounting recording and reporting, IT mapping in the core banking system, marketing material, and relevant SOPs/manuals/product programmes—whereas non-standard products (bespoke transactions such as Sukuk, syndication, club-deals, or investment proposals) require reviewing the structure/legal documentation, accounting recording/reporting, and/or approving after review Shari'ah pronouncements issued by other SSBs.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 8(a)–(b) & Appendix G, BC27–BC31 (Par. 8(a): standard products require reviewing at minimum (i) product concept paper, (ii) final version of legal documentation, (iii) transaction recording and reporting for accounting purposes, (iv) IT mapping in core banking system, (v) marketing material, and (vi) relevant SOPs, manuals, and product programmes; Par. 8(b): non-standard products [bespoke transactions e.g. Sukuk, syndication, club-deals, investment proposals] require (i) review of structure and legal documentation, (ii) review of transaction recording and reporting for accounting purposes, and/or (iii) approval, after necessary review, of Shari'ah pronouncements issued by other SSBs).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraph 9 (including Footnote 13) of AAOIFI GS 18, how are queries raised by management and governance organs to the SSB classified?
en.A: Solely into urgent queries and routine queries, with all product improvement inquiries treated as non-transactional.
en.B: Into three categories: (a) transactional queries (which also include queries regarding non-standard products), (b) non-transactional queries (divided into financial queries such as accounting policies, provisions, Zakah calculation, charity disbursement, cost allocation, and tax adjustments; and non-financial queries such as marketing, HR, or PR activities), and (c) development queries (related to improvements in standard products to enhance processes, cost efficiency, or customer experience).
en.C: Into internal audit queries and external rating queries, while accounting and Zakah questions are barred from being submitted to the SSB.
en.D: Only transactional queries may be submitted to the SSB; marketing, HR, and Zakah questions are decided exclusively by senior management.
en.True answer: Into three categories: (a) transactional queries (which also include queries regarding non-standard products), (b) non-transactional queries (divided into financial queries such as accounting policies, provisions, Zakah calculation, charity disbursement, cost allocation, and tax adjustments; and non-financial queries such as marketing, HR, or PR activities), and (c) development queries (related to improvements in standard products to enhance processes, cost efficiency, or customer experience).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 9(a)–(c) & Footnote 13 (Classifies queries into three categories: (a) transactional queries [Footnote 13 clarifies queries regarding non-standard products are transactional queries]; (b) non-transactional queries, comprising (i) financial queries [accounting policies/practices, provisions, Zakah calculation, charity disbursement, cost/expense allocation, tax adjustments] and (ii) non-financial queries [marketing/promotion, HR, public relations]; and (c) development queries [improvements in standard products to enhance processes, cost efficiency, or customer experience]).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 12–14 and Appendix G (BC7–BC9) of AAOIFI GS 18, why might a Central Shari'ah Board's (CSB's) SDM process lead to different decisions from an individual institution's SSB, and who holds authority to interpret and apply a CSB ruling within a specific institution?
en.A: A CSB focuses solely on maximizing individual bank profits, whereas an institution's SSB may freely ignore CSB rulings whenever they reduce commercial margins.
en.B: A CSB has no authority over Maqasid Al-Shari'ah, and only external financial auditors may interpret CSB rulings for individual banks.
en.C: A CSB considers a broader macro vision, wider industry-wide and public interest, national/global socio-economic objectives, overall industry ethical conduct, and greater emphasis on Maqasid Al-Shari'ah (including reconsidering individual permissions of controversial products not aligned with Maqasid Al-Shari'ah), whereas an individual SSB has a micro vision specific to one institution; once a CSB ruling/resolution is issued, the SSB of the respective institution holds authority to interpret and apply it in the specific context of that institution.
en.D: CSBs are excluded from the scope of GS 18, and institutional management unilaterally interprets CSB resolutions without SSB involvement.
en.True answer: A CSB considers a broader macro vision, wider industry-wide and public interest, national/global socio-economic objectives, overall industry ethical conduct, and greater emphasis on Maqasid Al-Shari'ah (including reconsidering individual permissions of controversial products not aligned with Maqasid Al-Shari'ah), whereas an individual SSB has a micro vision specific to one institution; once a CSB ruling/resolution is issued, the SSB of the respective institution holds authority to interpret and apply it in the specific context of that institution.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 12–14 & Appendix G, BC7–BC9 (Par. 13(a)–(g): CSB considers broader macro vision vs SSB's micro vision, wider industry interests/long-term development, public interest, national/global socio-economic objectives, overall industry ethics, greater consideration of Maqasid Al-Shari'ah [including reconsidering individual permission of controversial products], and precepts of do no harm/non-malevolence/justice; Par. 14: CSB has authority to interpret and decide on these matters in the jurisdiction, and once a CSB ruling/resolution is issued, the SSB of the respective institution has authority to interpret and apply it in the specific context of that institution).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 15–20 and Paragraph 32 of AAOIFI GS 18, when two or more product options are permissible under Shari'ah principles and rules but differ in their alignment with Maqasid Al-Shari'ah and higher ethical values, how are roles divided between the SSB and TCWG/Senior Management?
en.A: The SSB exercises direct executive authority to force commercial selection of a product based solely on non-mandatory ethical preferences.
en.B: Senior management may launch any controversial product without SSB review as long as it generates higher short-term revenue.
en.C: Neither the SSB nor TCWG considers Maqasid Al-Shari'ah; selection among permissible products is determined exclusively by external rating agencies.
en.D: The SSB's primary role does not include business decisions and it cannot impose non-mandatory higher ethical standards, though it identifies/justifies the permissibility of the options and provides guidance/recommendations on which option is more worthy under Maqasid Al-Shari'ah; TCWG and senior management hold the crucial responsibility to make the most desirable business choice among the SSB-approved permissible options while giving due weightage to ethics, stakeholder rights, and Maqasid Al-Shari'ah.
en.True answer: The SSB's primary role does not include business decisions and it cannot impose non-mandatory higher ethical standards, though it identifies/justifies the permissibility of the options and provides guidance/recommendations on which option is more worthy under Maqasid Al-Shari'ah; TCWG and senior management hold the crucial responsibility to make the most desirable business choice among the SSB-approved permissible options while giving due weightage to ethics, stakeholder rights, and Maqasid Al-Shari'ah.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 15–20, Par. 32 & Par. 68 (Par. 15: SSB's primary role does not include business decisions [such as choosing which product to adopt when multiple options are permissible but differ under Maqasid Al-Shari'ah], its involvement is advisory/supervisory, and it may suggest but cannot impose non-mandatory higher standards of ethics; Par. 16, 19 & 32: TCWG and senior management have the crucial test/role to choose the most desirable option among multiple SSB-approved permissible options while balancing stakeholder expectations, ethics, and Maqasid Al-Shari'ah; Par. 68: SSB provides guidance/recommendation when some permissible options are more worthy under Maqasid Al-Shari'ah).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 22–28 of AAOIFI GS 18, what rules apply to preventing 'Fatwa shopping' and the intentional replacement of SSB scholars to obtain a predetermined Fatwa?
en.A: An institution must never proactively search for scholars or Shari'ah consultancy firms with the intent to obtain favorable Fatwas for a predetermined outcome (including replacing SSB members for such purpose), and if a Shari'ah scholar becomes aware that the primary purpose of his appointment in place of another scholar is non-disciplinary Fatwa, accepting such an appointment constitutes a breach of good governance and ethical requirements.
en.B: An institution may freely replace dissenting SSB scholars mid-year whenever they reject a high-margin retail product.
en.C: A scholar who knowingly accepts an appointment intended to overturn a predecessor's strict Fatwa commits no ethical breach as long as he cites at least one classical text.
en.D: Continuing SSB members must remain silent and take no action if they discover management is replacing colleagues to secure predetermined Fatwas.
en.True answer: An institution must never proactively search for scholars or Shari'ah consultancy firms with the intent to obtain favorable Fatwas for a predetermined outcome (including replacing SSB members for such purpose), and if a Shari'ah scholar becomes aware that the primary purpose of his appointment in place of another scholar is non-disciplinary Fatwa, accepting such an appointment constitutes a breach of good governance and ethical requirements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 22–26 (Par. 23: if continuing SSB members become aware of intentional replacement of scholars within SSB aimed at attaining non-disciplinary Fatwa, they shall consider an appropriate course of action; Par. 25: institution shall in no case be involved in proactive search for scholar(s) and/or Shari'ah consultancy firm(s) with intent to provide favorable Fatwas for a predetermined outcome, including replacement of SSB members primarily with such intention; Par. 26: where a Shari'ah scholar becomes aware that primary purpose of his appointment in place of another scholar is non-disciplinary Fatwa, accepting such appointment is a breach of good governance and ethical requirements).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 69–71 (and Footnote 30) of AAOIFI GS 18, what rules govern limited delegation of authority by the SSB to one of its members?
en.A: Once authority is delegated to a single SSB member, the remaining SSB members are permanently absolved of all responsibility, and no subsequent ratification is needed.
en.B: The delegated member must have knowledge of and keep in view the hierarchy of Shari'ah principles and rules, respond in line with the specific delegation terms of reference, and be free of any conflict of interest; the Shari'ah decision made by the delegated person MUST be ratified in the next SSB meeting or via circulation (or per the terms of reference), and delegating specific responsibility does NOT absolve the other SSB members of their responsibilities.
en.C: The SSB may delegate full Fatwa-issuing authority to the bank's Chief Executive Officer during peak commercial periods.
en.D: Delegated decisions require ratification only once every five years during external regulatory inspections.
en.True answer: The delegated member must have knowledge of and keep in view the hierarchy of Shari'ah principles and rules, respond in line with the specific delegation terms of reference, and be free of any conflict of interest; the Shari'ah decision made by the delegated person MUST be ratified in the next SSB meeting or via circulation (or per the terms of reference), and delegating specific responsibility does NOT absolve the other SSB members of their responsibilities.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 69(a)–(c), Par. 70–71 & Footnote 30 (Par. 69: delegated member/person must (a) have knowledge of and keep in view hierarchy of Shari'ah principles and rules, (b) respond in line with specific delegation terms of reference, and (c) be free of conflict of interest with business/operational functions; Par. 70: Shari'ah decision by delegated person must be ratified in the next SSB meeting or via circulation or per terms of reference; Par. 71: delegating specific responsibility to a member with more expertise 'does not absolve the other SSB members of their responsibilities').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 72–73 and Appendix G (BC36–BC40) of AAOIFI GS 18, how must reservations and dissenting opinions of SSB members be treated in a Fatwa document?
en.A: Dissenting opinions must be excluded completely from all internal and external versions of a Fatwa to prevent market confusion.
en.B: Dissenting opinions are recorded only if at least half of the SSB disagrees with the ruling, and must always be published on billboards.
en.C: Reservations and dissenting opinions (if any), along with the reasons for such reservation or dissent and the name and signature of the respective member(s), MUST always be documented as part of the minimum contents of the Fatwa document; however, when publishing a Fatwa, the dissenting opinion is to be made available to the general public ONLY if so required by the respective Regulatory and Supervisory Authority (RSA).
en.D: Any dissenting scholar is prohibited from signing his name or stating reasons in the Fatwa document.
en.True answer: Reservations and dissenting opinions (if any), along with the reasons for such reservation or dissent and the name and signature of the respective member(s), MUST always be documented as part of the minimum contents of the Fatwa document; however, when publishing a Fatwa, the dissenting opinion is to be made available to the general public ONLY if so required by the respective Regulatory and Supervisory Authority (RSA).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 72(g) Note & Appendix G, BC36–BC40 (Par. 72(g) lists as a mandatory minimum content of a Fatwa: 'reservations and dissenting opinions, if any, along with the reasons for such reservation or dissent, and the name and signature of the respective member(s) [Note: Dissenting opinion is to be made available (in case of publishing of Fatwa) to the general public only if so required by the respective regulator]').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 75–81 of AAOIFI GS 18, what responsibilities rest with the Shari'ah Compliance Department (SCD) before and after an SSB resolution, and what five minimum items must be included in the format for presenting queries to the SSB?
en.A: SCD forwards raw business proposals directly to the SSB without legal or accounting checks, and query formats require only a one-sentence question.
en.B: SCD unilaterally revokes outdated Fatwas without SSB involvement, and query formats exclude identifying the query owner.
en.C: SCD reviews only marketing brochures, while legal and risk reviews are postponed until after product launch.
en.D: Before forwarding a query/proposal to the SSB, the SCD must review legal documentation, risk management analysis, accounting treatment, and the resultant operational/reputational impact (and after the SSB resolution, revert to legal, accounting, and risk departments to examine operational impact); SCD must also maintain an SSB-approved mechanism for reviewing previous Fatwas and inform the SSB of new regulations or contradicting views; and the query presentation format must include at minimum: (a) query owner, (b) nature of query (transactional, non-transactional, or observation), (c) type of query, (d) background/purpose, and (e) necessary detail (complete and correct information).
en.True answer: Before forwarding a query/proposal to the SSB, the SCD must review legal documentation, risk management analysis, accounting treatment, and the resultant operational/reputational impact (and after the SSB resolution, revert to legal, accounting, and risk departments to examine operational impact); SCD must also maintain an SSB-approved mechanism for reviewing previous Fatwas and inform the SSB of new regulations or contradicting views; and the query presentation format must include at minimum: (a) query owner, (b) nature of query (transactional, non-transactional, or observation), (c) type of query, (d) background/purpose, and (e) necessary detail (complete and correct information).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 75–81 (Par. 75–76: SCD reviews legal documentation, risk management analysis, accounting treatment, and resultant impact before forwarding query/proposal to SSB, and reverts to legal, accounting, and risk departments after SSB resolution to examine operational impact; Par. 77–79: SCD maintains SSB-approved mechanism for reviewing previous Fatwas and informs SSB of new regulations and contradicting views; Par. 81(a)–(e): minimum query format requires (a) query owner, (b) nature of query [transactional, non-transactional, or observation], (c) type of query, (d) background/purpose, and (e) necessary detail).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 29–33 and Appendix G (BC15–BC20) of AAOIFI GS 18, how is the relationship between 'Shari'ah principles and rules' and 'Maqasid Al-Shari'ah' structured in the SDM hierarchy, and how did the Board address the so-called 'Maqasid tendency'?
en.A: Shari'ah principles and rules rank first in the SDM hierarchy, followed by Maqasid Al-Shari'ah (incorporating Maqasid Al-Uqood, ethics/values including Adl and Ihsaan, legitimate business objectives, and CSR/public interest); the Board affirmed that Maqasid Al-Shari'ah is subordinate to and cannot override or violate Shari'ah principles and rules (as the sole path to achieve Maqasid Al-Shari'ah is by following Shari'ah principles and rules), while whenever two conclusions under Shari'ah principles and rules are acceptable, preference should be given to the conclusion more aligned with Maqasid Al-Shari'ah.
en.B: Maqasid Al-Shari'ah ranks above explicit Shari'ah principles and rules, allowing decision-makers to set aside clear AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard prohibitions whenever commercially advantageous.
en.C: Maqasid Al-Uqood applies only to non-profit Waqf institutions and is irrelevant to commercial banking contracts like Murabaha and Ijarah.
en.D: When two conclusions are equally permissible under Shari'ah principles and rules, the decision-maker must always choose the option with higher short-term fee income regardless of Maqasid Al-Shari'ah.
en.True answer: Shari'ah principles and rules rank first in the SDM hierarchy, followed by Maqasid Al-Shari'ah (incorporating Maqasid Al-Uqood, ethics/values including Adl and Ihsaan, legitimate business objectives, and CSR/public interest); the Board affirmed that Maqasid Al-Shari'ah is subordinate to and cannot override or violate Shari'ah principles and rules (as the sole path to achieve Maqasid Al-Shari'ah is by following Shari'ah principles and rules), while whenever two conclusions under Shari'ah principles and rules are acceptable, preference should be given to the conclusion more aligned with Maqasid Al-Shari'ah.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 29(a)–(b), Par. 30 & Appendix G, BC15–BC20 (Par. 29 sets SDM hierarchy: (a) Shari'ah principles and rules, followed by (b) Maqasid Al-Shari'ah [incorporating Maqasid Al-Uqood, ethics/values—Adl and Ihsaan, legitimate business objectives/sustainability, CSR/public interest/laws]; BC15–BC17 address the 'Maqasid tendency' by confirming that Maqasid Al-Shari'ah cannot violate or override Shari'ah principles and rules and that the sole path to achieve Maqasid is by following Shari'ah principles and rules; Par. 30 recommends giving preference to the conclusion more aligned with Maqasid Al-Shari'ah whenever two conclusions under Shari'ah principles and rules are acceptable).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 38–45 and Appendix G (BC25–BC26) of AAOIFI GS 18, why did the Board adopt the term 'psychological tendency' instead of 'cognitive bias,' and what are the three specific situations through which 'Status quo tendency' can influence an SSB?
en.A: The Board adopted 'psychological tendency' because cognitive biases do not exist in financial institutions; status quo tendency occurs solely due to external central bank audits.
en.B: The Board selected 'psychological tendency' (instead of 'cognitive bias') to avoid the negative connotation attached to the word 'bias' given the respect due to Shari'ah scholars while accurately reflecting the substance; Status quo tendency (treating prevailing practice as a baseline and rendering alternatives inferior) can influence SDM through three situations: (a) managerial influence (management favoring current product features/practices), (b) resistance against new initiatives (inertia and perceived challenges toward innovative proposals), and (c) scholarly reputation (reluctance to question or suggest alternatives to a product previously approved or rejected by a reputed/influential scholar).
en.C: Status quo tendency refers to giving disproportionate weight to the very first number heard in a negotiation, and applies exclusively to external auditors.
en.D: The Board prohibited using any psychological terminology in GS 18 and restricted status quo analysis solely to IT software upgrades.
en.True answer: The Board selected 'psychological tendency' (instead of 'cognitive bias') to avoid the negative connotation attached to the word 'bias' given the respect due to Shari'ah scholars while accurately reflecting the substance; Status quo tendency (treating prevailing practice as a baseline and rendering alternatives inferior) can influence SDM through three situations: (a) managerial influence (management favoring current product features/practices), (b) resistance against new initiatives (inertia and perceived challenges toward innovative proposals), and (c) scholarly reputation (reluctance to question or suggest alternatives to a product previously approved or rejected by a reputed/influential scholar).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 44–45(a)–(c) & Appendix G, BC25–BC26 (BC26: Board decided to use 'psychological tendency' instead of 'cognitive bias' to avoid the negative connotation attached to 'bias' and reflect substance appropriately; Par. 44–45: Status quo tendency occurs when prevailing practice is treated as a reference point rendering alternatives inferior, and can influence SSB through three situations: (a) managerial influence, (b) resistance against new initiatives due to inertia/perceived challenges, and (c) scholarly reputation where a product was approved/rejected by a reputed/influential scholar).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 46–53 of AAOIFI GS 18, how must an institution and its SSB counter (1) Confirming-evidence tendency, (2) Exaggerated threat of financial loss tendency, and (3) Availability tendency?
en.A: (1) Present only classical texts supporting management's preferred product; (2) treat normal commercial profit declines as Shari'ah necessity (Dharurah); (3) apply the most recent Fatwa from another bank without reviewing details of the current case.
en.B: (1) Allow management to pressure the SSB using competitor approvals; (2) prohibit management from submitting any financial data during SSB meetings; (3) ignore all historical Fatwas when evaluating new products.
en.C: (1) The SSB must consider information challenging its prevailing view and ensure multiple solutions with supporting evidence are available, while management must never pressure the SSB to approve a product merely on grounds of contemporary precedence (e.g., approval by other scholars, peers, another Madhhab, or a competitor); (2) when genuine risk of significant financial loss exists, management must provide factual, statistical, financial, and economic evidence rather than stretching 'necessity' to cover normal business losses or using mere threats of loss; and (3) Shari'ah decision-makers must examine specific case details rather than relying solely on immediate recent examples, while being provided complete information on similar cases and earlier Fatwas.
en.D: (1) Confirming-evidence tendency is encouraged to speed up Fatwa issuance; (2) exaggerated loss claims automatically justify approving controversial products; (3) availability tendency applies only to IT system downtime.
en.True answer: (1) The SSB must consider information challenging its prevailing view and ensure multiple solutions with supporting evidence are available, while management must never pressure the SSB to approve a product merely on grounds of contemporary precedence (e.g., approval by other scholars, peers, another Madhhab, or a competitor); (2) when genuine risk of significant financial loss exists, management must provide factual, statistical, financial, and economic evidence rather than stretching 'necessity' to cover normal business losses or using mere threats of loss; and (3) Shari'ah decision-makers must examine specific case details rather than relying solely on immediate recent examples, while being provided complete information on similar cases and earlier Fatwas.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 46–53 (Par. 48–49: to counter confirming-evidence tendency, SSB considers challenging information and ensures multi-solution research, while management shall in no case exert pressure on SSB to approve a product merely on ground of contemporary precedence [other scholars, peers, another school of jurisprudence, or competitor]; Par. 50–51: to counter exaggerated threat of financial loss [loss aversion bias], management must not stretch necessity to normal business losses and must provide factual, statistical, financial, and economic data when genuine risk of significant loss exists; Par. 52–53 & Appendix C Ex. 26: to counter availability tendency, decision-makers must be given complete information on similar cases/earlier Fatwas while evaluating specific details of each case).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 54–60 and 64–67 of AAOIFI GS 18, which definitions and SSB safeguards accurately address 'Fundamental attribution error,' 'Halo/reverse-Halo effect,' and 'Confirming-evidence tendency'?
en.A: Fundamental attribution error means blaming external regulations for every internal failure; Halo effect means assuming all bank departments are corrupt; and SSB members must avoid appointing any member to play an opponent role.
en.B: Overconfidence tendency improves SDM by eliminating the need for research, and SSB members should always ask leading questions to experts.
en.C: Self-serving tendency refers to donating excess profits to charity, and the SSB must accept management's initial framing without challenge.
en.D: Fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias) is over-emphasizing personal traits/internal factors while under-emphasizing situational/external influences; Halo effect (and reverse-Halo effect) is allowing a positive (or negative) impression about an individual, department, or institution in one area to positively (or negatively) influence a decision in another area; and to safeguard SDM objectivity, the SSB must challenge initial framings, evaluate all options independently before consulting third parties, examine evidence with equal rigor—including appropriately having one SSB member act as an opponent to argue against the contemplated decision—and avoid leading questions when seeking expert advice.
en.True answer: Fundamental attribution error (correspondence bias) is over-emphasizing personal traits/internal factors while under-emphasizing situational/external influences; Halo effect (and reverse-Halo effect) is allowing a positive (or negative) impression about an individual, department, or institution in one area to positively (or negatively) influence a decision in another area; and to safeguard SDM objectivity, the SSB must challenge initial framings, evaluate all options independently before consulting third parties, examine evidence with equal rigor—including appropriately having one SSB member act as an opponent to argue against the contemplated decision—and avoid leading questions when seeking expert advice.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 18, Par. 54–60 & Par. 64–67 (Par. 54–55: Fundamental attribution error [correspondence bias / over-attribution effect] over-emphasizes personal traits/internal factors and under-emphasizes situational/external forces; Par. 56–58: Halo effect and reverse-Halo effect allow positive or negative impressions in one area to influence decisions in another area; Par. 64–67: SSB should challenge initial framing, analyze independently before consulting third parties to avoid anchoring, examine evidence with equal rigor, consider having one SSB member act as an opponent to argue against the contemplated decision, and avoid leading questions that invite confirming evidence).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 18: Shari'ah Decision-Making Process
