en.A: (1) Compliant—unresolved material breaches belong in 'Other significant reporting matters' under a clean primary opinion; (2) Compliant—dissenting members never sign the main report and dissent anonymously; (3) Non-compliant—SSB advisors are prohibited from signing; (4) Non-compliant—reading the report at the AGM is prohibited.
en.B: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 22(d)(ii) & Appendix B ('Exceptions', p. 18 & Note on pp. 22–23), material unresolved Shari'ah non-compliances MUST be reported as 'Exceptions' and require modifying the primary opinion paragraph (listing the non-compliant items and stating that the SSB cannot provide an opinion that the institution's arrangements were in compliance), rather than issuing a clean opinion; (2) Non-compliant—violates Par. 22(h)–(i) & Appendix B ('Report approval and authentication' and 'Dissenting opinion [if any]', p. 22), under which all SSB members sign the main report (indicating agreement on all matters except the documented dissent) and the dissenting opinion must include the dissenting member's name and signature; (3) Compliant—follows Par. 22(j) (date and place of report) and Appendix B (p. 22), which explicitly notes: '[Preferably, the report shall be signed by the SSB advisors, if any]'; (4) Compliant—satisfies Par. 6 & Par. 18 of GS 21 (published in annual report and read at AGM) as well as GS 20 Par. 80 (presented at AGM by an SSB member, preferably the chairman).
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 22(d)(ii) & Appendix B ('Exceptions', p. 18 & Note on pp. 22–23), material unresolved Shari'ah non-compliances MUST be reported as 'Exceptions' and require modifying the primary opinion paragraph (listing the non-compliant items and stating that the SSB cannot provide an opinion that the institution's arrangements were in compliance), rather than issuing a clean opinion; (2) Non-compliant—violates Par. 22(h)–(i) & Appendix B ('Report approval and authentication' and 'Dissenting opinion [if any]', p. 22), under which all SSB members sign the main report (indicating agreement on all matters except the documented dissent) and the dissenting opinion must include the dissenting member's name and signature; (3) Compliant—follows Par. 22(j) (date and place of report) and Appendix B (p. 22), which explicitly notes: '[Preferably, the report shall be signed by the SSB advisors, if any]'; (4) Compliant—satisfies Par. 6 & Par. 18 of GS 21 (published in annual report and read at AGM) as well as GS 20 Par. 80 (presented at AGM by an SSB member, preferably the chairman).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 21 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 22(d)(ii) & Appendix B ('Exceptions', p. 18 & modified primary opinion Note on pp. 22–23) mandate reporting unresolved material Shari'ah non-compliances as Exceptions and modifying the primary opinion paragraph; (2) Par. 22(h)–(i) & Appendix B (p. 22) require all SSB members to sign the main report (confirming agreement except for the documented dissent) and require the dissenting member's name and signature in the Dissenting opinion section; (3) Par. 22(j) requires date and place of report, and Appendix B (p. 22) states '[Preferably, the report shall be signed by the SSB advisors, if any]'; (4) Par. 6 & Par. 18 require publishing the SSB report in the annual report and reading it at the AGM (aligned with GS 20 Par. 80).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the scope of AAOIFI GS 22 ('Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates'), its relationship with GS 1 (2024), and its effective date?
en.A: GS 22 describes the requirements related to Principle 11 ('Islamic finance subsidiaries / associates') of AAOIFI GS 1 (2024), applies to all Islamic finance subsidiaries and associates of conventional financial institutions irrespective of the conventional parent's ownership percentage (100%, majority, or minority) insofar as the parent can exercise control or significant influence over governance and managerial decision-making, and is effective on or after 1 January 2026.
en.B: GS 22 applies exclusively to unincorporated Islamic banking windows inside conventional banks and became effective retroactively on 1 July 2021.
en.C: GS 22 applies only when a conventional parent owns 100% of the shares of an Islamic subsidiary, exempting majority and minority associates.
en.D: GS 22 supersedes all other AAOIFI Governance Standards for subsidiaries and becomes effective on 1 January 2030.
en.True answer: GS 22 describes the requirements related to Principle 11 ('Islamic finance subsidiaries / associates') of AAOIFI GS 1 (2024), applies to all Islamic finance subsidiaries and associates of conventional financial institutions irrespective of the conventional parent's ownership percentage (100%, majority, or minority) insofar as the parent can exercise control or significant influence over governance and managerial decision-making, and is effective on or after 1 January 2026.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Preface PR5, Par. 2, Par. 5 & Par. 25 (PR5: describes requirements related to Principle 11 'Islamic finance subsidiaries / associates' of GS 1 (2024); Par. 2 & Par. 5: applies to all Islamic finance subsidiaries and associates of conventional financial institutions irrespective of ownership percentage [100%, majority, or minority] insofar as the conventional parent has the ability to exercise control/significant influence in respect of governance processes and managerial decision-making; Par. 25: effective on or after 1 January 2026).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 3(b)–(c) and 6–7 of AAOIFI GS 22, how are an 'Islamic finance subsidiary' and an 'Islamic finance associate' distinguished, and when does External Shari'ah Audit become mandatory for them?
en.A: Neither subsidiaries nor associates require their own SSB, and external Shari'ah audit is strictly optional for all subsidiaries regardless of size.
en.B: Both are independent, legally constituted, licensed IFIs, where a subsidiary is controlled by a conventional financial institution while an associate is subject to significant influence of a conventional financial institution (directly or via a common conventional parent); both must have the same four Shari'ah governance components as any full-fledged IFI (SSB, Shari'ah compliance function, internal Shari'ah audit, and external Shari'ah audit), and external Shari'ah audit becomes mandatory for Islamic finance subsidiaries/associates that are 'public interest institutions' after a period of three years from GS 22's effective date (1 January 2026).
en.C: An Islamic finance associate is an unincorporated division of a conventional bank, and external Shari'ah audit is mandatory from day one for all entities regardless of public interest status.
en.D: A subsidiary relies exclusively on its conventional parent's internal audit department without its own Shari'ah compliance or internal Shari'ah audit functions.
en.True answer: Both are independent, legally constituted, licensed IFIs, where a subsidiary is controlled by a conventional financial institution while an associate is subject to significant influence of a conventional financial institution (directly or via a common conventional parent); both must have the same four Shari'ah governance components as any full-fledged IFI (SSB, Shari'ah compliance function, internal Shari'ah audit, and external Shari'ah audit), and external Shari'ah audit becomes mandatory for Islamic finance subsidiaries/associates that are 'public interest institutions' after a period of three years from GS 22's effective date (1 January 2026).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 3(b)–(c), Par. 3(f) & Par. 6–7 (Par. 3(b)–(c): both are independent legally constituted licensed IFIs, distinguished by control [subsidiary, per FAS 44] vs significant influence [associate, per FAS 24]; Par. 6: Shari'ah governance framework consists of (a) SSB, (b) Shari'ah compliance function, (c) internal Shari'ah audit function, and (d) external Shari'ah audit; Par. 7: external Shari'ah audit shall be mandatory for Islamic finance subsidiaries/associates as public interest institutions after a period of three years from the effective date of GS 22, and strongly recommended during that period and for all other institutions).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraph 3(f) of AAOIFI GS 22, which retail Islamic finance subsidiary or associate qualifies as a 'public interest institution' based on stakeholder count (unless differently defined by the respective regulator)?
en.A: Any retail IFI with more than 1,000 investment accounts.
en.B: Any retail IFI with more than 5,000 investment accounts.
en.C: Any retail IFI dealing with a large number of common stakeholders (e.g., investment accountholders, depositors, unitholders, participants, employees), where the number of investment accounts, unitholders, or participants is in excess of 10,000 (in addition to listed entities and entities with publicly traded securities such as Sukuk).
en.D: Only retail IFIs with more than 50,000 common shareholders listed on an international stock exchange.
en.True answer: Any retail IFI dealing with a large number of common stakeholders (e.g., investment accountholders, depositors, unitholders, participants, employees), where the number of investment accounts, unitholders, or participants is in excess of 10,000 (in addition to listed entities and entities with publicly traded securities such as Sukuk).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 3(f)(i)–(iii) & Explanation (Defines 'public interest institutions' as: (i) all listed institutions/entities whose common shares are listed and publicly traded; (ii) all institutions/entities with publicly traded securities other than common shares e.g. Sukuk; and (iii) all retail IFIs dealing with a large number of common stakeholders—where Explanation specifies: 'the number of investment accounts, unitholders or participants for the purpose of this standard shall be considered large if it is in excess of 10,000 unless differently defined by the respective regulator').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 11–14 of AAOIFI GS 22, how may a conventional parent influence decision-making at an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate, and can the fiduciary responsibility of the subsidiary's TCWG be transferred to the conventional parent?
en.A: The conventional parent may issue direct daily operational directives to the subsidiary's CEO and assume the subsidiary's fiduciary responsibility toward IAHs.
en.B: The conventional parent may appoint 100% of the subsidiary's board regardless of shareholding percentage and override the subsidiary's SSB decisions.
en.C: Fiduciary responsibility toward the subsidiary's IAHs automatically transfers to the conventional parent whenever the parent owns more than 50% of the equity.
en.D: The Islamic finance subsidiary/associate must act as an independent IFI without unnecessary and undue interference from the conventional parent's management; the conventional parent may influence decision-making at a strategic level ONLY through board memberships and board committees where it is represented in line with its shareholding percentage; and the fiduciary responsibility of the subsidiary/associate's TCWG toward its stakeholders (including shareholders and IAHs) CANNOT be transferred or delegated to TCWG of the conventional parent simply because of ownership.
en.True answer: The Islamic finance subsidiary/associate must act as an independent IFI without unnecessary and undue interference from the conventional parent's management; the conventional parent may influence decision-making at a strategic level ONLY through board memberships and board committees where it is represented in line with its shareholding percentage; and the fiduciary responsibility of the subsidiary/associate's TCWG toward its stakeholders (including shareholders and IAHs) CANNOT be transferred or delegated to TCWG of the conventional parent simply because of ownership.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 11–14 (Par. 11: must be and act as an independent IFI without unnecessary and undue interference from management of conventional parent; Par. 13: 'TCWG of an Islamic finance subsidiary / associate shall bear the entire fiduciary responsibility towards its stakeholders, including the shareholders and the IAHs... This fiduciary responsibility cannot be transferred or delegated to TCWG of the conventional parent simply because of the ownership'; Par. 14: 'The conventional parent may influence decision-making at the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate at a strategic level only through board memberships and board committees, where it shall be represented in line with its shareholding percentage').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraph 16 and Appendix B (BC3–BC6) of AAOIFI GS 22, which executives from a conventional parent are prohibited from being appointed to the TCWG (board of directors) of an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate, and who MAY be appointed?
en.A: The conventional parent must NOT appoint any members of its executive management heading or significantly involved in business functions as a member of the subsidiary/associate's TCWG; however, it MAY appoint members of its executive management heading functions independent of business functions (such as the heads of compliance, internal audit, and risk management) as well as any of the non-executive members of its own TCWG (subject to regulatory requirements and GS 1 (2024)).
en.B: The conventional parent's Chief Commercial Officer and Head of Corporate Lending are encouraged to chair the Islamic subsidiary's board, while the Head of Internal Audit is barred.
en.C: No individual associated with the conventional parent in any executive or non-executive capacity may ever sit on the Islamic subsidiary's board.
en.D: Any executive director of the conventional parent's commercial sales division may serve on the Islamic subsidiary's board as long as he waives his director fee.
en.True answer: The conventional parent must NOT appoint any members of its executive management heading or significantly involved in business functions as a member of the subsidiary/associate's TCWG; however, it MAY appoint members of its executive management heading functions independent of business functions (such as the heads of compliance, internal audit, and risk management) as well as any of the non-executive members of its own TCWG (subject to regulatory requirements and GS 1 (2024)).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 16 & Appendix B, BC3–BC6 (Par. 16 & BC5–BC6: conventional parent shall NOT appoint any members of its executive management heading or significantly involved in business functions as a member of TCWG of the Islamic finance subsidiary/associate; however, it CAN appoint members of executive management of functions independent of business functions—specifically citing the heads of compliance, internal audit, and risk management—and can also appoint any non-executive members of its own TCWG subject to regulations and GS 1 (2024) Par. 36–46).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraph 17 of AAOIFI GS 22, how does the rule on dotted-line management reporting to a conventional parent differ between an Islamic finance subsidiary and an Islamic finance associate?
en.A: Both subsidiaries and associates must report directly via solid-line executive authority to the conventional parent's business department heads.
en.B: A conventional parent may have a dotted-line reporting of key business departments/functions with those of an Islamic finance subsidiary (but NOT an associate), whereby the parent's function heads have the right to certain relevant information (as approved by both boards, subject to regulatory requirements) without having authority to control or influence managerial decision-making of the Islamic finance subsidiary.
en.C: Dotted-line reporting is permitted for Islamic finance associates only, and is strictly prohibited for Islamic finance subsidiaries.
en.D: Dotted-line reporting grants the conventional parent's department heads full veto power over the Islamic subsidiary's daily financing approvals.
en.True answer: A conventional parent may have a dotted-line reporting of key business departments/functions with those of an Islamic finance subsidiary (but NOT an associate), whereby the parent's function heads have the right to certain relevant information (as approved by both boards, subject to regulatory requirements) without having authority to control or influence managerial decision-making of the Islamic finance subsidiary.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 17 ('A conventional parent may have a dotted-line reporting of key business departments / functions with those of an Islamic finance subsidiary (but not an associate) whereby the conventional parent's function heads can have the right to certain relevant information (as approved by both the respective boards, subject to regulatory requirements) without having an authority to control or influence the managerial decision-making of the Islamic finance subsidiary').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 18–19 of AAOIFI GS 22, what restrictions govern customer-level information sharing and market competition between a conventional parent and an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate?
en.A: The Islamic subsidiary must share all confidential customer records with its conventional parent's sales team and refrain from competing in lucrative corporate banking segments.
en.B: The conventional parent may prohibit the Islamic subsidiary from onboarding high-net-worth clients so they remain with the parent's conventional division.
en.C: Any sharing of customer-level information between the Islamic finance subsidiary/associate and the conventional parent must NOT be detrimental to the long-term interests of the subsidiary/associate's minority shareholders and IAHs; and the conventional parent must NOT devise any strategy or tactics to adversely influence competition from the Islamic subsidiary/associate (e.g., by prohibiting it from approaching certain categories of customers or business segments) if deemed against the interests of its minority shareholders and/or IAHs.
en.D: Information sharing is governed solely by the conventional parent's commercial marketing policy without regard to IAHs or minority shareholders.
en.True answer: Any sharing of customer-level information between the Islamic finance subsidiary/associate and the conventional parent must NOT be detrimental to the long-term interests of the subsidiary/associate's minority shareholders and IAHs; and the conventional parent must NOT devise any strategy or tactics to adversely influence competition from the Islamic subsidiary/associate (e.g., by prohibiting it from approaching certain categories of customers or business segments) if deemed against the interests of its minority shareholders and/or IAHs.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 18–19 (Par. 18: 'Any sharing of customer-level information between the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate and the conventional parent shall not be detrimental to the long-term interests of the minority shareholders and IAHs of the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate'; Par. 19: 'A conventional parent shall not devise any strategy or tactics to adversely influence competition from the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate (e.g., by prohibiting the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate from approaching certain categories of customers or business segments), if it is deemed to be against the interests of the minority shareholders and / or IAHs of the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 20–22 of AAOIFI GS 22, which rules govern shared services arrangements, employee secondments/coercion, infrastructure leasing, and co-located premises between a conventional parent and an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate?
en.A: The Islamic subsidiary may lease its IT systems and branch premises to the conventional parent and second Islamic bank tellers to work at conventional interest counters.
en.B: Shared services agreements require only CEO signature without SSB approval, and parent board representatives vote on the contract at the subsidiary board.
en.C: Co-locating branches is strictly prohibited under all circumstances even if brand identities are clearly separated.
en.D: Shared services for cost saving must be on an arm's length basis approved by the TCWGs of BOTH institutions and the SSB of the subsidiary/associate (with TCWG representing the conventional parent abstaining from voting when the subsidiary/associate's TCWG votes); no employee of the Islamic subsidiary/associate may be coerced directly or indirectly to work for the conventional parent; the Islamic subsidiary/associate CANNOT lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent; and if co-located, the arrangement must not affect the Islamic entity's brand identity in public perception.
en.True answer: Shared services for cost saving must be on an arm's length basis approved by the TCWGs of BOTH institutions and the SSB of the subsidiary/associate (with TCWG representing the conventional parent abstaining from voting when the subsidiary/associate's TCWG votes); no employee of the Islamic subsidiary/associate may be coerced directly or indirectly to work for the conventional parent; the Islamic subsidiary/associate CANNOT lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent; and if co-located, the arrangement must not affect the Islamic entity's brand identity in public perception.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 20–22 (Par. 20: arm's length shared services approved by TCWGs of both institutions and SSB of subsidiary/associate, with TCWG representing conventional parent abstaining from voting when subsidiary/associate's TCWG votes; Par. 21: no employee of Islamic subsidiary/associate can be coerced directly or indirectly to work for conventional parent, 'nor can the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent'; Par. 22: co-location must not affect brand identity in public perception).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraph 23 of AAOIFI GS 22, what rule governs internal fund placements and funding flows between an Islamic finance subsidiary/associate and its conventional parent or other conventional financial institutions?
en.A: An Islamic finance subsidiary/associate may receive funds from its conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract in line with Shari'ah principles and rules; HOWEVER, it CANNOT place funds with its conventional parent or with any other conventional financial institution, either directly or through a third party.
en.B: An Islamic finance subsidiary may place excess overnight liquidity in interest-bearing accounts at its conventional parent as long as the interest is donated to charity.
en.C: An Islamic finance subsidiary is prohibited from receiving any funding from its conventional parent, even under a Shari'ah-compliant Mudaraba or Wakalah contract.
en.D: An Islamic finance subsidiary may place funds with conventional banks indirectly through a commodity broker intermediary.
en.True answer: An Islamic finance subsidiary/associate may receive funds from its conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract in line with Shari'ah principles and rules; HOWEVER, it CANNOT place funds with its conventional parent or with any other conventional financial institution, either directly or through a third party.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 23 ('An Islamic finance subsidiary / associate may receive funds from its conventional parent under a Shari'ah compliant contract, in line with Shari'ah principles and rules. However, it cannot place funds with its conventional parent or with any other conventional financial institution, either directly or through a third party').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraph 24 of AAOIFI GS 22, what financial statement disclosure requirements apply to an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate regarding its dealings with the conventional parent?
en.A: Related-party transactions with the conventional parent may be netted and aggregated with general customer balances without separate identification.
en.B: The Islamic finance subsidiary/associate must make adequate and duly segregated disclosures in its financial statements regarding related-party transactions and balances with the conventional parent in line with relevant AAOIFI FASs, and must identify the nature of contracts and transactions, particularly those covered under Paragraphs 20–23 (shared services, premises, and internal fund flows).
en.C: Disclosures of transactions with the conventional parent are required only in confidential regulatory filings and omitted from published financial statements.
en.D: Only equity dividend payments to the parent need to be disclosed, while shared-service fees and funding contracts are exempt.
en.True answer: The Islamic finance subsidiary/associate must make adequate and duly segregated disclosures in its financial statements regarding related-party transactions and balances with the conventional parent in line with relevant AAOIFI FASs, and must identify the nature of contracts and transactions, particularly those covered under Paragraphs 20–23 (shared services, premises, and internal fund flows).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 24 ('An Islamic finance subsidiary / associate shall make adequate and duly segregated disclosures in their financial statements, in respect of related party transactions and balances with the conventional parent, in line with the requirements of relevant AAOIFI FASs. Additionally, it shall identify the nature of contracts and transactions, particularly those in line with the requirements of paragraphs 20-23').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: In Appendix B (Basis for Conclusions, BC1–BC2) of AAOIFI GS 22, why did the Board choose to draft GS 22 as a concise standard focusing on special considerations for Islamic finance subsidiaries/associates rather than a self-contained encyclopedic standard repeating all AAOIFI Governance Standards?
en.A: Because general AAOIFI Governance Standards do not apply to Islamic finance subsidiaries or associates.
en.B: Because AAOIFI lacks authority to regulate subsidiaries of conventional banks.
en.C: Because Islamic finance subsidiaries and associates are licensed IFIs to which all common requirements of relevant AAOIFI GSs already apply (subject only to proportionality flexibilities within those standards), and a self-contained standard would require constant revision whenever other AAOIFI GSs are updated.
en.D: Because Islamic finance subsidiaries are governed exclusively by conventional Basel corporate governance rules.
en.True answer: Because Islamic finance subsidiaries and associates are licensed IFIs to which all common requirements of relevant AAOIFI GSs already apply (subject only to proportionality flexibilities within those standards), and a self-contained standard would require constant revision whenever other AAOIFI GSs are updated.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 8–9 & Appendix B, BC1–BC2 (BC2 explains that the Board opted for a concise standard referring to other relevant AAOIFI GSs and addressing specific subsidiary/associate considerations because all common requirements of relevant AAOIFI GSs already apply to Islamic finance subsidiaries/associates as licensed IFIs [subject only to proportionality flexibilities], and a self-contained standard would need regular updating whenever other standards change).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraph 15 of AAOIFI GS 22, when must representatives of the conventional parent sitting on the TCWG (board of directors) of an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate abstain from voting?
en.A: Never—parent representatives may vote on every board resolution proportional to the parent's equity stake.
en.B: Only when voting on the annual external financial auditor's fee.
en.C: Only when the conventional parent owns less than 20% of the associate's shares.
en.D: On any issue which is, or is reasonably perceived to be, benefiting the conventional parent at the cost of the interests of the stakeholders of the Islamic finance subsidiary/associate, or creating a reputational risk for the overall Islamic finance industry (as well as when the subsidiary/associate's TCWG votes on a shared services arrangement with the parent per Paragraph 20).
en.True answer: On any issue which is, or is reasonably perceived to be, benefiting the conventional parent at the cost of the interests of the stakeholders of the Islamic finance subsidiary/associate, or creating a reputational risk for the overall Islamic finance industry (as well as when the subsidiary/associate's TCWG votes on a shared services arrangement with the parent per Paragraph 20).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 15 & Par. 20 (Par. 15: 'representatives of the conventional parent who are part of TCWG (normally, the board of directors) of an Islamic finance subsidiary / associate shall not be allowed to vote on any issue which is, or is reasonably perceived to be, benefiting the conventional parent at the cost of the interests of the stakeholders of the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate, or creating a reputational risk for the overall Islamic finance industry'; Par. 20 also requires abstention when voting on a shared services arrangement).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: In Appendix B (Basis for Conclusions, BC3–BC6) and Paragraph 16 of AAOIFI GS 22, how did the Board resolve the debate over whether a conventional parent may appoint its executives to the board of directors (TCWG) of an Islamic finance subsidiary or associate?
en.A: The Board prohibited the conventional parent from appointing any members of its executive management belonging to or heading business functions to the TCWG of the Islamic subsidiary/associate (to prevent direct conflicts of interest and safeguard stakeholder interests), while explicitly allowing the appointment of executive management members from functions independent of business functions (such as heads of compliance, internal audit, and risk management) as well as any non-executive members of the conventional parent's TCWG.
en.B: The Board allowed all conventional business-line executives to sit on the Islamic subsidiary's board because corporate governance is purely a commercial matter outside AAOIFI's mandate.
en.C: The Board prohibited even the conventional parent's non-executive board directors from serving on the Islamic subsidiary's board.
en.D: The Board allowed the conventional parent's Chief Lending Officer to serve on the Islamic subsidiary's board provided he does not chair the board.
en.True answer: The Board prohibited the conventional parent from appointing any members of its executive management belonging to or heading business functions to the TCWG of the Islamic subsidiary/associate (to prevent direct conflicts of interest and safeguard stakeholder interests), while explicitly allowing the appointment of executive management members from functions independent of business functions (such as heads of compliance, internal audit, and risk management) as well as any non-executive members of the conventional parent's TCWG.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 16 & Appendix B, BC3–BC6 (BC3–BC6: after considering counterarguments that board appointments are a business/corporate governance matter, the Board concluded that to avoid direct conflict of interest and safeguard stakeholders, the conventional parent shall NOT appoint any members of its executive management belonging to business functions on the TCWG of the Islamic subsidiary/associate, while allowing members of executive management of functions independent of business functions [such as heads of compliance, internal audit, and risk management] and categorically allowing any non-executive members of the parent's TCWG).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Comparing an 'Islamic finance subsidiary' versus an 'Islamic finance associate' under Paragraphs 3(b)–(c), 5, and 17 of AAOIFI GS 22, which distinction regarding parent influence and management reporting lines is accurate?
en.A: GS 22 applies only to subsidiaries (where parent ownership exceeds 50%), whereas associates (minority ownership) are exempt from GS 22 and may use solid-line executive reporting to parent business heads.
en.B: GS 22 applies to BOTH subsidiaries (controlled by the conventional parent) and associates (subject to significant influence of the conventional parent) irrespective of ownership percentage (100%, majority, or minority) insofar as control or significant influence can be exercised over governance and managerial decision-making; however, under Paragraph 17, dotted-line reporting of key business departments/functions to the conventional parent's function heads is permitted ONLY for an Islamic finance subsidiary (and NOT for an Islamic finance associate).
en.C: Dotted-line reporting to the conventional parent is mandatory for associates and prohibited for subsidiaries.
en.D: Neither subsidiaries nor associates are licensed IFIs; both operate as internal divisions on the conventional parent's balance sheet.
en.True answer: GS 22 applies to BOTH subsidiaries (controlled by the conventional parent) and associates (subject to significant influence of the conventional parent) irrespective of ownership percentage (100%, majority, or minority) insofar as control or significant influence can be exercised over governance and managerial decision-making; however, under Paragraph 17, dotted-line reporting of key business departments/functions to the conventional parent's function heads is permitted ONLY for an Islamic finance subsidiary (and NOT for an Islamic finance associate).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 3(b)–(c), Par. 5 & Par. 17 (Par. 3(b)–(c) & Par. 5: GS 22 applies to both Islamic finance subsidiaries [controlled] and associates [subject to significant influence], both being separate legally constituted licensed IFIs, irrespective of ownership percentage [100%, majority, or minority]; Par. 17: 'A conventional parent may have a dotted-line reporting of key business departments / functions with those of an Islamic finance subsidiary (but not an associate)...').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: A conventional bank owns 70% of an Islamic banking subsidiary. To reduce expenses, the two institutions propose entering into a shared IT/back-office services agreement and co-locating several branches. Under Paragraphs 20–22 and 24 of AAOIFI GS 22, which governance and operational conditions must be satisfied?
en.A: The shared services agreement may be priced below cost to subsidize the subsidiary, approved solely by the conventional parent's board, and allow the Islamic subsidiary to lease its core banking servers to the conventional parent.
en.B: Parent board representatives on the Islamic subsidiary's board vote in favor of the shared services contract to pass it quickly, and subsidiary IT engineers are seconded involuntarily to the parent's conventional treasury unit.
en.C: The shared services arrangement must be on an arm's length basis, approved by the TCWGs of BOTH institutions AND the SSB of the Islamic subsidiary (with TCWG members representing the conventional parent abstaining from voting when the subsidiary's TCWG votes on the arrangement); no employee of the Islamic subsidiary may be coerced directly or indirectly to work for the conventional parent; the Islamic subsidiary cannot lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent; co-located branches must preserve the subsidiary's distinct brand identity in public perception; and segregated related-party disclosures identifying the nature of contracts must be made in the financial statements.
en.D: Shared services agreements are exempt from SSB review, and related-party balances with the parent need not be segregated in financial statement notes.
en.True answer: The shared services arrangement must be on an arm's length basis, approved by the TCWGs of BOTH institutions AND the SSB of the Islamic subsidiary (with TCWG members representing the conventional parent abstaining from voting when the subsidiary's TCWG votes on the arrangement); no employee of the Islamic subsidiary may be coerced directly or indirectly to work for the conventional parent; the Islamic subsidiary cannot lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent; co-located branches must preserve the subsidiary's distinct brand identity in public perception; and segregated related-party disclosures identifying the nature of contracts must be made in the financial statements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 20–22 & Par. 24 (Par. 20: arm's length basis, approved by TCWGs of both institutions and SSB of subsidiary/associate, with TCWG representing conventional parent abstaining from voting when subsidiary/associate's TCWG votes; Par. 21: no employee coerced to work for conventional parent, nor can subsidiary/associate lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to conventional parent; Par. 22: co-location must not affect brand identity in public perception; Par. 24: segregated disclosures in financial statements identifying nature of contracts/transactions per Par. 20–23).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: An Islamic finance subsidiary has 14,500 retail investment accountholders (IAHs) and is owned 80% by a conventional bank and 20% by minority shareholders. GS 22 becomes effective on 1 January 2026 (assuming no different local regulatory threshold). Which combination of governance conclusions is completely accurate under AAOIFI GS 22?
en.A: The subsidiary is not a public interest institution (threshold is 50,000 IAHs); external Shari'ah audit is permanently optional; and the conventional parent may instruct the subsidiary not to compete for corporate clients.
en.B: External Shari'ah audit becomes mandatory immediately in 2026; fiduciary responsibility toward the 14,500 IAHs rests primarily with the conventional parent's board; and the subsidiary may place excess cash in overnight deposits at its conventional parent.
en.C: Because the conventional parent owns 80%, the subsidiary does not need its own SSB and may lease its branch network to the parent.
en.D: Because the retail subsidiary deals with >10,000 investment accountholders (14,500 IAHs), it is a 'public interest institution' under Par. 3(f)(iii), so external Shari'ah audit becomes mandatory after a 3-year transition period from 1 January 2026 (i.e., from 2029) and is strongly recommended during 2026–2028 (Par. 7); the subsidiary's TCWG bears the entire fiduciary responsibility toward its minority shareholders and 14,500 IAHs without transferring it to the parent (Par. 13); and the parent must not restrict the subsidiary's market competition against the interests of minority shareholders and IAHs (Par. 19).
en.True answer: Because the retail subsidiary deals with >10,000 investment accountholders (14,500 IAHs), it is a 'public interest institution' under Par. 3(f)(iii), so external Shari'ah audit becomes mandatory after a 3-year transition period from 1 January 2026 (i.e., from 2029) and is strongly recommended during 2026–2028 (Par. 7); the subsidiary's TCWG bears the entire fiduciary responsibility toward its minority shareholders and 14,500 IAHs without transferring it to the parent (Par. 13); and the parent must not restrict the subsidiary's market competition against the interests of minority shareholders and IAHs (Par. 19).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 3(f)(iii), Par. 7, Par. 13 & Par. 19 (Par. 3(f)(iii): retail IFI with >10,000 investment accounts/participants is a public interest institution; Par. 7: external Shari'ah audit is mandatory for public interest institutions after 3 years from the 1 January 2026 effective date [from 2029], and strongly recommended during the 3-year transition period; Par. 13: subsidiary's TCWG bears entire fiduciary responsibility toward stakeholders including minority shareholders and IAHs, non-transferable to parent; Par. 19: parent shall not devise strategy/tactics to adversely influence competition if against interests of minority shareholders and/or IAHs).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 14–17 of AAOIFI GS 22, how are strategic influence, board representation, executive board appointments, and management reporting lines structured for an Islamic finance associate in which a conventional bank holds a 30% minority equity stake?
en.A: Strategic influence by the conventional bank is exercised only through board and board committee memberships in line with its 30% shareholding percentage; parent representatives on the associate's board must abstain from voting on any issue benefiting the parent at the cost of the associate's stakeholders; the parent may appoint non-executive TCWG members or heads of independent control functions (compliance, internal audit, risk management) but NOT business-line executives to the associate's board; and dotted-line management reporting of business departments to the conventional parent is NOT permitted for an Islamic finance associate.
en.B: Because 30% is a minority stake, the conventional bank is completely exempt from GS 22 and may appoint its Head of Commercial Banking to the associate's board.
en.C: The conventional bank may establish dotted-line reporting from the associate's treasury department to the parent's conventional treasury head and hold 60% of the associate's board seats.
en.D: The conventional bank may freely vote on inter-company contracts benefiting itself as long as its shareholding is below 50%.
en.True answer: Strategic influence by the conventional bank is exercised only through board and board committee memberships in line with its 30% shareholding percentage; parent representatives on the associate's board must abstain from voting on any issue benefiting the parent at the cost of the associate's stakeholders; the parent may appoint non-executive TCWG members or heads of independent control functions (compliance, internal audit, risk management) but NOT business-line executives to the associate's board; and dotted-line management reporting of business departments to the conventional parent is NOT permitted for an Islamic finance associate.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 3(b), Par. 5 & Par. 14–17 (Par. 3(b) & Par. 5: GS 22 applies to Islamic finance associates even with minority ownership insofar as significant influence is exercised; Par. 14: strategic influence only through board/board committee memberships in line with shareholding percentage [30%]; Par. 15: abstain from voting on issues benefiting parent at cost of associate's stakeholders; Par. 16: cannot appoint business-line executives, only non-executive TCWG or heads of compliance/internal audit/risk management; Par. 17: dotted-line reporting of key business departments is allowed for a subsidiary 'but not an associate').

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 11, 18–19, and 23–24 of AAOIFI GS 22, which combination of operational, competitive, and liquidity rules governs an Islamic finance subsidiary's relationship with its conventional parent?
en.A: The Islamic subsidiary may place excess funds in interest-free call accounts at the conventional parent and transfer its retail customer database to the parent's conventional credit card unit.
en.B: The Islamic subsidiary may receive funds from its conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract, but CANNOT place funds with its conventional parent or any other conventional financial institution (directly or via a third party); customer-level information sharing must not harm the long-term interests of minority shareholders and IAHs; the parent must not restrict competition against minority shareholders' and IAHs' interests; and all related-party transactions/balances with the parent must receive segregated financial statement disclosures identifying contract nature.
en.C: The Islamic subsidiary may place funds with third-party conventional banks if its conventional parent guarantees the principal.
en.D: The conventional parent may divide the market by barring the Islamic subsidiary from serving manufacturing clients so the parent's conventional loan book faces no competition.
en.True answer: The Islamic subsidiary may receive funds from its conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract, but CANNOT place funds with its conventional parent or any other conventional financial institution (directly or via a third party); customer-level information sharing must not harm the long-term interests of minority shareholders and IAHs; the parent must not restrict competition against minority shareholders' and IAHs' interests; and all related-party transactions/balances with the parent must receive segregated financial statement disclosures identifying contract nature.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22, Par. 18–19 & Par. 23–24 (Par. 18: customer-level information sharing shall not be detrimental to long-term interests of minority shareholders and IAHs; Par. 19: conventional parent shall not devise strategy/tactics to adversely influence competition if against interests of minority shareholders and/or IAHs; Par. 23: subsidiary/associate may receive funds from conventional parent under Shari'ah-compliant contract, but cannot place funds with conventional parent or any other conventional financial institution, directly or through a third party; Par. 24: segregated financial statement disclosures identifying nature of contracts/transactions).

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question:
In March 2026, Global Conventional Bank (GCB) holds a 65% controlling equity stake in Al-Salam Islamic Bank (a separately licensed Islamic finance subsidiary), while 35% is held by public minority shareholders. Evaluate the following four governance actions:
(1) GCB appoints two individuals to Al-Salam's 5-member Board of Directors (TCWG): GCB's Head of Conventional Corporate Banking and GCB's Head of Group Internal Audit.
(2) GCB establishes a dotted-line reporting arrangement between Al-Salam's Corporate Financing Department and GCB's Group Corporate Credit Head, under which GCB's Credit Head receives board-approved portfolio risk reports without having authority to approve or block Al-Salam's financing decisions.
(3) Al-Salam enters into an arm's length shared IT infrastructure agreement with GCB; the agreement is approved by GCB's board, Al-Salam's SSB, and Al-Salam's board—where GCB's board representatives abstain from voting during Al-Salam's board vote.
(4) Under the same agreement, Al-Salam leases two floors of its headquarters building and its secondary data-center servers to GCB to generate extra rental income.
According to AAOIFI GS 22, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Both appointees are compliant; (2) Non-compliant—dotted-line reporting is prohibited for subsidiaries; (3) Non-compliant—GCB representatives must vote; (4) Compliant—leasing spare premises to the parent is allowed.
en.B: (1) Both appointees are non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Partially non-compliant—under Par. 16 & Appendix B (BC5–BC6), GCB's Head of Group Internal Audit IS eligible because internal audit is independent of business functions, whereas GCB's Head of Conventional Corporate Banking is PROHIBITED from sitting on Al-Salam's TCWG because he heads a business function; (2) Compliant—Par. 17 permits dotted-line reporting of key business departments/functions of an Islamic finance subsidiary (though not an associate) to the conventional parent's function heads to receive board-approved information without authority to control or influence managerial decision-making; (3) Compliant—satisfies Par. 20 (arm's length basis, approved by TCWGs of both institutions and Al-Salam's SSB, with GCB's representatives abstaining from voting at Al-Salam's board); (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 21, which explicitly prohibits an Islamic finance subsidiary/associate from leasing any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Partially non-compliant—under Par. 16 & Appendix B (BC5–BC6), GCB's Head of Group Internal Audit IS eligible because internal audit is independent of business functions, whereas GCB's Head of Conventional Corporate Banking is PROHIBITED from sitting on Al-Salam's TCWG because he heads a business function; (2) Compliant—Par. 17 permits dotted-line reporting of key business departments/functions of an Islamic finance subsidiary (though not an associate) to the conventional parent's function heads to receive board-approved information without authority to control or influence managerial decision-making; (3) Compliant—satisfies Par. 20 (arm's length basis, approved by TCWGs of both institutions and Al-Salam's SSB, with GCB's representatives abstaining from voting at Al-Salam's board); (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 21, which explicitly prohibits an Islamic finance subsidiary/associate from leasing any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 16 & Appendix B BC5–BC6 prohibit appointing members of the conventional parent's executive management heading/involved in business functions (Head of Conventional Corporate Banking is invalid), while permitting executives of functions independent of business functions such as heads of compliance, internal audit, and risk management (Head of Group Internal Audit is valid); (2) Par. 17 allows dotted-line reporting of key business departments/functions of an Islamic subsidiary (not an associate) to receive board-approved relevant information without controlling/influencing managerial decision-making; (3) Par. 20 requires arm's length shared services approved by TCWGs of both institutions and subsidiary's SSB, with parent representatives abstaining from voting at the subsidiary's TCWG; (4) Par. 21 explicitly states: 'nor can the Islamic finance subsidiary / associate lease any part of its physical infrastructure or systems to the conventional parent'.

en.Theme: AAOIFI GS 22: Application of Shari'ah Governance Principles to Islamic Finance Subsidiaries / Associates
en.Question:
In June 2026, Meridian Conventional Bank (MCB) holds a 25% equity stake in Al-Noor Islamic Finance (a separately licensed Islamic finance associate over which MCB exercises significant influence). Examine the following four events:
(1) Because MCB holds only a 25% minority stake, MCB argues that AAOIFI GS 22 does not apply to Al-Noor Islamic Finance.
(2) To manage seasonal liquidity, Al-Noor receives USD 15 million from MCB under a Shari'ah-compliant Mudaraba contract approved by Al-Noor's SSB, and later places USD 5 million of surplus overnight liquidity in a short-term deposit at a third-party conventional bank through an intermediary broker.
(3) MCB instructs its board representative at Al-Noor to push through a policy prohibiting Al-Noor from offering SME financing to manufacturing companies so that MCB's own conventional SME lending unit faces less competition—a policy detrimental to Al-Noor's minority shareholders and IAHs.
(4) In its 2026 financial statements, Al-Noor discloses the USD 15 million Mudaraba funding balance and contract nature with MCB in a segregated related-party note in accordance with relevant AAOIFI FASs.
According to AAOIFI GS 22, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—GS 22 applies only when parent ownership exceeds 50%; (2) Compliant—receiving funds from the parent and placing funds via a third party are both permitted; (3) Compliant—protecting parent business lines is permitted; (4) Non-compliant—parent funding balances must not be segregated.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 2, Par. 3(b), and Par. 5, GS 22 applies to all Islamic finance associates of conventional financial institutions irrespective of ownership percentage (whether 100%, majority, or minority) insofar as the conventional parent exercises significant influence over governance and managerial decision-making; (2) Partially non-compliant—under Par. 23, receiving funds from the conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract IS permitted, HOWEVER placing funds with the conventional parent OR with any other conventional financial institution—either directly or through a third party—is strictly PROHIBITED; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. 19, which prohibits a conventional parent from devising any strategy or tactics to adversely influence competition from the Islamic subsidiary/associate (e.g., prohibiting it from approaching certain categories of customers or business segments) if against the interests of minority shareholders and/or IAHs; (4) Compliant—satisfies Par. 24, which requires adequate and duly segregated financial statement disclosures of related-party transactions and balances with the conventional parent identifying the nature of contracts and transactions per relevant AAOIFI FASs.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 2, Par. 3(b), and Par. 5, GS 22 applies to all Islamic finance associates of conventional financial institutions irrespective of ownership percentage (whether 100%, majority, or minority) insofar as the conventional parent exercises significant influence over governance and managerial decision-making; (2) Partially non-compliant—under Par. 23, receiving funds from the conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract IS permitted, HOWEVER placing funds with the conventional parent OR with any other conventional financial institution—either directly or through a third party—is strictly PROHIBITED; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. 19, which prohibits a conventional parent from devising any strategy or tactics to adversely influence competition from the Islamic subsidiary/associate (e.g., prohibiting it from approaching certain categories of customers or business segments) if against the interests of minority shareholders and/or IAHs; (4) Compliant—satisfies Par. 24, which requires adequate and duly segregated financial statement disclosures of related-party transactions and balances with the conventional parent identifying the nature of contracts and transactions per relevant AAOIFI FASs.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI GS 22 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 2, Par. 3(b) & Par. 5 apply GS 22 to all Islamic finance subsidiaries and associates irrespective of ownership percentage (100%, majority, or minority) insofar as control or significant influence is exercised over governance and managerial decision-making; (2) Par. 23 permits receiving funds from the conventional parent under a Shari'ah-compliant contract, but strictly prohibits placing funds with the conventional parent or any other conventional financial institution, 'either directly or through a third party'; (3) Par. 19 prohibits the conventional parent from devising strategies/tactics to adversely influence competition from the Islamic subsidiary/associate (such as barring it from approaching certain customer categories or business segments) against the interests of minority shareholders and/or IAHs; (4) Par. 24 requires segregated financial statement disclosures of related-party transactions/balances with the parent identifying contract nature per AAOIFI FASs.

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the purpose, adoption date, and effective date of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1 ('Objective and Principles of Auditing')?
en.A: It governs internal Shari'ah compliance reviews of non-financial corporations, was adopted in December 2024, and is effective from 1 January 2026.
en.B: It establishes standards and provides guidance on the objective and general principles governing an audit of financial statements prepared by a financial institution conducting business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles; it was adopted on 19–20 May 1996 (2–3 Muharram 1417 A.H.) and became effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1418 A.H. or 1 January 1998 A.D.
en.C: It sets out accounting recognition rules for Murabaha receivables and became effective on 1 July 2021.
en.D: It applies solely to government central bank monetary policy audits and has no specified effective date.
en.True answer: It establishes standards and provides guidance on the objective and general principles governing an audit of financial statements prepared by a financial institution conducting business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles; it was adopted on 19–20 May 1996 (2–3 Muharram 1417 A.H.) and became effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1418 A.H. or 1 January 1998 A.D.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 1, Par. 14 & Adoption of the Standard (Par. 1: establishes standards and provides guidance on the objective and general principles governing an audit of financial statements prepared by a financial institution which conducts business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles; Par. 14: effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1418 A.H. or 1 January 1998 A.D.; Adoption: adopted by the Board in meeting No. 11 on 2–3 Muharram 1417 A.H. / 19–20 May 1996 A.D.).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 2 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, what is the objective of an audit of financial statements of an Islamic financial institution, and what exact phrase is used to express the auditor's opinion?
en.A: To enable the auditor to express an opinion as to whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with (1) Shari'a Rules and Principles, (2) AAOIFI accounting standards, and (3) relevant national accounting standards and practices in the country in which the institution operates, using the phrase 'give a true and fair view'.
en.B: To certify that the institution is 100% free from all operational errors and guaranteed to remain profitable for the next five years, using the phrase 'absolute financial guarantee'.
en.C: To evaluate whether the financial statements comply solely with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), using the phrase 'present fairly in accordance with IFRS'.
en.D: To replace the Shari'ah Supervisory Board's annual Fatwa report, using the phrase 'certified as a Shari'ah ruling'.
en.True answer: To enable the auditor to express an opinion as to whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with (1) Shari'a Rules and Principles, (2) AAOIFI accounting standards, and (3) relevant national accounting standards and practices in the country in which the institution operates, using the phrase 'give a true and fair view'.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 2 ('The objective of an audit of financial statements is to enable the auditor to express an opinion as to whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the Shari'a Rules and Principles, the accounting standards of the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) and relevant national accounting standards and practices in the country in which the financial institution operates. The phrase used to express the auditor's opinion is "give a true and fair view"').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 3 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, although the auditor's opinion enhances the credibility of the financial statements, what two assumptions CANNOT be made by a user of the financial statements?
en.A: That the financial statements were prepared by management, or that historical transactions occurred during the reporting period.
en.B: That the auditor complied with AAOIFI auditing standards, or that the institution has an appointed Shari'ah Board.
en.C: That the auditor's opinion is an assurance as to (1) the future viability of the financial institution, or (2) the efficiency or effectiveness with which management has conducted the affairs of the financial institution.
en.D: That accounting estimates were reviewed during the audit, or that sampling was applied to test balances.
en.True answer: That the auditor's opinion is an assurance as to (1) the future viability of the financial institution, or (2) the efficiency or effectiveness with which management has conducted the affairs of the financial institution.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 3 ('Although the auditor's opinion enhances the credibility of the financial statements, the user cannot assume that the opinion is an assurance as to the future viability of the financial institution or as to the efficiency or effectiveness with which management has conducted the affairs of the financial institution').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 4 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, which ethical codes must the auditor comply with, and which of the following lists ethical principles explicitly enumerated in Paragraph 4?
en.A: Exclusively national bar association ethics rules, focusing solely on commercial profitability and client advocacy.
en.B: Only the IFAC Code of Ethics even where it conflicts with Shari'a Rules and Principles, omitting righteousness and trustworthiness.
en.C: Internal corporate HR handbooks of the audited Islamic bank, prioritizing confidentiality above regulatory compliance.
en.D: The 'Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants' issued by AAOIFI, and that issued by the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC) which do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles, encompassing principles such as righteousness, integrity, trustworthiness, fairness, honesty, independence, objectivity, professional competence, due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour, and technical standards.
en.True answer: The 'Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants' issued by AAOIFI, and that issued by the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC) which do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles, encompassing principles such as righteousness, integrity, trustworthiness, fairness, honesty, independence, objectivity, professional competence, due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour, and technical standards.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 4(a)–(l) (Auditor should comply with the 'Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants' issued by AAOIFI, and that of IFAC which do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles; enumerates 12 ethical principles: (a) Righteousness, (b) Integrity, (c) Trustworthiness, (d) Fairness, (e) Honesty, (f) Independence, (g) Objectivity, (h) Professional Competence, (i) Due Care, (j) Confidentiality, (k) Professional Behaviour, and (l) Technical Standards).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 5 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, what do Auditing Standards for Islamic Financial Institutions (ASIFIs) contain?
en.A: Basic principles and essential procedures together with related guidance in the form of explanatory and other material, approved by AAOIFI.
en.B: Exclusively non-binding academic essays on Islamic history with no essential audit procedures.
en.C: Only national tax calculation tables applicable to conventional commercial banks.
en.D: Confidential internal memos issued by individual bank Shari'ah Supervisory Boards.
en.True answer: Basic principles and essential procedures together with related guidance in the form of explanatory and other material, approved by AAOIFI.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 5 ('The auditor should conduct an audit in accordance with ASIFIs, which are auditing standards approved by the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions. These contain basic principles and essential procedures together with related guidance in the form of explanatory and other material').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 6 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, how should the auditor treat management representations when planning and performing the audit?
en.A: The auditor should automatically assume management representations are accurate unless whistleblowers prove fraud in court.
en.B: The auditor should plan and perform the audit with professional competence and due care recognizing that circumstances may exist which cause the financial statements to be materially misstated—for example, expecting to find evidence to support management representations and NOT automatically assuming that they are necessarily correct.
en.C: The auditor is prohibited from requesting written representations from management.
en.D: Management representations eliminate the need to obtain external corroborating audit evidence.
en.True answer: The auditor should plan and perform the audit with professional competence and due care recognizing that circumstances may exist which cause the financial statements to be materially misstated—for example, expecting to find evidence to support management representations and NOT automatically assuming that they are necessarily correct.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 6 ('The auditor should plan and perform the audit with professional competence and due care recognizing that circumstances may exist which cause the financial statements to be materially misstated. For example, the auditor would usually expect to find evidence to support management representations and not automatically assume that they are necessarily correct').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 7 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, what does 'scope of an audit' refer to, and when do International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) apply?
en.A: Scope refers solely to the audit fee budget, and ISAs never apply to Islamic financial institutions.
en.B: Scope is determined unilaterally by the bank's CEO, and ISAs override ASIFIs whenever a conflict arises.
en.C: 'Scope of an audit' refers to the audit procedures deemed necessary by the auditor in the circumstances to achieve the audit objective (determined having regard to appropriate Islamic Rules and Principles, ASIFIs, relevant professional bodies, legislations/regulations not contravening Islamic Rules and Principles, and engagement/reporting terms); International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs, provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles.
en.D: ISAs apply exclusively to Zakah audits, while ASIFIs apply only to conventional commercial loans.
en.True answer: 'Scope of an audit' refers to the audit procedures deemed necessary by the auditor in the circumstances to achieve the audit objective (determined having regard to appropriate Islamic Rules and Principles, ASIFIs, relevant professional bodies, legislations/regulations not contravening Islamic Rules and Principles, and engagement/reporting terms); International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs, provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 7 ('The term "scope of an audit" refers to the audit procedures deemed necessary by the auditor in the circumstances to achieve the objective of the audit... International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) shall apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs providing these do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 8–9 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, what does 'reasonable assurance' encompass in an audit of an Islamic financial institution?
en.A: Absolute 100% certainty that every single transaction in the bank's history is free from immaterial clerical errors.
en.B: Assurance that the bank's share price will increase over the next 12 months.
en.C: A personal Fatwa issued by the external financial auditor overriding the institution's Shari'ah Board.
en.D: Accumulating the audit evidence necessary for the auditor to conclude that there are no material misstatements in the financial statements taken as a whole (relating to the whole audit process), AND satisfying himself that the transactions examined during his audit comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution.
en.True answer: Accumulating the audit evidence necessary for the auditor to conclude that there are no material misstatements in the financial statements taken as a whole (relating to the whole audit process), AND satisfying himself that the transactions examined during his audit comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 8–9 (Par. 8: audit provides reasonable assurance that financial statements taken as a whole are free from material misstatement, relating to accumulation of audit evidence across the whole audit process; Par. 9: 'Reasonable assurance also means that the auditor has satisfied himself that the transactions he examined during his audit comply with Sharia Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 10 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, which three factors give rise to inherent limitations in an audit that affect the auditor's ability to detect material misstatements?
en.A: (a) The use of sampling while testing transactions and balances, (b) the inherent limitations of any accounting and internal control system (including, for example, the possibility of collusion), and (c) the fact that most audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive.
en.B: (a) Prohibition of computer usage in auditing, (b) inability to inspect bank contracts, and (c) statutory ban on speaking with management.
en.C: (a) Mandatory 100% transaction testing, (b) infallibility of internal controls, and (c) conclusive legal proof in every voucher.
en.D: (a) Lack of AAOIFI accounting standards, (b) absence of Shari'ah Boards in IFIs, and (c) client refusal to pay audit fees.
en.True answer: (a) The use of sampling while testing transactions and balances, (b) the inherent limitations of any accounting and internal control system (including, for example, the possibility of collusion), and (c) the fact that most audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 10(a)–(c) (Lists the three factors causing inherent limitations in an audit: (a) the use of sampling while testing transactions and balances; (b) the inherent limitations of any accounting and internal control system [including, for example, the possibility of collusion]; and (c) the fact that most audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 11 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, in which two primary areas is the work undertaken by the auditor to form an opinion based on professional judgement?
en.A: (a) Setting profit-sharing ratios for Mudaraba depositors, and (b) drafting new Shari'ah Fatwas.
en.B: (a) The gathering of audit evidence (for example, in deciding the nature, timing, and extent of audit procedures), and (b) the drawing of conclusions based on the audit evidence gathered (for example, assessing the reasonableness of the estimates made by management in preparing the financial statements).
en.C: (a) Approving employee salaries, and (b) negotiating vendor lease contracts.
en.D: (a) Selecting the bank's Board of Directors, and (b) determining Zakah rates.
en.True answer: (a) The gathering of audit evidence (for example, in deciding the nature, timing, and extent of audit procedures), and (b) the drawing of conclusions based on the audit evidence gathered (for example, assessing the reasonableness of the estimates made by management in preparing the financial statements).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 11(a)–(b) ('Also the work undertaken by the auditor to form an opinion is based on judgement, regarding in particular: (a) The gathering of audit evidence, for example, in deciding the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures, and (b) The drawing of conclusions based on the audit evidence gathered, for example, assessing the reasonableness of the estimates made by management in preparing the financial statements').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 12 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, when inherent limitations affect the persuasiveness of audit evidence on certain aspects (such as transactions between related parties), when do specified procedures identified in certain ASIFIs provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence?
en.A: Even when clear evidence of material fraud exists, as long as management signs a waiver.
en.B: Never—related party transactions always require an automatic disclaimer of opinion.
en.C: In the absence of (a) unusual circumstances which increase the risk of material misstatement beyond that which would ordinarily be expected, or (b) any indication that material misstatement exists.
en.D: Only when the related party is a government agency.
en.True answer: In the absence of (a) unusual circumstances which increase the risk of material misstatement beyond that which would ordinarily be expected, or (b) any indication that material misstatement exists.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 12(a)–(b) ('In these cases certain ASIFIs identify specified procedures which may, because of the nature of these aspects, provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence in the absence of: (a) Unusual circumstances which increase the risk of material misstatement beyond that which would ordinarily be expected, or (b) Any indication that material misstatement exists').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 13 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, how are responsibilities divided between the auditor and the management of the financial institution, and does the audit relieve management of its responsibility?
en.A: The audit transfers legal responsibility for preparing financial statements from management to the external auditor.
en.B: Management is responsible only for bookkeeping, while the auditor is responsible for ensuring the bank complies with Shari'a Rules and Principles.
en.C: The Shari'ah Supervisory Board is responsible for preparing the financial statements, and the audit relieves management of all statutory duties.
en.D: While the auditor is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the financial statements, the responsibility for preparing and presenting the financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation and regulations is that of the management of the financial institution (considering the definition of management in relevant national legislation/regulations), and the audit of the financial statements does NOT relieve management of this responsibility.
en.True answer: While the auditor is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the financial statements, the responsibility for preparing and presenting the financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation and regulations is that of the management of the financial institution (considering the definition of management in relevant national legislation/regulations), and the audit of the financial statements does NOT relieve management of this responsibility.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 13 ('While the auditor is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the financial statements, the responsibility for preparing and presenting the financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation and regulations is that of the management of the financial institution. (Consideration should be given to the definition of management in relevant national legislation and regulations.) The audit of the financial statements does not relieve the management of the financial institution of this responsibility').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: An external auditor issues an unqualified audit report expressing that an Islamic bank's financial statements 'give a true and fair view' under ASIFI No. 1.
