Ten months later, the bank suffers severe liquidity distress due to poor commercial credit decisions, and an institutional investor claims the audit opinion assured the bank's future viability and managerial efficiency. Meanwhile, the bank's CFO argues that compliance with national GAAP alone suffices for the audit opinion even where AAOIFI accounting standards apply. Under Paragraphs 2–3 of ASIFI No. 1, which evaluation is accurate?
en.A: Both the investor and the CFO are incorrect: under Par. 2, the audit opinion evaluates whether financial statements are prepared in all material respects in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, AAOIFI accounting standards, AND relevant national accounting standards/practices; and under Par. 3, while the opinion enhances credibility, the user cannot assume it is an assurance as to the institution's future viability or the efficiency/effectiveness with which management conducted its affairs.
en.B: Both the investor and the CFO are correct: a 'true and fair view' opinion certifies managerial efficiency and future solvency, and national GAAP always supersedes AAOIFI standards.
en.C: The investor is correct regarding future viability, whereas the CFO is incorrect regarding AAOIFI accounting standards.
en.D: The CFO is correct that national GAAP alone suffices, whereas the investor is incorrect regarding managerial efficiency.
en.True answer: Both the investor and the CFO are incorrect: under Par. 2, the audit opinion evaluates whether financial statements are prepared in all material respects in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, AAOIFI accounting standards, AND relevant national accounting standards/practices; and under Par. 3, while the opinion enhances credibility, the user cannot assume it is an assurance as to the institution's future viability or the efficiency/effectiveness with which management conducted its affairs.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 2–3 (Par. 2 requires financial statements to be prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, AAOIFI accounting standards, AND relevant national accounting standards and practices; Par. 3 explicitly states that although the auditor's opinion enhances credibility, the user cannot assume it is an assurance as to future viability of the financial institution or as to the efficiency or effectiveness with which management conducted its affairs).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question:
During an audit of an Islamic bank, the external auditor encounters two methodological situations:
(1) A specific audit sampling detail is not covered in detail by ASIFIs, so the auditor proposes applying an International Standard on Auditing (ISA) procedure that is fully consistent with Islamic Rules and Principles.
(2) A provision in a professional code of ethics or national regulation conflicts directly with Islamic Rules and Principles.
According to Paragraphs 4 and 7 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, how must the auditor resolve both situations?
en.A: In (1), ISAs are strictly prohibited even when ASIFIs are silent; in (2), national regulations and IFAC ethical rules override Islamic Rules and Principles.
en.B: In (1), applying the ISA procedure is valid because Paragraph 7 states that ISAs shall apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles; in (2), the conflicting provision cannot be applied because both Paragraph 4 (ethical codes) and Paragraph 7 (audit scope/regulations/ISAs) apply ONLY insofar as they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles.
en.C: Both situations are resolved solely by asking the bank's Chief Executive Officer which standard he prefers.
en.D: In (1), the auditor must skip the audit area completely; in (2), the auditor must apply the conflicting rule and note it in a private letter.
en.True answer: In (1), applying the ISA procedure is valid because Paragraph 7 states that ISAs shall apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles; in (2), the conflicting provision cannot be applied because both Paragraph 4 (ethical codes) and Paragraph 7 (audit scope/regulations/ISAs) apply ONLY insofar as they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 4 & Par. 7 (Par. 4: comply with AAOIFI Code of Ethics and IFAC Code of Ethics 'which do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles'; Par. 7: audit scope considers Islamic Rules and Principles, ASIFIs, relevant professional bodies, legislations/regulations 'which do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles', and explicitly states: 'International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) shall apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs providing these do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 8–9 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, what dual dimension distinguishes 'reasonable assurance' in an audit of an Islamic financial institution from a purely conventional financial audit, and whose Shari'ah rulings serve as the benchmark for examined transactions?
en.A: The external auditor issues his own independent Fiqh rulings overriding the bank's Shari'ah Board, and provides 100% absolute assurance.
en.B: Reasonable assurance covers only mathematical trial-balance accuracy, leaving Shari'ah compliance of examined transactions entirely outside the financial statement audit.
en.C: In addition to providing reasonable assurance (across the whole audit process) that the financial statements taken as a whole are free from material misstatement (Par. 8), reasonable assurance under ASIFI No. 1 also means that the auditor has satisfied himself that the transactions he examined during his audit comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution (Par. 9).
en.D: Reasonable assurance applies solely to Zakah disclosures and relies exclusively on management's oral assurances.
en.True answer: In addition to providing reasonable assurance (across the whole audit process) that the financial statements taken as a whole are free from material misstatement (Par. 8), reasonable assurance under ASIFI No. 1 also means that the auditor has satisfied himself that the transactions he examined during his audit comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution (Par. 9).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 8–9 (Par. 8 defines reasonable assurance regarding absence of material misstatement in the financial statements taken as a whole; Par. 9 adds the distinct Islamic audit dimension: 'Reasonable assurance also means that the auditor has satisfied himself that the transactions he examined during his audit comply with Sharia Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: During an audit, an auditor obtains a signed representation letter from senior management stating that all Mudaraba valuation estimates are reasonable. Months after the audit concludes, a sophisticated collusion scheme between two senior officers and an external appraiser is uncovered that inflated asset values in transactions outside the auditor's sample. Under Paragraphs 6, 10, and 11 of ASIFI No. 1, which assessment is correct?
en.A: The auditor should have accepted management's representation letter without seeking any supporting evidence (Par. 6), and any undetected fraud automatically proves audit negligence because audits provide absolute assurance.
en.B: Audit evidence is always conclusive rather than persuasive, so collusion can never prevent detection of material misstatements.
en.C: Auditor judgement applies only to clerical formatting of the audit report and not to assessing management estimates.
en.D: Under Par. 6, the auditor must not automatically assume management representations are correct and must seek evidence supporting them; under Par. 11(b), assessing the reasonableness of management's estimates requires auditor judgement; however, under Par. 10(a)–(c), an audit has inherent limitations—specifically (a) use of sampling, (b) inherent limitations of accounting and internal control systems (explicitly including the possibility of collusion), and (c) the fact that most audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive—meaning an audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
en.True answer: Under Par. 6, the auditor must not automatically assume management representations are correct and must seek evidence supporting them; under Par. 11(b), assessing the reasonableness of management's estimates requires auditor judgement; however, under Par. 10(a)–(c), an audit has inherent limitations—specifically (a) use of sampling, (b) inherent limitations of accounting and internal control systems (explicitly including the possibility of collusion), and (c) the fact that most audit evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive—meaning an audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 6, Par. 10(a)–(c) & Par. 11(a)–(b) (Par. 6: expect evidence to support management representations and do not automatically assume they are correct; Par. 11(b): drawing conclusions involves auditor judgement in assessing reasonableness of management's estimates; Par. 10(a)–(c): inherent limitations arise from sampling, inherent limitations of accounting/internal control systems [specifically citing collusion], and persuasive rather than conclusive nature of most audit evidence).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Under Paragraph 12 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, an auditor examines related-party financing transactions where limitations affect the persuasiveness of available audit evidence. Compare two scenarios: (I) routine related-party transactions with normal commercial terms, no unusual risk factors, and no indication of material misstatement; versus (II) related-party transactions structured off-market at year-end with unusual circumstances elevating the risk of material misstatement beyond ordinary expectations. How do specified ASIFI procedures apply in (I) and (II)?
en.A: In Scenario (I), performing the specified procedures identified in the relevant ASIFIs provides sufficient appropriate audit evidence because neither unusual risk-elevating circumstances nor indications of material misstatement are present; in Scenario (II), the specified procedures alone are NOT sufficient because unusual circumstances increase the risk of material misstatement beyond what would ordinarily be expected, requiring extended audit procedures.
en.B: In both Scenarios (I) and (II), the specified ASIFI procedures are automatically sufficient without any further inquiry.
en.C: In both Scenarios (I) and (II), the auditor must immediately issue an adverse opinion without performing any procedures.
en.D: Specified ASIFI procedures apply only in Scenario (II) and are prohibited in Scenario (I).
en.True answer: In Scenario (I), performing the specified procedures identified in the relevant ASIFIs provides sufficient appropriate audit evidence because neither unusual risk-elevating circumstances nor indications of material misstatement are present; in Scenario (II), the specified procedures alone are NOT sufficient because unusual circumstances increase the risk of material misstatement beyond what would ordinarily be expected, requiring extended audit procedures.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 12(a)–(b) (Explains that where limitations affect persuasiveness of evidence [e.g. related-party transactions], certain ASIFIs identify specified procedures which may provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence 'in the absence of: (a) Unusual circumstances which increase the risk of material misstatement beyond that which would ordinarily be expected, or (b) Any indication that material misstatement exists'. Scenario I meets both conditions for sufficiency; Scenario II triggers (a), requiring additional procedures).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question: Following a regulatory inspection of an Islamic bank, the regulator discovers that the bank's annual financial statements omitted mandatory disclosures required under national banking regulations and Shari'a Rules and Principles. During the enforcement hearing, the bank's executive directors argue that because the external auditor completed a statutory audit and issued an unqualified opinion, legal responsibility for preparing compliant financial statements shifted to the external auditor. Under Paragraph 13 of ASIFI No. 1, which conclusion is correct?
en.A: The executive directors are correct: once an external audit is completed, management is legally relieved of responsibility for financial statement preparation and compliance.
en.B: The executive directors are incorrect: while the auditor is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the financial statements, the responsibility for preparing and presenting the financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation and regulations rests with the management of the financial institution (taking into account the definition of management in relevant national legislation and regulations), and the audit does NOT relieve management of this responsibility.
en.C: Responsibility for preparing compliant financial statements rests exclusively with the external rating agency.
en.D: Management is responsible only for Shari'a compliance, while the external auditor is legally responsible for statutory regulatory compliance.
en.True answer: The executive directors are incorrect: while the auditor is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the financial statements, the responsibility for preparing and presenting the financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation and regulations rests with the management of the financial institution (taking into account the definition of management in relevant national legislation and regulations), and the audit does NOT relieve management of this responsibility.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1, Par. 13 ('While the auditor is responsible for forming and expressing an opinion on the financial statements, the responsibility for preparing and presenting the financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation and regulations is that of the management of the financial institution. (Consideration should be given to the definition of management in relevant national legislation and regulations.) The audit of the financial statements does not relieve the management of the financial institution of this responsibility').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question:
An external audit firm is conducting the statutory financial statement audit of an Islamic bank under AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1. Examine the following four audit engagement actions:
(1) The audit partner plans the engagement solely to opine on whether the financial statements conform to national accounting standards, omitting AAOIFI accounting standards and Shari'a Rules and Principles from the audit opinion framework.
(2) For a specific IT data-extraction audit procedure not covered in detail by ASIFIs, the audit team applies an International Standard on Auditing (ISA) procedure after verifying that it does not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles.
(3) During audit fieldwork, the CFO provides a signed representation letter confirming the completeness of off-balance-sheet Mudaraba commitments; the audit team relies on this representation letter without seeking any supporting evidence.
(4) When testing examined financing transactions for Shari'a compliance as part of reasonable assurance, the lead auditor rejects a transaction structure approved by the bank's Shari'a Board solely because the lead auditor personally prefers a different classical Fiqh school's opinion.
According to ASIFI No. 1, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—national accounting standards alone define the opinion framework; (2) Non-compliant—ISAs are prohibited; (3) Compliant—written CFO representations require no corroborating evidence; (4) Compliant—auditors apply their own preferred Fiqh opinions.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 2, the audit objective is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, AAOIFI accounting standards, AND relevant national accounting standards and practices; (2) Compliant—Par. 7 explicitly states that ISAs shall apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. 6, which stipulates that the auditor should usually expect to find evidence to support management representations and NOT automatically assume they are necessarily correct; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 9, which defines reasonable assurance as the auditor satisfying himself that examined transactions comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles 'as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution' (not the auditor's personal Fiqh preference).
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 2, the audit objective is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, AAOIFI accounting standards, AND relevant national accounting standards and practices; (2) Compliant—Par. 7 explicitly states that ISAs shall apply in respect of matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles; (3) Non-compliant—violates Par. 6, which stipulates that the auditor should usually expect to find evidence to support management representations and NOT automatically assume they are necessarily correct; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 9, which defines reasonable assurance as the auditor satisfying himself that examined transactions comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles 'as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution' (not the auditor's personal Fiqh preference).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1 integrates four core provisions: (1) Par. 2 requires the opinion to cover Shari'a Rules and Principles, AAOIFI accounting standards, AND relevant national accounting standards and practices; (2) Par. 7 authorizes applying ISAs on matters not covered in detail by ASIFIs provided they do not contravene Islamic Rules and Principles; (3) Par. 6 requires expecting evidence to support management representations and not automatically assuming they are correct; (4) Par. 9 specifies that reasonable assurance means the auditor satisfies himself that examined transactions comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles 'as determined by the Shari'a Board of the financial institution'.

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 01: Objective and Principles of Auditing
en.Question:
Following the issuance of an unqualified 'give a true and fair view' audit opinion on an Islamic bank's financial statements under AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 1, four disputes and audit review issues arise:
(1) Nine months later, the bank's profitability drops sharply due to poor commercial expansion decisions by management, and minority shareholders sue the external auditor alleging the audit opinion guaranteed future viability and managerial effectiveness.
(2) A subsequent forensic review reveals a well-concealed collusion scheme between a branch manager and an outside vendor involving falsified shipping documents in transactions not selected in the audit sample, despite the auditor having properly designed and executed sampling and control tests.
(3) For routine related-party transactions with a subsidiary where no unusual risk-elevating circumstances and no indications of material misstatement existed, the auditor performed the specific procedures prescribed by the relevant ASIFI and concluded sufficient appropriate evidence was obtained.
(4) When the regulator orders a restatement of omitted Zakah disclosures, management claims that because the external auditor audited the financial statements, management was relieved of its legal responsibility for preparing compliant financial statements.
According to ASIFI No. 1, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Auditor is liable—audit opinions guarantee future viability and managerial effectiveness; (2) Auditor is negligent—audits detect 100% of collusion schemes; (3) Non-compliant—specified ASIFI procedures never suffice for related parties; (4) Management is right—audits relieve management of preparation responsibility.
en.B: (1) Auditor is not liable; (2) Auditor is negligent; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Management is right.
en.C: (1) Auditor is liable; (2) Auditor is not negligent; (3) Compliant; (4) Management is right.
en.D: (1) Auditor is not liable—under Par. 3, while the opinion enhances credibility, users cannot assume it is an assurance as to future viability or the efficiency/effectiveness with which management conducted the institution's affairs; (2) Properly executed audit—under Par. 10(a)–(c), inherent limitations of an audit arise from sampling, inherent limitations of accounting and internal control systems (explicitly including the possibility of collusion), and the persuasive rather than conclusive nature of most audit evidence; (3) Compliant—under Par. 12(a)–(b), specified procedures identified in relevant ASIFIs provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence for related-party aspects in the absence of unusual risk-elevating circumstances or indications of material misstatement; (4) Management is wrong—under Par. 13, preparing and presenting financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation/regulations is management's responsibility, and the audit does NOT relieve management of this responsibility.
en.True answer: (1) Auditor is not liable—under Par. 3, while the opinion enhances credibility, users cannot assume it is an assurance as to future viability or the efficiency/effectiveness with which management conducted the institution's affairs; (2) Properly executed audit—under Par. 10(a)–(c), inherent limitations of an audit arise from sampling, inherent limitations of accounting and internal control systems (explicitly including the possibility of collusion), and the persuasive rather than conclusive nature of most audit evidence; (3) Compliant—under Par. 12(a)–(b), specified procedures identified in relevant ASIFIs provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence for related-party aspects in the absence of unusual risk-elevating circumstances or indications of material misstatement; (4) Management is wrong—under Par. 13, preparing and presenting financial statements in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and relevant legislation/regulations is management's responsibility, and the audit does NOT relieve management of this responsibility.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 1 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 3 states users cannot assume the opinion is an assurance as to future viability or efficiency/effectiveness of management; (2) Par. 10(a)–(c) explains inherent audit limitations due to sampling, inherent limitations of accounting and internal control systems (explicitly citing collusion), and persuasive rather than conclusive nature of most audit evidence; (3) Par. 12(a)–(b) confirms specified ASIFI procedures provide sufficient appropriate evidence in the absence of unusual circumstances increasing misstatement risk beyond ordinary expectations or any indication that material misstatement exists; (4) Par. 13 establishes that preparing and presenting compliant financial statements is management's responsibility and that the audit does NOT relieve management of this responsibility.

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 1–4 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2 ('Auditor's Report'), which three benchmarks must the auditor consider when reviewing and assessing conclusions drawn from audit evidence, and can ASIFI 2 guidance be adapted to financial information other than financial statements?
en.A: The auditor must consider whether the financial statements have been prepared in accordance with (1) AAOIFI accounting standards, (2) relevant national standards or practices, and (3) statutory requirements; and much of the guidance in ASIFI 2 CAN be adapted to auditor's reports on financial information other than financial statements.
en.B: The auditor considers only IFRS standards, and ASIFI 2 is strictly prohibited from being adapted to any financial information other than annual statutory financial statements.
en.C: The auditor considers only national tax laws, and the auditor's report may express an oral rather than a written opinion.
en.D: ASIFI 2 applies exclusively to internal Shari'ah audit reports and became effective on 1 January 2026.
en.True answer: The auditor must consider whether the financial statements have been prepared in accordance with (1) AAOIFI accounting standards, (2) relevant national standards or practices, and (3) statutory requirements; and much of the guidance in ASIFI 2 CAN be adapted to auditor's reports on financial information other than financial statements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 1–4 & Par. 47 (Par. 1: 'Much of the guidance provided can be adapted to auditor's reports on financial information other than financial statements'; Par. 3: 'This review and assessment involves considering whether the financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the accounting standards of the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) and relevant national standards or practices. It will also be necessary to consider whether the financial statements comply with statutory requirements'; Par. 4: clear written expression of opinion on financial statements taken as a whole; Par. 47: effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1418 A.H. / 1 January 1998 A.D.).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraph 5(a)–(j) of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, which option lists all ten basic elements of an auditor's report in their proper structural sequence?
en.A: Opinion paragraph → Scope paragraph → Title → Addressee → Auditor's signature → Opening paragraph → Date of report → Auditor's address.
en.B: (a) Title, (b) Addressee, (c) Opening or introductory paragraph, (d) Scope paragraph (describing the nature of the audit), (e) Reference to the ASIFIs and relevant national standards or practices, (f) Description of the work the auditor performed, (g) Opinion paragraph containing an expression of opinion on the financial statements, (h) Date of report, (i) Auditor's address, and (j) Auditor's signature.
en.C: (a) Addressee, (b) Management's letter of representation, (c) Shari'ah Supervisory Board Fatwa list, (d) Opinion paragraph, and (e) Zakah calculation schedule.
en.D: (a) Title, (b) Scope paragraph, (c) Emphasis of matter paragraph, (d) Opening paragraph, and (e) Date of financial statement approval by shareholders.
en.True answer: (a) Title, (b) Addressee, (c) Opening or introductory paragraph, (d) Scope paragraph (describing the nature of the audit), (e) Reference to the ASIFIs and relevant national standards or practices, (f) Description of the work the auditor performed, (g) Opinion paragraph containing an expression of opinion on the financial statements, (h) Date of report, (i) Auditor's address, and (j) Auditor's signature.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 5(a)–(j) (Enumerates the exact 10 basic elements of the auditor's report: (a) Title, (b) Addressee, (c) Opening or introductory paragraph, (d) Scope paragraph [describing nature of audit], (e) Reference to ASIFIs and relevant national standards or practices, (f) Description of the work the auditor performed, (g) Opinion paragraph containing an expression of opinion on the financial statements, (h) Date of report, (i) Auditor's address, and (j) Auditor's signature).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 13 and 15 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, which two statements must be included in the Scope paragraph of the auditor's report regarding assurance level and opinion basis?
en.A: That the audit provides an absolute 100% guarantee against all fraud, and that management's estimates were approved by the external auditor.
en.B: That the audit was limited to verifying mathematical addition, and that no sampling was applied.
en.C: A statement that the audit was planned and performed to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of material misstatements (Par. 13), AND a statement by the auditor that the audit provides a reasonable basis for the opinion (Par. 15).
en.D: A statement that the Shari'ah Supervisory Board audited the accounting ledgers, and that the external auditor is not responsible for expressing an opinion.
en.True answer: A statement that the audit was planned and performed to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of material misstatements (Par. 13), AND a statement by the auditor that the audit provides a reasonable basis for the opinion (Par. 15).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 13 & Par. 15 (Par. 13: 'The report should include a statement that the audit was planned and performed to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of material misstatements'; Par. 15: 'The report should include a statement by the auditor that the audit provides a reasonable basis for the opinion').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 17–20 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, what does the opinion phrase 'give a true and fair view' indicate regarding materiality, and how is the financial reporting framework communicated to readers?
en.A: It indicates that the auditor verified every single immaterial transaction down to the smallest cent, without needing to identify the accounting framework.
en.B: It guarantees that the bank achieved its annual profit budget under IFRS only.
en.C: It indicates that only Shari'a compliance was examined, ignoring accounting standards and statutory laws.
en.D: The term 'give a true and fair view' indicates, amongst other things, that the auditor considers only those matters that are material to the financial statements; and to advise the reader of the context in which 'fairness' is expressed, the opinion indicates the framework using wording such as 'in accordance with the Sharia Rules and Principles (as determined by the Shari'a Board of the Financial Institution) and in accordance with the accounting standards of the AAOIFI and relevant national legislation, regulations and standards or practices' (plus compliance with other statutory requirements where applicable).
en.True answer: The term 'give a true and fair view' indicates, amongst other things, that the auditor considers only those matters that are material to the financial statements; and to advise the reader of the context in which 'fairness' is expressed, the opinion indicates the framework using wording such as 'in accordance with the Sharia Rules and Principles (as determined by the Shari'a Board of the Financial Institution) and in accordance with the accounting standards of the AAOIFI and relevant national legislation, regulations and standards or practices' (plus compliance with other statutory requirements where applicable).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 17–21 (Par. 17: state opinion as to whether statements give a true and fair view in accordance with Sharia Rules and Principles as determined by the SSB and the financial reporting framework, plus statutory compliance where appropriate; Par. 18: 'The term used to express the auditor's opinion is "give a true and fair view". This term indicates, amongst other things, that the auditor considers only those matters that are material to the financial statements'; Par. 19–21: specify framework wording).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 22, 25, and 26 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, which requirements govern (1) identifying the country of accounting principles in cross-border distributions, (2) the auditor's address, and (3) the auditor's signature?
en.A: (1) Where it is not evident which country's accounting principles were used (or when statements are distributed extensively outside or prepared specifically for another country), the country of origin's accounting principles should be stated; (2) the report must name a specific location, ordinarily the city where the auditor maintains the office responsible for the audit; and (3) the report must be signed either in the name of the audit firm, the personal name of the auditor, or both, as appropriate.
en.B: (1) The country of accounting principles is never mentioned in cross-border reports; (2) the auditor's address must be the client's headquarters; and (3) only the client's CEO signs the auditor's report.
en.C: (1) Cross-border reports automatically substitute the host country's GAAP without disclosure; (2) no city location is required; and (3) electronic stamps without firm or personal names suffice.
en.D: (1) Only AAOIFI's headquarters city in Bahrain may be listed; (2) the report is signed solely by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board Chairman.
en.True answer: (1) Where it is not evident which country's accounting principles were used (or when statements are distributed extensively outside or prepared specifically for another country), the country of origin's accounting principles should be stated; (2) the report must name a specific location, ordinarily the city where the auditor maintains the office responsible for the audit; and (3) the report must be signed either in the name of the audit firm, the personal name of the auditor, or both, as appropriate.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 22 & Par. 25–26 (Par. 22: state country where not evident, and when distributed extensively outside country of origin or prepared specifically for another country [e.g. translated into another language/currency in cross-border financing], refer to accounting principles of the country of origin; Par. 25: name specific location, ordinarily the city where auditor maintains the office responsible for the audit; Par. 26: signed either in name of audit firm, personal name of auditor, or both, as appropriate).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraph 27 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, what does an unqualified audit opinion implicitly indicate regarding changes in accounting principles or in the method of their application?
en.A: That no changes in accounting principles ever occurred during the financial year.
en.B: That any changes in accounting principles or in the method of their application, and the effects thereof, have been properly determined and disclosed in the financial statements.
en.C: That management is free to change accounting methods mid-year without disclosing the financial effects.
en.D: That accounting method changes are reviewed exclusively by tax inspectors rather than the auditor.
en.True answer: That any changes in accounting principles or in the method of their application, and the effects thereof, have been properly determined and disclosed in the financial statements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 27 ('An unqualified opinion should be expressed when the auditor concludes that the financial statements give a true and fair view in accordance with the identified financial reporting framework. An unqualified opinion also indicates implicitly that any changes in accounting principles or in the method of their application, and the effects thereof, have been properly determined and disclosed in the financial statements').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraph 29 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, how are 'Modified Reports' categorized into matters that do NOT affect the auditor's opinion versus matters that DO affect the auditor's opinion?
en.A: Matters NOT affecting the opinion: Qualified opinion; Matters AFFECTING the opinion: Emphasis of matter, Adverse opinion, and Disclaimer of opinion.
en.B: Matters NOT affecting the opinion: Adverse opinion; Matters AFFECTING the opinion: Emphasis of matter only.
en.C: Matters that do NOT affect the auditor's opinion: Emphasis of a matter; Matters that DO affect the auditor's opinion: (a) Qualified opinion, (b) Disclaimer of opinion, or (c) Adverse opinion.
en.D: All modified reports automatically express an Adverse opinion without sub-categories.
en.True answer: Matters that do NOT affect the auditor's opinion: Emphasis of a matter; Matters that DO affect the auditor's opinion: (a) Qualified opinion, (b) Disclaimer of opinion, or (c) Adverse opinion.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 29 (Classifies modified reports into two groups: 1. Matters that do not affect the auditor's opinion: Emphasis of a matter; 2. Matters that do affect the auditor's opinion: (a) Qualified opinion, (b) Disclaimer of opinion, or (c) Adverse opinion).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 30 and 35 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, where should an 'Emphasis of Matter' paragraph preferably be placed in the auditor's report, and for what non-financial-statement matters may it also be used?
en.A: Preferably before the Title, used exclusively to replace a Qualified opinion.
en.B: Preferably inside the Scope paragraph, used exclusively to list audit staff names.
en.C: Preferably after the Auditor's signature, used only when management refuses to pay audit fees.
en.D: Preferably AFTER the opinion paragraph (ordinarily referring to the fact that the auditor's opinion is not qualified in this respect), and it may also be used to report on matters other than those affecting the financial statements—such as when an amendment is necessary to other information in a document containing audited financial statements and the institution refuses to make the amendment, or when there are additional statutory reporting responsibilities.
en.True answer: Preferably AFTER the opinion paragraph (ordinarily referring to the fact that the auditor's opinion is not qualified in this respect), and it may also be used to report on matters other than those affecting the financial statements—such as when an amendment is necessary to other information in a document containing audited financial statements and the institution refuses to make the amendment, or when there are additional statutory reporting responsibilities.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 30 & Par. 35 (Par. 30: emphasis of matter paragraph 'would preferably be included after the opinion paragraph and would ordinarily refer to the fact the auditor's opinion is not qualified in this respect'; Par. 35: may also be used, preferably after the opinion paragraph, to report on matters other than those affecting the financial statements, e.g., when an amendment is necessary to other information in a document containing audited financial statements and the financial institution refuses to make the amendment, or when there are additional statutory reporting responsibilities).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraph 34 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, when may an auditor consider expressing a 'disclaimer of opinion' instead of merely adding an 'emphasis of matter' paragraph for going concern problems or significant uncertainties?
en.A: In extreme cases, such as situations involving multiple uncertainties that are significant to the financial statements.
en.B: Whenever a single minor lawsuit with negligible financial impact is disclosed in Note 15.
en.C: Never—uncertainties can never result in a disclaimer of opinion under ASIFI 2.
en.D: Whenever management requests a disclaimer of opinion to avoid tax inspections.
en.True answer: In extreme cases, such as situations involving multiple uncertainties that are significant to the financial statements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 34 ('The addition of a paragraph emphasizing a going concern problem or significant uncertainty is usually adequate to meet the auditor's reporting responsibilities regarding such matters. However, in extreme cases, such as situations involving multiple uncertainties that are significant to the financial statements, the auditor may consider it appropriate to express a disclaimer of opinion instead of adding an emphasis of matter paragraph').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraph 36 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, which reporting outcomes can result from (a) a material limitation on the scope of the auditor's work versus (b) a material disagreement with management?
en.A: (a) Scope limitation leads to Qualified or Adverse opinion; (b) Disagreement with management leads to Qualified or Disclaimer of opinion.
en.B: (a) Limitation on scope could lead to a Qualified opinion or a Disclaimer of opinion; (b) Disagreement with management (regarding implementation of Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board, acceptability of accounting policies, method of application, or adequacy of disclosures) could lead to a Qualified opinion or an Adverse opinion.
en.C: Both scope limitations and disagreements with management lead exclusively to an Emphasis of Matter paragraph.
en.D: (a) Scope limitation leads to Adverse opinion; (b) Disagreement with management leads to Disclaimer of opinion.
en.True answer: (a) Limitation on scope could lead to a Qualified opinion or a Disclaimer of opinion; (b) Disagreement with management (regarding implementation of Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board, acceptability of accounting policies, method of application, or adequacy of disclosures) could lead to a Qualified opinion or an Adverse opinion.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 36(a)–(b) (Explicitly maps the two triggers: (a) limitation on the scope of the auditor's work could lead to a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion; (b) disagreement with management [regarding implementation of Sharia Rules and Principles as determined by the Shari'a Board, acceptability of accounting policies, method of application, or adequacy of disclosures] could lead to a qualified opinion or an adverse opinion).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: In the illustrative wording for 'Limitation on scope — disclaimer of opinion' in Paragraph 44 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2 (p. 836), how are the opening (introductory) paragraph and the auditor's responsibility sentence modified compared to an unqualified report?
en.A: The opening paragraph states 'We have audited...' and retains the sentence 'Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit.'
en.B: The opening paragraph omits management's responsibility for Shari'a compliance.
en.C: The opening paragraph begins with 'We were engaged to audit...' (instead of 'We have audited...') and explicitly OMITS the sentence stating the responsibility of the auditor ('Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit').
en.D: The disclaimer of opinion omits any description of the scope limitation.
en.True answer: The opening paragraph begins with 'We were engaged to audit...' (instead of 'We have audited...') and explicitly OMITS the sentence stating the responsibility of the auditor ('Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit').
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 44 Illustration 'Limitation on scope-disclaimer of opinion' (p. 836) (Shows two key changes in the opening paragraph: changes 'We have audited' to 'We were engaged to audit', and explicitly instructs: '(Omit the sentence stating the responsibility of the auditor)').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraph 40 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, where should the clear description of substantive reasons and quantification of possible financial statement effects normally be placed when the auditor expresses an opinion other than unqualified?
en.A: In a footnote at the very bottom of the page after the auditor's address.
en.B: Inside the opening introductory paragraph before naming the financial statements.
en.C: In a separate confidential letter sent solely to the bank's internal audit department.
en.D: In a separate paragraph PRECEDING the opinion or disclaimer of opinion paragraph (and it may include a reference to a more extensive discussion, if any, in a note to the financial statements).
en.True answer: In a separate paragraph PRECEDING the opinion or disclaimer of opinion paragraph (and it may include a reference to a more extensive discussion, if any, in a note to the financial statements).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 40 ('Whenever the auditor expresses an opinion that is other than unqualified, a clear description of all the substantive reasons should be included in the report and, unless impracticable, a quantification of the possible effect(s) on the financial statements. Usually, this information will be set out in a separate paragraph preceding the opinion or disclaimer of opinion and may include a reference to a more extensive discussion, if any, in a note to the financial statements').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: In the Paragraph 46 illustration ('Disagreement on accounting policies — inappropriate accounting method — qualified opinion', p. 837) of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, an Islamic financial institution failed to record straight-line depreciation on its building (cost USD 2,000,000, annual rate 5%) and equipment (cost USD 500,000, annual rate 20%) for the year ended 31 December 2025. What is the exact total depreciation adjustment for the year that must be quantified in the explanatory paragraph preceding the qualified opinion?
en.A: USD 200,000 (USD 100,000 for the building [5% × $2,000,000] + USD 100,000 for the equipment [20% × $500,000]), reducing fixed assets by accumulated depreciation of USD 200,000 and increasing the loss for the year and accumulated deficit by USD 200,000 respectively.
en.B: USD 125,000 (5% of the combined USD 2,500,000 asset base), leaving fixed assets unchanged.
en.C: USD 500,000 (20% of the combined USD 2,500,000 asset base), reducing cash balances by USD 500,000.
en.D: No numerical quantification is required in the audit report under Paragraph 40 or Paragraph 46.
en.True answer: USD 200,000 (USD 100,000 for the building [5% × $2,000,000] + USD 100,000 for the equipment [20% × $500,000]), reducing fixed assets by accumulated depreciation of USD 200,000 and increasing the loss for the year and accumulated deficit by USD 200,000 respectively.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 40 & Par. 46 Illustration (p. 837) (Building depreciation = 5% × $2,000,000 = $100,000; Equipment depreciation = 20% × $500,000 = $100,000; Total provision = $200,000. Per Par. 46 illustration, the report quantifies the exact adjustment: fixed assets reduced by accumulated depreciation of $200,000, and loss for the year and accumulated deficit increased by $200,000 respectively).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Comparing the three modified-opinion formulations in Paragraph 46 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2 (pp. 837–838)—(1) Qualified opinion for inappropriate accounting method, (2) Qualified opinion for inadequate disclosure, and (3) Adverse opinion—which phrasing accurately reflects the standard's exact opinion wording for each?
en.A: All three use the exact phrase 'do not give a true and fair view' regardless of whether the effect is pervasive.
en.B: (1) Qualified opinion (inappropriate accounting method): 'In our opinion, except for the effect on the financial statements of the matter referred to in the preceding paragraph, the financial statements give a true and fair view...'; (2) Qualified opinion (inadequate disclosure): 'In our opinion, except for the omission of the information included in the preceding paragraph, the financial statements give a true and fair view...'; and (3) Adverse opinion: 'In our opinion, because of the effects of the matters discussed in the preceding paragraph(s), the financial statements do not give a true and fair view...'
en.C: (1) and (2) use 'subject to the adjustments', while (3) uses 'we are unable to express an opinion'.
en.D: Adverse opinion uses 'except for the omission of information', while Qualified opinion uses 'do not give a true and fair view'.
en.True answer: (1) Qualified opinion (inappropriate accounting method): 'In our opinion, except for the effect on the financial statements of the matter referred to in the preceding paragraph, the financial statements give a true and fair view...'; (2) Qualified opinion (inadequate disclosure): 'In our opinion, except for the omission of the information included in the preceding paragraph, the financial statements give a true and fair view...'; and (3) Adverse opinion: 'In our opinion, because of the effects of the matters discussed in the preceding paragraph(s), the financial statements do not give a true and fair view...'
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 46 Illustrations (pp. 837–838) (Provides the exact wording for each: (1) inappropriate accounting method qualified: 'except for the effect on the financial statements of the matter referred to in the preceding paragraph, the financial statements give a true and fair view...'; (2) inadequate disclosure qualified: 'except for the omission of the information included in the preceding paragraph, the financial statements give a true and fair view...'; (3) adverse opinion: 'because of the effects of the matters discussed in the preceding paragraph(s), the financial statements do not give a true and fair view...').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 12 and 22 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, an Islamic bank headquartered in Country A prepares financial statements translated into the language and currency of Country B specifically for cross-border financing in Country B. Meanwhile, the audit firm's office responsible for the audit is located in Country A, and the report does not explicitly name the country of the national auditing standards followed. How are the auditing standards and accounting principles frameworks determined and disclosed?
en.A: The auditing standards are presumed to be those of Country B, and the auditor must omit any reference to Country A's accounting principles.
en.B: The auditing standards are presumed to be those of Switzerland, and cross-border translations require no reference to the country of origin's accounting principles.
en.C: Under Paragraph 12, unless otherwise stated, the national auditing standards or practices followed are presumed to be those of the country indicated by the auditor's address (Country A); and under Paragraph 22, when reporting on financial statements distributed extensively outside the country of origin or prepared specifically for use in another country (e.g., translated into another country's language and currency in cross-border financing), the auditor must refer to the accounting principles of the country of origin where prepared (Country A) and consider whether appropriate disclosure has been made in the statements.
en.D: Both auditing standards and accounting principles are presumed to be those of Country B without any explanatory disclosure.
en.True answer: Under Paragraph 12, unless otherwise stated, the national auditing standards or practices followed are presumed to be those of the country indicated by the auditor's address (Country A); and under Paragraph 22, when reporting on financial statements distributed extensively outside the country of origin or prepared specifically for use in another country (e.g., translated into another country's language and currency in cross-border financing), the auditor must refer to the accounting principles of the country of origin where prepared (Country A) and consider whether appropriate disclosure has been made in the statements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 12 & Par. 22 (Par. 12: 'Unless otherwise stated, the national auditing standards or practices followed are presumed to be those of the country indicated by the auditor's address'; Par. 22: when reporting on financial statements distributed extensively outside the country of origin or prepared specifically for use in another country—such as translated into the language and currency of another country in cross-border financing—the auditor recommends/considers referring to the accounting principles of the country of origin where prepared and considers whether appropriate disclosure has been made).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 41–44 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, how do the auditor's duties differ when a scope limitation is (1) imposed by the institution's proposed engagement terms (which would require a disclaimer of opinion) versus (2) imposed by external circumstances (such as appointment after physical inventory count or inadequate accounting records)?
en.A: (1) The auditor must accept every engagement with contractual scope restrictions and issue a clean opinion; (2) when appointed after inventory count, the auditor must immediately issue an adverse opinion without attempting alternative procedures.
en.B: (1) Contractual scope limitations are acceptable if the client pays double the standard audit fee; (2) alternative audit procedures are prohibited under ASIFI 2.
en.C: Both types of scope limitations are resolved by adding an Emphasis of Matter paragraph after the opinion.
en.D: (1) When a proposed engagement contains a limitation that the auditor believes would require a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor would usually NOT accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement unless required by statute (and a statutory auditor would not accept it where the limitation infringes statutory duties); (2) when a scope limitation is imposed by circumstances (e.g., late appointment preventing inventory observation or inadequate records), the auditor should attempt to carry out reasonable alternative procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support an unqualified opinion (and if a qualified or disclaimer opinion is still required, describe the limitation and indicate possible adjustments).
en.True answer: (1) When a proposed engagement contains a limitation that the auditor believes would require a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor would usually NOT accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement unless required by statute (and a statutory auditor would not accept it where the limitation infringes statutory duties); (2) when a scope limitation is imposed by circumstances (e.g., late appointment preventing inventory observation or inadequate records), the auditor should attempt to carry out reasonable alternative procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support an unqualified opinion (and if a qualified or disclaimer opinion is still required, describe the limitation and indicate possible adjustments).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 41–43 (Par. 41: when limitation in terms of proposed engagement is such that auditor believes need to express disclaimer of opinion exists, auditor would usually not accept such limited engagement as an audit engagement unless required by statute, and statutory auditor would not accept where limitation infringes statutory duties; Par. 42: when imposed by circumstances [timing of appointment, inadequate records, inability to perform desirable procedure], auditor attempts reasonable alternative procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence supporting an unqualified opinion; Par. 43: if qualified or disclaimer opinion is required, describe limitation and indicate possible adjustments).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question:
Under Paragraphs 8–11 and 23–24 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, evaluate two audit reporting scenarios:
(1) An Islamic bank's management prepares the financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2025 and signs/approves them on 18 March 2026. The auditor finishes all audit procedures on 14 March 2026 and dates the auditor's report 14 March 2026.
(2) In the opening (introductory) paragraph, the auditor states that management is responsible for preparing the financial statements, but omits mentioning management's undertaking to operate in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles.
Which evaluation is completely accurate?
en.A: Both (1) and (2) violate ASIFI 2: under Par. 24, the auditor must NOT date the report earlier than the date on which the financial statements are signed or approved by management (18 March 2026, not 14 March 2026); and under Par. 9 & Par. 11, the opening paragraph MUST include a statement that BOTH the financial statements AND the financial institution's undertaking to operate in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles are the responsibility of management.
en.B: Both (1) and (2) are compliant: dating the report on fieldwork completion (14 March) is required, and management's Shari'a undertaking is mentioned only in the opinion paragraph.
en.C: (1) Is compliant, whereas (2) violates Paragraph 9.
en.D: (1) Violates Paragraph 24, whereas (2) is compliant because Shari'a compliance is exclusively the auditor's responsibility.
en.True answer: Both (1) and (2) violate ASIFI 2: under Par. 24, the auditor must NOT date the report earlier than the date on which the financial statements are signed or approved by management (18 March 2026, not 14 March 2026); and under Par. 9 & Par. 11, the opening paragraph MUST include a statement that BOTH the financial statements AND the financial institution's undertaking to operate in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles are the responsibility of management.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 9, Par. 11 & Par. 23–24 (Par. 24: 'Since the auditor's responsibility is to report on the financial statements as prepared and presented by management, the auditor should not date the report earlier than the date on which the financial statements are signed or approved by management' [18 March 2026]; Par. 9 & Par. 11: the opening paragraph must include a statement that the financial statements AND the financial institution's undertaking to operate in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles are the responsibility of the financial institution's management).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 30–35 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, which four situations may lead an auditor to add an 'Emphasis of Matter' paragraph WITHOUT qualifying the audit opinion?
en.A: (1) Fraudulent misstatement of revenue by 40%, (2) refusal by management to provide any accounting records, (3) intentional violation of Shari'a Board Fatwas across all Mudaraba pools, and (4) complete omission of the cash flow statement.
en.B: (1) A material matter regarding a going concern problem (Par. 31), (2) a significant uncertainty (other than a going concern problem) whose resolution depends on future events and which may affect the financial statements (Par. 32), (3) a material inconsistency in other information in a document containing audited financial statements where the institution refuses to make a necessary amendment (Par. 35), and (4) additional statutory reporting responsibilities (Par. 35).
en.C: (1) Minor clerical typos in branch addresses, (2) routine audit fee negotiations, (3) normal quarterly dividend declarations, and (4) staff training schedules.
en.D: Emphasis of Matter paragraphs are permitted solely for going concern problems and are prohibited for legal uncertainties or other information inconsistencies.
en.True answer: (1) A material matter regarding a going concern problem (Par. 31), (2) a significant uncertainty (other than a going concern problem) whose resolution depends on future events and which may affect the financial statements (Par. 32), (3) a material inconsistency in other information in a document containing audited financial statements where the institution refuses to make a necessary amendment (Par. 35), and (4) additional statutory reporting responsibilities (Par. 35).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2, Par. 30–35 (Enumerates the specific uses of an emphasis of matter paragraph that does not affect the opinion: (1) Par. 31: material matter regarding a going concern problem; (2) Par. 32: significant uncertainty [other than going concern] dependent on future events; (3) Par. 35: necessary amendment to other information in a document containing audited financial statements when the institution refuses to amend; and (4) Par. 35: additional statutory reporting responsibilities).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question:
During the statutory audit of Al-Barakah Islamic Bank for the year ended 31 December 2025, the external auditor encounters four distinct reporting issues:
(1) The bank entered into commodity financing agreements restricting future cash dividends to post-year-end earnings, and management refused to disclose this restriction in the notes; the auditor concludes the omission is material but not pervasive, and drafts a qualified opinion stating: 'In our opinion, except for the omission of the information included in the preceding paragraph, the financial statements give a true and fair view...'
(2) For a separate major Murabaha portfolio representing 65% of total assets, a system crash destroyed all digital and physical records, and no alternative procedures could confirm recoverability; because the scope limitation is so material and pervasive that the auditor cannot form an opinion, the auditor drafts a disclaimer of opinion beginning with 'We were engaged to audit...' and omits the sentence describing the auditor's responsibility.
(3) In the Chairman's Statement accompanying the audited financial statements in the Annual Report, the Chairman claims net profit grew by 35% (whereas audited net profit actually declined by 5%), and management refuses to amend the Chairman's Statement; the auditor concludes the financial statements themselves are fairly presented and plans to add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph after the opinion paragraph describing the material inconsistency.
(4) Management refuses to record AAOIFI-mandated Zakah and investment-account profit adjustments across the entire bank, resulting in a material and pervasive distortion that makes the financial statements misleading as a whole; the auditor proposes issuing an 'except for' qualified opinion.
According to AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Non-compliant—inadequate disclosure always requires an adverse opinion; (2) Non-compliant—disclaimer reports must retain the auditor responsibility sentence; (3) Non-compliant—Chairman's Statement errors require an adverse opinion on the financial statements; (4) Compliant—qualified opinion suffices.
en.B: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant—matches Par. 45 & Par. 46 ('Disagreement on accounting policies — inadequate disclosure — qualified opinion', p. 838); (2) Compliant—matches Par. 38 & Par. 44 ('Limitation on scope — disclaimer of opinion', p. 836), which uses 'We were engaged to audit...' and explicitly omits the auditor responsibility sentence; (3) Compliant—matches Par. 35, which provides for adding an emphasis of matter paragraph (preferably after the opinion paragraph) when an amendment is necessary to other information in a document containing audited financial statements and the institution refuses to amend; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 39, which mandates expressing an ADVERSE opinion when the effect of a disagreement is so material and pervasive that a qualification is inadequate to disclose the misleading or incomplete nature of the financial statements.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Compliant—matches Par. 45 & Par. 46 ('Disagreement on accounting policies — inadequate disclosure — qualified opinion', p. 838); (2) Compliant—matches Par. 38 & Par. 44 ('Limitation on scope — disclaimer of opinion', p. 836), which uses 'We were engaged to audit...' and explicitly omits the auditor responsibility sentence; (3) Compliant—matches Par. 35, which provides for adding an emphasis of matter paragraph (preferably after the opinion paragraph) when an amendment is necessary to other information in a document containing audited financial statements and the institution refuses to amend; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 39, which mandates expressing an ADVERSE opinion when the effect of a disagreement is so material and pervasive that a qualification is inadequate to disclose the misleading or incomplete nature of the financial statements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 45 & Par. 46 (p. 838) prescribe the exact qualified opinion wording 'except for the omission of the information included in the preceding paragraph' when a material non-pervasive disclosure is omitted; (2) Par. 38 & Par. 44 (p. 836) require a disclaimer of opinion for a material and pervasive scope limitation, opening with 'We were engaged to audit...' and omitting the auditor responsibility sentence; (3) Par. 35 authorizes an emphasis of matter paragraph (preferably after the opinion paragraph) when other information in a document containing audited financial statements requires amendment and the institution refuses; (4) Par. 39 mandates an ADVERSE opinion when a disagreement is so material and pervasive that a qualification is inadequate.

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 02: Auditor’s Report
en.Question:
Evaluate the following four audit engagement and reporting scenarios under AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 2:
(1) A prospective Islamic finance client proposes engagement terms prohibiting the external auditor from auditing the institution's compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, and the auditor determines that this limitation would require a disclaimer of opinion; the auditor accepts the engagement anyway in order to issue a disclaimer at year-end (there is no statutory requirement to accept).
(2) In another engagement, the auditor is appointed after year-end physical inventory count for a Salam commodity portfolio; by performing reasonable alternative audit procedures, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence confirming physical existence and valuation, and issues an unqualified opinion.
(3) An Islamic bank faces a material going concern uncertainty that is adequately disclosed in Note 28 to the financial statements, alongside multiple other major unresolved uncertainties affecting core asset recoverability and regulatory capital; the auditor considers whether to add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph or, given the extreme multiple uncertainties, express a disclaimer of opinion.
(4) In an unqualified audit report on a bank that omitted depreciation of USD 80,000 on equipment (a material, non-pervasive disagreement), the auditor issues a qualified opinion but omits quantifying the USD 80,000 effect even though quantification is entirely practicable.
According to ASIFI No. 2, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—auditors should accept restricted engagements to issue disclaimers; (2) Non-compliant—late appointment after inventory count always requires a qualified opinion; (3) Non-compliant—multiple uncertainties can never lead to a disclaimer; (4) Compliant—quantification is optional even when practicable.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 41, when a limitation in the terms of a proposed engagement (such as barring Shari'a compliance audit) is such that the auditor believes a disclaimer of opinion would be needed, the auditor would usually NOT accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement unless required by statute; (2) Compliant—under Par. 42, when a scope limitation is imposed by circumstances (such as appointment timing preventing inventory observation), the auditor should attempt reasonable alternative procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence supporting an unqualified opinion; (3) Compliant—under Par. 31 & Par. 34, while an emphasis of matter paragraph is usually adequate for a going concern problem or significant uncertainty, in extreme cases involving multiple uncertainties significant to the financial statements, the auditor may consider it appropriate to express a disclaimer of opinion; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 40, which mandates that whenever the auditor expresses an opinion other than unqualified, a clear description of substantive reasons AND, unless impracticable, a quantification of the possible effect(s) on the financial statements MUST be included.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—under Par. 41, when a limitation in the terms of a proposed engagement (such as barring Shari'a compliance audit) is such that the auditor believes a disclaimer of opinion would be needed, the auditor would usually NOT accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement unless required by statute; (2) Compliant—under Par. 42, when a scope limitation is imposed by circumstances (such as appointment timing preventing inventory observation), the auditor should attempt reasonable alternative procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence supporting an unqualified opinion; (3) Compliant—under Par. 31 & Par. 34, while an emphasis of matter paragraph is usually adequate for a going concern problem or significant uncertainty, in extreme cases involving multiple uncertainties significant to the financial statements, the auditor may consider it appropriate to express a disclaimer of opinion; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 40, which mandates that whenever the auditor expresses an opinion other than unqualified, a clear description of substantive reasons AND, unless impracticable, a quantification of the possible effect(s) on the financial statements MUST be included.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 2 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 41 states that when a limitation in proposed engagement terms (specifically citing not auditing compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles) would require a disclaimer of opinion, the auditor would usually NOT accept such a limited engagement as an audit engagement unless required by statute; (2) Par. 42 directs the auditor, when facing a scope limitation imposed by circumstances (such as appointment timing preventing physical inventory count observation), to attempt reasonable alternative procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence supporting an unqualified opinion; (3) Par. 31 & Par. 34 allow expressing a disclaimer of opinion instead of an emphasis of matter paragraph in extreme cases involving multiple uncertainties significant to the financial statements; (4) Par. 40 mandates quantifying the possible effect(s) on the financial statements unless impracticable whenever an opinion other than unqualified is expressed.

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the main points, adoption date, and effective date of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3 ('Terms of Audit Engagement')?
en.A: It governs external credit ratings of Islamic banks, was adopted in May 2024, and is effective from 1 January 2026.
en.B: It establishes standards and provides guidance on appointing an auditor for an IFI, focusing on (a) agreeing the terms of the engagement with the client and (b) the auditor's response to a client request to change engagement terms to one providing a lower level of assurance; it was adopted on 15–16 June 1997 (10–11 Safar 1418 A.H.) and became effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1419 A.H. or 1 January 1999 A.D.
en.C: It applies exclusively to internal Shari'ah audit charters and became effective retroactively on 1 January 1995.
en.D: It prohibits issuing audit engagement letters whenever audit objectives are established by national law.
en.True answer: It establishes standards and provides guidance on appointing an auditor for an IFI, focusing on (a) agreeing the terms of the engagement with the client and (b) the auditor's response to a client request to change engagement terms to one providing a lower level of assurance; it was adopted on 15–16 June 1997 (10–11 Safar 1418 A.H.) and became effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1419 A.H. or 1 January 1999 A.D.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 1–4, Effective Date & Adoption (Par. 1: main points are (a) agreeing the terms of the engagement with the Islamic financial institution [client], and (b) the auditor's response to a request by a client to change the terms of an engagement to one that provides a lower level of assurance; Par. 4: even where objectives/scope are established by law, engagement letters may still be informative; Effective Date: financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1419 A.H. or 1 January 1999 A.D.; Adoption: 10–11 Safar 1418 A.H. / 15–16 June 1997 A.D.).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 3–6 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, when should an audit engagement letter preferably be sent, what four core matters does it document and confirm, and how should non-audit services (such as tax, accounting, or management advisory services) be handled?
en.A: Preferably before the commencement of the engagement to avoid misunderstandings; it documents and confirms (1) the auditor's acceptance of the appointment, (2) the objectives and scope of the audit, (3) the extent of the auditor's responsibilities to the client, and (4) the form of any reports to be provided; and when other services such as tax, accounting, or management advisory services are provided, separate letters may be appropriate to distinguish clearly the statutory audit from other services.
en.B: After the audit opinion is published; it confirms only the audit fee schedule; and tax and management advisory services must always be merged into the statutory audit engagement letter.
en.C: Preferably midway through fieldwork; it documents only management's tax liability; and non-audit services require no written contract.
en.D: Only when requested by external banking regulators; it documents board remuneration; and separate letters for related services are prohibited.
en.True answer: Preferably before the commencement of the engagement to avoid misunderstandings; it documents and confirms (1) the auditor's acceptance of the appointment, (2) the objectives and scope of the audit, (3) the extent of the auditor's responsibilities to the client, and (4) the form of any reports to be provided; and when other services such as tax, accounting, or management advisory services are provided, separate letters may be appropriate to distinguish clearly the statutory audit from other services.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 3, Par. 5 & Par. 6 (Par. 3: when other services such as tax, accounting, or management advisory services are to be provided, separate letters may be appropriate to distinguish clearly the statutory audit from other services; Par. 5: auditor should send an engagement letter, preferably before the commencement of the engagement, to help in avoiding misunderstandings; Par. 6: documents and confirms (1) auditor's acceptance of the appointment, (2) objectives and scope of the audit, (3) extent of auditor's responsibilities to client, and (4) form of any reports to be provided).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 7–10 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, what is the auditor's specific responsibility with respect to the fatwas, rulings, and guidelines issued by the Islamic financial institution's Shari'a Supervisory Board (SSB)?
en.A: The auditor drafts and issues new Shari'a fatwas on behalf of the institution's SSB.
en.B: The auditor evaluates whether the SSB's fatwas are commercially profitable and modifies any fatwa that reduces net income.
en.C: The auditor is responsible for expressing an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared in accordance with the fatwas, rulings, and guidelines issued by the SSB (alongside AAOIFI accounting standards, national standards, and legislation) and attesting as to whether management has adhered to those fatwas, rulings, and guidelines—which management must provide in full to the auditor.
en.D: The auditor is prohibited from reviewing SSB fatwas or rulings during a financial statement audit.
en.True answer: The auditor is responsible for expressing an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared in accordance with the fatwas, rulings, and guidelines issued by the SSB (alongside AAOIFI accounting standards, national standards, and legislation) and attesting as to whether management has adhered to those fatwas, rulings, and guidelines—which management must provide in full to the auditor.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 7–10 (Par. 7: audit objective includes expressing an opinion as to whether financial statements are prepared in accordance with fatwas, rulings, and guidelines issued by the SSB of the IFI; Par. 9: 'The auditor is responsible for attesting as to whether the management has adhered to the fatwas, rulings and guidelines issued by the Shari'a supervisory board of the Islamic financial institution'; Par. 10: management should provide the auditor with all fatwas, rulings, and guidelines issued by its SSB and other relevant documents e.g. SSB reports).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 11 and 13–16 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which provisions must be addressed in the engagement letter regarding access to information, written confirmations from management, additional reports to management, fees, and client acknowledgment?
en.A: The engagement letter may restrict auditor access to sensitive Sukuk contracts and omit any mention of fee billing arrangements.
