en.B: Oral assurances from management suffice without written confirmation, and the client need not acknowledge receipt of the engagement letter.
en.C: The auditor is prohibited from sending a management letter on internal control weaknesses.
en.D: The engagement letter must state that the auditor must have unrestricted access to whatever records, documentation, and information are requested; state expectations of receiving written confirmation from management concerning representations made (including oral representations); refer to other reports/communications to be issued (such as a report to management on material weaknesses in accounting and internal control systems); state the basis on which fees are computed and billing arrangements; and request the client to confirm the terms by acknowledging receipt of the engagement letter.
en.True answer: The engagement letter must state that the auditor must have unrestricted access to whatever records, documentation, and information are requested; state expectations of receiving written confirmation from management concerning representations made (including oral representations); refer to other reports/communications to be issued (such as a report to management on material weaknesses in accounting and internal control systems); state the basis on which fees are computed and billing arrangements; and request the client to confirm the terms by acknowledging receipt of the engagement letter.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 11 & Par. 13–16 (Par. 11 & 14: unrestricted access to requested records/documentation/information and written confirmation of representations made in connection with the audit; Par. 13: refer to other reports/communications such as a report to management on material weaknesses in or observations on accounting and internal control systems; Par. 15: basis on which fees are computed and billing arrangements; Par. 16: request client to confirm terms by acknowledging receipt of the engagement letter).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraph 18 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, when the auditor of a parent Islamic financial institution is also the auditor of its subsidiary, branch, or division (component), which six factors influence the decision on whether to send a separate engagement letter to the component?
en.A: (1) Who appoints the auditor of the component, (2) whether a separate audit report is to be issued on the component, (3) legal requirements, (4) the extent of any work performed by other auditors, (5) degree of ownership by the parent, and (6) degree of independence of the component's management.
en.B: (1) Geographic distance from headquarters, (2) number of ATM machines, (3) branch marketing budget, (4) retail deposit interest rates, (5) employee turnover rate, and (6) software vendor brand.
en.C: Separate engagement letters are always mandatory for every single domestic branch regardless of ownership or legal requirements.
en.D: Separate engagement letters are strictly prohibited whenever the parent owns more than 50% of the subsidiary.
en.True answer: (1) Who appoints the auditor of the component, (2) whether a separate audit report is to be issued on the component, (3) legal requirements, (4) the extent of any work performed by other auditors, (5) degree of ownership by the parent, and (6) degree of independence of the component's management.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 18 (Lists the six factors influencing whether to send a separate engagement letter to a subsidiary, branch, or division: (1) who appoints the auditor of the component; (2) whether a separate audit report is to be issued on the component; (3) legal requirements; (4) the extent of any work performed by other auditors; (5) degree of ownership by parent; and (6) degree of independence of the component's management).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 19–20 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, on recurring audits, must the auditor send a new engagement letter each period, and which five factors may make it appropriate to send a new letter?
en.A: A brand-new engagement letter must be sent every single year without exception, even when no terms, management, or business circumstances have changed.
en.B: The auditor may decide NOT to send a new engagement letter each period; however, five factors may make it appropriate to send a new letter: (1) any indication that the client misunderstands the objective and scope of the audit, (2) any revised or special terms of the engagement, (3) a recent change of senior management, equity holders, members of the board of directors, or in ownership (such as in a new holding IFI), (4) a significant change in nature or size of the client's business, and (5) legal requirements.
en.C: A new engagement letter is required only when the audit firm changes its office telephone number.
en.D: Recurring audits are exempt from any written engagement terms after the first year.
en.True answer: The auditor may decide NOT to send a new engagement letter each period; however, five factors may make it appropriate to send a new letter: (1) any indication that the client misunderstands the objective and scope of the audit, (2) any revised or special terms of the engagement, (3) a recent change of senior management, equity holders, members of the board of directors, or in ownership (such as in a new holding IFI), (4) a significant change in nature or size of the client's business, and (5) legal requirements.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 19–20 (Par. 20: 'The auditor may decide not to send a new engagement letter each period. However, the following factors may make it appropriate to send a new letter: (1) Any indication that the client misunderstands the objective and scope of the audit; (2) Any revised or special terms of the engagement; (3) A recent change of senior management, equity holders, members of the board of directors or in ownership, such as in a new holding Islamic financial institution; (4) A significant change in nature or size of the client's business; (5) Legal requirements').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 22–23 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which circumstances ordinarily constitute a reasonable basis for a client requesting a change in engagement terms prior to completion, versus what is NOT considered reasonable?
en.A: A request driven by incomplete or incorrect information provided by the client is reasonable, whereas a genuine misunderstanding of the service originally requested is unreasonable.
en.B: Any client request to downgrade an audit to a review is automatically reasonable as long as the audit fee is paid in full.
en.C: A change in circumstances affecting the IFI's requirements or a misunderstanding concerning the nature of the service originally requested would ordinarily be considered a reasonable basis; in contrast, a request for a change is NOT considered reasonable if it appears that the change relates to information provided by the client that is incorrect, incomplete, or otherwise unsatisfactory.
en.D: Neither a change in circumstances nor a misunderstanding ever justifies changing engagement terms.
en.True answer: A change in circumstances affecting the IFI's requirements or a misunderstanding concerning the nature of the service originally requested would ordinarily be considered a reasonable basis; in contrast, a request for a change is NOT considered reasonable if it appears that the change relates to information provided by the client that is incorrect, incomplete, or otherwise unsatisfactory.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 22–23 (Par. 23: 'A change in circumstances that affects the Islamic financial institution's requirements or a misunderstanding concerning the nature of the service originally requested would ordinarily be considered a reasonable basis for the client requesting a change in the terms of engagement. In contrast, a request for a change by the client would not be considered reasonable if it appeared that the change related to information provided by the client that is incorrect, incomplete or otherwise unsatisfactory').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraph 25 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, when an auditor agrees with reasonable justification to change an audit engagement to a lower-assurance engagement, what two items must the revised report NOT refer to (and what is the sole exception)?
en.A: The revised report must prominently describe the original audit engagement and list every audit procedure performed before the change.
en.B: The revised report must omit the date and auditor's signature.
en.C: The revised report must include a disclaimer of opinion on the original audit.
en.D: To avoid confusing the reader, the revised report must NOT include reference to (1) the original engagement or (2) any procedures that may have been performed in the original engagement—EXCEPT where the engagement is changed to an engagement to undertake agreed-upon procedures, in which case reference to the procedures performed is a normal part of the report.
en.True answer: To avoid confusing the reader, the revised report must NOT include reference to (1) the original engagement or (2) any procedures that may have been performed in the original engagement—EXCEPT where the engagement is changed to an engagement to undertake agreed-upon procedures, in which case reference to the procedures performed is a normal part of the report.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 25 ('In order to avoid confusing the reader, the report would not include reference to: • The original engagement; or • Any procedures that may have been performed in the original engagement, except where the engagement is changed to an engagement to undertake agreed-upon procedures and thus reference to the procedures performed is a normal part of the report').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 27–28 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, what must the auditor do if a client requests changing an audit engagement to a review engagement without reasonable justification (e.g., to avoid a qualified or disclaimer opinion on unverified receivables) and refuses to permit the auditor to continue the original audit?
en.A: The auditor must NOT agree to the change, should withdraw from the engagement, and should consider whether there is any obligation (either contractual or otherwise) to report to other parties, such as the board of directors or equity holders, the circumstances necessitating the withdrawal.
en.B: The auditor must accept the change to a review engagement and issue a clean review conclusion without mentioning the unverified receivables.
en.C: The auditor must remain in the engagement and issue an unqualified audit opinion based solely on management's oral assurances.
en.D: The auditor must withdraw quietly and is strictly barred from ever reporting the withdrawal circumstances to the board of directors or equity holders.
en.True answer: The auditor must NOT agree to the change, should withdraw from the engagement, and should consider whether there is any obligation (either contractual or otherwise) to report to other parties, such as the board of directors or equity holders, the circumstances necessitating the withdrawal.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 27–28 (Par. 27: auditor should not agree to change of terms where there is no reasonable justification, e.g., unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence on receivables and client asks to change to a review engagement to avoid a qualified or disclaimer opinion; Par. 28: 'If the auditor is unable to agree to a change of the terms of engagement and is not permitted to continue the original engagement, the auditor should withdraw and consider whether there is any obligation, either contractual or otherwise, to report to other parties, such as the board of directors or equity holders, the circumstances necessitating the withdrawal').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: In Appendix (A) ('Example of an Audit Engagement Letter', pp. 854–855) of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which four statutory matters must the auditor consider and report on if not satisfied, and what right does the auditor have regarding the client's Shari'a Supervisory Board?
en.A: The auditor checks only branch profitability and is barred from ever speaking directly with the client's Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
en.B: The auditor considers and reports on any of the following four matters if not satisfied: (1) whether proper accounting records have been kept, (2) whether the statement of financial position and income statement are in agreement with the accounting records, (3) whether all information and explanations deemed necessary for the audit have been obtained, and (4) whether the information in the directors' report is consistent with that in the audited financial statements; and the auditor has the right to seek independent consultation with the client's Shari'a Supervisory Board.
en.C: The auditor reports only on employee attendance records and must obtain CEO approval before contacting the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
en.D: The auditor is prohibited from reviewing the directors' report or consulting the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
en.True answer: The auditor considers and reports on any of the following four matters if not satisfied: (1) whether proper accounting records have been kept, (2) whether the statement of financial position and income statement are in agreement with the accounting records, (3) whether all information and explanations deemed necessary for the audit have been obtained, and (4) whether the information in the directors' report is consistent with that in the audited financial statements; and the auditor has the right to seek independent consultation with the client's Shari'a Supervisory Board.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Appendix (A) (pp. 854–855) (Lists the four statutory matters to consider and report on if not satisfied: (1) whether proper accounting records have been kept; (2) whether statement of financial position and income statement are in agreement with accounting records; (3) whether all information and explanations necessary for the audit have been obtained; and (4) whether information in the directors' report is consistent with the audited financial statements; and states on p. 855: 'We understand that we have the right to seek independent consultation with the Shari'a supervisory board').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraph 12 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, what is the auditor's responsibility regarding the detection of fraud, instances of non-compliance, or errors, and why is there an unavoidable risk that some material misstatement may remain undetected?
en.A: The auditor guarantees 100% detection of every fraud or irregularity committed anywhere in the institution.
en.B: The auditor ignores fraud and non-compliance completely, focusing solely on arithmetic totals.
en.C: The auditor must endeavor to plan the audit so that he has a reasonable expectation of detecting material misstatement in the financial statements or accounting records resulting from fraud, instances of non-compliance, or errors; however, due to the test nature and other inherent limitations of an audit, together with the inherent limitations of any accounting and internal control system, there is an unavoidable risk that even some material misstatement may remain undetected.
en.D: Undetected material misstatements occur solely because auditors are prohibited from testing internal controls.
en.True answer: The auditor must endeavor to plan the audit so that he has a reasonable expectation of detecting material misstatement in the financial statements or accounting records resulting from fraud, instances of non-compliance, or errors; however, due to the test nature and other inherent limitations of an audit, together with the inherent limitations of any accounting and internal control system, there is an unavoidable risk that even some material misstatement may remain undetected.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 12 ('The auditor shall endeavour to plan his audit so that he has a reasonable expectation of detecting material misstatement in the financial statements or accounting records resulting from fraud, instances of non-compliance or errors which may exist. • Due to the test nature and other inherent limitations of an audit, together with the inherent limitation of any accounting and internal control system, there is an unavoidable risk that even some material misstatement may remain undetected').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraph 17 and Appendix (B) ('Example of Audit Re-Engagement Letter', pp. 857–858) of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which matters are typically covered in a re-engagement letter for a recurring audit?
en.A: A completely new audit methodology overriding all AAOIFI standards and removing fee billing terms.
en.B: A waiver of management's responsibility for Shari'ah compliance and internal control.
en.C: A confidential agreement exempting the client from providing SSB Fatwas in future years.
en.D: Confirmation of re-appointment on the same terms as set out in the original engagement letter, the updated fee estimate for the current year (plus out-of-pocket expenses and advance/progress payment arrangements), and a request for the client to sign and return the acknowledgment copy.
en.True answer: Confirmation of re-appointment on the same terms as set out in the original engagement letter, the updated fee estimate for the current year (plus out-of-pocket expenses and advance/progress payment arrangements), and a request for the client to sign and return the acknowledgment copy.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Appendix (B) 'Example of Audit Re-Engagement Letter' (pp. 857–858) (Confirms re-appointment on the same terms as set out in the original letter of engagement, states the estimated fee for the current financial year plus out-of-pocket expenses and advance/progress billing arrangements, and requests client signature/acknowledgment).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question:
Under Paragraphs 21–28 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, evaluate two client requests to change an audit engagement before completion:
• Request X: An Islamic finance company originally requested a statutory audit by mistake when its board actually needed an agreed-upon procedures engagement on a specific Sukuk asset pool, and all client records are complete and transparent.
• Request Y: During a statutory audit, the auditor discovers that a major Murabaha receivables portfolio lacks valid contracts and customer confirmations; management asks the auditor to convert the engagement into a review engagement so that a qualified or disclaimer opinion is avoided.
How must the auditor respond to Request X and Request Y?
en.A: For Request X, the auditor may accept the change because a misunderstanding of the service originally requested is a reasonable basis (Par. 23), agree on new terms (Par. 26), and issue an agreed-upon procedures report that omits reference to the original engagement while referring to the agreed-upon procedures performed (Par. 25); for Request Y, the auditor MUST NOT agree to the change because avoiding a qualified/disclaimer opinion on unverified receivables lacks reasonable justification (Par. 27), and if not permitted to continue the audit, must withdraw and consider reporting obligations to the board or equity holders (Par. 28).
en.B: Both Request X and Request Y must be accepted as long as the client signs a revised fee addendum.
en.C: Both Request X and Request Y must be rejected, and the auditor must withdraw from both engagements immediately.
en.D: For Request X, the revised report must describe the original audit engagement in full; for Request Y, the auditor should issue a clean review report.
en.True answer: For Request X, the auditor may accept the change because a misunderstanding of the service originally requested is a reasonable basis (Par. 23), agree on new terms (Par. 26), and issue an agreed-upon procedures report that omits reference to the original engagement while referring to the agreed-upon procedures performed (Par. 25); for Request Y, the auditor MUST NOT agree to the change because avoiding a qualified/disclaimer opinion on unverified receivables lacks reasonable justification (Par. 27), and if not permitted to continue the audit, must withdraw and consider reporting obligations to the board or equity holders (Par. 28).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 23, Par. 25, Par. 27 & Par. 28 (Par. 23 & 25: Request X reflects a genuine misunderstanding of the service originally requested—a reasonable basis—and because the revised engagement is agreed-upon procedures, the report omits reference to the original engagement while normally referring to the agreed-upon procedures performed; Par. 27 & 28: Request Y is the exact example in Par. 27 of an unjustified request to avoid a qualified/disclaimer opinion on receivables, requiring the auditor to refuse and withdraw if barred from continuing the audit).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: An external audit firm is appointed as auditor of both a parent Islamic bank and its wholly-owned Islamic leasing subsidiary, and is also entering its third recurring audit year for the parent bank. Under Paragraphs 18–20 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which combination of factors governs (1) whether to send a separate engagement letter to the leasing subsidiary and (2) whether to send a new engagement letter for the parent bank's recurring audit?
en.A: (1) Only the subsidiary's asset size matters; (2) a new engagement letter is required every year even when nothing has changed.
en.B: (1) Sending a separate engagement letter to the subsidiary depends on six factors: who appoints the component's auditor, whether a separate audit report is issued on the component, legal requirements, extent of work performed by other auditors, degree of ownership by parent, and degree of independence of the component's management (Par. 18); (2) for the parent's recurring audit, a new letter is not required every period unless triggered by factors such as client misunderstanding of audit objective/scope, revised/special terms, recent change in senior management/equity holders/board/ownership, significant change in nature/size of business, or legal requirements (Par. 20).
en.C: (1) Separate engagement letters for subsidiaries are prohibited; (2) recurring audits never require a new engagement letter even after a complete change of ownership and board of directors.
en.D: (1) Only the parent CEO decides whether the subsidiary gets a separate letter; (2) a new engagement letter is triggered solely by inflation adjustments to audit fees.
en.True answer: (1) Sending a separate engagement letter to the subsidiary depends on six factors: who appoints the component's auditor, whether a separate audit report is issued on the component, legal requirements, extent of work performed by other auditors, degree of ownership by parent, and degree of independence of the component's management (Par. 18); (2) for the parent's recurring audit, a new letter is not required every period unless triggered by factors such as client misunderstanding of audit objective/scope, revised/special terms, recent change in senior management/equity holders/board/ownership, significant change in nature/size of business, or legal requirements (Par. 20).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 18–20 (Par. 18 sets the 6 factors for component engagement letters: who appoints component auditor, separate audit report, legal requirements, work by other auditors, degree of ownership by parent, degree of independence of component's management; Par. 19–20 set the 5 triggers for sending a new engagement letter on recurring audits: client misunderstanding of objective/scope, revised/special terms, recent change of senior management/equity holders/board/ownership, significant change in nature/size of business, legal requirements).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 7–14 and Appendix (A) (pp. 853–856) of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, how are governance, Shari'ah, and internal control responsibilities divided between the Islamic financial institution's management and the external auditor in the engagement letter?
en.A: The external auditor is responsible for maintaining the bank's internal control system, safeguarding assets, and issuing Shari'ah fatwas, while management only pays the audit invoice.
en.B: Management is responsible only for commercial marketing, while the external auditor prepares the financial statements and approves Zakah policies.
en.C: Management is responsible for preparing and presenting financial statements that give a true and fair view in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles (as determined by the SSB) and relevant legislation/regulations, maintaining an effective internal control system, properly recording transactions, safeguarding assets, and making available all accounting records, meeting minutes, and SSB fatwas/rulings/guidelines; whereas the auditor is responsible for auditing the financial statements to express an opinion on whether they give a true and fair view in accordance with SSB fatwas/rulings, AAOIFI accounting standards, national standards, and legislation, attesting whether management adhered to SSB fatwas/rulings, and providing a separate letter on material weaknesses in accounting and internal control systems noticed during the audit.
en.D: Both management and the external auditor share joint executive responsibility for operating the bank's daily treasury desk.
en.True answer: Management is responsible for preparing and presenting financial statements that give a true and fair view in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles (as determined by the SSB) and relevant legislation/regulations, maintaining an effective internal control system, properly recording transactions, safeguarding assets, and making available all accounting records, meeting minutes, and SSB fatwas/rulings/guidelines; whereas the auditor is responsible for auditing the financial statements to express an opinion on whether they give a true and fair view in accordance with SSB fatwas/rulings, AAOIFI accounting standards, national standards, and legislation, attesting whether management adhered to SSB fatwas/rulings, and providing a separate letter on material weaknesses in accounting and internal control systems noticed during the audit.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 7–14 & Appendix (A) (pp. 853–855) (Clearly separates management's responsibility for financial statements, Shari'a undertaking, internal controls, proper accounting records, safeguarding assets, and providing all records/minutes/SSB fatwas from the auditor's responsibility to express an opinion on true and fair view, attest adherence to SSB fatwas/rulings/guidelines, and report material weaknesses in accounting/internal control systems).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraph 12 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which of the following accurately synthesizes the relationship between ASIFIs, International Standards on Auditing (ISAs), national standards, internal control assessment, and audit evidence in defining the scope of an audit?
en.A: National standards and ISAs always override ASIFIs even when they contradict Shari'a Rules and Principles, and audit procedures remain identical regardless of internal control quality.
en.B: The auditor need not obtain an understanding of the accounting system if management provides an annual representation letter.
en.C: Because audit evidence is conclusive rather than persuasive, there is zero risk that any material misstatement could remain undetected.
en.D: The audit is conducted in accordance with ASIFIs, with ISAs and national standards applying to matters not covered by ASIFIs provided they do NOT contravene Shari'a Rules and Principles; the auditor obtains an understanding of the accounting system to assess its adequacy as a basis for preparing financial statements, obtains relevant and reliable evidence sufficient to draw reasonable conclusions, and varies the nature and extent of audit procedures according to his assessment of the internal control system.
en.True answer: The audit is conducted in accordance with ASIFIs, with ISAs and national standards applying to matters not covered by ASIFIs provided they do NOT contravene Shari'a Rules and Principles; the auditor obtains an understanding of the accounting system to assess its adequacy as a basis for preparing financial statements, obtains relevant and reliable evidence sufficient to draw reasonable conclusions, and varies the nature and extent of audit procedures according to his assessment of the internal control system.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 12 (States that: (1) audit is conducted in accordance with ASIFIs, while ISAs and national standards apply to matters not covered by ASIFIs providing they do not contravene Shari'a Rules and Principles; (2) auditor obtains understanding of accounting system to assess its adequacy; (3) obtains relevant and reliable evidence sufficient to draw reasonable conclusions; and (4) nature and extent of auditor's procedures vary according to assessment of internal control system).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: In Appendix (A) ('Example of an Audit Engagement Letter', pp. 855–856) of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, how are audit fee computation, out-of-pocket expenses, payment timing, and multi-year effectiveness of the engagement letter structured?
en.A: Fees are billed as work progresses based on time occupied and expenses incurred (having regard to the degree of responsibility involved and the experience and skills required), out-of-pocket expenses are added to the estimated fee, an advance payment is requested at commencement with one or more payments on account during the work, and the engagement letter remains effective for future years unless terminated, amended, or superseded.
en.B: Fees are calculated as a contingent percentage of the bank's annual net profit, payable only if an unqualified opinion is issued, and the letter automatically expires after 12 months.
en.C: Fees are fixed identically for all banks regardless of time occupied or skill required, out-of-pocket expenses are absorbed by the auditor, and payment is due only 5 years after report issuance.
en.D: Advance payments are prohibited by ASIFI 3, and the engagement letter applies only to interim quarterly reviews.
en.True answer: Fees are billed as work progresses based on time occupied and expenses incurred (having regard to the degree of responsibility involved and the experience and skills required), out-of-pocket expenses are added to the estimated fee, an advance payment is requested at commencement with one or more payments on account during the work, and the engagement letter remains effective for future years unless terminated, amended, or superseded.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Appendix (A) (p. 856) ('Our fees, which will be billed as work progresses, are based on the time occupied and expenses incurred having regard to the degree of responsibility involved and the experience and skills required... Out of pocket expenses will be added to this fee. It is our practice to request an advance payment at the commencement of our work and one or more payments on account during the course of our work. This letter will be effective for future years unless it is terminated, amended or superseded').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 17 and 24–26 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which considerations and additional arrangements are relevant when (1) drafting an initial audit engagement letter or (2) evaluating a client's request to convert an audit engagement into a review engagement?
en.A: (1) Predecessor auditors may never be contacted in an initial audit; (2) converting an audit into a review requires no evaluation of legal or contractual implications.
en.B: (1) In an initial audit, the engagement letter may include arrangements to be made with the predecessor auditor (if any), alongside consultation arrangements with the client's SSB, involvement of other auditors/experts, and any permissible liability restrictions (Par. 17); (2) before agreeing to change an audit engagement to a related service (such as a review), the auditor must consider any legal or contractual implications of the change (Par. 24), verify reasonable justification (Par. 23), and agree on the new terms with the client (Par. 26).
en.C: (1) Consultation with the client's SSB is prohibited in engagement letters; (2) changing an audit to a review requires no new agreement on terms.
en.D: (1) Liability restrictions are mandatory in every audit letter; (2) legal and contractual implications are assessed only by the client's marketing team.
en.True answer: (1) In an initial audit, the engagement letter may include arrangements to be made with the predecessor auditor (if any), alongside consultation arrangements with the client's SSB, involvement of other auditors/experts, and any permissible liability restrictions (Par. 17); (2) before agreeing to change an audit engagement to a related service (such as a review), the auditor must consider any legal or contractual implications of the change (Par. 24), verify reasonable justification (Par. 23), and agree on the new terms with the client (Par. 26).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3, Par. 17(a)–(d), Par. 24 & Par. 26 (Par. 17: other matters in engagement letter include planning arrangements, other letters/reports, consultation with client's SSB, involvement of other auditors/experts, arrangements with predecessor auditor in case of an initial audit, and any restrictions of auditor's liability when such possibility exists; Par. 24: before agreeing to change an audit engagement to a related service [such as a review], consider any legal or contractual implications; Par. 26: agree on new terms).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question:
In March 2026, an external audit firm is preparing engagement letters and handling recurring audit updates for Al-Manar Islamic Financial Group:
(1) Al-Manar asks the audit firm to provide both the statutory financial statement audit and corporate tax compliance advisory services; the audit partner drafts a single combined letter blurring statutory audit responsibilities with tax advisory deliverables.
(2) Al-Manar's CFO requests inserting a clause in the statutory audit engagement letter restricting the auditor from inspecting confidential Sukuk SPV contracts and barring the auditor from consulting Al-Manar's Shari'ah Supervisory Board independently.
(3) For a recurring audit of Al-Manar's parent bank, a new holding Islamic financial institution acquired 60% ownership and replaced the majority of the Board of Directors and senior management during the year; the audit partner concludes that no new engagement letter is needed because the original engagement letter from four years ago states it remains effective for future years.
(4) For Al-Manar's 80%-owned Takaful subsidiary, which has an independent management team, its own statutory audit report requirement, and a separate board appointment process, the audit partner evaluates whether to issue a separate engagement letter by examining who appoints the subsidiary's auditor, whether a separate audit report is issued, legal requirements, work by other auditors, parent ownership degree, and component management independence.
According to AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—statutory audit and tax advisory must be combined in one letter; (2) Compliant—management may restrict access to Sukuk contracts and SSB consultations; (3) Compliant—ownership and board changes never require a new engagement letter; (4) Non-compliant—separate engagement letters are banned for subsidiaries.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.C: (1) Sub-optimal / non-aligned with Par. 3—when other services such as tax, accounting, or management advisory services are provided, separate letters may be appropriate to distinguish clearly the statutory audit from other services; (2) Non-compliant—violates Par. 14 (requiring unrestricted access to requested records, documentation, and information) and Appendix (A) (confirming the auditor's right to seek independent consultation with the client's SSB); (3) Non-compliant—under Par. 20, a recent change of senior management, equity holders, members of the board of directors, or ownership (such as in a new holding IFI) is an explicit factor making it appropriate to send a new engagement letter; (4) Compliant—applies all six component factors listed in Par. 18.
en.D: (1) Compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.True answer: (1) Sub-optimal / non-aligned with Par. 3—when other services such as tax, accounting, or management advisory services are provided, separate letters may be appropriate to distinguish clearly the statutory audit from other services; (2) Non-compliant—violates Par. 14 (requiring unrestricted access to requested records, documentation, and information) and Appendix (A) (confirming the auditor's right to seek independent consultation with the client's SSB); (3) Non-compliant—under Par. 20, a recent change of senior management, equity holders, members of the board of directors, or ownership (such as in a new holding IFI) is an explicit factor making it appropriate to send a new engagement letter; (4) Compliant—applies all six component factors listed in Par. 18.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3 integrates four provisions: (1) Par. 3 states that when other services such as tax, accounting, or management advisory services are provided, separate letters may be appropriate to distinguish clearly the statutory audit from other services; (2) Par. 14 mandates unrestricted access to requested records/documentation/information, and Appendix (A) (p. 855) confirms the auditor's right to seek independent consultation with the SSB; (3) Par. 20 identifies a recent change of senior management, equity holders, members of the board of directors, or in ownership (such as in a new holding IFI) as a specific factor warranting a new engagement letter; (4) Par. 18 enumerates the exact six factors governing whether to send a separate engagement letter to a component.

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 03: Terms of Audit Engagement
en.Question:
Midway through the 2026 statutory audit of Safa Islamic Bank, the auditor encounters significant missing supporting documentation and contradictory valuation records for a USD 40 million Istisna financing portfolio. Evaluate the following four actions by the bank's management and the external auditor:
(1) Because management's incomplete and unsatisfactory documentation prevents the auditor from obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence on the Istisna receivables, management asks the auditor to change the engagement from a statutory audit to a lower-assurance review engagement; the auditor agrees in order to preserve the client relationship.
(2) In a separate engagement for a different client where a genuine change in regulatory circumstances justified converting a non-statutory audit into an agreed-upon procedures engagement, the auditor issues the agreed-upon procedures report while omitting reference to the original audit engagement and describing the agreed-upon procedures performed.
(3) Returning to Safa Islamic Bank, after the auditor refuses the unjustified downgrade to a review engagement, management refuses to permit the auditor to continue the original audit; the auditor withdraws from the engagement and evaluates whether contractual or statutory obligations require reporting the withdrawal circumstances to the Board of Directors or equity holders.
(4) In another engagement where management refuses to provide written confirmation letters for oral representations made during the audit regarding off-balance-sheet guarantees, the auditor treats oral assurances as completely sufficient under ASIFI 3.
According to AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 3, which evaluation across (1)–(4) is completely accurate?
en.A: (1) Compliant—auditors should downgrade audits to reviews when client records are incomplete; (2) Non-compliant—agreed-upon procedures reports must never mention procedures performed; (3) Non-compliant—auditors may never withdraw mid-engagement; (4) Compliant—oral assurances require no written confirmation.
en.B: (1) Non-compliant; (2) Non-compliant; (3) Compliant; (4) Compliant.
en.C: (1) Compliant; (2) Compliant; (3) Non-compliant; (4) Non-compliant.
en.D: (1) Non-compliant—violates Par. 23 & Par. 27, which establish that a change request related to incorrect, incomplete, or unsatisfactory client information—or aimed at avoiding a qualified/disclaimer opinion on unverified receivables—lacks reasonable justification and MUST NOT be accepted; (2) Compliant—follows Par. 25, which requires omitting reference to the original engagement while permitting reference to the procedures performed when the revised engagement is agreed-upon procedures; (3) Compliant—follows Par. 28, which directs the auditor to withdraw when unable to agree to a change and not permitted to continue the original engagement, and to consider contractual or other obligations to report withdrawal circumstances to parties such as the board of directors or equity holders; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 11 & Par. 14, under which the auditor should obtain written representation letters from management confirming oral representations made during the audit.
en.True answer: (1) Non-compliant—violates Par. 23 & Par. 27, which establish that a change request related to incorrect, incomplete, or unsatisfactory client information—or aimed at avoiding a qualified/disclaimer opinion on unverified receivables—lacks reasonable justification and MUST NOT be accepted; (2) Compliant—follows Par. 25, which requires omitting reference to the original engagement while permitting reference to the procedures performed when the revised engagement is agreed-upon procedures; (3) Compliant—follows Par. 28, which directs the auditor to withdraw when unable to agree to a change and not permitted to continue the original engagement, and to consider contractual or other obligations to report withdrawal circumstances to parties such as the board of directors or equity holders; (4) Non-compliant—violates Par. 11 & Par. 14, under which the auditor should obtain written representation letters from management confirming oral representations made during the audit.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 3 integrates four rules: (1) Par. 23 & Par. 27 prohibit accepting a change to a lower-assurance engagement when based on incorrect/incomplete/unsatisfactory client information or when aimed at avoiding a qualified or disclaimer opinion on unverified receivables; (2) Par. 25 requires omitting reference to the original engagement in the revised report, while noting that reference to procedures performed is a normal part of the report when changed to agreed-upon procedures; (3) Par. 28 requires withdrawing if unable to agree to a change and barred from continuing the original engagement, while considering contractual or other obligations to report withdrawal circumstances to the board of directors or equity holders; (4) Par. 11 & Par. 14 require obtaining written confirmation/representation letters from management regarding oral representations made in connection with the audit.

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Which of the following accurately describes the purpose, adoption date, and effective date of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4 ('Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles by an External Auditor')?
en.A: It establishes standards and provides guidance on testing for compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles by an external auditor in connection with the audit of financial statements of an institution conducting business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles; it was adopted on 21 May 2000 (17 Safar 1421 A.H.) and became effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H. or 1 January 2002 A.D.
en.B: It establishes standalone internal Shari'ah audit procedures for internal audit departments, was adopted in May 1996, and became effective on 1 January 1998.
en.C: It governs how Shari'ah Supervisory Board members derive classical Fiqh rulings, was adopted in December 2024, and is effective from 1 January 2026.
en.D: It applies exclusively to government tax audits of conventional banks and has no effective date.
en.True answer: It establishes standards and provides guidance on testing for compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles by an external auditor in connection with the audit of financial statements of an institution conducting business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles; it was adopted on 21 May 2000 (17 Safar 1421 A.H.) and became effective for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H. or 1 January 2002 A.D.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 1, Par. 18 & Adoption of the Standard (Par. 1: establishes standards and provides guidance on testing for compliance with Sharia Rules and Principles by an external auditor in connection with the audit of financial statements of a financial institution conducting business in conformity with Shari'a Rules and Principles; Par. 18: effective for financial statements for financial periods beginning 1 Muharram 1423 A.H. or 1 January 2002 A.D.; Adoption: adopted by the Accounting and Auditing Standards Board in meeting No. 19 on 17 Safar 1421 A.H. / 21 May 2000 A.D.).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 2–3 (including Footnote 1) of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, how are the terms 'auditor' and 'institution/institutions' defined, and what dual definition of 'reasonable assurance' is incorporated from ASIFI No. 1?
en.A: 'Auditor' includes both external auditors and internal Shari'ah reviewers; 'institution' excludes Islamic banks; and 'reasonable assurance' means an absolute 100% guarantee of financial solvency.
en.B: 'Auditor' refers to the external auditor ONLY (excluding any internal audit function associated with the IFI); 'institution/institutions' represents Islamic financial institutions, including banks; and 'reasonable assurance' encompasses both accumulating sufficient appropriate audit evidence to conclude there are no material misstatements in the financial statements taken as a whole AND the auditor satisfying himself that examined transactions comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the IFI's SSB.
en.C: 'Auditor' refers exclusively to members of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, and 'reasonable assurance' relates solely to arithmetic trial balance checks.
en.D: 'Auditor' refers to central bank inspectors, and 'reasonable assurance' excludes Shari'a compliance of examined transactions.
en.True answer: 'Auditor' refers to the external auditor ONLY (excluding any internal audit function associated with the IFI); 'institution/institutions' represents Islamic financial institutions, including banks; and 'reasonable assurance' encompasses both accumulating sufficient appropriate audit evidence to conclude there are no material misstatements in the financial statements taken as a whole AND the auditor satisfying himself that examined transactions comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the IFI's SSB.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 2–3 & Footnote 1 (Par. 2: 'auditor' refers to the external auditor only and shall not apply to any internal audit function associated with the IFI; Footnote 1: 'institution/institutions' represents Islamic financial institutions, including banks; Par. 3: cites ASIFI No. 1 defining reasonable assurance both as accumulating evidence that financial statements taken as a whole are free from material misstatement AND satisfying himself that examined transactions comply with Sharia Rules and Principles as determined by the SSB).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 5–8 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, what is the exact division of responsibilities between IFI management, the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB), and the external auditor regarding Shari'ah compliance?
en.A: The external auditor interprets Shari'ah rules, the SSB prepares the accounting ledgers, and management expresses the statutory audit opinion.
en.B: Management interprets Fiqh rulings, the external auditor certifies the competence of SSB scholars, and the SSB prepares financial statements.
en.C: IFI management is responsible for ensuring that the financial statements and the IFI's activities comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the SSB; the SSB holds responsibility to interpret the Rules and Principles of Shari'a; and the external auditor (while knowledgeable about Shari'a, without possessing the same level of knowledge as SSB members and without being expected to interpret Shari'a rules) uses the fatwas, rulings, and guidance issued by the SSB as the basis for concluding whether the financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles.
en.D: The external auditor and the SSB share joint executive responsibility for day-to-day branch operations.
en.True answer: IFI management is responsible for ensuring that the financial statements and the IFI's activities comply with Shari'a Rules and Principles as determined by the SSB; the SSB holds responsibility to interpret the Rules and Principles of Shari'a; and the external auditor (while knowledgeable about Shari'a, without possessing the same level of knowledge as SSB members and without being expected to interpret Shari'a rules) uses the fatwas, rulings, and guidance issued by the SSB as the basis for concluding whether the financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Shari'a Rules and Principles.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 5–8 (Par. 5: auditor forms/expresses opinion on financial statements, while management is responsible for ensuring financial statements and IFI activities comply with Sharia Rules and Principles as determined by SSB; Par. 6: per GSIFI No. 1, responsibility to interpret Rules and Principles of Shari'a lies with the SSB; Par. 7: auditor shall be knowledgeable about Sharia Rules and Principles, would not possess the same level of knowledge as SSB members, and shall not be expected to provide interpretation; Par. 8: fatwas, rulings, and guidance issued by the SSB form the basis on which the auditor considers compliance and concludes whether financial statements are prepared in accordance with Sharia Rules and Principles).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 10–11 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, what is the external auditor's responsibility regarding (1) assessing the competence of SSB members and (2) evaluating the IFI's process for introducing new products or modifying existing products?
en.A: (1) The external auditor must examine and grade the Fiqh credentials of every SSB member; (2) new product launch procedures are reviewed only if requested by marketing.
en.B: (1) The external auditor certifies SSB members' academic degrees; (2) product modifications are exempt from Shari'ah review.
en.C: (1) The external auditor may dismiss SSB members who lack banking degrees; (2) only SSB approval is needed for new products, without management or internal audit review.
en.D: (1) The auditor has NO responsibility for assessing the competence of the members of the SSB (Par. 10); and (2) the auditor MUST satisfy himself that the IFI's process for introducing new products or modifying existing products includes appropriate procedures for ensuring compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, including reviews by IFI management, internal audit, and the SSB (Par. 11).
en.True answer: (1) The auditor has NO responsibility for assessing the competence of the members of the SSB (Par. 10); and (2) the auditor MUST satisfy himself that the IFI's process for introducing new products or modifying existing products includes appropriate procedures for ensuring compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, including reviews by IFI management, internal audit, and the SSB (Par. 11).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 10 & Par. 11 (Par. 10: 'The auditor shall have no responsibility for assessing the competence of the members of the SSB'; Par. 11: 'The auditor shall satisfy himself that the IFI's process for introducing new products or modifying existing products includes appropriate procedures for ensuring compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles including reviews by IFI management, internal audit and the SSB').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 12–13 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, which documents and fatwa updates must the external auditor identify and review for each period under examination?
en.A: All new fatwas, rulings, and guidance as well as modifications to existing fatwas, rulings, and guidance for each period under examination (Par. 12), AND available documents—specifically including reports issued by the SSB to the IFI concerning Shari'a compliance and the SSB's minutes of meetings—to ensure all types of products offered by the IFI have been reviewed by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2 and found compliant (Par. 13).
en.B: Only fatwas issued in the current month, while SSB minutes of meetings are strictly confidential and off-limits to the external auditor.
en.C: Only product marketing brochures, without reviewing SSB reports or modifications to earlier fatwas.
en.D: Only fatwas issued by foreign central banks, disregarding the IFI's own SSB minutes.
en.True answer: All new fatwas, rulings, and guidance as well as modifications to existing fatwas, rulings, and guidance for each period under examination (Par. 12), AND available documents—specifically including reports issued by the SSB to the IFI concerning Shari'a compliance and the SSB's minutes of meetings—to ensure all types of products offered by the IFI have been reviewed by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2 and found compliant (Par. 13).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 12 & Par. 13 (Par. 12: ensure all new fatwas, rulings, and guidance, and modifications to existing fatwas, rulings, and guidance are identified and reviewed for each period under examination; Par. 13: review available documents—specifically including reports issued by the SSB to the IFI concerning Sharia compliance and the SSB's minutes of meetings—to ensure all types of products offered by the IFI have been subject to review by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2 and found compliant, considering the effect of matters in these documents on the auditor's work).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraph 14 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, how does the external auditor verify that transactions entered into by the IFI are consistent with the SSB's fatwas, rulings, and guidelines, and what determines the nature and extent of this testing?
en.A: By examining 100% of every single transaction across all branches using a fixed statutory sample formula identical for every bank.
en.B: By carrying out verification on a test basis, where the nature and extent of the testing is subject to the individual circumstances of the IFI and is determined by the auditor after careful consideration of those circumstances.
en.C: By relying exclusively on a signed representation letter from the branch operations manager without testing any individual transactions.
en.D: By delegating transaction testing entirely to the external credit rating agency.
en.True answer: By carrying out verification on a test basis, where the nature and extent of the testing is subject to the individual circumstances of the IFI and is determined by the auditor after careful consideration of those circumstances.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 14 ('The auditor shall also verify that the transactions entered into by the IFI are consistent with the fatwas, rulings and guidelines of the SSB. This verification shall be carried out by the auditor on a test basis. The nature and extent of the testing is subject to the individual circumstances of the IFI and shall be determined by the auditor after careful consideration of these circumstances').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraph 15 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, the findings of which three internal reviews must the external auditor review, and how do those findings affect the external auditor's examination?
en.A: External credit rating reports, competitor annual reports, and tax authority circulars—which replace the external auditor's own testing.
en.B: Only external financial audit working papers from prior years—which have no effect on current-year audit timing.
en.C: Internal reviews carried out by (1) IFI management, (2) internal audit, and (3) an internal Shari'a review (as set out in GSIFI No. 3)—considering whether their findings affect the nature, timing, or extent of the work carried out by the auditor during his examination.
en.D: Only customer satisfaction surveys—which determine the external auditor's fee structure.
en.True answer: Internal reviews carried out by (1) IFI management, (2) internal audit, and (3) an internal Shari'a review (as set out in GSIFI No. 3)—considering whether their findings affect the nature, timing, or extent of the work carried out by the auditor during his examination.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 15 ('The auditor shall also review the findings of all internal reviews carried out by the IFI management, the internal audit, and as set out in GSIFI No. 3, by an internal Shari'a review. Consideration shall be given to the findings of these reviews and whether these findings effect the nature, timing or extent of the work carried out by the auditor during his examination').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 16–17 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, what bidirectional draft report exchange is mandated between the external auditor and the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB)?
en.A: Neither party may see the other's draft report until after both final reports are published in the newspaper.
en.B: Only the SSB sees the auditor's draft report, while the auditor issues his final report before the SSB prepares a draft report.
en.C: Only the auditor sees the SSB's draft report, while the SSB issues its final report without seeing the auditor's draft conclusions.
en.D: (1) Prior to issuance of the final report of the SSB, the external auditor must make available to the SSB his draft report and conclusions related to Shari'a compliance (Par. 17); and (2) the external auditor must make available the auditor's report ONLY after he has taken note of the SSB's draft report on the IFI's compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles—providing an adequate explanation of the nature and reasons if he decides to modify his draft report based on the SSB's draft report (Par. 16).
en.True answer: (1) Prior to issuance of the final report of the SSB, the external auditor must make available to the SSB his draft report and conclusions related to Shari'a compliance (Par. 17); and (2) the external auditor must make available the auditor's report ONLY after he has taken note of the SSB's draft report on the IFI's compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles—providing an adequate explanation of the nature and reasons if he decides to modify his draft report based on the SSB's draft report (Par. 16).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 16 & Par. 17 (Par. 17: 'Prior to issuance of the final report of the SSB, the auditor shall make available to the SSB his draft report and conclusions related to Shari'a compliance'; Par. 16: 'The auditor shall make available the auditor's report only after he has taken note of the SSB's draft report on the IFI's compliance with Sharia Rules and Principles. If the SSB's draft report indicates that compliance with Sharia Rules and Principles is lacking, and the auditor decides, based on the SSB's draft report, to modify his draft report, he shall provide an adequate explanation of the nature of and reasons for the modification').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraph 16 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, what must the external auditor include in his report if the SSB's draft report indicates a lack of compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles and the auditor consequently decides to modify his draft report?
en.A: An adequate explanation of the nature of and reasons for the modification.
en.B: A demand that the shareholders replace all members of the Shari'ah Supervisory Board.
en.C: A complete omission of the Shari'ah non-compliance details in order to protect the bank's stock price.
en.D: A personal Fiqh refutation arguing that the SSB's draft report is incorrect.
en.True answer: An adequate explanation of the nature of and reasons for the modification.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 16 ('If the SSB's draft report indicates that compliance with Sharia Rules and Principles is lacking, and the auditor decides, based on the SSB's draft report, to modify his draft report, he shall provide an adequate explanation of the nature of and reasons for the modification').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraph 13 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, why must the external auditor review both the reports issued by the SSB to the IFI concerning Shari'a compliance AND the SSB's minutes of meetings?
en.A: To grade the Arabic grammar and literary style of the SSB's secretary.
en.B: To ensure that all types of products offered by the IFI have been subject to a review by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2, to satisfy himself that the SSB has found these products to be in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, and to give consideration to the matters contained in these documents and their effect on the work to be carried out by the auditor.
en.C: To calculate the exact bonus payable to each SSB member based on meeting length.
en.D: To replace the SSB's annual report with the external auditor's own Shari'ah certificate.
en.True answer: To ensure that all types of products offered by the IFI have been subject to a review by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2, to satisfy himself that the SSB has found these products to be in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles, and to give consideration to the matters contained in these documents and their effect on the work to be carried out by the auditor.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 13 ('As part of his own scope of work, the auditor shall review available documents to ensure that all types of products offered by the IFI have been subject to a review by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2, and shall satisfy himself that the SSB has found these products to be in compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles. The documents to be reviewed shall include the reports issued by the SSB to the IFI concerning the Sharia compliance as well as the SSB's minutes of meetings. The auditor shall give consideration to the matters contained in these documents and their effect on the work to be carried out by him').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraph 11 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, which three internal governance/control reviews must be included in an IFI's process for introducing new products or modifying existing products to satisfy the external auditor?
en.A: Reviews by (1) external credit rating agencies, (2) retail marketing consultants, and (3) external tax lawyers.
en.B: Reviews by (1) branch tellers, (2) IT hardware vendors, and (3) minority shareholders.
en.C: Reviews by (1) IFI management, (2) internal audit, and (3) the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB).
en.D: Only a review by the external financial auditor prior to product launch.
en.True answer: Reviews by (1) IFI management, (2) internal audit, and (3) the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB).
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 11 ('The auditor shall satisfy himself that the IFI's process for introducing new products or modifying existing products includes appropriate procedures for ensuring compliance with Shari'a Rules and Principles including reviews by IFI management, internal audit and the SSB').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 7–9 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, what level of Shari'ah knowledge is expected of the external auditor, and what is the auditor's precise opinion objective regarding the IFI's transactions?
en.A: The external auditor must possess classical Ijtihad mastery equal to SSB jurists and issue independent Fatwas on novel contracts.
en.B: The external auditor needs zero knowledge of Shari'ah principles and tests transactions solely against conventional interest benchmarks.
en.C: The external auditor assesses whether SSB scholars followed classical Usul al-Fiqh methodology when issuing their rulings.
en.D: The auditor must be knowledgeable about Shari'a Rules and Principles (though not possessing the same level of knowledge as SSB members and not expected to interpret those rules and principles), and his responsibility is to form an opinion on whether the transactions of the IFI are in compliance with the fatwas, rulings, and guidance issued by the SSB of the IFI.
en.True answer: The auditor must be knowledgeable about Shari'a Rules and Principles (though not possessing the same level of knowledge as SSB members and not expected to interpret those rules and principles), and his responsibility is to form an opinion on whether the transactions of the IFI are in compliance with the fatwas, rulings, and guidance issued by the SSB of the IFI.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 7–9 (Par. 7: 'The auditor shall be knowledgeable about Shari'a Rules and Principles. However, he would not possess the same level of knowledge as that of SSB members and thus the auditor shall not be expected to provide interpretation of these rules and principles'; Par. 9: 'The responsibility of the auditor is to form an opinion on whether the transactions of the IFI are in compliance with the fatwas, rulings and guidance issued by the SSB of the IFI').

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: During the annual audit of an Islamic bank, the external auditor reviews three internal control findings: (1) a management compliance review noting minor delays in filing branch Shari'ah checklists, (2) an internal audit report identifying missing customer signatures on 12% of Salam contracts, and (3) an internal Shari'a review (conducted under GSIFI No. 3) revealing systematic execution of Tawarruq trades without prior commodity ownership. Meanwhile, the bank's newly launched digital Murabaha product was approved by management and internal audit, but was never reviewed by the SSB. Under Paragraphs 11, 13, and 15 of ASIFI No. 4, how must the external auditor respond?
en.A: Under Par. 15, the external auditor must review the findings of ALL three internal reviews (management, internal audit, and internal Shari'a review under GSIFI No. 3) and evaluate how they affect the nature, timing, or extent of his own examination (such as expanding sample sizes and substantive testing on Salam and Tawarruq); and under Par. 11 & Par. 13, because the new digital Murabaha product lacked SSB review and compliance approval under GSIFI No. 2, the product introduction process is deficient and the auditor must consider the effect of this unapproved product on his work and audit opinion.
en.B: The external auditor may ignore internal Shari'a review findings under GSIFI No. 3 because ASIFI No. 4 restricts external auditors to financial ledger reviews only.
en.C: Management and internal audit approval of the new digital Murabaha product is sufficient without SSB review, so no audit adjustment or follow-up is needed.
en.D: The external auditor should personally issue a retroactive Fatwa approving the digital Murabaha product and reduce sample sizes to zero.
en.True answer: Under Par. 15, the external auditor must review the findings of ALL three internal reviews (management, internal audit, and internal Shari'a review under GSIFI No. 3) and evaluate how they affect the nature, timing, or extent of his own examination (such as expanding sample sizes and substantive testing on Salam and Tawarruq); and under Par. 11 & Par. 13, because the new digital Murabaha product lacked SSB review and compliance approval under GSIFI No. 2, the product introduction process is deficient and the auditor must consider the effect of this unapproved product on his work and audit opinion.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 11, Par. 13 & Par. 15 (Par. 15 requires reviewing findings of all internal reviews by IFI management, internal audit, and internal Shari'a review under GSIFI No. 3, and considering whether they affect the nature, timing, or extent of external audit work; Par. 11 & 13 require verifying that new/modified products undergo management, internal audit, AND SSB reviews under GSIFI No. 2 and considering the impact of unreviewed/non-compliant products on the auditor's work).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: During the year-end reporting process of an Islamic financial institution, the external auditor and the Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB) are finalizing their respective reports under Paragraphs 16–17 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4. Which sequence of actions violates the reporting coordination protocol?
en.A: The external auditor provides his draft report and Shari'ah compliance conclusions to the SSB prior to issuance of the SSB's final report; the SSB issues its draft report to the auditor; and after reviewing the SSB's draft report, the external auditor finalizes and releases his audit report.
en.B: The external auditor issues and publishes his final audit report before receiving or taking note of the SSB's draft report, and refuses to share his draft report and Shari'ah compliance conclusions with the SSB prior to the issuance of the SSB's final report.
en.C: Upon noting that the SSB's draft report identifies material unresolved Shari'ah non-compliance in a Sukuk pool, the external auditor modifies his draft audit report and includes an adequate explanation of the nature of and reasons for the modification.
en.D: The SSB reviews the external auditor's draft Shari'ah compliance conclusions before finalizing its own SSB report, and the external auditor takes note of the SSB's draft report before releasing the final audit report.
en.True answer: The external auditor issues and publishes his final audit report before receiving or taking note of the SSB's draft report, and refuses to share his draft report and Shari'ah compliance conclusions with the SSB prior to the issuance of the SSB's final report.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 16 & Par. 17 (Par. 17 mandates that prior to issuance of the SSB's final report, the auditor shall make available to the SSB his draft report and conclusions related to Shari'a compliance; Par. 16 mandates that the auditor shall make available the auditor's report ONLY after taking note of the SSB's draft report on Shari'a compliance, and if modifying his draft report based on the SSB's draft report, provide an adequate explanation of the nature and reasons. Option B violates both Par. 16 and Par. 17).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question:
Under Paragraphs 5–10 and 12–14 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, compare two situations encountered by an external auditor:
• Situation 1: The IFI's Shari'ah Supervisory Board (SSB) issued a modified ruling in Q3 changing the conditions for late-payment charity collection on Ijarah contracts, and the external auditor tests Q4 Ijarah transactions against the Q3 modified SSB ruling.
• Situation 2: An external audit partner believes that an SSB fatwa permitting a specific Salam Salam-parallel arrangement is overly lenient compared to the audit firm's internal Shari'ah consultant's view, and proposes qualifying the audit opinion on the ground that the SSB members lack sufficient Fiqh competence.
Which evaluation of Situations 1 and 2 is completely accurate?
en.A: Both Situation 1 and Situation 2 are compliant with ASIFI No. 4.
en.B: Situation 1 violates ASIFI No. 4 (auditors test only against initial fatwas, ignoring modifications), whereas Situation 2 is compliant.
en.C: Situation 1 is compliant—under Par. 12 & Par. 14, the auditor must identify and review all modifications to existing fatwas/rulings during the examination period and verify on a test basis that transactions are consistent with them; Situation 2 violates ASIFI No. 4—under Par. 6–8, the SSB's fatwas/rulings form the authoritative basis for concluding on Shari'a compliance (the auditor does not interpret Shari'a rules), and under Par. 10, the auditor has NO responsibility for assessing the competence of SSB members.
en.D: Both Situation 1 and Situation 2 violate ASIFI No. 4.
en.True answer: Situation 1 is compliant—under Par. 12 & Par. 14, the auditor must identify and review all modifications to existing fatwas/rulings during the examination period and verify on a test basis that transactions are consistent with them; Situation 2 violates ASIFI No. 4—under Par. 6–8, the SSB's fatwas/rulings form the authoritative basis for concluding on Shari'a compliance (the auditor does not interpret Shari'a rules), and under Par. 10, the auditor has NO responsibility for assessing the competence of SSB members.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 6–10, Par. 12 & Par. 14 (Situation 1 follows Par. 12 [identify and review all new fatwas/rulings/guidance and modifications to existing ones for each period under examination] and Par. 14 [verify on a test basis that transactions are consistent with SSB fatwas/rulings/guidelines]; Situation 2 violates Par. 6–8 [SSB fatwas/rulings form the basis for concluding on Shari'a compliance; auditor is not expected to interpret Shari'a rules] and Par. 10 ['The auditor shall have no responsibility for assessing the competence of the members of the SSB']).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: Under Paragraphs 13–15 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4, how do Governance Standards for Islamic Financial Institutions (GSIFIs) No. 2 and No. 3 interface with the external auditor's Shari'ah compliance testing procedures?
en.A: GSIFI No. 2 and GSIFI No. 3 apply exclusively to external auditors, while the SSB and internal Shari'ah reviewers perform no reviews.
en.B: Because GSIFI No. 2 and GSIFI No. 3 exist, the external auditor is exempt from reviewing SSB minutes or testing individual transactions.
en.C: The external auditor directly supervises the SSB's GSIFI No. 2 review and grades the internal Shari'ah reviewer's GSIFI No. 3 report for the central bank.
en.D: Under Paragraph 13, the external auditor reviews available documents (including SSB reports and minutes) to ensure all types of products offered by the IFI have been reviewed by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2 and found compliant; and under Paragraph 15, the external auditor reviews the findings of all internal reviews—including an internal Shari'a review conducted as set out in GSIFI No. 3 (alongside management and internal audit reviews)—and considers whether those findings affect the nature, timing, or extent of his own examination.
en.True answer: Under Paragraph 13, the external auditor reviews available documents (including SSB reports and minutes) to ensure all types of products offered by the IFI have been reviewed by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2 and found compliant; and under Paragraph 15, the external auditor reviews the findings of all internal reviews—including an internal Shari'a review conducted as set out in GSIFI No. 3 (alongside management and internal audit reviews)—and considers whether those findings affect the nature, timing, or extent of his own examination.
en.main: Rationale: AAOIFI ASIFI No. 4, Par. 13 & Par. 15 (Par. 13 explicitly references GSIFI No. 2: external auditor reviews available documents [including SSB reports and minutes] to ensure all types of products offered by the IFI have been subject to a review by the SSB in accordance with GSIFI No. 2 and found compliant; Par. 15 explicitly references GSIFI No. 3: external auditor reviews findings of all internal reviews carried out by IFI management, internal audit, and 'as set out in GSIFI No. 3, by an internal Shari'a review', considering their effect on nature, timing, or extent of external audit work).

en.Theme: AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 04: Testing for Compliance with Shari'a Rules
en.Question: When planning Shari'ah compliance testing across two different Islamic financial institutions—Bank X (a newly licensed Islamic bank with high transaction volume, complex Sukuk/Mudaraba structures, and weak internal Shari'ah review documentation) versus Bank Y (a mature Islamic bank with strong internal Shari'ah controls and clean prior-year findings)—how does Paragraph 14 of AAOIFI Auditing Standard No. 4 direct the external auditor to determine the nature and extent of transaction testing?
en.A: Under Paragraph 14, transaction verification is carried out on a test basis, and the nature and extent of testing is subject to the individual circumstances of each IFI and must be determined by the auditor after careful consideration of those circumstances (resulting in more extensive, substantive test coverage for Bank X than for Bank Y).
en.B: ASIFI No. 4 mandates an identical fixed 10% transaction sample size for both Bank X and Bank Y regardless of individual circumstances.
